en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Sub-Commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
Commentary on the Twenty Verses: 1.
Desiring to explain the meaning of the *Abhidhamma-saṃvaṇṇanā*, the author first determines the meaning of its opening verse by way of its purpose (*payojana*) and connection (*sambandha*).
He does so as follows: "The practice of those with noble aspirations who act with reflection has as its purpose the production of various kinds of welfare and happiness for others."

Just as, at the beginning of the Teacher’s own commentary on the Dhamma, the act of revering the Teacher serves to dispel obstacles, so too, in this case, it may serve to produce the jewel of faith—which leads others to the attainment of ultimate happiness—toward both the Teacher and the Dhamma.
To show this, he said, "of the commentary on the Dhamma," and so forth. In that regard, for one who practices according to the instructions...

The word *dhamma* is a general term meaning "that which holds one back from falling into the states of misery (*apāya*)," yet through the proximity of other words, it here refers specifically to the particular teaching (*pariyatti*).
It is called *saṃvaṇṇanā* because the meaning is fully described by it; thus, it is a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
He is the Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs the Dhamma of liberation as is appropriate by means of the threefold vehicle. *Paṇāma* is the act of bowing.

The state of being inclined toward the Teacher’s virtues by means of body, speech, and mind. *Kiriya* means an act; *paṇāmakaraṇaṃ* is the performance of prostration, that is, the application of homage.

Although this [term] will later demonstrate the intended nature of the prostration in such passages as “having bowed at his feet” (via the phrase beginning with) “now, performing the intended prostration,” it nevertheless [serves as a designation] for such passages as “like compassion.”

It should also be understood by way of the praise of everything that has been stated. For this [praise] proceeds by way of extolling the specific qualities of the Teacher’s great compassion and so forth;

and by means of the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma—which is manifested through the eulogy and is inseparable from those specific qualities such as great compassion—it generates faith in those who have not yet developed faith in the Teacher, the one whose Dhamma is well-expounded.
And it leads to the further increase of faith in those who have already arisen in it.

By the phrase "in the Dhamma, which is a teaching not otherwise than true because of the Teacher’s quality of teaching the Dhamma without error," he states that the Dhamma inspires confidence precisely because it possesses the capacity to produce specific fruits from the Teacher’s own qualities, such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). For the Teacher’s success is established through the Dhamma, and the Dhamma’s success is established through the Teacher; and by the perfection of the Dhamma...
"It is accomplished by means of the Teacher’s qualities and by the manifestation of those qualities.
Having thus shown one purpose for performing this salutation to the Teacher, he now clarifies the connection with the words, "For, through faith in both of these," and so forth.
Indeed, one who lacks faith in the Teacher or the Dhamma [would not apply themselves] when that which is to be attained is being extolled.
Furthermore, one who practices correctly according to the Dhamma does not achieve the great goal that culminates in final Nibbāna through non-clinging,
such as virtue and so forth; therefore, the intention is that in the expositions of the Dhamma, for those who desire correct practice and who receive such Dhamma,
the generation of confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma, as well as the act of paying homage to the Teacher, are prescribed.
Since the proclamation of the Blessed One’s qualities is indeed a praise of his Dhamma and Saṅgha as well, it is called “the word of salutation to the Triple Gem.

Likewise, he will say later, “by means of the praise of the Blessed One alone,” and so forth. Or rather, it was said with reference to what is to be stated later, such as “having honored his True Dhamma,” and so on.
Alternatively, it should be connected as “for the purpose of making known to other wise people”; for there is no measure [of wisdom] among those who are unwise.
And there is the grasping by the wise because of [the speaker’s] being a worthy vessel.

For they, knowing that one who possesses reverence for the Buddha and others has become an authority, consider his word to be worth hearing and worth having faith in; and by practicing it correctly, they fulfill his intention.

Here too, the connection should be understood in the same manner as before, since [the teaching] was proclaimed through the means of manifesting confidence and so forth, out of a desire for right practice.

And here, the first alternative of meaning is stated with reference to persons who are followers by faith (*saddhānusārī*), while the second is with reference to those who are followers by Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*).
Alternatively, the first is stated with reference to those for whom the Teacher’s Dhamma has not yet been fully established, while the second is with reference to those for whom it has.

Likewise, the first is intent upon showing the act of salutation toward the first Jewel (the Buddha), whereas the second is so toward the others as well; this is the distinction that should be understood.
"Paṇāmakaraṇaṃ" means that by which salutation is performed; it is the volition (cetanā) that brings about the act of saluting.

For, through the excellence of the field (the recipient) and the excellence of the teacher's intention, that volition—being experienced in the present life—serves as a cause for the attainment of whatever prosperity has been obtained, by way of reinforcing the power of the karma;
thus, it occurs in the midst of the stream of result (vipākasantāna) produced by previous karma.

This demonstrates the meaning that there is an extraordinary excellence of merit capable of destroying—whether by warding off, suppressing, or cutting off—the karma that brings about misfortunes such as disease, which have acquired the name "obstacles" (*antarāya*) because they come and descend upon one;
this is shown by the phrase: "Because of the state of distinction [in the salutation] to the Three Jewels...
And having done so, by the statement regarding the absence of the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of lust and the other defilements, [the text refers to] the cause of the obstacle...
The Mahānāma Sutta itself has been cited here to illustrate: the absence of failure in application;
the presence of success in application—which serves as the cause for the absence of obstacles—as expressed by the words "attainment of wealth" and so forth;
and the dwelling in happiness in this very life, as expressed by the words "he dwells without affliction amidst an afflicted populace."

"‘For the purpose of showing a distinction of qualities’—by this, he shows that although bowing with body and mind is also capable of dispelling obstacles, the verbal bow is performed as particularly preeminent by way of manifesting the state of being worthy of such bowing on the part of the object of the bow.
‘One who possesses a distinction of qualities,’ etc., shows the teacher’s propriety and fitness in acting. ‘The teaching in the Vinaya Piṭaka’..."
Here, one might object: "Since there is no teaching of the Vinaya Piṭaka here either, is it not improper to speak of a distinction between the Teaching (Dhamma) and the Vinaya Piṭakas?

This is not improper; for, as in the passage, "In these three [Piṭakas], there are these [fourfold categories of] Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration," the teaching of the parts is contained within the teaching of the whole. Or else, at the time of the teaching, [the Vinaya] was determined by the mind.
The term "division" (bheda) is used because the Vinaya Piṭaka constitutes the Vinaya Canon and because it contains the teaching that establishes its subject matter.

Alternatively, "desanā" (teaching) refers to that by which something is taught—namely, the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that originates the teaching—and since this [consciousness] has the Vinaya Piṭaka as its object and is preceded by compassion (karuṇā), the application of the term "division" here should be understood in this way. The same principle applies to the expressions "Suttanta Piṭaka" and so forth.
But how is it understood that the Blessed One’s teaching in the Vinaya Piṭaka is dominated by compassion (*karuṇā*),
while in the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas it is dominated by wisdom (*paññā*) and compassion-wisdom (*paññā-karuṇā*) respectively?

Because even the Blessed One— who possessed shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) reaching the highest limit— employed expressions such as “Sikharaṇī” and so forth, which ought to be avoided even by worldly virtuous people, and [used] words according to the offense.
He spoke words of censure in the midst of the great assembly, his mind impelled by great compassion, out of regard for the reasons for the promulgation of various training rules (*sikkhāpada*);

he even experienced physical exhaustion in Verañjā and other places. Therefore, although the originators of the Vinaya rules are like those of different locations, causal conditions, modes of occurrence, and periods of time, they are indeed the originators of the Vinaya promulgations.
Wisdom possesses an extraordinary function because it is not shared by others; however, with the intention that the function of compassion is even greater than that, it is said:
"In the Vinaya Piṭaka, compassion is predominant. Indeed, the predominance of compassion in the teaching is due to the preeminence of compassionate activity;
for in the teaching of the Suttanta, there is an abundance of the attainment of Great Compassion, which conforms to the inclinations within the mental continuums of those to be trained.
"He established the profound meaning and the words" refers to the predominance of compassion and wisdom;

however, in the teaching of the Abhidhamma, because the analysis of the material and immaterial—which is capable of becoming the objective domain of omniscient knowledge—proceeds in accordance with the intrinsic nature of phenomena, there is a predominance of wisdom.
And for that very reason, by the passage beginning "and for this cause," the suitability of the teaching is described in its respective commentary.
This shows that it is the nature of the teacher to offer praise.

For the employment of words for the purpose of comprehending the meaning—just as one who possesses sight perceives ten pomegranates and so forth by way of a collection—is dependent solely upon oneself and constitutes the mere denotation of the meaning;
[yet] this is subverted by one who effects a reversal of the word-meaning.
He says, "By the word *iti*, the meaning of the phrase 'compassion arises' is produced," and adds, "'Like compassion' is an illustrative statement.
For an illustration (*nidassana*) occurs only when there is a relationship between the thing to be illustrated and that by which it is illustrated, and not otherwise.
Thus, clarifying its nature as an illustration, he says: "The meaning is: for whom, in whatever manner... [etc. ...it proceeds."

In the passage beginning with “*Tattha karuṇā viyā ti nidassanavacanan*,” the true meaning of the verse is shown by way of illustrating the relationship between the illustration (*nidassana*) and the thing illustrated (*nidassitabba-dhamma*), together with their specific distinctions regarding their locus, object, and function.

Then, in order to show the meaning according to the analysis of its constituent parts, it is said: “*Kiratīti karuṇā*,” and so forth. Therein, for those who were formerly free from desire and lust, by way of their past state...
Or it should be understood as seventy. Because even a single phenomenon possesses many modes of commonality, it is said:

"in its various ways according to its true nature. For it has been stated: "all phenomena in all their aspects"—this rejects the notion that phenomena are unknowable, because there is no state of being impossible to know.
By this, he expresses that this wisdom proceeds without difficulty.
For just as, although the intended meaning is established by the mere phrase "arising with respect to all that is knowable" (*ñeyyesu sabbesu pavatti*),

the objects of knowledge (*ñeyyā*) must nevertheless be qualified by the word "phenomena" (*dhamma*)— in order to indicate their lack of selfhood or belonging to a self and to negate the false graspings of others such as [the notion of] a sentient being (*satta*)—

so too, although the intended meaning is established by the mere phrase "arising with respect to all phenomena" (*dhammesu sabbesu pavatti*), [this qualification is necessary] because that wisdom is dependent upon desire regarding phenomena.
In order to show that their mode of existence is difficult to master, the phenomena (*dhammā*) are qualified by the word "knowable" (*ñeyya*) through the negation of anything else being knowable.

Since the terms *ñeyya-dhamma* (knowable phenomena) and *nīla-uppala* (blue lotus) are joined in a relationship of both difference and non-difference, it is said: "those which are knowable and those which are phenomena.
The word *yā* indicates the meaning of the term *yathā*. For this word *yathā* is used here in the sense of distribution (*byāpanī*).
The connection is: "Wisdom proceeds according to its various classifications.
Regarding the phrase "proceeding in the Blessed One": this is stated because, for the most part, the relationship between the simile and the subject of the simile involves different bases;
and because here, a simile whose referent has a different base is impossible. [This refers to] the state of the Blessed One’s compassion being uncommon to others.

It should be understood that his sole aspiration for absolute welfare was such that he would even sacrifice his own body and life to lift beings out of the suffering of *saṃsāra* and establish them in the ultimate bliss of *nibbāna*;
for this reason, he even manifested for those to be trained the concealment of the male organ within a sheath and the appearance of a long tongue, so that these beings might know:
"The teaching of the Blessed One is as cool as a lake, yet it is also ablaze."
One might even plunge into a mass of fire. The connection is with the phrase "of others who are looking on.

With reference to the word *uddhaṭā* ("drawn out"), the genitive case in *sattānaṃ* ("of beings") is used in the sense of the object, meaning "of those beings who have plunged into the great flood of sensual desire and so forth. This is the summary of the meaning here:

for one who sees that there is no one else to draw out beings who have plunged into the great flood of sensual desire and so forth except oneself, just as [there was] through the compassion of the Blessed One.
It is an "entering" (āvisanaṃ), for others do not possess such a vision; or alternatively,
regarding the phrase "of others who see," even if others were to see [the Buddha], they nevertheless lack the arising of compassion as the Blessed One possesses it,
because they have failed to practice and instead practice only for their own benefit— this is the meaning.
It is unobstructed because its activity is unimpeded at all times and in all places; it is uncommon because, by way of comprehending the causes and conditions of all phenomena without exception,
and through the thorough knowledge of their specific natures, functions, and states, it discerns— at the very moment of the accumulation [of karma]—
the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior among those various fruits of various karmas, whether they pertain to the bound-by-faculties or the non-bound-by-faculties.

Furthermore, this [knowledge] is to be understood through the complete penetration of the specific distinctions of color, shape, odor, taste, touch, and so forth in their respective effects, by means of discerning the combination of their various causes— even for material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) that are extremely subtle, hidden, remote, and differentiated by such categories as the past and the future.
And this meaning [was realized] by the Blessed One through his knowledge of the world as it truly is, in terms of its many elements and its manifold elements.

It is to be understood. And as for the phrase "and as he sees": this statement regarding the Blessed One’s vision of the world’s habitation as being ablaze with the fires of lust and so forth is spoken with reference to the means by which his Great Compassion arises.

Indeed, Great Compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, toward sentient beings as they perceive it through many modes: "The world’s habitation is ablaze... [it is] engaged in effort... and so on.

“Great compassion descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, toward sentient beings as they perceive: ‘The world is swept away...’; ‘...the world has entered upon a wrong path...’; ‘...the world is led along, unstable...’;
‘...the world is without refuge, without a protector...’; ‘...the world is ownerless, everything must be abandoned and departed from...’;
‘...the world is deficient, unsatisfied, a slave to craving’—thus it is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* by more than a hundred modes.”

To avoid excessive textual expansion and to show the method for its exposition, he said: "All of that should be understood by way of the analysis of Great Compassion and Knowledge (*mahākaruṇāñāṇavibhaṅga*) in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

The knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriyaparopariyatta*), the knowledge of their inclinations and underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya*), the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), and the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇa*) are the remaining unique knowledges. For their analysis as well—
The phrase beginning with “Here the Tathāgata sees beings with little dust in their eyes,” and so forth, has been shown in various ways in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*;

thus, it is referred to here by way of the previous method. It should be understood that by the word “etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), the knowledge of truth (*sacca-ñāṇa*), and so on, which are analyzed therein, is intended.
Just as compassion has both unlimited and limited objects, so too the Blessed One’s wisdom here is intended to be entirely without remainder, encompassing both unlimited and limited objects.
Showing that by means of this, the remaining types of wisdom should be understood through the method of illustration by pointing out a few of its divisions, he says:
"And by the mention of 'wisdom'... These, moreover, are virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

The seventy-two sets of two dhammas; the twenty-two sets of three dhammas; the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the fruits of recluseship, the noble lineages, and so forth;

the five destinations, the five factors of striving, the five-factored concentration, the faculties, the powers, the elements leading out [from the world], the bases of liberation, the perceptions that ripen liberation, and so forth; and the six qualities that provide a refuge.
The bases of recollection; disrespect and respect; grounds for expulsion; constant abodes; the unsurpassed; wisdom conducive to penetration and so forth;

the seven factors of non-decline; the noble treasures; the factors of enlightenment; the grounds for the wearing away of the qualities of a true person; perceptions; persons worthy of offerings, those whose taints are exhausted, their powers, and so forth;
the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom; the wrong, the right, and the worldly conditions; the modes of speech of the noble and the ignoble; and the grounds for undertaking [tasks].
The bases of laziness, the unfavorable occasions, the reflections of a Great Man, the bases of mastery, the liberations and so forth;

the ninefold states rooted in wise attention, the factors of purification, the factors of striving, the abodes of beings, the grounds for resentment, the removal of resentment, the diversity of perceptions, the successive dwellings and so forth;

the ten qualities that provide protection, the kasiṇa bases, the unwholesome courses of action, the wholesome courses of action, wrongness, rightness, the noble abodes, and the knowledge of the ten powers.

The qualities of one beyond training (*asekkhadhammādi*), the eleven benefits of virtue (*sīlānisaṃsa*), the natural law as the cause of growth, the twelve bases (*dvādasāyatana*) and dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) as the form of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkākāra*),
the thirteen ascetic virtues (*dhutaguṇa*), the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha (*buddhañāṇa*), the fifteen qualities that ripen the liberation of conduct (*caraṇavimuttiparipācanīyadhamma*),

the sixteen mindfulnesses of breathing (*ānāpānassati) and the aspects of truth (*saccākāra*) according to the Suttanta and Paṭṭhāna, and the eighteen elements of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadhammadhātu*) as the grounds for differentiation.
It is the manifestation of the modes of penetration and teaching of phenomena categorized as nineteen kinds of reviewing, twenty-four conditions, twenty-eight suttanta-foundations,
fifty views of arising and passing away, more than fifty wholesome states, sixty-two types of speculative views,
and the hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering, as well as the various divisions of the Great Vajira-knowledge that traverses twenty-four million meditative attainments.

And those modes of the Blessed One’s wisdom that proceed by way of teaching the analysis of the *Paṭṭhāna* (Fundamental Conditions) through infinite methods, and those that proceed by way of discerning the inclinations, latent tendencies, temperaments, and so forth of infinite beings in infinite world-systems—all such varieties of the Blessed One’s wisdom are to be understood here as being included under the term "method" (*naya*) by means of the word "etc. (*ādi*). For who is capable [of enumerating them]?
In order to demonstrate, step by step and without omission, the various classifications of the Blessed One’s wisdom, even the Elder Sāriputta—
the Commander-in-Chief of the Dhamma and the foremost among the wise after the Blessed One— devoted himself to defining the Buddha’s qualities and said:
"Furthermore, venerable sir, the method of inference regarding the Dhamma is known to me."

For the sake of delivering across [the ocean] those beings who have plunged into the great flood of saṃsāra, one who has set out [on the path] is said to be "instigated" by them, even though they lack such an intention;
thus it is said, "Beings indeed instigate the Great Awakening (mahābodhi).

By all this—that is, by the demonstration of the root of the Great Awakening and so forth—it should be connected with the phrase "absence of departure" (*apagamana*) as "freedom from defilement" (*nirupakkilesa*).
By showing the state of being born and having grown, wrong views such as "the sentient being is without beginning and without end" are refuted. [The passage] "...conventional designation...
and so forth shows that even though a sentient being does not exist in the ultimate sense, there is still the conventional expression and usage of the term "sentient being.

The statement "compassion is the beginning and wisdom is the end" is said with reference to the sequence of the time of gathering the requisites and their final accomplishment, not because they possess temporal limits.

For this very reason it was said: "Because they have that as their cause, and because there is nothing further to be done beyond them. By way of this method (*nayato*), all the qualities of a Buddha are shown;
for this indeed is the means for showing the qualities of a Buddha without exception, namely, the grasping of the method.
Even the abstinence from seizing the property of others and so forth may serve as a proximate cause (*upanissaya*) for compassion, by way of its proceeding through the prevention of harm to others.
Virtue has compassion as its cause; for that very reason, it is said: "because of the occurrence of abstention from killing living beings and so forth.
By the passage beginning with "The commentary on which," etc., he shows the connection with the praise beginning with "of compassion.
The purpose, however, should be understood according to the method already stated. That which is internal is one's own internal self; that which exists outside of that is external.

"Compassion (dayā) is intended" is stated because the word *dayā* denotes both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*), and having taken into account the subsequent application that will be explained.

For it is by means of that [compassion] that one is incited, not by loving-kindness; this is the intended meaning. He states the meaning of the word *taṃ* as a reference back to what was previously mentioned.
By specifying wisdom (*paññā*) through its function as a simile, he sets it aside [from the other factors].
Because it abides in its own nature. It does not deserve a further explanation because, among the primary and secondary meanings, the function is seen to reside in the primary meaning.

The intention is that since the word *ta-* is spoken in grammatical coreferentiality (*ekādhikaraṇabhāva*) with the word *dayā*—which expresses compassion—within the context of "of the two words... [etc.]...

because of the word," it is not appropriate for that word *ta-* to have as its object a phenomenon other than that [compassion]. This is because words that do not have synonymous meanings cannot stand in a relationship of coreferentiality.
He says, "When there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*visesanavisesitabbabhāva*), it occurs, and not otherwise," thus stating: "Being common... [etc. ...occurs.

For here, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is established by way of having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*); and since that state of having a common substratum does not exist for those with different case-endings (*vibhatti*), it establishes that very same thing through having identical case-endings as well.
Thus, in the phrase "compassion... [etc. ...consciousness," this [term] belongs to compassion.
This is a statement of the reason for that which is to be qualified. For she (compassion) has become something to be qualified by virtue of her preeminence and her universality.
In this context, her universality is to be understood because she expresses the compassion of both the Blessed One and others.

And the phrase "of that" refers to the word *dayā* (compassion). Although wisdom was the preeminent factor in the preceding verse—as indicated by the words "and wisdom is preeminent"—[the pronoun] "by that" [refers back to compassion].

However, he shows that because it is stated as a qualification of compassion rather than being mentioned alone, it is appropriate to provide a further description of compassion even though it is subordinate.
And the subordination of compassion was stated by way of the preceding verse, but here it is indeed predominant.
Thus it has been said: "It is predominant in the sense of being impelled by compassion."
"But how... and so forth—having kept in mind the very meaning that is about to be explained, he raises an objection. "If it were thus" means:
if you were to take only the literal words without grasping the intended meaning of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "And 'loving-kindness' would not be appropriate" means:
just as, according to this commentary, "having attained a state of loving-kindness" does not refer to pity or compassion, so too [the term] "cruelty" (*nikkaruṇatā*)...
By means of this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), he demonstrates that there is even a contradiction among the commentaries if one takes the mere words "dayā" and "mettā" [as being identical].
Having stated, "It should be construed according to the underlying intention (*adhippāya*"), he explains that very intention with the words beginning "For the word *dayā*...
Grammarians indeed record the word *dayā* in the senses of giving, going, and protecting. And as for protecting...

Loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) have a common function (*samānakicca*) because they operate respectively in the manner of bestowing benefit and removing suffering; therefore, it is said that the word "compassion" (*dayā*) applies to both.

"Included within" (*antonīta*) means contained within; the meaning is that the sense of "protecting," just as the general term "tree" includes specific trees like the *dhava* and *khadira*, is the commonality (*sāmañña*) of loving-kindness and compassion.
However, the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) here [in the phrase] "one who has become compassionate" (*dayāpanno*) is...

Because the term *karuṇā* (compassion) was mentioned immediately prior [to the phrase] "one who is compassionate toward the welfare of all living beings," it is understood that the word *dayā* (pity) is a synonym for *mettā* (loving-kindness).
For *mettā*, like *karuṇā*, is a cause for abstaining from taking life.

However, in the expression "not being devoid of pity" (*adayāpanno*), a compassionate person—due to having an inclination toward non-harming—does not even inflict mere harm upon others, let alone [greater violence].
It should be understood that by the phrase "taking life," the state of being merciless in taking life is indicated.
With reference to this very meaning, he said: "For in this way, there is no contradiction with the commentaries.

If the word *dayā* is a designator for both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*), then the objection—"In that case, how is it to be known that compassion is 'dayā'?"—remains just as it was; thus one should take this challenge to heart.
By the passage beginning with "having done so, compassion and the teaching," he states the reason for mentioning compassion alone. With the words "Is it not by that...

and so forth, he shows that even by way of implication (*sāmatthiya*), the context (*pakaraṇa*) is powerful; thus, by means of the context itself, he demonstrates that the object of compassion is understood.
As for the phrase "it proceeded according to his wish," this refers to the preceding verse whose object consisted of both specific and non-specific beings.

This is a statement of the reason for having adopted [the term] *karuṇā* (compassion). For its application according to preference consists in its application in accordance with one's desire toward both a single [being] and many [beings].

By the phrase "but here, in order to include the scope of all beings without exception," it is shown that since this is already established, the undertaking [of the further specification] has an indicative purpose;
thus, the repeated mention of "toward beings" (*sattesu*) indicates this specific meaning. This is also shown by the passage beginning with "not only toward gods," etc.

He shows that although the capacity [of the discourse] to have sentient beings as its object is already established by the fact that it incites one to the means for developing compassion, the explicit mention of the word "towards sentient beings" (sattesu) indicates this specific qualification:

that its intended scope is the totality of sentient beings without exception. Regarding the external introduction (bāhiranidāna), which illustrates the time, place, teacher, assembly, and so forth, he says "at what time," etc., while determining those factors such as time.
By the statement, "Dwelling in the final [state] in the abode of the Thirty-three," he shows that the manifestation of that miracle is delimited by the proximity of other sounds.

Furthermore, it is not possible [to speak of it] by means of conventional usage occurring therein; for since there is an absence of the removal of the opposites of lust and so forth even in the mental continuum of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), the designation "sentient being" applies to those whose desire has ceased, just as it does to the mental continuum of an ordinary person by way of the removal of the opposites of lust and so forth.

The intention [of the author] is that it cannot be maintained that even in the absence of such an occurrence, what happens within the continuum of the Blessed One may still be called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*) by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*).
This is because there are those who become established in right view through the removal of wrong views— such as Acelaka Kassapa and others— and those who,
due to their inability to explain [the truth], fall into a state of being speechless and so forth, such as Saccaka and others.
3. "The mountains named Sītapabbata" refers to the mountains mentioned as "Yugandhara... [and so on] ...the lofty mountain," which stand surrounding Sineru. 4–5.
Three interpretations are appropriate based on the connection with the phrase "having come from all around the thousandfold world-systems and having sat down completely";
however, the interpretation "ten by ten from all around the thousandfold world-systems" is not suitable because it establishes what is undesirable.
It is prohibited. "Those that should be avoided" refers to those which can be avoided, namely: "too close to the front," "too near," and "a high place.
However, the others cannot be shunned because of the great size of that assembly.
Having stated, "All-knowing... [and so on]... capable," the statement [means] they are capable of knowing the various types of things that should be taught.
It is said [in the text] because even the Master of Dhamma, who has personally realized the mode of being, would be unable to teach it to others;

otherwise, all sentient beings would have already seen the Truths. The "power" as previously described is precisely the capacity to know all objects of knowledge according to their true nature and so forth.
The intention is that this demonstrates the capacity to grasp those [truths], and that the additional statement makes another meaning known.
6. By the passage beginning with “The Tathāgata is worthy of veneration,” he explains that specific actions such as “having paid homage” are performed in accordance with their respective suttas.

By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “the excellence of the physical form, etc.,” qualities such as the excellence of his speech, sovereignty, and the perfection of his retinue are included.
7. “Having made to disappear” means having suppressed. And here, suppression occurs by way of removing the causes of their arising.

It should be understood as "making [the offense] not arise again. The connection is: "I shall clarify the meaning. The phrase "having withered" is stated because a prior action depends upon a subsequent action.
8. To illustrate the state of being difficult:
the intention is that what is not difficult would not be requested in such a manner. Regarding the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses...

Because failure in virtue (*sīla-vipatti*) consists mostly of grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) and the like, while failure in conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*) consists mostly of lapses in deportment, the application [of the term] is made thus to both conduct and virtue.
Furthermore, because the virtue of behavior (*cāritta-sīla*) has the nature of conduct (*ācāra*), the second [case ending] is used by taking the other [virtue] as its very nature.
"Incapable" (*asakkuṇeyya*) means: by a fellow practitioner endowed with qualities such as pure conduct, for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dhamma.

The intention [of the author] is that, having been respectfully requested by him who was rightly assessed as being capable of elucidating the *Abhidhammattha*, it is not easy to turn away from that task. 9.
The meaning of the term *Devadeva* has been explained in detail in the commentary on the *Paṭṭhāna-ṭīkā*, so we have not elaborated upon it here.
13. Regarding the statement that "the commentary was recited at the First Council," this implies that the commentary existed even during the Blessed One’s lifetime;
therefore, it is understood that like the text itself, it is rooted in the Blessed One. Having asked, "Whose commentary is that?
[the author] connects the word "of the Abhidhamma" with the phrase "I shall explain the meaning."

By virtue of its governing authority (*adhikāra*), it draws forth that very term from the *Abhidhammapada*. Alternatively, this meaning is to be clarified by means of repetition (*āvutti*) and so forth.

16. The doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga, which proceeds according to the method beginning with "the preparatory jhāna itself determines the specific factors of the noble path—namely, the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*), path factors (*maggaṅga*), and jhāna factors (*jhānaṅga*)"—is indicated by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*);
[it also includes the view that] the aggregates (*khandha*) which serve as the object of insight (*vipassanā*) determine [the path].

The statement "the inclination of the individual determines [the interpretation]" and so forth includes the views of such masters as the Elder Mahādatta, resident of Moravāpi, and the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya.
"By the very elucidation of that" means by the elucidation of the meaning of the Abhidhamma. "That" refers to the methodological determination (*vinicchaya*) of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
"In that manner" means by way of being unmixed and unconfused. Or rather, the determination of the Mahāvihāravāsins is itself unmixed and unconfused.
By the phrase "in the state of being his own," he shows that the exposition of the Mahāvihāravāsins is produced here precisely through this elucidation of the meaning of the Abhidhamma.
Alternatively, "by its very elucidation" means by the elucidation of its unmixed and unconfused nature.
"It" refers to the meaning of the Abhidhamma being elucidated. "In that manner" means by way of the exposition of the Mahāvihāravāsins. In this...
In the *Atthavikappa*, it should be connected thus: “I shall clarify the meaning unmixed and unconfused. 17.

“And all other elucidation of the meaning is a gratification”—this is the sense. For this very reason he said: “By all of that, gratification is produced. This is a suitable construction (*yuttarūpā yojanā*).
The commentary on the twenty stanzas is concluded.

The *Nidānakathāvaṇṇanā* (Commentary on the Introductory Story) is the section concerning the nature of the seven treatises (*sattappakaraṇa*). "Arrangement" (*sannivesa*) refers to the determination of the seven treatises and their constituent parts.
Regarding the phrase "thus considered by the Sāgaras": it means that four oceans [were used] for the purpose of making known the profound nature of this Abhidhamma.
The investigation of the ocean of methods together with the oceans of water and so forth is presented by way of the passage beginning, “It should be understood,” and so on.

The profundity of the Abhidhamma through its teachings is the discourse on its depth by means of the distinctions in teaching, such as: “Having transitioned from one state of phenomena to another a hundredfold and a thousandfold, he taught.
This is the profundity of the teachings.
“‘Thus, while teaching continuously for three months’ and so forth refers to the consideration of the manner in which the Blessed One’s body was sustained during the time of the teaching;

this is the exposition... [and] the grasping. Likewise, ‘the path of recitation in the Abhidhamma belongs to the Elder Sāriputta,’ and so forth, indicates that the path of recitation in the Abhidhamma is connected to the Elder Sāriputta and that it was produced by him alone.”

For that method taught by the Blessed One to the deities is endless and immeasurable due to its system of an unlimited number of recitations, and thus it is not suitable for the recitation of the monks;
whereas that method taught to the Elder is [too] excessively abbreviated. However, the method of recitation propagated by the Elder is one that is neither too concise nor too prolix.

By the phrase "through understanding the meaning of the words" and so forth, he states the connection for the investigation of the term *abhidhamma*, rather than providing a commentary on the meaning of the specific terms such as "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*).

Although the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) are indeed [the subject] according to such suttas as: "Those states which have been taught by me through direct knowledge—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness...
[and so on]... two bhikkhus who had trained themselves held different views regarding the Abhidhamma," etc.
"They are called ‘Abhidhamma’; and since the word *dhamma* is seen to be used in the sense of concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth, he said, ‘the meaning is:
the Pāḷi texts pertaining to the Suttantas,’ in order to show that here it is intended specifically as the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*).

In this context, even the Suttanta is called ‘Dhamma’ because it possesses the quality of not deviating from the Dhamma, just like the Abhidhamma. ‘O Ānanda, that Dhamma which has been taught by me to you...’"

In such passages as "the Vinaya has been taught and established," and because [the term *abhidhamma*] could otherwise be understood in other ways, the word "Suttantas" is used to clarify that the meaning is to be excluded by the prefix *abhi-*.

But is it not the case that [the Suttantas and Abhidhammas] possess the sense of being "excessive" (*atireka*) and "distinguished" (*visesa*), and are of distinct natures, since they are respectively indicated by the terms "additional" (*adhika*) and "variegated" (*vicitra*)?
Therefore, [should it not have been expressed] with a plural form, as in "by the senses of 'excess' and 'distinction' of the Dhamma"? [This is answered as follows:]...
Considering that it ought not to be expressed with a single word, he said: "For both... [the] singular-number designation was made.
Indeed, it does not even deserve to be employed, because prefixes (*upasagga*) must be employed only before verbal roots (*dhātu*).

Even if one were to employ them—as in *atimālā* and so forth, where words such as *ati* are used—nevertheless, just as in the case of "atimālā," where by means of a compound (*samāsa*), [the meaning is established].
The prefix *ati* is a qualifier for the action of "desiring" (*kamanakiriyā*) when it is not yet manifested, but not for a "garland" (*mālā*);
likewise, here too, the intention is that the prefix *abhi* is not appropriately a qualifier of the Dhamma.

As for the phrase "of another prefix as well," this is stated either by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), or by taking the etymological definition of a prefix (*upasagga*)—namely, that it "attaches itself to a meaning. This applies in cases such as *aticchatta* and so forth.

For here, the word *ati* is intended as a prefix (*upasagga*). In this regard, just as a man who is excellent or honored becomes "an eminent man" (*atipuruṣa*), so too, since the meanings of excellence and being honored can apply to the sense of "surpassing" (*atireka*) and "distinction" (*visesa*), the linguistic principle should be understood as follows:
an umbrella that is excellent or honored is an "eminent umbrella" (*aticchattra*). For the states of being excellent and being honored arise through connection with specific qualities.
It is to be desired. This is a distinction of quality, namely, its exceeding of measure and its variegated nature.

And by doing so, the statement "even for non-action" becomes justified. And just as it should be understood in the case of *aticchatta* and other such terms, so too should it be seen in the word *abhidhamma*.
For particles (*nipāta*) have many meanings. "Because it indicates that state" means because it indicates the state of exceeding and being distinguished.
“Because they have come down singly” means that since the Suttanta-bhājaniya has been seen for the aggregates, bases, and so forth that have come down singly in the Suttas—
such as “These six, monks, are faculties,” and so on, referring to the six beginning with the eye-faculty,
the three beginning with the femininity-faculty, the five beginning with the pleasure-faculty, and the five beginning with the ‘I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown’ faculty— [the exposition follows].

It is stated [thus] because the twenty-two faculties—which have not come down as a single sutta—have each arrived separately as distinct suttas according to the three [categories], and because the *Suttanta-bhājanīya* for them has not yet been seen;

it is not because arriving together as one in the Suttanta is the cause for a *Suttanta-bhājanīya*. For indeed, the *Paṭisambhidā* concerning the delimitation of the planes (*bhūmantara*) has not come down at all in its entirety within the Suttanta.
They are seen analyzed according to the Suttanta-bhājaniya method; however, the training rules (sikkhāpada) that have come down as a single unit are not analyzed in that way.

Furthermore, unlike the case of the abstentions (veramaṇī), there is no uniform mode of analysis for the twenty-two faculties (indriya) that is free from distinctions such as their intrinsic nature and function—such a mode of analysis would constitute a Suttanta-bhājaniya—and thus, in the Indriya-vibhaṅga, there is a Suttanta-bhājaniya.
It would be logical to say that it does not exist.
Even though there is no such thing as a "conditionality" (paccayabhāva) separate from the conditioned phenomena themselves, nevertheless,

the specific mode of occurrence of a conditioning phenomenon that serves as a condition for the phenomena produced by that condition— namely, its status as a cause (hetu) and so forth— is distinct from those [phenomena].

It is said that the state of being a condition for a conditioned phenomenon is as if it were something distinct; and that [state] is spoken of as the primary factor in such passages as, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
In that context, ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth—which function as cause and effect—are subordinate [to that state];

thus it is said, "the state of being a condition has been indicated. The phrase beginning with "of the phenomena indicated" refers specifically to those phenomena delimited by the enumeration (uddesa).

It is stated that the method of interrogation by question (*pañhapucchakanaya*) regarding the aggregates and so forth has been shown in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* and other such texts, and not otherwise than this.
In the *Suttanta*, such as the *Saṅgītisuttanta* and others, the five training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are recited thus: "Abstaining from taking life...
[and so on] ...from occasions of negligence. However, there is no other way to analyze these abstentions; this refers to the analysis of the past, impermanence, and so forth.

This is stated with the intention that, because the abstentions (*veramaṇī*) are included within the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, they should be understood by way of those very categories;
furthermore, there is no other mode of analyzing the abstentions apart from this that would be inconsistent with the method of the Abhidhamma.

And likewise, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, in the discourse on the contemplation of phenomena one by one (*anupadadhammasammasana-kathā*), it says: "The eye is impermanent... [and so on] ...aging-and-death is impermanent."
The abstentions have not been extracted. [Objection:
Should it not be shown that the Abhidhamma Piṭaka possesses a superior distinction even by way of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, the *Dhātukathā*, and so forth? [Reply:
This is true; however, since that [distinction] is established even without being stated—being dependent exclusively on the method of the Abhidhamma—it was not shown here.

By this illustration, all of that [remaining material] should also be understood. Alternatively, because it has already been stated through the common method of the Abhidhamma in the *Abhidhammabhājaniya* and the *Pañhāpucchaka*, it should be regarded as not needing to be repeated here.
"Question-sections" (*pañhavāra*) refers to the textual methods proceeding by way of questions and answers. "Right here" refers to the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*.

Thus it is. Because the state of being "not great" (appa-mahanta) is governed by relative expectation (*apekkhā*), the remaining portion is called the "Great Discourse on Elements" (*Mahādhātukathā*) in accordance with the words of the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*.
To demonstrate this, it is said: "Without coming from the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, [it is taken] from the discourse that has come down in the Great Heart of the Dhamma (*Mahādhammahadaya*).
From the phrase "Dhammahadaya... onwards, it means that without coming from the *Rūpakaṇḍa*, the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*, and so forth, [it is taken] from within this *Mahādhātukathā*.
The connection is: "the thread that has come down [in the *Mahādhātukathā*] is but a small portion. Now, one should construe it thus:

since the detailed exposition of the *Dhātukathā*—the *Mahādhātukathā*—does not appear in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, but appears in the *Mahādhammahadaya*, the thread that has come down in the *Mahādhātukathā* (as opposed to the *Dhātukathā*) is but a small portion.

"It is apprehended" is stated by way of characterizing the fivefold positive-negative [formula], while "it is not apprehended" is stated by way of characterizing the fivefold negative-positive [formula].

By the phrase "relying on the true goal" (*saccikaṭṭhaṃ*), through the non-specification of location and so forth in the passage beginning with "in all places," it is the true goal itself—divided into the seventy-seven categories of phenomena such as form—that serves as the basis. Regarding the term "in all places" (*sabbattha*) here as well...
The phrase "whether it is apprehended or not apprehended" should be connected by supplying the words "when a proposition has been accepted, for the purpose of grasping its negation";

the same applies here to the terms "always" and "in all. If the aggregates, bases, and so forth are included according to the method transmitted in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), then the connection is "if, however, it has been stated [as such].
The expression "the true goal" (*saccikaṭṭha*) characterizes that which is based upon the true goal. By these...
By these words. How is it that the "portion" (*padesa*)—which is a single part (*ekadesa*) of the "real object" (*saccikaṭṭha*), the "place" (*desa*), and the "time" (*kāla*)—is called "all"?

Because of the multiplicity of portions. Furthermore, this question proceeds by way of indicating the distinction for each [term] as "in all portions," and thus it is not a remainder of the preceding ones.
"Is it apprehended...? and so on, up to "is it wrong?"—the phrase "it is apprehended as one" refers to the first pentad (*pañcaka*).

Its meaning is that it is a single factor or a single constituent part consisting of the occurrence of the acceptance of a proposition, the rejection of that acceptance, the refutation of the opponent, and, by way of direct and reverse order, the establishment of the proposition, the bringing about of defeat, and the imposition [of the charge].
This should be applied similarly to the remaining pentads as well. [This establishes] the state of being a sound refutation for the refutation itself.
If the proponent desires [to establish his point], by means of establishing a formal admission (*paṭiññā*) such as, "But if you think so,
you must indeed say that 'the person is not apprehended,'" and by saying, "Since you admit this as the reason for that [position] and thus acknowledge it,
you are to be refuted; therefore, we shall refute you, and you will be well-refuted," [the opponent replies] with, "If indeed the person is not apprehended," and so forth.
*Paṭikammaveṭhana* (the veiling of the counter-argument) is the opponent’s method of counter-arguing in such a way that the proponent cannot extricate himself.
When the proponent desires to demonstrate the difficulty of the opponent’s counter-argument, he does so by pointing to that very counter-argument, saying:
"If this [position] is indeed difficult to refute... and by pointing to the counter-argument itself, saying: "One must say, 'A person is apprehended... and so forth.
"Regarding 'in the ultimate sense' (paramatthena): we are not to be refuted by you for making such a claim while asserting it as such.

If you have refuted us, then we are poorly refuted. Having said this, one effects the non-refutation [of the opponent] by demonstrating that the refutation—starting with "If a person is indeed apprehended"—is a poor refutation; this is the "untying of the refutation" (niggahanibbeṭhana).
“Then, having said, ‘If a person is indeed apprehended, then that which you have refuted...

and so forth, [the opponent] effects the cutting off and destruction of the opponent’s refutation by establishing that his own refutation is not actually a refutation, and by making his own counter-argument a well-formed counter-argument through the statement:
‘In that case, those refutations you made are [themselves] faulty refutations, while the remedies you applied are well-applied remedies.’”

Because it arises by way of refuting the doctrine of a person (puggalavāda). Having arisen in accordance with the nature of things (dhammatā), that which proceeds in opposition to it is the "fivefold set of the conformable and the contrary" (anulomapaccanīka-pañcaka);
this second fivefold set should be understood as the reverse of what was stated [in the first].

"Having that as its basis" (tadādhāra) means: those forms and so forth, which are the true and ultimate reality, are the basis (ādhāra) for this; thus, it is "having that as its basis. By this, [the phrase] "in form... [is explained].
The doctrine of a person (*puggalavāda*) is shown in such forms as "the self" (*attā*). Or, by the phrase "the basis for them," such forms as "form in the self" (*attani rūpaṃ*) are indicated.
Or, "apart from those" means without those [aggregates] such as form; it is unmingled with them in the sense of being neither the support nor the supported, but separate and distinct.
By this, such expressions as "a person unmixed with qualities like existence" (*satta*) and so forth are intended. This is because [the self] is the owner thereof.
Or, by way of dependence upon that, it is said, "or apart from them"; thus it should be understood that a doctrine of a person (*puggalavāda*) of such a kind as "the self possesses form" is shown.

By the term "not other," a doctrine of such a kind as "form is the self" is shown. The specific characteristic (*visesalakkhaṇa*) of the aggregates of form and so forth is their intrinsic nature of being subject to change and so on;
their general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) is their intrinsic nature of being conditioned and so on. Whether [the self] is other than or not other than form and the rest—if it were other...

The proponent of our own view (Sakavādī) pursues the argument that [the person], being perceived as the basis for those [aggregates] and so forth, would necessarily follow [as being identical to them], because no other alternative is possible.

The Proponent of the Person (Puggalavādī) does not accept that the person is different from form and the other aggregates, because it is impossible to apprehend it either through direct perception or through inference—just as one can apprehend form and the rest—and because its status as an agent or an experiencer is untenable. Nor, however, is it non-different.
Because it would follow that the person possesses the very nature of being subject to change and having conditions, and because it would follow that the person is non-existent.
For just as fire is not designated without fuel, yet one cannot assert that fire is other than the fuel, nor that it is not other;
if it were other, the fuel would not be hot; if it were not other, it would be nothing but that which is to be burned.

It might be a burner. In the same way, a person (puggala) is not designated apart from form and the other aggregates, yet it is neither different from them nor non-different, as that would entail the consequences of eternalism or annihilationism.
Standing upon this position, the proponent of the person (puggalavādin) rejects [the opponent's argument] by saying, "Not so.
In that regard, if the simile of fire and fuel is stated according to worldly convention, then the fuel—such as wood—is unignited and is what must be burned.

Fire is burning, radiant, hot, and burning; and that [fire], consisting of the eight material qualities beginning with nutritive essence (*ojas*), is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen in both its prior and subsequent phases.
If this is so, it follows that the person is other than the form and the rest, and is likewise impermanent.
Now, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), fire is the heat itself within that very burning wood and so forth, together with those [eight] co-nascent [qualities].
The three primary elements (*bhūta*) are the fuel; thus, it is established that fire and fuel are distinct due to the difference in their characteristics.

Consequently, it should be understood that the person (*puggala*), like fire, would result in being something other than the material form (*rūpa*) and so forth that constitute the fuel, and would therefore be impermanent;
thus, [the opponent's position] is contradicted. For one who asserts that "the person is perceived," since no other mode of existence is possible, [it must be among] the modes already stated.
Because it is apprehended as being apprehended in one way, it is called "entered" (*āpanna*); thus it is said, "entered into oneness by way of admission.

Precisely because of this entry into oneness, it is not to be rejected. When the person (*puggala*) has been refuted, the adherence to it—even for the proponent of a person (*puggalavādin*)—is indeed refuted and removed from its own position by the revelation of the emptiness of the mode in which it was grasped as something unreal.
Thus it is said: "refuting the view of a person (puggaladiṭṭhi). Or rather, the person itself is called a "view" because it is to be viewed in such a manner.

For here, what is rejected is the person established as a mere conceptual construct, which serves as the object of dogmatic adherence—such as [the notions] that he is "a master, a dweller, an agent, an experiencer, permanent, and eternal"—and not the conventional person spoken of in such expressions as, "O monks, these four persons... and so forth.
The meaning is that non-inquiry [into it] is like an investigation into whether a sky-flower is red, blue, or otherwise.

Having previously asserted "it is not apprehended," one does not incur a specific objection; therefore, the subsequent denial "it is not so" bears the taint of contradicting one's own prior admission.
It is like an inquiry into whether the son of a barren woman is tall or short—[an inquiry into something] which is in every respect entirely unapprehended from the perspective of ultimate reality.
In this context, the meaning of "non-perverted" (*aviparīta*) is precisely the state of not engaging in the pursuit of the identity or difference of a person (*puggala*) from form and so forth.

By the phrase "for what reason" (*yaṃkāraṇā*), it is shown that one should understand the elision of a case ending (*vibhattialopa*) in the expression "from which source" (*yatonidāna*). "They transgress" (*ajjhācaranti*) means they overcome.
The terms "delight" (*abhinandana*) and so forth should be construed respectively with "craving" (*taṇhā*) and so forth; or alternatively, they may be construed with "craving" and "views" (*diṭṭhi*).

Regarding "delighting" (*abhinandanā*) and "clinging" (*ajjhosāna*): either the act of greeting (*abhivadana*) is to be applied without distinction to all three, or the three [terms] should be joined with the three [objects].

Here, by indicating the absence of delighting and so forth through the phrase "there is nothing to be delighted in," the Path and Fruition—which constitute the total eradication and subsiding of delighting and so forth—are spoken of by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit. And this very [designation] is what is referred to by "this" (*idaṃ*).
Having said this, it was stated: "The fruit of [the knowledge] that knows...

As for the phrase "it is known (jānāti), therefore it is knowledge (jānan)": because the entire range of knowable objects (ñeyyajāta) is grasped without exception through the comprehension of the highest possible state, the instrument (karaṇa) for the act of knowing—which has that as its object—must necessarily be the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) itself; thus, "that which is to be known by omniscient knowledge..."
It is said, "he knows. Alternatively, this meaning is to be clarified either by the context of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*) or by the proximity of another word, namely "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*).
The same method applies here to the expression "seeing, he sees.

Even those who know—such as the heretics (*titthiya*) who claim to have full comprehension (*pariññā*) of sense-desires and form through the first jhāna and the formless jhānas—know [only] by way of perversion (*vipallāsa*); yet one who truly knows indeed knows.

The Blessed One [is so called] because he has taught the full understanding (*pariññā*) by means of the paths of non-returning and arahantship. And this meaning should be clarified by way of the *Dukkha-khandha Sutta*.
Or, he is "become vision" (*cakkhubhūta*) because he has arisen with the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*). The same method applies to the terms "become knowledge" (*ñāṇabhūta*), and so forth.
Alternatively, he is "become vision" because he has become—that is, attained—the fivefold vision beginning with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*). The same applies to "become knowledge," and so forth.
It should be seen. Because the Blessed One’s state as a speaker and so forth is preeminent in his teaching of the Dhamma that is self-exalting, it is said:

“He speaks on the Dhamma of the Four Truths, thus he is a ‘speaker’ (vattā),” and so on. Regarding the term “pavattā,” in order to show that the letter *pa* has the sense of being distinguished (*pakaṭṭha*), he says:
“He causes [the Dhamma] to proceed for a long time... thus he is a ‘proclaimer’ (pavattā). He who leads after having extracted [the truth] is a “guide” (*ninnetā*).
The phrase “eighty-nine states of consciousness” is stated by way of association with consciousness, just as one says, “the spears are moving.

Although each individual word of those scriptural passages has been extracted, and although the states of consciousness have been analyzed in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* by extracting only the terms of the triad of the wholesome (*kusala-ttika*), nevertheless, by means of the triad of the wholesome, those things comprised within the categories of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*)— [...]* (Note: The source text provided ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects this.)

It is said that because there are no terms for the "sixfold dyads" (sesattika-duka) that are not included [in the triplets], the terms for the other triplets and dyads are also effectively extracted by the extraction of the terms for the "threefold wholesome" (kusalattika). By doing so, the inclusion of the matrix (mātikā) becomes justified.
And that phenomenon (dhamma) refers to each subsequent term in such passages as "the three wholesome roots," etc., in relation to each preceding textual passage.

It is said, "the exposition of the meaning. To show that the word *samānentī* should be understood according to the method of verbal derivation (*saddanaya*), as in the case of the word *paṭapaṭāyati*, it is said, "making equal" (*samānaṃ karontī*).

And since making equal occurs either by adding what is deficient or by removing what is excessive, it is said, "filling up," to show that in this instance it occurs by adding what is deficient. [The word] *samānetabbaṃ*...
“In this case too” means in the phrase “the *Paṭṭhāna* should be brought together.
By the powerful momentum of knowledge proceeding through the reviewing of the *Abhidhamma*. Of the powerful momentum of knowledge proceeding by way of casting out all defilements.

“Deep indeed” (*gambhīraṃ eva*) means “deeply gone” (*gambhīragata*), as in the expressions “deeply gone into views” (*diṭṭhigata*) and so forth. “Without remainder” (*niravasesena*) means without leaving anything remaining.
"Free from the five stakes" means free from the five mental stakes.
Regarding "the one hundred and eight defilements plus one": there are seventy-three enumerated by way of single units such as "pride of birth";
thirty-six by way of pairs such as "anger and resentment"; and [nine] by way of triplets such as "the three unwholesome roots."
There are one hundred and five [categories]: fifty-six by way of groups of four, such as “the four taints” (āsavā);
seventy-five by way of groups of five, such as “the five lower fetters” (orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni); eighty-four by way of groups of six, such as “the six roots of dispute” (vivādamūlāni);
forty-nine by way of groups of seven, such as “the seven underlying tendencies” (anusayā); and [fifty-three] by way of groups of eight, such as “the eight bases of defilement” (kilesavatthūni).
By way of groups of eight, there are sixty-four; by way of groups of nine, such as "the nine grounds for resentment" and so forth, there are eighty-one;

by way of groups of ten, such as "the ten grounds for defilement" and so forth, there are seventy; and by way of groups of eighteen, such as "the eighteen modes of craving's movement for the arising of the internal [person]" and so forth, there are one hundred and eight.
Thus, among the eight hundred and one defilements, the remainder—ninety-three in addition—[are to be understood].
The defilements (*kilesā*) consist of the sixty-two views found in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, which together with those [other defilements] total seven hundred and fifty-five.

Alternatively, there are eighty factors: fourteen unwholesome states, twenty-five common to the wholesome and indeterminate, fourteen common to the wholesome triad, and twenty-seven material phenomena—counting the two, such as accumulation (*upacaya*), as one. Within these two categories of existence...
Excluding one, there are seventy-nine internal factors and seventy-nine external factors;
thus, all together they amount to one hundred and fifty-eight. Since ten defilements arise in relation to each of these, there are one thousand five hundred and eighty defilements in total.

Alternatively, there are fifty-three immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), eighteen material phenomena (*rūpa*), the space element (*ākāsadhātu*), and the characteristic material phenomena (*lakkhaṇarūpa*);

thus, these seventy-five phenomena become one hundred and fifty when divided into internal and external. In that regard, since there are ten defilements (*kilesa*) for each [of those], there are one thousand five hundred defilements.
Likewise, here, feeling (*vedanā*) is analyzed by way of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and so forth.
By making fivefold, there are fifty-seven immaterial phenomena and eighteen material phenomena;
thus, the seventy-five phenomena that are objects of insight (vipassanūpagadhammā) become one hundred and fifty when divided into internal and external categories.
Within each of these, there are ten defilements (kilesa), making one thousand five hundred defilements in total.

Another method: among the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising, there are six defilements in the first, seven in the second, six in the third, seven in the fourth, six in the fifth, seven in the sixth, six in the seventh, seven in the eighth, five in the ninth, six in the tenth, five in the eleventh, and four in the twelfth;
thus, all seventy-two of these belong to the five doors.
Regarding the five objects such as visible forms and so forth, there are seventy-two for each, totaling three hundred and sixty;
however, regarding the mind-door with respect to the six objects, there are seventy-two for each, totaling four hundred and thirty-two.
Thus, all together they amount to seven hundred and ninety-two. These, by way of being internal and external objects—
It should be understood that there are one thousand eight hundred and eighty-four defilements (*kilesa*).
Alternatively, there are five objects consisting of visible forms and so forth;

the remaining five—namely, the objects consisting of the remaining aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—make ten. These become twenty when divided into internal and external categories, plus the concept (*paññatti*), making twenty-one.
Regarding the twenty-one types of objects, there are seventy-two defilements for each, which amounts to one thousand two hundred and twelve defilements in total.
Alternatively, among the twelve unwholesome consciousness-arising states: in the first, there are twenty mental factors; in the second, twenty-two; in the third, twenty;
in the fourth, twenty-two; in the fifth, nineteen; in the sixth, nineteen; and in the seventh, nineteen.
In the eighth [jhāna] there are twenty-one; in the ninth, nineteen; in the tenth, twenty-one; in the eleventh, sixteen; and in the twelfth, sixteen.
Thus, all unwholesome states (*akusaladhammā*) total two hundred and thirty-six. These two hundred and thirty-six occur individually for each of the six objects.
All together, they amount to one thousand four hundred and sixteen.
In this way, one thousand five hundred defilements are to be understood.
As for the phrase "the others," it refers to the designation of the past and so forth for the "thirty-six wanderings of craving" by means of such expressions as "thirty-six past [wanderings].
"In their exhaustion" means in their total eradication by the Noble Path; for it is said, "having exhausted one thousand five hundred defilements. In the ultimate sense...
Because the past and so forth are not to be abandoned by the path, it is said: "The non-apprehension of the past and so forth as existing is 'dispelling' (khepana).

Furthermore, regarding that which is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna* in the triads such as: "A state to be abandoned by seeing is a condition, by way of proximity-condition, for a state to be abandoned by seeing," and likewise in the triad of the past states to be abandoned by seeing: "Past states to be abandoned by seeing [are conditions for future states to be abandoned by seeing]," and so forth.

Furthermore, the statement that [the defilements] are to be abandoned through vision and so forth with respect to the three times should be understood as being said because they do not differ from those things to be abandoned through vision in terms of their being defiled and leading to rebirth in the states of misery (apāya).
The phrase "not a statement of the literal meaning" is a partial explanation intended to exclude what was previously termed "a figurative expression for welfare."
Just as this word *attha* does not signify the meaning of what was spoken (*bhāsita-attha*), so too it does not signify the object (*visaya*) or the purpose (*payojana*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of what has been stated," this refers to the synonym for welfare (*hita*). Although in the commentary on the passage "Neither for one's own sake nor for another's sake, nor for praise or gain" (Dhp 128), the terms "one's own welfare" (*attattha*) and so forth are mentioned independently of the Sutta—beginning with "either one's own welfare or another's welfare"—[the term *attha* here is understood differently].

Because they have not been defined as being of the nature of the meaning of the discourses (*sutta*), yet not even a single one of those varieties of meaning transcends the necessity of being illustrated by the discourse, he said:
"It clarifies (*sūceti*) those [meanings] through the discourse. In this alternative interpretation, the word *attha* also denotes the expressed meaning (*bhāsitattha*).
For the preceding five varieties of meaning are synonyms for benefit (*hita*), while the six subsequent ones are varieties of the expressed meaning.

The latter two, however, possess both characteristics. In that regard, for the purpose of clarifying the difficulty of attainment: "profound" (gambhīra) means having no bottom reached; "hidden" (guḷha) means not revealed;
"concealed" (paṭicchanna) means covered over by the arrangement of syllables and so forth, like roots or water by soil;

"to be inferred" (neyya) means to be made known by extracting [the meaning]; "definitive" (nīta) means to be understood according to the literal expression alone. [These qualities] consist in being blameless, free from defilements, and pure.

[The term "sutta"] is spoken of by way of a figurative method (pariyāya), or by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional states (dhamma). The ultimate meaning (paramattha) is Nibbāna, or simply that which possesses an unerring intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

[The word] *sutta* is used in such expressions as “this much of the Blessed One’s teaching has come down in the Suttas and is included in the Suttas,” and “there are five hundred suttas in our own school,” and so forth, because it is explained as being preeminent due to its being the foremost among them.
He said, "This very thing is called a *sutta* because it indicates the meaning," with the intention of using this as a metaphorical designation (*upacara*).

Furthermore, the statement that "the teaching of a *suttanta* leads to the attainment of absolute welfare" is also said with reference to the fact that the teaching of a *suttanta* has that very welfare as its primary purpose in bringing about the benefit of those to be trained.

And that state of having that as its primary purpose should be understood from its conformity to the inclinations of those to be trained; likewise, so too should its predominance in revealing one's own welfare and so forth.
"By the others" means by the Vinaya and Abhidhamma.

"In the night, etc. means when the night, the king, and the Vinaya have become the objects [of the prefix]. But is it not the case that since "delight" (*abhirati*) is not explicitly mentioned, the inclusion of "night" need not be made;
and furthermore, that the word *abhi* is a qualifier of the specific action characterized by knowledge, as in "well-known" (*abhiññāta*) and "distinguished" (*abhilakkhita*)?
No; for the words *ñāta* and *lakkhita*, when qualified by the prefix *abhi*, have as their referent the night, because they stand in grammatical apposition with the word *ratti*.

Furthermore, since particles merely illuminate the meaning of a word when placed in proximity to a denotative term, it is said that the prefix *abhi* functions here in the sense of "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*), as it illuminates the meaning of the word *lakkhita*. It is a synonym for the word *abhilakkhita*.

And it should be understood that the word *abhiññāta* [functions as a prefix]; however, the formation of the compound for the word *abhivinaya* should be seen as being established like that of *abhipurisa*.
For particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings, and the differentiation of these multiple meanings is the domain of the application of words.
Although teaching (*desanā*) and the like do not exist independently of the object to be taught and so forth, commands (*āṇā*) and the like depend specifically upon the teacher and others.
The distinction between them is stated by way of their respective specific applications.

For just as the formulation of an injunction depends specifically on those worthy of the injunction due to the application of skill therein, so too the formulations of conventional and ultimate truth depend upon the formulators;

thus, the dependence of the formulation of injunctions and the like on the teacher is stated. Furthermore, just as [the teaching] conforms to the offender's disposition, the Dispensation likewise conforms specifically to the Dhamma.
"Depending on the persons to be trained accordingly" means "by way of being those who are to be instructed... and those to be trained," as it has been stated.

Since speech exists when there is a view to be dispelled—just as there is name-and-form (nāmarūpa) for the sake of restraint and non-restraint—but not when it does not exist, he said, "the discourse on that which is to be spoken...
the discourse," indicating that it is specifically dependent upon that. "Censure and so forth" refers to censure, the means of escape from it, the Dhamma, and the protection of one's treasure.
“Mastery and so forth” refers to mastery, right practice, and wrong practice.
The aggregate of the whole (tanti-samudāya) is the locus for the aggregate of its parts (avayava-tanti), just as one says, “the branch is on the tree.

This should not be questioned either directly or by way of the relationship between object and subject, because the intention is that the profundity of the Vinaya and other texts has already been stated. Dhamma.
For the Vinaya and so forth exist, and their object is the meaning (attha); and both teaching and penetration have the Dhamma and its meaning as their object.

By the words “of penetration,” etc., he shows that it is difficult to fathom because the Dhamma and its meaning are hard to penetrate, and because it is impossible to produce a teaching [without them];
furthermore, it is difficult to fathom because it is impossible to produce and to penetrate that penetration.

The meaning “in accordance with the Dhamma” (*dhammānurūpa*) and “according to the Dhamma” (*yathādhamma*) is also appropriate. For the teaching, like the penetration (*paṭivedha*), proceeds in accordance with the Dhamma because it reveals its own object without error;
hence it is called “unmistaken expression. By the phrase “it shows the linguistic expression of the Dhamma,” he illuminates that this is the intrinsic nature of the word for teaching.
For indeed, the state of having a limited object and so forth belongs to the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).

In the Pāḷi it is stated, and in the Aṭṭhakathā as well, that sound has the quality of being an object (*saddārammaṇatā*), by way of such passages as "having made the sound of the respective intrinsic nature and designation its object.

For the teaching is the sound that functions by way of clarifying each respective referent, having established the relationship between the word and the thing signified (*vacanavacanīya*) as "this sound is the designator of this meaning. But is it not said that "the Dhamma is the string"?
In this position, since *dhamma* also has the nature of sound, would there not be no distinction between *dhamma* and the teaching of *dhamma* (*dhammadesanā*)?
