"Without applied thought and with sustained thought, and with applied thought and without sustained thought"—this should be construed as "without applied thought and without sustained thought, and with applied thought and without sustained thought.

The phrase "if [they were] with applied thought and sustained thought," and so forth, was stated with the intention that even the demonstration of one part of both constitutes a demonstration of both.
"In order to reveal the other as well" means that just as in the arising of consciousnesses with applied thought and sustained thought, applied thought...
It is called "without applied thought and with sustained thought" (*avitakkavicāramatta*) by virtue of being without applied thought but possessing sustained thought;

this was said with reference to the fact that, among the aforementioned types of consciousness, sustained thought can be understood as "with applied thought and without sustained thought" (*savitakkavicāra*).

Furthermore, the statement that these [types of consciousness] are "mere sustained thought" due to the absence of applied thought is also made by employing the word *matta* (mere) for the purpose of excluding the qualifying attribute [of applied thought].

For since the term *vicāramattā* is understood to mean "possessing mere investigation" (*vicāramattavantī*), it excludes [the first jhāna] by virtue of its commonality—namely, the absence of other specific qualities—and thus the word *avitakka* ("without applied thought"), signifying the absence of that specific quality of *vitakka*, is brought forward to distinguish the factors of the second jhāna.
As it is said: "Not from investigation," and so forth.
7. "Vedayamānā" means experiencing. "In the mode of pleasure" (sukhākāra) means in the mode of the desirable, or in the mode of experiencing what is desirable.
"Udāsīnā" means devoid of inclination or aversion. It is not opposed to pleasure and pain because it does not act as an obstacle to them.
For, like pleasure and pain themselves, it proceeds immediately after them; thus, being an intervening factor, it is not in conflict with them.

But it is not because of the immediate succession of pleasure and pain. As for the meaning, "It looks on by way of rebirth (*upapatti*), thus it is equanimity (*upekkhā*)," this is not stated here as the definition of the word *upekkhā*, because that would include all types of equanimity. For the equanimity associated with greed and so forth does not "look on by way of rebirth.
Therefore, [it is] because it is accompanied by joy alone and not accompanied by pleasure; and even when accompanied by pleasure...
"They are not accompanied by rapture alone" means that those accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagata*) and those accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagata*) are distinct from one another; therefore,

even though those accompanied by pleasure are for the most part accompanied by rapture, that pleasure with which they are endowed makes them "accompanied by pleasure" rather than "accompanied by rapture"—
this is the distinction made by this triad, namely, "pleasure devoid of rapture" (*nippītikasukha*).
Explaining the meaning of "shown," he said, "having stated 'accompanied by rapture,'" and so forth.
"Established" means that, having included both the remaining and non-remaining forms of happiness and rapture within the first and second terms occurring in the sequence,
that specific state which is accompanied by rapture is happiness, and that specific state which is accompanied by happiness is rapture.
Even though there is mutual association (*saṃsaṭṭha*), the meaning is that it is established, known, and understood because it is shown to be included within the other terms.

Some say: "This triad was stated in order to show the exquisite nature of the bliss of the fourth jhāna by extracting it from the coarse factors, as that bliss is exceedingly sublime. However, this [explanation] applies to all phenomena associated with pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*).
Here, because it is stated as "accompanied by pleasure" (*sukhasahagatā*), this must be investigated.

For indeed, the exposition proceeds by way of such statements as "in the realm of sense-desire (*kāmāvacara*) on the plane of pleasure," and "from wholesome states of the sense-sphere, four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by joy. 8.
This was said with reference to having Nibbāna as its object, not to the penetration of Nibbāna; otherwise, the state of *gotrabhū* would entail being [itself] a stage of seeing (*dassana*).

The intended meaning is that it should not be objected to. [Objection: But surely, since the very path of stream-entry is "seeing" by virtue of performing the duty to be done upon seeing, and the penetration of Nibbāna through the knowledge of its superior state is itself "seeing," then the status of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) as "seeing" should not be challenged.
[Response: No, because "seeing" is heard of as a common term, and because there is a performance of duties to be done through seeing.

Because it is stated with distinction. In that context, although the use of distinct terminology is appropriate—since, as in passages such as "Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed," a distinction is figuratively applied even when there is no difference in time—it is not proper to employ a term for the commonality of seeing when a specific kind of seeing is intended;
thus, it is merely the commonality of seeing [that is meant].
It is said that "the charge was made after taking [it up]" with the intention of referring to Nibbāna as the object.
Because the expression "the eye of Dhamma" (dhammacakkhu) is also applicable to the second and third paths, it is said that "[it] has not reached the state of cultivation" (bhāvanā).
In this context, "cultivation" (bhāvanā) means increasing; and since that occurs through frequent arising, he says, "by way of repeated production. For it is thus:
Regarding the word *satīti* (“when there is”), it means when there is the sense of “by way of rejecting both,” namely, by way of rejecting [the paths of] seeing and cultivation.
One might object: “Are not mundane serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) also, according to their respective capacities, abandoners of sensual desire and the other hindrances?
How then can it be said that there is no other abandoner? Anticipating this objection, he says “by others,” and so forth.

9. *Appahātabbahetumattesu* means "in those cases where there is merely a cause that is not to be abandoned. This refers to all wholesome (*kusala*) and indeterminate (*abyākata*) phenomena according to their intended meaning.
A compound (*samāsa*) is not applicable because of the lack of semantic compatibility. *Yesaṃ* means "of those" phenomena which have been stated as belonging to the third category;
this is their meaning. Regarding *ubhinnaṃ*, since they must be construed separately, it is understood as referring to two instances of the term *pahātabbahetu*.
It has been stated. "This" refers to the statement: "These possess a cause to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.
This is [stated] by means of the term "possessing a cause to be abandoned," which is joined with those two terms, "vision" and "cultivation.

And "having done so" means having thus joined the term "possessing a cause to be abandoned" individually with each of the terms "vision" and "cultivation. For in this way, the first two terms... [etc. ...this is the vision.
"Is it so?"—if this meaning is intended, namely that "these [states] have a cause that is not to be abandoned by vision or cultivation," then, having explained the meaning of the phrase "The cause...
might be" by way of showing that those without a cause were not included under the previous meaning with the words "For in the first meaning...
and so forth, he now says "Or rather... and so on, demonstrating the appropriateness of the second meaning alone, beginning with "Of that very meaning which is to be accepted."
For it is indeed the meaning that is to be grasped because it has been stated, "The meaning should be understood in this way.
10. "Otherwise" means when the mere making of an object is intended.

But how is it to be known that by the phrase "having made an object," the making of an object that accomplishes the four functions is expressed? [It is known] from the specific sense within a general description.
Because it is the state of persistence and because the noble path-dhammas alone lead to diminution. For it is said: "The four paths, being not included [in the mundane], lead to diminution.
It is for this very reason that he says: "This is a designation for the noble paths.
Or rather, by this very expression—which serves as a cause for distinguishing the specific quality—it is understood that the aforementioned distinction in the way the object is made is intended.
Or this meaning should be understood by way of knowing the highest possible state (*ukkaṃsagati*). By the phrase "reviewing, etc.," the stages of purification (*vodāna*) and so forth are included.

"By way of being a cause" means by way of being a cause that brings about [the result]. For a cause is threefold: the informer (*ñāpaka*), the producer (*kāraka*), and the bringer-about (*sampāpaka*);

likewise, the fruit is threefold by way of being that which is to be informed, and so forth. Just as unwholesome states, mundane wholesome states, and the arising of consciousness are so called because they are the paths leading to states such as hell or the human condition.
When it is said, “states leading to accumulation,” this does not refer only to mundane states such as wrong view or right view;

likewise, because they constitute the path leading to Nibbāna, the arising of supramundane wholesome consciousness should be understood as “leading to dispersal,” and not only the factors of the Noble Path.
Demonstrating this point, he says, “of the former and the latter,” and so forth. Therein:
Since it is the noble path alone whose nature as the practice leading to Nibbāna is clearly manifest, it is logical that it alone possesses the quality of leading to diminution (*apacayagāmin*).
However, because they follow that [path], the remaining factors are included and mentioned [as such].

Those for whom there is an especially superior going toward diminution through the full understanding of suffering and so forth are "those leading to diminution"; thus it is said, "the paths themselves are those leading to diminution. Regarding the phrase "of the former and the latter":
And in this triplet, the meaning is "of the meanings included in the first and second words.
In such passages as "Victory breeds enmity, whether one is moving or standing," the word *ācaya* has a nasalized vowel (*sānunāsika*);

thus it is said, "the elision of the nasal was made. Furthermore, it should be understood that although one ought to say "accumulating" (*ācinan*), it is stated as "accumulation" (*ācaya*) by way of a grammatical variation (*byattaya*).

By the phrase "going as accumulations," it should be understood that the meaning shown through the method of exposition is: "they go by way of diminishing" (apacaya), that is, they proceed as diminutions.
Regarding the statement, "Among worldly [phenomena], the state of one beyond training (asekkha-bhāva) is not possible," why was this said? Is it not the case that—
“Monk, one is called a ‘trainee’ (sekha) because he trains. And what does he train in?
He trains in higher virtue, he trains in higher mind, and he trains in higher wisdom. Monk, one is called a ‘trainee’ because he trains.
This includes even a virtuous worldling who fulfills the practice in accordance with the truth, who is perfected in virtue, and [restrained] in the sense-faculties...”

"One who dwells with guarded doors of the sense faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to the practice of wakefulness, and devoted to the practice of developing the states conducive to enlightenment during the first and last watches of the night,
thinking, 'Today or tomorrow I shall attain one of the fruits of recluseship'—
he too trains, and thus he is a trainee (sekha)."

Is it because of the statement that even the virtues and other qualities of the aforementioned "good worldling" (kalyāṇaputhujjana) are called "of one in training" (sekha)? No, because this is said figuratively (pariyāya).
For the status of being "in training" or "beyond training" (asekha) applies, according to possibility, only to the states of the path and its fruits;

thus, since there is no suspicion of the status of being "in training" regarding mundane (lokiya) states, it is stated that they do not possess the status of being "beyond training. Therefore he said, "virtue and concentration," and so forth. This also applies to the states of the fruit of Arhatship.

Considering the objection that "since they proceed by way of being the fruit of training, like the states of the lower fruits, they would be *sekkhā* (in training) in the sense of having been born into the trainings, etc.";

or alternatively, that "even the states of the lower fruits, because they proceed by way of being the fruit of training, would be *asekkhā* (beyond training), like the states of the fruit of Arahantship," it is said: "Because the duty of training has been brought to completion. Likewise, regarding the lower fruits...

"Panā" and so forth. In such expressions as "I eat that very same rice," "that very same partridge," and "those very same medicinal herbs," the designation of the original term should be understood as referring to things similar to them.
By this, others maintain that non-trainees (asekkhas) who resemble trainees (sekkhas) are referred to as "amanusso" (non-human).
Elsewhere, in words such as "ariṭṭha," the letter *a* is seen even in the sense of growth; thus, the trainees who have attained growth [are meant].
"Those beyond training" (asekkhā)—this meaning has also been stated.

"Because of their capacity to suppress the defilements" (kilesavikkhambhanasamatthatāya): this should be regarded as a mere illustration; for here, the capacity to suppress applied thought (vitakka) and so forth is also obtained.
Or else, because wholesome states have the function of destroying the unwholesome, they possess a particularly distinguished role therein.
In order to show that the sublime states (mahaggata) are distinguished from the limited states (paritta), it is said:

"by way of their capacity to suppress the defilements. This means that among the resultant and functional states, there is indeed long continuity, but not the capacity to suppress the defilements nor the possession of abundant fruit.
However, if the meaning is taken as "abundant fruit" (*vipulaṃ phalaṃ vipulaphalan*), then even among the resultants, there is the quality of having abundant fruit.
It can indeed be so obtained. It should be understood that this [explanation] is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* by way of the "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*).
Furthermore, the meaning "those who have gone or have entered upon the path by means of the great ones" is common to all three [terms].

Because they proceed as if setting a limit for beings by saying "this is the extent of their qualities," the gross defilements are called "limit-setters" (*pamāṇakarā*). By these, they are completely broken and delimited.
They are limited (*paritta*). Although they may be delimited by certain factors, they are called "lofty" (*mahaggata*) because they proceed with a great measure.
Because they are not the domain even of the subtle defilements that create delimitation, they are not delimited by them in any way;
thus they are "unlimited" (*appamāṇa*), which is why they are also called "not included" (*apariyāpanna*).

14. They do not produce satiety because they are exceedingly peaceful and because they are insatiable. Furthermore, the alternative explanation of the meaning beginning with “by those which make a measure” is written in many manuscripts after the commentary on the inferior set of terms beginning with “in the sense of being insatiable”;
however, it should be brought back and stated in its proper place.

15. Even among worldly good people, activity regarding things that are extremely loathsome—such as the denial of the existence of karma with immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*)—does not occur without the power of perversion (*vipallāsa*);

therefore, it is said: "due to the strength of inversion. By this [phrase], namely "when there is the giving of a result" and so forth, it is indicated that even though there is a fixed time [for results], the statement regarding the arising of the result is one made with reservation. "Therefore" means because, according to the method already stated...
Because of their fixed nature, an over-extension [of the definition] would be difficult to avoid; therefore, by the phrase "the occurrence...

by a powerful [kamma]," he shows that for the *anantarika* kammic deeds, there is an inevitability of fruition because they cannot be turned back by a kamma of a different class, and even when a kamma of the same class occurs, they cannot be obstructed due to their capacity to produce fruition immediately after it.
For this reason, their quality of being subject to fruition is established by their very nature.
“Certainty and immediate succession. By the phrase “from another... from giving,” he likewise clarifies that the fruit is not precluded by things of a different class and so forth.
The objector, not understanding the underlying intention, raises a challenge regarding an over-extension with the words “Is it not so?

and so on. The other [the respondent] reveals his own intention with the words “He does not incur [the fault],” and so forth. “Inevitably” means necessarily occurring. “Because of being fixed” refers to the accomplishment or production [of the result].
Because of their fixed nature. Those in which the suspicion of non-ripening has ceased are "those in which the suspicion of non-ripening has ceased" (*uparatāvipaccana...saṅkāni*);
their state is "the state of having ceased... suspicion" (*upa...saṅkattaṃ*); therefore [it is said].

"Because there is no impairment of capability" expresses the fact that they cannot be obstructed even by a powerful *ānantariya* (immediate) karma. They are supportive, providing auxiliary strength for the arising of the continuum.
Because they are specified [as such]. By this, he states that their activity is never fruitless, even when no kamma-result (vipāka) is produced.

16. The function of the Path consists of full understanding and so forth. This is because, by means of the path-factors known as the path-roots—namely, right view associated with the Eightfold Path and non-greed and non-hate—it demonstrates that the remaining path-factors associated with the path, including right view itself, possess the state of being "with root" (sahetuka).
It is said: "By way of including those not included in the three methods. Regarding "by way of the multiplicity of causes":

immediately after the first method, which possesses multiple causes, the third method—stated in the *Nikkhepa-kanda* text by virtue of the commonality of having multiple causes—is stated here in the commentary as the second.
[This refers to] among inactive phenomena that proceed according to their respective conditions...

The state of being followed by some [mental factors] arises not only from the intrinsic nature of the phenomena (*dhamma-sabhāva*), but also from the specific mode of occurrence of preceding phenomena;
thus he says, "by way of prior volitional formations" (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra-vasena*).

For the specific mode of occurrence is the "prior volitional formation of cultivation," which is the imparting of excellence to each successive [moment] of the preceding minds and mental concomitants (*citta-cetasika*). "Following along" (*anuvattayamāno*)...
"Treating with respect. "By way of illustration" means by way of an example, not by way of showing everything without exception.
With the words "But because," etc., he establishes the meaning already stated by means of an alternative reading.

For in that context, since it stands as the opposite of the predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), the meaning "the path is the predominance; [thus] path-predominance" is obtained. "By way of the meaning of the word *samāna*" (common).

This was stated with reference to the absence of any difference in the meaning of the term *maggādhipati*, despite the differences in the meanings of compounds where the referent is distinct from the other members (*aññapadattha*) or where they share the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

17. Regarding the word *uppanna*: since it functions as a derivative of the root *uppāda* (to arise), it denotes both types of meanings—namely, "having arisen" and "having reached and then passed away.
To show that it expresses both meanings and not only the former ones, he said "unarisen" (*anuppannā*), and so forth. In this context, the state of having arisen...
The state of having reached arising and so forth. By this, even past [phenomena] are included. For this very reason, it says:

"the entire state of being arisen. The state of being an arisen phenomenon means the state of being a phenomenon grasped by the phrase "arisen phenomena," that is to say, the state of being a present phenomenon.
Or rather, that which has reached arising and so forth, which maintains its own intrinsic nature and is maintained by conditions—this is [what is meant].
"Arisen phenomenon" (*uppannadhamma*) means the state of being present; thus, this is how the meaning should be understood here.
Having spoken of "arisen phenomena," the statement "unarisen" (*anuppanna*) is not a negation of what has already been attained. How, then, is this to be understood?
He says, "If indeed," and so forth. Some, however, hold that in this context the word "arisen" includes the past as well.
If they are not included, one might argue that they should be called "inexpressible" (navattabba) just like Nibbāna;
however, they do not state it thus. But that is merely their own opinion. As for this triad, the commentary will explain that it is shown by way of fulfilling two time-periods (addhāna).
This being so, why were the past states not called "inexpressible"?
Because it does not exist as something included within the category of "dhammas. For Nibbāna, which is not included among dhammas, cannot be described there as "arisen" (*jāta*);
nor are there any dhammas whatsoever that are called "past" such that, by virtue of not being included here [in the present], they would have to be described as "not to be spoken of.
Here, the term "completed" (*pariniṭṭhita*) refers to the arising of the cause prior to the production of the fruit.
Because it does not exist for him as something that has already passed away, he says, "or in the future. For even the fruit of the Blessed One Metteyya’s arising is called "arising.

By the passage beginning with "For one who has emerged from jhāna," etc., he demonstrates the preceding portion of the text—beginning with "Therefore, Ānanda"—by way of its meaning. For this is the text therein:
"And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu settle his mind internally, compose it, and make it one-pointed?"
He concentrates. Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, quite secluded... [as before] ...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
In this way... he concentrates. He directs his mind to internal emptiness;
as he directs his mind to internal emptiness, his mind does not leap forward into emptiness... [as before] ...it is liberated. This being so, Ānanda, it is thus.
A bhikkhu understands thus: "While attending to emptiness internally, my mind does not leap forward into internal emptiness...
[and so on] ...it is not liberated. Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard. He attends to emptiness externally...
[and so on] ...he attends to emptiness both internally and externally... [and so on] ...he attends to the imperturbable; while he is attending to the imperturbable...
“‘The mind does not leap forward into the imperturbable… it is liberated’—thus, in this regard, he is clearly comprehending. Therefore, Ānanda, by that bhikkhu.
In that context, “in internal emptiness and so forth” means in internal emptiness, external emptiness, both internal and external emptiness, and in the imperturbable.
“In the sign of concentration such as the first jhāna” means in the sign of concentration such as the first jhāna which serves as the basis. From the jhāna that is the unskilled basis...
For when he has emerged [from concentration] and is attending to internal emptiness, his mind does not leap forward into it.
Then he attends externally, thinking, "How is it in another's continuum? There too it does not leap forward.
Then he attends both internally and externally, thinking, "At one time in my own continuum, and at another time in another's continuum, how is it?"

He applies his mind to it, yet he does not leap forward into it. Then, desiring to be liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), he applies his mind to the imperturbable (*āneñja*), thinking, "What now is the method for the formless attainments? Yet even there he does not leap forward.
Thinking, "Now my mind does not leap forward," he must not relax his energy; rather, he must thoroughly [cultivate] the foundational jhāna itself.

It must be brought to mind again and again. Thus, just as for one cutting down a tree who has the axe sharpened repeatedly while it is being struck, the attention flows toward the object of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) as it is being cut;
it is with this in view that the passage beginning with "In that very same [object]" was spoken.

Regarding the phrase "and because they are not identical in meaning": why was this stated? Is it not the case that after showing all those meanings in which the word *ajjhatta* occurs, this was stated by way of an enumeration of meanings (*atthuddhāra*) for the purpose of determining the specific meaning intended here?

Furthermore, the term *ajjhattika* regarding the eye and so forth occurs by taking into account the specific quality of being internal (*abbhantara*) to those that are internal (*ajjhatta*). Therefore, they are called "internal-internal" (*ajjhatta-ajjhatta*).

...are so called. Furthermore, the phrase "the six internal [bases]" is stated here by way of illustration because the term *ajjhattika* (internal) exists as a designation for the internal nature of the eye and the other [senses].
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* regarding the dyad of the internal: "Those which are simply internal are the internal bases.
This being the case, there would be no lack of terminological consistency here; therefore, the aforementioned objection does not apply.

Clarifying this, he said, "But here, however... and so forth. "By that" means for that reason. "Of that which expresses it" refers to that which expresses the internal [state], because it can be said that the state of being internal exists as its referent. As it is said:
"Indeed, Ānanda, a bhikkhu who delights in company, who takes pleasure in company, and who is devoted to delighting in company, does not shine. And so on.

And by seeing the absence of the attainment of one’s desires for the happiness of renunciation and so forth—which is unsuitable for one who has gone forth—and the delight in company, as well as the delight in form and so forth, [the Blessed One said]:

"Ānanda, I do not perceive even a single form such that, for one who is attached to it and takes pleasure in it, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise due to its change and alteration. Thus [he spoke] regarding delight in form and the other sense objects.
Having thus stated the danger, if some person of poor wisdom who has gone forth should say, "The Perfectly Enlightened One is like one who drives cattle into a field;
he draws us away from the group and enjoins us to live in solitude, yet he himself dwells surrounded by kings, royal ministers,
and others," then for the purpose of cutting off the ground for such speech, [he speaks] before an assembly extending to the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
He said, "In order to show that even while sitting in the midst [of the assembly], the Tathāgata is alone," the teaching beginning with "But this... was commenced;
he stated this "in order to show the dwelling in the opposite state. In that context, "all signs" refers to the conditioned signs of form and so forth.
"Internally" means within the range of the sense objects. "Emptiness" refers to the fruition attainment produced through the power of the contemplation of non-self.
For this very reason, he said, "internally" (*ajjhattam*), and so forth. Therein, in the second alternative, the word "basis" (*ṭhāna*) should be understood as a synonym for "cause.
"By the *Saccaka Sutta*" refers to the *Mahāsaccaka Sutta*. For therein it is said:
"Moreover, Aggivessana, I recall teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds; yet even then..."
Each one of them thinks thus: "The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma for my sake alone.
But this, Aggivessana, should not be viewed in such a way. It is only for the purpose of making it understood that the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others.
At the conclusion of that very discourse, Aggivessana, right there at that previous [moment]...
“With respect to the sign of concentration, I settle the mind internally, I compose it, I unify it, and I concentrate it—
by means of which I indeed dwell constantly throughout the aeon”—
thus it is said to have “come.”
22. By making something appear as if it were other than what it is through other non-indicative [factors], as in the expression "the body of a stone statue.

By means of the commonality of the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena, etc., although there is no such thing as a state of being indicative distinct from the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), there is nevertheless the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Therefore, since the distinction of the sense-sphere of form is made by way of its state of being indicative, this state of being indicative is that which effects the distinction of other phenomena.

This shows that although it is not other than the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), it is designated [as such] by treating it as if it were other. "Distinction in meaning" refers to the differentiation between the general meaning and the specific meaning.
[The objects are] those tangible phenomena that have reached [the senses] themselves; those of the nose, tongue, and body which have reached [them] by way of their support;
and the odors and tastes, which are otherwise unapproached. "Mutual falling upon" means the abiding of one in the suitable location of the other.

"By which state of resistance": "Activity, etc. refers to the occurrence of the downward sinking and upward leaping of the eye-lids and so forth, by way of the mental activity and the expansion of the air-element. "The arising of a modification" means the arising of something dissimilar;
the meaning is that there is assistance or injury [to the object] by way of its being desirable or undesirable.
The commentary on the words of the Tikamātikā is finished.
Commentary on the words of the Dukamātikā 1–6:
Regarding the inclusion of those [factors] to be taken together in the same location, which must be taken with respect to one and the same object, having a single object as their domain.

Or alternatively, the meaning is: because those factors existing in the same location have a single basis (*ekavatthu*) and a state of being grasped together (*samānagahetabbabhāva*), they are said to be "arisen together" (*ekuppādi*).

Those phenomena that are accompanied by roots (*hetusahagata*) are included together with the roots. And as for their state of being rooted (*sahetukabhāva*), it is stated as "simultaneity... and existence" (*samā...pe...
sabbhāva*) on the grounds that it is produced by the roots through such relations as co-nascence (*sahajāta*). Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the other relations are implied].
It grasps [the mind] in its operation as the cause for accomplishing the state of being well-established, and so forth.

"Attaining a state of unity" is said with reference precisely to the fact that the mind and mental factors, occurring as a single aggregate through their mutual association, have distinctions between them that are difficult to discern due to their dense mass-like nature.

"Even in the absence of diversity among phenomena" means even in the absence of a distinction in their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) or objective referent (attha). "By way of the diversity of word-meanings" (padatthana-nānatta): *Note: The term *padatthana* here refers to the various modes or bases of the mental factors' activity.*
By way of the distinction of being designated by various terms. By this, he shows that the statement regarding the "other pair" (*dukantara*) is in consideration of another category.
For phenomena (*dhammā*) are of many kinds. For this very reason it is said: "All phenomena in all their aspects come within the range of the knowledge of the Blessed Buddha.
And this meaning is to be seen even in the *Tika* (triplets). Of those disciples (*vineyyāna*) by whom...

When the manifestation of phenomena is accomplished through various modes, there is penetration (*paṭivedha*); the manifestation of those phenomena according to their respective specific modes is [the penetration].

However, for those cases where penetration occurs through the manifestation by means of even a single mode, the Teacher’s mastery over the Dhamma consists in teaching that mode and manifesting all other remaining modes without exception;
thus he said, "the knowledge of the modes to be taught," and so forth.
Is it not the case that for one who knows by one mode, the manifestation of other modes is fruitless?

It is not so, because it serves as a supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for the differentiation of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). "Those modes belong to these" means *tappakārā*; the state of being such is *tappakāratā*.
By this, he shows that the manifestation of the specific distinctions of modes that actually exist among phenomena is the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*).
"In other places as well" refers to such passages as "states that are both rootless and not roots," and so forth.

Just as by taking one part of the first dyad and joining it with the second and third dyads, three dyads are obtained in the method of the sixth dyad— namely, "root states are both with-roots and rootless," and so on— so too,
by taking one part of the second and third dyads and joining them with the first dyad, [other combinations are formed].
“States with roots are both roots and not roots; states without roots are both roots and not roots; states associated with roots are both roots and not roots;
states dissociated from roots are both roots and not roots”—thus four dyads are obtained.

However, it should be understood that these are not shown because they can be demonstrated by the same method already explained. Alternatively, [they are omitted] because they are included within those stated in the Pāḷi...
Because these [two] are not different from the first two shown in the commentary in the fourth and fifth [sections], they are not mentioned here.
For the distinction here consists merely in a difference of arrangement. Precisely because they do not have a distinct meaning, he said "But among these...
and so forth, in order to show that those dyads not mentioned [in the text] are included within the dyads as they have been determined according to their occurrence among the dyads found in the Pāḷi.

Alternatively, when there is a compendium of possible dyads (duka) such as "states that are both causes and rootless," according to the method to be explained in the passage beginning with "Or by this demonstration of the destiny," there would also be a compendium of these [present states].
Or, having extracted a term from a dyad, another dyad is stated; thus, when there is a difference [in meaning], another dyad is obtained, but not [when there is no difference].
It should be understood that no distinction exists here between these and the aforementioned pairs, as such has not been shown in the commentaries. Furthermore,

just as there is a difference in the mere meaning of the terms between the "With-cause" pair and the "Associated-with-cause" pair, and between the "With-cause-and-with-cause" pair and the "Cause-and-associated-with-cause" pair,
but no difference in their essential nature (*sabhāva*), so too it is with the "With-cause-and-with-cause" pair.

Having spoken thus, the others were also addressed; for it was stated that even though there is no diversity in the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the dyads such as "root-associated root" and "root-root-associated," because a diversity of word-meanings (*padatthana*) is possible, another dyad is expressed through the diversity of word-meanings despite the absence of a diversity of phenomena (*dhamma*), such as:
"phenomena accompanied by roots" and "phenomena not accompanied by roots," "phenomena co-nascent with roots" and "phenomena not co-nascent with roots."
“States: states associated with a root, states dissociated from a root; states originated by a root, states not originated by a root;
states co-existent with a root, states not co-existent with a root. And likewise: “States that are both roots and accompanied by roots,” and so forth; and also:
“States that are not roots, yet are accompanied by roots, or are not accompanied by roots,” and so forth.
It appears that a collection of various dyads (dukas) that are possible has been permitted; for he will say, "By this demonstration of the paths," and so forth.
In the same way, this meaning should be stated as applicable to the group of taints (āsava-gocchaka) and the rest.
Or rather, it was spoken by the Lord of Dhamma, who knows the intrinsic nature, function, and other characteristics of phenomena, as well as their mode of being understood, exactly as they are.
One should abide by as many dyads (duka) as have been stated. Indeed, it should be understood that those dyads which were not stated by the Blessed One must certainly not be spoken of [as valid].
The intention is that the dyad of "cause and associated-with-cause" (hetu-hetusampayutta-duka) does not differ in meaning from the sixth dyad. Regarding the phrase "among them":
this refers to the first and third dyads. If [there is a question] because of the identity of meaning between one dyad and the terms of another dyad...

Regarding the non-statement of these dyads and the intermediate phrases of the dyads: if this were the case, even the first phrase of the sixth dyad should not be stated, because its meaning is identical to the second phrase of the fourth dyad.
Thus, with reference to the objection that "in that case, the sixth dyad would not even exist," he says, "In the fourth dyad," and so forth.
The phrase "for the purpose of completing the dyad" refers precisely to this identity of meaning.
This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*), for indeed there exists a distinction in the teaching (*desanāvisesa*).

Even in the absence of a difference in meaning (*atthantaratā*), the statement of a separate dyad (*dukantara*) is due to a difference in mode of presentation; for this is the meaning demonstrated here.

By this "demonstration of the method" (*gatidassana*)—that is, by the demonstration of the principle known as the completion of the sixth dyad—even in the absence of a difference in meaning—the [meaning] is shown in the first dyad... as stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
[This is] by means of the fourth and fifth [dukas], by the two preceding ones shown in the Aṭṭhakathā, and by the four shown here.
Regarding the phrase "among those": it should be understood that what is shown by the first duka is presented in the Pāḷi by the sixth duka, and in the other cases by the remaining dukas.

7–13. By the phrase "by way of mere conditionality" ... up to "... exists," it is shown that existence does not consist merely in the possession of an intrinsic nature (sasabhāvatā) defined as having been acquired;

rather, it shows this meaning: non-ceasing by way of its opposite, non-abandonment, the state of not yet having produced its fruit, and the fitness for the production of a fruit through the non-eradication of the cause.
For thus it is said: "When this exists, that comes to be."
Here, by the word "satī" (being), that cause—whether past or otherwise—without which something does not exist, is indeed included. For this very reason, he said:
"Not without a cause... [etc. ...of times. "Same... [etc. ...dīpeti": "Conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) means made by conditions having come together and combined.
This is their distinction: namely, that these things produced by conditions possess conditions and are brought about by multiple conditions.
And in the two dyads, the distinction lies in the meaning of the preceding term; for the others, however, it lies in their having a nature devoid of the factors included in the preceding term.

Regarding the phrase "because they are not excluded... nor set aside": this is stated because, in the Abhidhamma matrix (mātikā), there is no explicit determination or definition of the number of factors by saying "there are so many," whereas in the Suttanta matrix, such specific designations of the types of formations have already been determined.
Ignorance and the other factors are mentioned specifically for the purpose of defining their determined meanings.

Regarding the interpretation of the meaning as "earth and so forth are matter," just as the state of being accompanied by roots is established for the roots within those states of consciousness that possess multiple roots, so too is the state of being material established for all earth and so forth;
thus he says, "The preceding... [etc. ...is not possible. For among them, there is no fixed state of being a transmigrator anywhere. [This concludes] the contemplation of impermanence.
Or, "the world" (loka) should be understood as that which breaks up, disintegrates, and perishes; for those supramundane states (lokuttara) that are devoid of such grasping, there is no "world-ness.
"By that very fact" means by way of being the truth of suffering and by way of being something to be fully understood (pariññeyya).

Why is it said, "a plurality of du-kas [sufferings] results"? Is it not the case that twenty du-kas have been analyzed? [The answer is: "Even though not explicitly stated, they are included according to what is available."
And since he will say, "it should be understood," is it not then intended that there is a plurality of *dukkhas*? True, this is so;
however, one who does not accept that very plurality of *dukkhas* speaks thus. Furthermore, a plurality of *dukkhas* follows from the classification of consciousness;

therein, from wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*), those associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*) [are distinguished], and likewise from great functional consciousness (*mahākiriyā*), mind-door adverting (*manodvārāvajjana*). It is in this manner that such types [of consciousness] [differ].

By the phrase "due to the multiplicity of pairs" (*dukkabahutā*) and so forth, he shows that [consciousness] is not all-pervasive because it does not touch upon consciousnesses that have all phenomena as their object.
Furthermore, showing the fault in its being non-pervasive, he says: "And thus... it would be," etc. And it is contradicted by the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), such as:

"Those phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness are not cognizable by ear-consciousness," and so on, [demonstrating] the distinctness of the sense-bases such as visible form (*rūpāyatana*) from the respective eye-consciousness and so forth.

By showing that [a phenomenon] is cognizable by some, such as ear-consciousness, and not cognizable by others, this statement—that "it is a dyad because of the difference in meaning between the two terms" according to the exposition of the *nikkheparāsi*—is contradicted;

likewise, it does not accord with the actual meaning even in the exposition of the extraction of meanings (*atthuddhāra*). "Therein" means in that commentary on the *nikkheparāsi*. And as for the negation...
The intention is to show how the dyads (duka) arise from the diversity of meaning. By the passage beginning with "For it is not the same...

and ending with "...to establish," he demonstrates that the occurrence of two dyadic terms within these sections of the Exposition (*niddesa*)—namely, "Those phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness are not those phenomena cognizable by ear-consciousness"—is understood directly from the Canon itself (*pāḷi*).

"Likewise" means that, because the two words "some" (keci) are used without restriction, it is shown by way of seeing that the phenomenon which has a distinct nature—such as eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness—is indeed the "object" (attha) through the conventional designation of its supports, namely the eye, ear, and so forth.

For the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) alone is said to be "cognizable by some and not cognizable by others," due to its being respectively cognizable and non-cognizable by eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness. If...
Having taken to heart the objection that "in this case as well, a plurality of dyads (duka) would result," he said, "But here there is not," and so forth.
"By way of the distinction of the cognizable" means by way of the specific difference of the cognizable; the meaning is: by way of a portion of what is to be known.

"Distinction of dyads" means a specific dyad, namely, a dyad cognizable by some [sense-faculty], or rather, a sub-division thereof. "Complete" means fully mastered, thoroughly acquired, and perfected. As many...
“Just as many [objects] are to be cognized, so many are the sufferings”: this shows the manner in which the classification of suffering is established.

With the words “And this being so,” etc., he demonstrates the merit gained by this commentary. Since it was stated that “those phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness are not cognizable by ear-consciousness,” and thus only the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is mentioned—there being no difference in their meaning—one might ask how this constitutes a dyad (*duka*). To this he replies: “By way of the diversity of consciousness,” and so forth.
But if there is only a brief summary in the inclusion of all that is cognizable, how is the exposition of the "sets of terms" (nikkheparāsi) to be understood?
To this he says, “But of this...,” and so forth.
Here, however, when the objects of cognition are divided according to the diversity of consciousness and expressed in pairs (duka), even though the objects of cognition [are many],...

Regarding their multiplicity: however many [factors] are to be known, there are not that many "dukkhas" (sufferings), because there is no plurality of suffering since the two terms "dukkha" are applied only to certain portions of the phenomena included within the category of suffering.

Thus, even when they are called "dukas" (pairs) due to the difference in meaning between the two terms, however many consciousnesses there may be, there are not that many "dukkhas," because there is no plurality of suffering... [as before] ...precisely because of the aforementioned state of affairs.
For it is not said that "by this or that" refers to only one single consciousness; rather, it refers to another as well.

Thus, in the inclusion of all consciousnesses, the dyad is completed, and there is no interruption of the dyad anywhere, because the objects of mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa) are distinct, just like those of the sense-faculties and their respective consciousnesses.
For a consciousness that has a past object does not have a future object, nor does one with a future object [have a past one].

Or [it may have] past and so forth as its object; therefore, it is impossible to prevent the occurrence of the two pairs of terms—“object” and “non-object”—in relation to each respective sense-field among the various types of mind-consciousness distinguished by their specific acquisitions.
For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary: “But as for the meaning that ‘some things are cognizable and some are not cognizable by mind-consciousness’...”

“It exists; therefore, even though it has not been mentioned, it should be understood according to what is available. Thus he will show it according to what is available by way of the distinction of planes.
As for the phrase “because of the absence of definition,” this too was stated taking only the generality of mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) without having grasped its specific distinctions.
However, it should be understood that the Pāḷi has come down showing the method by way of the sense-faculties and their respective consciousnesses.
And having done so, it is established that in this commentary on the meaning, the term "by anyone" (*kenaci*) is understood as an indefinite inclusion of all consciousness;

thus, there is no contradiction with the formal exposition (*niddesa*). The occurrence of the two pairs of terms is shown by way of being cognizable by the eye-consciousness and cognizable by the ear-consciousness, but not by way of being cognizable by the eye-consciousness and not cognizable by the eye-consciousness, because there is no distinguishing cause [in the latter case]. Furthermore, "those which... [and so forth].
Or rather, even from the combination of the other words, it is understood that by the extent of the statement, "Those states cognizable by the eye... [etc]...
those states are not cognizable by the eye," the occurrence of two pairs of terms (*duka*) is shown; for the word *vā pana* has the purpose of showing the existence of another term, just as in:
"Whatever states are wholesome, all those are wholesome roots; or else, whatever are wholesome roots..."
In such passages as “All those states are wholesome,” and so forth. Otherwise, the Canon would have read:

“Those states that are cognizable by the eye-consciousness are not cognizable by the ear-consciousness; those states that are cognizable by the ear-consciousness are not cognizable by the eye-consciousness.
As for what they say: “Those states that are cognizable by the eye-consciousness... [etc. ...are not cognizable by the eye-consciousness”—by this [statement]...

"The two pairs are stated in terms of meaning"—this too was said with reference to being cognizable by the eye and not cognizable by the eye, and being cognizable by the ear and not cognizable by the ear;
however, it should not be understood as "that which is cognizable by the eye but not by the ear" and "that which is cognizable by the ear but not by the eye.
By this, the rejection of the canonical text (pāḷi) should be seen as refuted, because there is no such rejection [in the text].
Likewise, when a certain object is spoken of as having the nature of cognizing, it is expressed by the word "by something" (*kenaci*) for the purpose of indicating non-restriction;
and when that very same object is spoken of as having the nature of not cognizing another thing, it is again expressed by the word "by something" for the purpose of indicating non-restriction.
Therefore, in demonstrating that meaning, the interpretation of the phrase "by that very [same thing]" (*teneva*) is not possible, and thus it cannot be maintained.
Thus, it should be understood that the meaning here is consistent with how the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) is established.

14–19. Because they cause the continuity of the stream (santāna) to become ignoble and defiled, and because they are impure due to being the cause for the ripening of dark kamma, it is said that "they flow with impurity.
Regarding the phrase "therein" (tattha), it refers to the wound. By the expression "the oozing... sound," the term *āsava* [is explained].
It should be understood that the meaning "like an outflow" (*āsava*) has also been shown here. Regarding the statement "The change-of-lineage... have been stated":
by this, the mention of "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhu*) is intended as an illustration, showing it is like the expression "butter is to be guarded from crows.

However, since there is a sense in which "change-of-lineage" means "that which resembles the change-of-lineage," and because things where a quality is the primary referent cannot be expressed by a single word [without qualification], only purification (*vodāna*) and the others were mentioned.
They would exist. Alternatively, it should be understood that this exposition is given by means of a collective singular (*ekasesa*) or a general term (*sāmañña*), namely "lineage" (*gotrabhū*).
Having transformed the case ending, it should be stated as "the limit (*avadhi*) which is the scope of pervasion (*abhividhi*).

"Accompanied by taints" (*āsavasahita*) means being accompanied by those taints through their associated states (*sampayutta*). This is what is meant: just as in the case of [states] possessing roots...

The state of being "with cause" (*sahetukatā*) is due to associated causes; it is not so with the states described as "with taints" (*sāsava*), for their state of being "with taints" is not through associated taints, but rather through dissociated ones.
Here, the fact that certain words were not stated in the other couplets is itself the method by which the application of the couplets is understood.
If this is so, why is it explained in the "Cluster of Causes" (*hetugocchaka*)? To this he says: "But in the Cluster of Causes," and so forth. In the first [verse]...
By adding the second [term] to the first dyad, he states the fourth dyad as "one. By adding the third [term] to the first dyad, he states the fifth dyad along with this:
"states that are both taints and dissociated from taints; and states that are dissociated from taints but are not taints.
By adding the second [term] to the first dyad, he states "one": "states that are not taints."
“Both with taints and without taints”—this is one. In the third [section], when the first is added, there are two: “Tainted phenomena are both associated with taints and dissociated from taints;
untainted phenomena are both associated with taints and dissociated from taints”—these are the two.
In the third [section], when the second is added, there is one: “Phenomena with taints are both associated with taints and dissociated from taints.”
One. When the second is added to the third, there is one; thus he states the sixth dyad. "By three" means by the fourth, fifth, and sixth.

"The others" refers to the five remaining. Of these, however, in the first case, when the second term of the third dyad is added, there is one; in the second case, when the second term of the first dyad is added, there is one;
in the third case, when each individual term of the first [dyad] is added, there are two; and in the third [case],...
In the first part of the second dyad, it should be understood as follows: "One [is] thus. This applies even to these: "Dhammas with taints (sāsavā) are both taints and not taints;

dhammas associated with taints are both taints and not taints; dhammas dissociated from taints are both taints and not taints," as well as to those such as "dhammas accompanied by taints" and "dhammas not accompanied by taints," when they are not included [in the definition].
The reason and the method of inclusion should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

"This method" means that this very approach—which was explained here in the group on the taints (*āsava*) starting with the insertion of the second dyad into the first dyad—is the method for determining the intermediate dyads in the groups on the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.
Among those, the dyads not found in the Pāḷi text are as follows:
In the *Saṃyojana-gocchaka* (Cluster of Fetters), first: "States that are both fetters and dissociated from fetters;
states that are dissociated from fetters but are not fetters; states that are fetters and are both associated with and dissociated from fetters;
states that are not fetters and are both associated with and dissociated from fetters. [End of] states that are not fetters.
“States that are conducive to fetters and states that are not conducive to fetters; states conducive to fetters are both associated with fetters and dissociated from fetters”—thus there are five.
In the same way, there are five each in the groups of knots (*gantha*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and clingings (*upādāna*).

However, in the group of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), because there is no state of being dissociated from the hindrances for the hindrances themselves, it is said: “States that are not hindrances are both conducive to hindrances and not conducive to hindrances.”
“Neither hindrances nor states associated with hindrances, yet states that are subject to hindrance may be either associated with hindrances or dissociated from hindrances”—thus there are three.
Likewise, in the Cluster on Misapprehensions: “Neither misapprehensions nor states misapprehended, yet states that are not misapprehensions may be either misapprehended or not misapprehended;

neither misapprehensions nor states misapprehended, yet states that are not misapprehensions may be either associated with misapprehension or dissociated from misapprehension”; [and] “states that are misapprehended...”
“Dhammas are both associated with perversions and dissociated from perversions. In the *Kilesagocchaka* (Cluster on Defilements):

“There are dhammas that are not defilements but are either subject to defilement (*saṃkilesika*) or not subject to defilement (*asaṃkilesika*); there are dhammas that are not defilements but are either defiled (*saṃkiliṭṭha*) or undefiled (*asaṃkiliṭṭha*);

there are dhammas that are not defilements but are either associated with defilements (*kilesasampayutta*) or dissociated from defilements (*kilesavippayutta*). Dhammas that are subject to defilement are either defiled or undefiled.”

"Defiled phenomena (*saṃkilesika-dhammā*) are both associated with defilements (*kilesa-sampayutta*) and dissociated from defilements (*kilesa-vippayutta*); non-defiled phenomena (*asaṃkiliṭṭha-dhammā*) are both defiled and non-defiled"—thus should the six dyads be understood.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated. (20–25) "By way of being a condition" demonstrates the sense of fetter (*saṃyojana*).
For it is precisely their respective status as conditions that constitutes the nature of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and the other [fetters].
“Fetters of the round” (*vaṭṭasaṃyojana*). If this is so, how is it that only sensual lust and the others have the status of fetters? To this he says: “Even though,” and so forth.

“Of others” means of other defilements, volitional formations, and so on, apart from the fetters themselves. “In their state of being conditions” means in their state of being conditions for those rounds of defilement, karma, and result.
“Included and delimited by way of being lower-bound and higher-bound” means included (*saṅgahitā*)—that is, delimited—by way of being lower-bound (*orambhāgiya*) and higher-bound (*uddhambhāgiya*).

“By those [fetters] such as sensual lust (kāmarāga), which serve as specific conditions”: having established that there is a fixed rule even regarding the production of the existence of rebirth in the sense-sphere (kāmūpapattibhava) and so forth from the karma-existence (kammabhava) and so forth of the sense-sphere, he says, “that respective... arises.

Having thus shown the presence of the karma-existences and rebirth-existences as previously described rules when the fetters (saṃyojana) are present, he says “and not... and so forth, showing their absence when those [fetters] are absent.
"Binding" means making one a slave, such as by shackles and the like. "Tying with knots" means making something cut off or severed.

A "circular ring" is a circle of rope used for wiping the feet. "It should not be urged" refers to the credibility of the aforementioned distinction, because it cannot be perceived by the wisdom-eye of ordinary people. For the meaning is threefold; some...

That which is established by direct perception (*paccakkhasiddha*) is the personally experienced, indefinable mode of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), which is said to be the characteristic of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāvalakkhaṇa*) of all phenomena.

Some [modes] are established by inference (*anumānasiddha*), such as the impermanence and other modes of pots, cloths, and so forth, which are known through their dependence on conditions as established in the cases of pots and cloths. Some are established by conviction (*okappanasiddha*), which...
Heaven, Nibbāna, and so forth, are objects of faith that are absolutely unseen by ordinary people.

In this regard, since the word of a Teacher does not deceive one concerning matters established through direct perception or inference—because it functions without error—the matters to be believed are established by his word;
and such is the Blessed One. Thus: "The intrinsic nature of phenomena... [and so on].
It is stated, "one should not urge [them]. This same method applies to subsequent instances of this kind as well. 26–37.

Just as a mountain range is to be crossed by means of *sarabhas*, so too the word-derivation (*saddasiddhi*) for *oghaniya* is established in the same way; thus he said, "by that," and so forth. 50–54. Grasping erroneously is "misapprehension" (*parāmasana*).

Regarding the term "the other" (*parato*), what is intended here is not merely being otherwise than the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), but rather its opposite; thus he said, "from the 'other,' i.e., from permanence and so forth."
55–68. If [the object] does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), how can it have the status of an objective support (*ārammaṇa*)? To this he says:

"It is designated as such by means of variegated perception (*vicittasaññā*)," the meaning being that it is established merely through conceptual construction (*parikappa*). Because their diversity is difficult to discern, they reach a state of continuity; thus it is said:

"Because their diversity is easily discerned, there is no state of being mixed (*saṃsaṭṭha*). "Of these" refers to those immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*). "By the others" refers to material form and Nibbāna.

But what is the reason that mutual association is stated only for immaterial phenomena—which arise and cease together and constitute a single group—and not likewise for material phenomena, even though they are of the same nature? To this he says: "For this is their intrinsic nature.

By this it is meant that although some immaterial phenomena may have separate objects, it is only because of the sluggishness of the occurrence of material phenomena [that such association is not predicated of them].

This shows that while the state of being conjoined and the absence thereof for those [material phenomena] is established by their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), this is not the case for immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).
Alternatively, because they are more difficult to distinguish due to their massed-togetherness (*samūhaghanatā*), immaterial phenomena do not exist as separate objects;
thus, their state of being conjoined is difficult to discern. This is because they function in dependence on those [material phenomena] without ever relinquishing them.
Because it is to be grasped by the intellect. 83–100.

Sensual craving is "kāma" through the elision of the latter member of the compound, just as "form-existence" (rūpabhava) is called "form" (rūpa). The same applies to the remaining [types of craving]. By the phrase "by way of making an object," this indicates that the state of being objects for sensual, fine-material, and immaterial craving is, respectively, the cause for their belonging to the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial spheres.
[The author] shows this. Indeed, it must necessarily be accepted in this way; otherwise, the status of [the planes] such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) would have an incomplete scope.

For if the delimitation of the planes were by way of the phenomena to be taken as objects (ālambitabbadhamma), then in that case there would be no inclusion of those things which are without an object (anārammaṇa).

If, on the other hand, it were by way of the giving of result (vipākadāna), even so there would be no inclusion of those things which do not give result (avipāka). Therefore, it is by way of making into an object (ārammaṇakaraṇa) [that the delimitation is established].

The delimitation of the planes for those states included within the mundane must be made; for if this is done, the status of being "belonging to the sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) and so forth will have its full range of objects.

That is why he said, "For if this is so," and so on. As for those states not included [within the mundane], because they have transcended the world, they possess the status of the "supreme plane" (anuttarabhūmi).

By stating that they do not fall into the category of "not belonging to the sense-sphere" and so forth, he avoids the fault of non-pervasiveness (abyāpitadosa); and by stating that they do not fall into the category of "belonging to the sense-sphere" and so forth, [he avoids the fault of over-extension].

The fault of being over-extensive (*ativyāpita-dosa*). But [one might object]: "In this position, what is sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*)? It is craving that has sense-sphere phenomena as its object. And what are the sense-sphere phenomena?
They are those things that are the objects of sensual craving. Thus, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itarītara-nissayatā*). [Response:

No, because by taking any craving whatsoever—whether it inclines toward the eleven realms such as the Avīci hell and so forth—as being of the nature of sensual craving, one grasps it as an object for that which possesses that same intrinsic nature.
Because the phenomena of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-dhamma) are to be characterized.
Now, supporting the aforementioned meaning with the text, he says: "In the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* as well," and so forth.

For therein, because they are to be taken as objects by sensual craving (*kāmatanha*), the phenomena included within the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) are submerged in the "sensual" (*kāma*) known as sensual existence (*kāmabhava*).
"Having offered, they perform [the rite], not otherwise"—here it is said "they range within.
To show this meaning—that a distinction is applied by one who seeks a distinction—he said: "Because of the determination of being included according to the world (*loka*).

By this, he shows that the word *pariyāpanna* (included) is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) for mundane phenomena (*lokīya-dhamma*), following the Blessed One’s utterance of it for those to be trained (*vineyya*).
Because it is the practice for that purpose. "Delimitation" is so called because it depends on a delimiting agent;
thus it is said, "by craving which acts as the delimiting agent. For that [craving] delimits the state of phenomena as belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.

Furthermore, here the prefix *pari-* should be understood to indicate an action together with its instrument, just as the prefix *upa-* does in words such as *upādinnā*; this is the meaning stated here.

They are "leading out" (niyyānika) because their nature is to lead out, just as one who has the habit of eating cakes is called a "cake-eater" (āpūpika); or rather, they are simply those whose nature is leading out.

It is understood that only lust, hatred, and delusion are included [here], for otherwise the statement regarding their being "conjoined with what is to be abandoned" (pahānekaṭṭha) would be purposeless.
In such passages as, "The moon, the sun, and the stars do not shine when struck by dust (raṇa)," the word *raṇa* should be seen as a synonym for *reṇu* (dust).
Because the word *sampahāra* (conflict) implies striking, and because that which is struck is the object of the strike, it is the unwholesome army itself that is called "the refuge" (*saraṇā*).
Regarding "of suffering, etc.": this refers to suffering, vexation, and feverish distress as effects, as well as to the corresponding wrong practice.
By the phrase "of the unwholesome states whose nature is to produce those [effects]," he shows that all unwholesome states constitute a refuge.
The commentary on the word-list of the *Duka-mātikā* of the *Abhidhamma* is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the word-list of the *Duka-mātikā* of the *Suttanta*, sections 101–108.
[They are so called] because of their commonality with true knowledge (*vijjā*), since they assist true knowledge, unlike resolve and the other [mental factors]. “Indivisible... [etc.]”
The statement “it grows again” is said with reference specifically to abandonment without remainder.

For although the defilements abandoned by the lower paths are indeed abandoned without remainder according to their respective categories, those remaining to be severed appear as if they have grown again due to their common nature as defilements such as greed (*lobha*). However, when the path of Arahantship has arisen...

It is not so, because nothing remains [of the defilements]. By way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), that is, by way of conventional expression regarding their support (*nissaya*). Or, "to be heated" (*tapaniya*) means they are to be tormented by wholesome states;

the meaning is that they are to be afflicted and abandoned by means of the "penetration of its constituent parts" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth. Terms such as "designation" (*adhivacana*) have identical meanings because they possess the nature of being enumerations (*saṅkhā*) and so on.
According to such passages as "All phenomena are the paths of designation," there is no phenomenon whatsoever that does not fall within the objective domain of designations and the rest.
With the intention that the very state of being speech is appropriate for designations (*adhivacana*) and so forth according to the method to be explained, he said:
"And all speech partakes of the state of being a designation, etc. (109–118).
The sense of "name-making" (*nāmakaraṇa*) is the nature of making a name for itself by its own power, without depending on anything else; by that—

In order to dispel the suspicion that earth and the other [elements] might also possess the status of "name" (nāma) simply by virtue of being called "spontaneously born" (opapātika), just as non-material phenomena (arūpadhamma) do, he said:

"because they do not incur another name. For non-material phenomena are not designated as a collective entity by some name other than those such as "feeling" (vedanā) and so on—just as material phenomena are designated by names such as "hair"—without the names "earth" and so forth. As for that which...

When one gives a name to another, that act of naming is dependent on another; thus, because it lacks the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of being an act of naming, it does not follow that the common names and so forth which are given possess the status of being "names.

Furthermore, for that person to whom a name is given by others, there is likewise an absence of the intrinsic nature of being an act of naming; therefore, they do not possess the status of being "names.
However, those things which have not yet received an external name and whose names are established by their own intrinsic nature—those [do possess the status of being names].
Showing that feeling and the rest alone constitute "name" (nāma), he said, "by itself," and so forth.
To show that the orientation of contact and the other factors toward an object is simply their non-arising in the absence of that [name], it was stated, "because of inseparability" (avinābhāvato).
Designation-contact (adhivacana-saṃphassa) is mind-contact; it is made manifest by way of illustration because it cannot be apprehended apart from name.
This has been stated. The phrase "by way of the nature of being affected" (ruppanasabhāvena) should be regarded as a mere illustration;

for material phenomena (rūpadhammā) are manifest even without a name, by way of the relationship between the manifester and the manifested. Alternatively, the relationship between the manifester and the manifested—that is, the subject-object relationship—is the specific nature (sabhāva) of the eye, visible forms, and so forth;
this should be understood as being included within the general nature of being affected.

119–123. From the passage beginning "The preliminary work prior to this," it appears as if mastery in attaining meditative absorption (*samāpatti-kusala*)—just like mastery in emerging from absorption—is possessed only by those who have attained the *jhānas*.

However, they say: "Even for others, the wisdom that delimits the absorption (*appanā-pariccheda-paññā*) of attainments is obtained by way of hearsay (*anussava*). Thus, one enters absorption through the purification of virtue and so forth.
Some say: "The wisdom that knows [the object] together with its preliminary work is the wisdom that knows the delimitation of absorption. Skillfulness in emerging is mastery over emergence.
"In the past" means prior to entering [absorption].
Regarding "delighting in what is beautiful," one who delights in what is beautiful is *surata*; the state of such a person is *soracca*. Thus he said: "Delight in beautiful action."
"Goodly" (*suṭṭhu*) means well-restrained; "gentle" (*sorata*) means one who is well-restrained, and the state of being so is "gentleness" (*soracca*).

This meaning, however, has already been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Lack of reflection is delusion (*moha*). The cultivation of the wholesome is the increase of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).

A sign (*saññāṇa*) is a distinguishing mark. "With its apprehension" (*saviggaha*) means with its image (*sabimbaka*). It refers to a class of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) that possesses the form to be distinguished, or else it refers to the object (*ārammaṇa*).

Non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is the opposite of mental distraction (*cittavikkhepa*). For, by way of being the direct antithesis and by emerging through abandonment, non-distraction rejects distraction and does not allow it to proceed. 135–142.

The morality of the cause (*kāraṇasīla*) is mundane (*lokiya*); the morality of the fruit (*phalasīla*) is supramundane (*lokuttara*), considering that [the former] is accomplished by means of the latter; thus, even mundane [morality...]
Or rather, the relationship between virtue as cause and its fruit should be understood through their temporal sequence (of preceding and succeeding).

"Of one who has perfected" means of one whose collection is complete. "Unwholesome virtues" refers to unwholesome modes of conduct. "Perfection of virtue" means the attainment of virtue or the qualities of virtue.
When it is said that "shame is accompanied by knowledge," this expresses that shame is dominated by knowledge, and not merely that knowledge is accompanied by shame. Not...

For there is indeed knowledge devoid of shame and fear. Inclination (*adhimuttatā*) is a state of proceeding without apprehension due to delight. Escape (*nissaṭatā*) is dissociation (*visaṃyuttatā*).

Here, by the expressions "inclination" and "escape," he shows that the two liberations—which are synonyms for those two respectively—are stated here as "liberation" (*vimutti*) by means of the method of mentioning one of a pair (*ekasesanaya*). For it has been said: "And the inclination of the mind..."
"And Nibbāna. "Arising" (*uppāda*) means that by means of this [path], there is arising; "non-arising" (*anuppāda*) means the absence of arising.

It should be understood that at the conclusion of non-arising—that is, at the moment of liberation which is the culmination of non-arising, or at the conclusion of the non-arising of defilements through the Noble Path—the noble fruit itself is characterized by its specific state and its result.
The commentary on the *mātikā* headings is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the analysis of the terms for wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala-padabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā*):
[the phrase] "to bring about" means to lead to absorption (*appanā*). By the non-statement of the analysis of the terms, there is an exclusion of absorption.
Having established [the point], while stating the reason for not providing a word-by-word commentary (*padabhājaniya*), he says, "By its own form," and so forth.
Therein, in phrases such as "contact exists" (*phasso hoti*), the word *hoti* is stated with the intention that it is synonymous with the word *atthi*; thus it is said, "by the second word *hoti*.

Having previously explained this according to the intention of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is now demonstrated that the aforementioned passage of the Canon (*Pāḷi*) is consistent with that [intention].
Showing his own intention, he said, "In brief," and so forth.

The phrase "desiring to know" is stated to show that the characteristic is the object of the inquiry. "By whatever means" refers either to that which is endowed with specific qualities such as seeing, or otherwise.
For the specific states of knowledge consist of seeing, weighing, and investigating. He says [this] regarding the phrases "not seen," and so on.

It should be applied; and in all cases, it is the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). That which is "additional" (*adhika*) here is this. "That by which what has not been seen is illuminated" (*adiṭṭhaṃ jotīyati etāya*);

"that by which what has been seen is harmonized" (*diṭṭhaṃ saṃsandati etāya*)—thus it is "the harmonization of the seen" (*diṭṭhasaṃsandana*). "That by which doubt is cut off" (*vimatiṃ chindati etāya*)—thus it is "the cutting off of doubt" (*vimaticchedana*).
The literal meaning (*saddattha*) of these [terms] has been shown by way of method (*naya*); but as for their meaning (*atthato*), all of them likewise proceed...
It should be understood as either the word itself or the arising of consciousness that produces it.
"Pabheda" means differentiation or distinction; [it is] by way of that differentiation. Regarding "the teaching of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ desanā*):

although this is indeed an exposition (*niddesa*) because it encompasses every possible differentiation by way of occasion, plane, class, object, intrinsic nature, and so forth, [it is still called a teaching].

Although it would be appropriate to speak [of all categories], nevertheless, here the "classification" (pabheda) intended is specifically that which is comprised by the terms of the Matika beginning with the wholesome (kusala), etc.;
thus it is said: "He gave the teaching on the classification... etc. For this very reason, the Commentary says: "Having illustrated the wholesome...
etc., [it says] 'there is contact'... etc., 'there is non-distraction. And by such statements as "contact is touching," it is precisely those things possessing classification that are emphasized.
