“Niddiṭṭhā” (pointed out) means that while [the categories] have been explained, they have not been stated as a formal matrix (mātikā); thus, “niddesa” is the demonstration of that which possesses such divisions.
With the words “This is what is meant,” etc., he states the summarized meaning of the sentence: “for the purpose of demonstrating the divisions...”.
If only the phenomena (dhammā) themselves were to be asked about and answered, why is there the statement of the division, namely “wholesome” (kusala)? To this he says: “But those...,” and so forth.
For there are no possessors of distinctions without the distinctions themselves.

By the statement "these states are wholesome," the wholesomeness of those states that were listed and defined by such expressions as "there is contact" and "contact is touching," etc., has been answered;
it is with this intention that he said, "even in the answer 'these states are wholesome. In the phrase "for in this [answer]," the word *hi* (for) is used.
The meaning is "for the sake of the cause. Therefore, the construction is as follows: "Since only phenomena (dhammas) are to be taught, and since those—beginning with the wholesome...
[and so on]... must be taught according to their divisions, therefore [it is said]. By the phrase "of phenomena alone," he demonstrates the result of the restriction [implied by the word "alone"].

By the word "and" in the phrase "and of meanings," he includes both the natural linguistic expressions such as "contact is touching" and so forth, as well as the knowledge of the aforementioned phenomena and so on.
“Itikattabbatā” (the state of being thus-to-be-done) is the state of being to be performed in such and such a manner, [expressed as] “Thus indeed this is to be set in motion and to be withdrawn.
It is “yutto” (joined) by means of that; the meaning is “of that which is to be performed. The intention is that because it is a qualification, there is a distinction.
Since that which is to be qualified is joined with “itikattabbatā,” the enumeration (uddesa) has the dhamma as its primary focus; therefore, therein, of the dhamma—

Because they must be qualified [by the term "wholesome"], this sequence of words, “wholesome states” (*kusalā dhammā*), has been established. The question is characterized by doubt, as it must be put forward for the purpose of determining what is not yet desired.
Therefore, even though all doubts and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have been eradicated regarding all phenomena, the question is formulated as if directed toward those who are still in doubt;
having projected onto oneself the state of doubt belonging to the person to whom the teaching is addressed, it proceeds as if one were oneself possessed of doubt.

[The author] shows this: Just as there is a distinction such as that of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth, the distinction of wholesome (kusala) and so forth is fixed by way of their being phenomena (dhamma).
Therefore, when the term "phenomena" (dhammā) is mentioned, because there is no certainty [as to which specific type], doubt arises as to whether they are "wholesome or unwholesome," and so on;

thus he says, "But the distinction of wholesome and so forth is subject to doubt. However, the state of being a phenomenon (dhammabhāva) is indeed certain among the wholesome and others, because it is exclusive to them.

It is said: "And the state of being a phenomenon (dhamma-bhāva) is not doubted. By this, he shows that it is the state of wholesomeness (kusala-bhāva) that is primary here, insofar as it is the state to be determined when there is doubt, whereas the state of being a phenomenon is not so [primary]; thus they are called "wholesome phenomena" (dhammā kusalā).
"At the time of the arising of consciousness" (cittuppāda-samaye) means at the moment of the consciousness's arising. Regarding the word "atha" in the phrase "atha vijjamāne":
He states the meaning with the word “afterwards. Having shown the diversity of partial time-frames through examples such as eating and walking, he says “assemblages, etc.
to show the remaining diversity. By the term “distinguished,” he clarifies the meaning of the word “restricted”;

therefore, the sense is “from time distinguished by the aforementioned specific states of consciousness. The phrase “of those intended” refers to those associated with specific categories such as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and so forth.

"At that time": although the time is to be qualified by the arising of consciousness, it is that very consciousness which, while arising, itself becomes the qualifier of the time in the phrase "at which time.
Likewise, the consciousness that serves as the qualifier in the phrase "at that time" [is mentioned] for the purpose of assisting the time that is to be qualified by it, [in the phrase] "at which..."
It attains the state of being qualified as "at the time... [pe] ...the mind. Furthermore, "assistance" should be understood as the mutual relationship between the delimiting and the delimited.

The non-interruption and non-separation of the preceding and succeeding phenomena means that the arising of the subsequent phenomena occurs either simultaneously with the dissolution of the preceding phenomena or immediately after their dissolution;
it is the state of being uninterrupted by anything whatsoever. By virtue of which, through the predominance of the positive side...
Because the side of non-existence does not appear as if it were concealed, the common person perceives it through the grasping of "it is that very same thing," thereby becoming deluded;
this matter is made very clear by the example of a firebrand's circle (*alātacakka*). For this reason, he said, "as if they had become one.

The occurrence of things "as if they had become one" is due to their being gathered into a single mass; it is a state of dense aggregation resulting from the difficulty of discerning the distinctions between their functions.
The construction is: "the density of the mass of functions [arising] as if they were unified.

And here, it should be understood that for the many phenomena occurring in the state of condition and conditioned, their individual distinctions are difficult to discern by way of time, intrinsic nature, function, and object;
thus, they are to be grasped as if unified, which constitutes, respectively, the density of the continuity (*santati*) and so forth.

"Samaya" means "coming together" (*sameti*) with the presence of cooperative causes; thus, showing that the word *samaya* has the sense of "conjunction" (*samavāya*), he said "the completeness of conditions" (*paccayasāmaggi*).
It is called "samaya" because the holy life of the path comes together (*sameti*) or meets (*samāgacchati*) here with the persons who are its support;

thus it is a "moment" (*khaṇa*). Alternatively, it is so called because phenomena come together (*samenti*) or meet (*samāgacchanti*) here, or by means of this [moment], with co-nascent phenomena such as arising and so forth.

The time has come; it is the moment. For although time does not exist as a substantial entity apart from the mere occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*), it is nevertheless designated by way of a form established through mere conceptualization, functioning as the locus or the instrument for the occurrence of phenomena.
"Samaya" means the going (*ayana*), proceeding, or persisting of parts together (*sama*) or simultaneously (*saha*); it is a collection, just as in the term "samudāya."
A collection (*samūha*) is indeed the abiding together of parts (*avayava*). A condition (*samaya*) is so called because the fruit comes (*eti*) from the meeting of various conditions;

it arises and proceeds from this, thus it is a cause, as in the term "origination" (*samudaya*). Or, it is a "condition" because it brings together (*sameti*) and connects, proceeding within its own domain;

or, it is a "condition" because connections (*sambandhā*) go forth (*ayanti*) by means of it—this refers to a view (*diṭṭhi*). For by the fetter of views (*diṭṭhisaṃyojana*), sentient beings are bound exceedingly tight.

*Samaya* means meeting, conjunction, or attainment; it is acquisition. It is *samaya* because it is the vehicle (*yāna*) to cessation (*sama*), or because it is the correct (*sammā*) departure and non-occurrence; thus, it is abandonment.

*Abhisamaya* is the unerring intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) that is to be approached correctly through direct confrontation, to be fully realized, and to be attained. Alternatively, one correctly goes toward or proceeds toward it through direct confrontation.
"Becoming enlightened" (*bujjhati*) means "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*); it is the unerring comprehension of the true nature of phenomena (*dhammā*) without deviation.
And here, because prefixes are merely indicators, the word *samaya* alone is the designator of each respective meaning; thus, it is spoken of even with its prefix.
"Those very same" refers to oppression and so forth. "Expansion" is the accomplishment of exertion in activities through the state of being masterful.
"In some" refers to unwholesome resultant states and so forth. Because there is no possibility of a moment [of existence] without that [condition], he said "Is it not," and so on.

"By the phenomenon itself" means by that which is devoid of any other distinction. For by that very restriction, he shows the excluded distinction with the words "its occurrence did not take place," and so forth.
"In whatever way or in that way" means that the world proceeds and ceases according to time.

Or "time" (kāla) is a real entity (bhāva) characterized by continuous succession, or that which provides the occasion for the occurrence of phenomena—this is according to whichever mode [of explanation].

Here, since there is simply no arising from a supreme cause (uttamahetu), he negates only the "cause-cause" (hetu-hetu) and the "common cause" (sādhāraṇa-hetu). "Conditionality by that" (tappaccayatam) means conditionality by many [causes].

The mention of the doctrine of the Primordial Nature (pakati) and the Lord (issara) should be regarded as merely illustrative; the doctrines of the Progenitor (pajāpati), the Person (purisa), Time (kāla), and so forth, are also included.
“Ekakāraṇavādo” (the doctrine of a single cause). By the word *vā* (or), their inclusion should also be understood.

The term *dāya* (collection) is stated by way of its constituent parts (*avayava*), because a whole (*samudāya*) may be designated by means of its component properties, just as in the expressions “powder is even” or “Devadatta is adorned.
*Anipphādanaṃ* is the absence of production; it is the state of being without a cause. However, for that which is incapable of producing [an effect], there are other conditions...
Even when a thousand [conditions] have come together, there is no capacity at all; thus he said, "of that which has the capacity for production.

And here, since the production of the fruit by the conditioning factors (paccayadhamma) depends upon cooperative causes (sahakārīkāraṇa), it is said that they are mutually expectant (aññamaññāpekkhā);
therefore, "expectancy" (apekkhā) should be understood as being like mutual expectation.
"In those who are inactive and unoccupied. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, [the phrase] "one by one" (*eka-ekasmiṃ*) indicates that the reduplicated expression has been shown as elided.

Furthermore, when there is a reduplication, plurality is established. Regarding the statement "a hundred blind men see," the nominative case (*paccattavacana*) is transformed into the locative case for the purpose of specification (*niddhāraṇe*), and thus he says "among a hundred blind men" (*andhasate*).
Likewise, by means of this [phrase] "one by one," it is distinguished separately.
He says, "The meaning 'a hundred blind people see' results in the sense that they see collectively;
thus, the intended meaning is 'a hundred blind people see together. "Otherwise" means when the meaning is grasped according to the literal expression.

Since [the capacity for seeing] is established in cases such as carrying a palanquin and so forth through the power of combination (*asāmaggi*), this [literal] meaning cannot be proven. Now, regarding that meaning...
Showing that [the moment] need not be established by means of its being very evident, he said, "separately," and so forth.
By this method: this refers to the time defined as a moment (*khaṇa*), which illustrates the rarity of the arising of wholesome states.
Regarding the phrase "due to its own rarity": here the word *samaya* has the sense of a moment; thus the meaning stated is "the time defined as a moment."
"By this which is the means and the method": here the construction is as follows—[the word] *samavāya*... [etc. ...
"illustrates the occurrence (*vutti*) because it itself is the state of the completeness of conditions. Alternatively, the word *samaya* has the sense of "coincidence" (*samavāya*);
that is, the *samaya* known as coincidence. It [is used] by way of explaining the meaning of the phrase "when there is such a completeness of conditions" for phenomena (*dhammānaṃ*).
It illustrates occurrence from multiple causes. It illustrates time... [etc. ...it illustrates limitation because of its own extreme limitation.
It illustrates simultaneous arising because it itself is a collective state of phenomena.
It illustrates occurrence because, only when it exists, do its own fruits come to be. And in both the sense-side and the word-side, that which is extremely limited—

In whatever time, within whatever collection of phenomena, and when whatever cause exists—by way of making known this meaning, it illustrates the difficulty of penetration, the simultaneous arising of many [factors], and the state of dependence upon others for the occurrence of wholesome states, which are supported by and dependent upon that [cause].
"Firm-bowed archers" refers to archers with strong bows. A "strong bow" is said to have a strength of two thousand [pounds].

"Having the strength of two thousand" means that when a bowstring is drawn with a force equal to two thousand [units], the load of iron balls and so forth attached to it is released from the ground once it has been lifted by the handle to the height of a *kaṇḍa*.
"Trained" means having mastered their craft in the teacher’s household for ten or twelve years.
"Skilled" means having attained mastery (*vasībhāva*) in archery. Some merely learn the craft, while others become skilled.
This shows that these [other things] are not like that. "Those who have displayed their craft" means those who have exhibited their skills among royal families and the like.
"They would stand facing the four quarters" means they would stand in one and the same place, leaning against a single pillar or tree, facing toward all four directions;
such is the meaning. "Of the swift man thus described" means there is no man of such a kind.
This has never happened before, except in the case of a Bodhisatta. For he did such a thing while he was a swift swan.
However, in the Sutta, this is merely brought forward as a simile by way of an imaginative supposition.

"Because its nature consists in that" means because its nature is exclusively occupied with illustrating the dependence of the time designated as the cause upon something else. As for those who say "its nature consists in that":

They recite [the text]; for them, because it illustrates dependence on conditions (*paccaya*), the state of being "intent upon that" (*tapparabhāva*) belongs to the time-period (*samaya*) reckoned as a cause.

Therefore, the construction is: "therefore, its state of illustrating dependence on another is stated. Regarding the phrase "because of not being intent upon that": when one is intent upon illustrating dependence on the whole (*samudāya*), one is intent upon that;
but when one is intent upon illustrating dependence on a single part (*ekadesa*) of it, one is not intent upon that—hence he says, "because of not being intent upon that."

But is it not the case that time is merely a conventional designation (vohāramattaka) established in dependence upon this or that [phenomenon]? How then can it be the locus for the phenomena mentioned therein?

To this he says: "For time also... and so forth. If the characteristic of one action by another action is a "characteristic of a state by a state" (bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa), what then is the characterizing action here?
To this he says: "In this case also... and so forth. In the phrase "endowed with a state that serves as a characteristic," the word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

This is what is meant: because the time [samaya] is associated with the activity of characterization (lakkhaṇakiriyā) consisting of sentient beings, therefore it is the "Exposition of the Grounds" (bhūminiddesa) therein.

"From the summary" (uddānato): if the meaning is "in brief" (saṅkhepato). But surely, just like the remaining defilements and so forth, sensual desire as defilement (kilesakāma) is also included within sensual objects as basis (vatthukāma) because it is to be relished; and just as knowledge is included within the knowable, would not desire be one and the same in brief?

He says "the defilement of sensual desire" and so forth, with reference to the inquiry "might it be? "Of one who is possessed" means of one who is established in the relationship of object and subject.

Although all sensual desires were indicated by the summary statement "in brief, there are two kinds of sensual desire," nevertheless, because the object has been specified by the passage beginning "of the four states of deprivation," it is the lust for sensual pleasure that constitutes the lower-fettering defilement which is understood here as "the defilement of sensual desire."
He said, “By that,” and so forth. Not understanding his intention, the accuser interrogates him with the words, “Is it not the case that...?
The other, however, reveals his own intention with the words, “Of one whose defilements are abundant,” and so forth.
[This refers to] among sense-sphere phenomena—such as celestial palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, and the like—or among limited wholesome states and so on. And is it not the case that... “of the four”?
Is it not the case that because the term "apāyānaṃ" (of the states of misery) qualifies the object, the inclusion of the form and formless realms is impossible?

No; for in the statement "In brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures," all sensual pleasures have been taught without exception. Even though the entire collection of sensual pleasures has been taught, only a portion of it is taken up here;
to show this, he says "twofold," and so forth. Sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) is the lust directed toward the five strands of sensual pleasure. Craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).
Craving has as its object the phenomena of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Craving for cessation is lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi).

"Here" refers to the elevenfold plane. If "unremaindered occurrence" were intended, one could not say "this is twofold," because a portion of the objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma) does not occur here;
therefore, the meaning is either that it is "as if unremaindered" due to its predominance, or that it is "unremaindered" [in the sense of being complete].
Showing that [it] is to be grasped, he says, "The sensual object of the basis (*vatthukāma*) as well," and so forth.

And here, "likeness to being without remainder" refers to the complete absence of anything whatsoever that is distinct in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). And by doing it thus, the meaning is: because the sensual object of the defilements (*kilesakāma*) and the sensual object of the basis are distinguished by their state of being entirely complete and without remainder.
He shows that the shortening of the vowel in the word *cā* (in *kāmacchanda*) indicates that the sense of the agent of the cause (*hetukattuattha*) is inherent within the term *kāmāvacara*.

"Object" (*visaya*) means in the sense of a basis or a denotable referent. By the phrase "devoid of a sign" (*nimittaviraha*), he shows that in conventional expressions (*ruḷhi*) there is an action for the purpose of making a distinction, not an action directed toward oneself.
"The state of wholesomeness" (*kusalabhāva*) refers to the quality of being wholesome as described according to the discourses on the Jātaka, the Bāhitika-sutta, and the Abhidhamma.
"Of that" (*tassa*) refers to the state of having a pleasant result (*sukhavipākabhāva*). [This is said] because of the desire to explain its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).

By this, he shows that in the phrase "characterized by the ripening of blameless happiness" (*anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇaṃ*), the word "happiness" (*sukha*) is used as a synonym for "the desirable" (*iṭṭha*).

The functions of perception (*saññā*) and wisdom (*paññā*) are, respectively, the making of a sign (*sañjānanakaraṇa*) and penetration (*paṭivijjhanā*). The apprehension of an object devoid of both of these is what is expressed by the term "it cognizes" (*vijānāti*);
thus he says: "Perception... [and so on]... grasping. But is it not the case that its function is also distinguished from the functions of contact (*phassa*) and the rest?
"Is it *citta*? This is true; however, that distinction is not as difficult to understand as [the distinctions between] perception (*saññā*), wisdom (*paññā*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
Because it possesses characteristics distinguished by the functions of perception and wisdom, he states the characteristic of consciousness (*viññāṇa*).

That which occurs as the cause for the state of proficiency and strength in immediately preceding phenomena is said to "accumulate" (*cinoti*) the continuum. And such an occurrence constitutes the condition of repetition (*āsevana-paccaya*).
He said: "It accumulates by way of being a condition through repeated practice.
"Consisting of what is made by mind" means consisting of volitional formation-consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*).

Regarding the "determination of diversity and so forth," here "determination" (*vavatthāna*) should be applied to each term individually. Determination is delimitation, the state of non-confusion. And by that, the phenomenon (*dhamma*) is ascertained.
He said, "It is called 'ascertainment' (nicchitatā). Regarding "the diversity of gender-marks" (liṅganānattādi):

here, the diversity of gender-marks (liṅganānatta) is by way of the physical forms of female and male. There is a plurality of the female gender-mark according to the divisions of devas, humans, animals, and so forth; likewise for the male gender-mark.
Within each of these various classes of females—such as devas and others—there exists a mutual dissimilarity consisting of a diversity of individual bodies (nānattakāyatā).

The classification [of gender] should be understood by way of the distinctions such as place (*desa*) and so forth that differentiate specific qualities. Likewise, this applies to the male characteristic (*purisaliṅga*).

Alternatively, the diversity and other attributes of the characteristic should be applied based on the diversity and other factors of the karma that produces that characteristic, as previously described.

Because perception (*saññā*) and the other [mental factors] operate within the diversity of characteristics and so forth, there is a diversity and so forth of those [perceptions]. For this very reason, it was said: "For they are produced by the diversity and other factors of karma."
By showing the various distinctions of the baseless (apada), etc., the diversity of gender (liṅga-nānatta) is demonstrated.
And when that is shown, the diversity of perception (saññā-nānatta), and so forth, are likewise shown; thus he says, "The wheel of existence (bhavacakkra) turns," demonstrating this.

The female gender, male gender, and so on, are specific modes of arrangement of the aggregate of form (rūpa-khandha) as determined by consciousness (viññāṇa-adhiṭṭhita). By way of the head-term "perception" (saññā-sīsa), the four aggregates [are indicated].
Thus it was said. By this conventional expression, the occurrence of the five aggregates as that which is to be conventionally designated is illustrated.
Showing the meaning that this [occurrence] has craving, views, and dogmatic adherence as its causes, he said: "The signs, etc.… down to the end. [As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, whatever states are unwholesome and partake of the unwholesome, all those have mind as their forerunner"; "mind as their forerunner..."
Because of such statements as "states" (*dhammā*), it is said that "kamma has consciousness as its cause," for "kamma is produced from consciousness.
"According to the respective order" means that gender (*liṅga*) arises from kamma, and designation (*saññā*) arises from gender;

this is not like the previous alternative where both gender-designation and gender-designation arise from kamma, but rather by way of showing the occurrence of both from both. "They undergo differentiation..."
Because the distinction is specified as "this is a woman" or "this is a man," the state of being designated by way of femininity and so forth is here called "distinction";
thus it is said, "they undergo the designation of woman, man, and so forth. "By way of two time-periods" means by way of the two periods of past and present. Fame is the manifestation of qualities;
therefore he says, "of wide-spread fame. Because there is no cause for the production of various types of kamma apart from the performance of various types of kamma.
It is said: “…by those born of kamma… [and so on] …the distinction. A non-occasion for ripening (*avipaccanokāsa*) refers to an unsuitable state or the time of rebirth (*gatikāla*).

Here, it should be illustrated by the case where the volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) of the sense-sphere, having produced eye-consciousness and so forth in the form realm, does not produce a registration (*tadārammaṇa*) due to the absence of an occasion.
This is because only a certain type of mental production is intended, owing to the deficiency of the eye and other faculties.
The kamma-consciousness that does not produce eye-consciousness and so forth should be seen as being "unplunged" (anogadha) when deficient in other conditions.
That too is included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the procedure at the time of death, etc.

And here, [it should be understood that] "that which is deficient in its cooperative cause does not obtain any space for fruition at all, whereas the other obtains space for a portion of fruition; this is the difference between them."
When they say "diversity," it is stated with the intention that, provided there is the acquisition of a spatial location for the result (vipāka), there is no lack of auxiliary causes.
Let it be, then, that what has existed and then passed away is "passed away after having been" (bhūtāpagata); but how is it that what has passed away after being experienced is so called?

Thus he says, "experienced and become" (anubhūtabhūtā), and so forth. By that word "experienced" (anubhūta), whatever meaning is expressed, for that very meaning the word "become" (bhūta) alone [is used].
It shows that *vācaka* (denoter) is not the same as *anu-sadda* (the prefix *anu*); rather, the prefix *anu* is an indicator (*jotaka*).

For prefixes and particles are like the breaking of branches. And because prefixes possess multiple meanings, they "delimit" (*avacchedana*) the specific sense to be expressed by verbal roots precisely through their function of indicating that specific sense;
thus, whatever specific meanings are to be denoted by the verbal root, [the prefix] delimits them.
The commonality (*sāmañña*) is that which is without distinction; its stabilization in specific instances is nothing other than the illumination of each respective particularity.

Thus he said: "The commonality... is specified. Since the word *anubhūta* is most frequently seen in the sense of the object (*kamma*), he said "And the word *anubhūta*" and so forth, in order to show that it here expresses the sense of the agent (*kattṛ*). Even though [this is true] for all mental states (*cittuppāda*)...

In order to show that the intended meaning here is this: "the mode of experiencing an object through the mental formation of consciousness proceeding within a continuum that is subject to perversion (vipallāsa), which—due to its state of being accompanied by feeling—is distinguished from the indeterminate (abyākata) and is preeminent among the wholesome and unwholesome," he said, "according to the intention of what is to be said.
[This is] by way of the intention of expressing the state of having departed from the primary elements (bhūta).
He states the means of attracting the wholesome and the unwholesome.
It is called "arisen" (*uppātita*) because it is similar to what has already arisen, in that it accomplishes its function as if it had already emerged.
He provides the reason for using the word "arisen" (*uppanna*) even for that which has not yet occurred, stating that it has "begun to arise. And here, by way of passion and so forth—

The experience of the flavor of the object (*ārammaṇarasa*) is preeminent; thus, both the unwholesome and the wholesome, having arisen and ceased, are said to be "devoid of the existent" (*bhūtāpagata*) by virtue of their commonality in having ceased.
However, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated: "It has that as its object by way of experiencing the result (*vipāka*).
And kamma is [said to be devoid of the existent] merely by virtue of having become and then passed away, because the result has not yet ripened and is therefore entirely non-existent."

"It is said to be 'devoid of beings' (*bhūtāpagata*). For that very reason, it is stated there that "arisen by way of providing space" refers specifically to *vipāka* (karmic result). But here, it refers to *kamma* as well.
The aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*) are called "planes" (*bhūmi*) because the collection of defilements (*kilesajāta*) exists therein by way of taking them as objects (*ārammaṇakaraṇa*).
He shows the means for designating it as "having attained the plane" (*bhūmiladdha*), as if fire had been taken up. By this [means], it is *kamma*. Of this...
It should be understood that "the result has been stated.
"Because it is not suppressed" means because it is not dispelled. "In its own plane" means in its own level. "Having severed" means not allowing it to arise again.
It is said that "having entered into a portion of the three moments" means having entered into the three moments; this refers to the example already mentioned.

He states the sense of figurative usage (*upacāra*). By this, he shows that the example "arisen phenomena are present phenomena" is appropriate here. "By means of the primary" means by way of being the principal factor.

"Mind is the forerunner of the teaching" shows that when mundane phenomena are to be taught, it is the custom for the Blessed One to teach having made the mind the forerunner. Or, it refers to the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.
This shows that the nature of mundane phenomena (*lokiyadhammā*) is such that they are preceded by mind and have mind as their chief;
thus he states the reason for teaching them in that manner, meaning that all unwholesome phenomena (*akusaladhammā*) are "with the exception of mind" (*cittavajjā*).

The word "some" (*keci*) refers to the authors of the *pada* [verses]. By the particle "also" (*api*) in the phrase "contact and so forth" (*phassādayopi*), he includes greed and the other [defilements]. Even though there is no difference in time...
A phenomenon that is required as a condition is conventionally described as if it were already previously produced; thus he said, "as if arisen first.
To show its status as a precursor in its literal, non-figurative sense, he stated, "the immediate condition," and so forth.
Because of such statements as "The conduit to existence is destroyed," the mind associated with craving—which acts as that conduit—is called the "leader."
He said, "Or associated with craving.

Because it was defined as "the mental pleasure at that time," the feeling of joy (*somanassavedanā*) has the nature of being pleasant; thus he said, "It is stated by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
In its primary sense, the word "sweet" (*madhura*) refers to a specific taste, but [here it is used] by way of the commonality of being desirable.

It is said here that it is expressed by way of figurative usage (upacāra) when one says, “as if sweet. In the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is no delight-and-lust (nandirāga) or state of delight-and-lust apart from craving;
thus, while there is no state of being accompanied [by it] by way of association (sampayoga), it is nevertheless called “accompanied by delight-and-lust.
By this it is understood that the word “accompanied” (sahagata) illuminates the state of delight-and-lust within craving. It is a term denoting a particular state (avatthāvisesa).

Alternatively, the word *saha* (together with) is used here as in expressions such as *sanidassana* (“visible”), indicating that in all its states craving has not abandoned its essential nature of delight-and-lust;

thus craving is described as “accompanied by delight-and-lust” (*nandirāgasahagatā*). Or else, since the word *gata* (gone) carries no change in meaning—as in expressions such as *diṭṭhigata* (“gone into views”)—craving, which possesses the essential nature of delight-and-lust, is called “accompanied by delight-and-lust,” meaning it has the essential nature of delight-and-lust.

The meaning. "In this case as well" means in this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "In this word as well" means even in the word "accompanied by joy" (*somanassasahagata*). "This very meaning" means precisely "conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*).

"The word *saṃsaṭṭha* as it has been shown" refers to the word *saṃsaṭṭha* as it occurs in the commentary based on its appearance in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), following the incidental discussion of the extraction of the meaning.
"In 'co-nascent'" (*sahajāte*) means in the sense of being co-nascent (*sahajāta*).
Showing that the word *ābhata* (brought forth) is a verbal noun (*kamma-sādhana*) independent of temporal distinctions and is a synonym for "spoken," he says:

"The state of not being spoken is non-brought-forthness (*anābhaṭṭhatā*). "In the text" means in this commentary on the first arising of consciousness. "Precisely because it has not been spoken" means precisely because the state of being unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) has not been mentioned.
Because the word *vatthu* (basis) is used as a synonym for cause, by virtue of its general sense of being a condition, it refers also to those phenomena that serve as doors.

Thinking that there might be a figurative application (*pariyāya*) regarding the "basis" (*vatthu*), he said: "The 'door' is called the 'basis'. By this, he shows that it is called a "basis" because it is like a basis.
Since mental states that constitute the mind-door generally function together with the heart-basis, he said:

"...by way of the door... the heart-basis is mentioned," just as one says, "the spears are walking. "By way of its own function" means by way of its own specific activity, due to its being accompanied by that activity.
Or: "Not shared by others" explains the meaning of the word *sa*. For that which has its own essence (*rasa*) is "with-essence" (*saraso*).
Because consciousness has the immediately preceding consciousness as its cause, it is said to have a single origination;

because mental factors have the co-nascent consciousness and contact as their causes, they have a double origination. "Mental states originate from consciousness; touched, O monks, one feels; touched..."
For it is said: "He perceives; being touched, he cognizes.
By the phrase "subtle matter such as dust," he refers to subtle matter like pollen and the like. However, there is nothing at all to be said regarding the matter of an atom (*paramāṇu*).

By the expression "due to the smallness of the physical basis" (*vatthuparittatāya*), he indicates that many instances of the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) contained within numerous groups (*kalāpa*) have combined and function together through collective action, according to the principle of carrying a palanquin.
This shows that [the object] is the objective condition for eye-consciousness, and not just one or a few [atoms].
But if this is so, does it not follow that eye-consciousness has a composite (samudāya) as its object? It does not so follow, because the composite itself does not exist.
For there is no such thing as a "composite" in the ultimate sense (paramattha). Rather, it is simply the sphere of visible form (vaṇṇāyatana) as much as is situated in a suitable location.

When other conditions are present, that [object] becomes the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for eye-consciousness to that extent, according to the principle already stated, because of its non-conceptual nature.

However, as for the mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) directed toward that [object], which arises many times, it proceeds by way of a collective mode and by way of modes such as shape, etc., through the power of prior established conceptualization; so what [is there] for the eye-consciousness?

One should not raise the objection as to whether the visible-object base (*vaṇṇāyatana*) is a single object or many; for it is not appropriate to seek logical consistency regarding an object that is directly perceived.

Furthermore, because consciousness arises in many millions of instances within the duration of a finger-snap, due to the mind’s rapid turnover, even when the colors of a jar, a bowl, or similar objects are situated in a suitable location, [the mind perceives them all].
In accordance with a preceding act of attention (*manasikāra*), first one [object]—such as a "jar" or a "bowl"—is delimited by a single stream of mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa-santāna*);
subsequently, the other is delimited by a process of visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa-vīthi*) that has intervened.

However, because of a lack of discernment, there arises the conceptualization of non-difference in the cognition of the jar, bowl, and so forth. Such an objection here should be regarded as no objection at all.
"By the brevity of the moment" means by the shortness of the duration of the continuous series (*pabandha*).

For, according to the continuous series, individual material and immaterial phenomena—due to the conjunction of opposing and non-opposing conditions—cease either quickly or slowly; thus they are of short duration or long duration.

However, from the perspective of their intrinsic nature and characteristic (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*), they are each of a single unit of measure. And just as with the sense-sphere of visible form, so too...
The others as well: for sound and the rest are also obtained by way of the limitedness of their physical basis (*vatthu*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by way of being very near, etc.," the word "etc. includes such factors as the absence of adverting (*anāvajjana*) and being concealed by something.

Because it specifically binds (*sinoti*) or fetters (*bandhati*) the object-dhamma, it is called an "object" (*visaya*); thus he says, "the object is by way of not having another meaning," since there is no other state [for it].
For visual consciousness and the rest do not occur with respect to an object other than the sense-base of visible form and so forth. "Gocara" means that which cows graze upon;
it is like a pasture (*gocara*). He said, "It is a pasture because of wandering there," referring to the state of frequent movement.
For visible forms and the rest are generally grasped by visual consciousness and the others, whereas they are not grasped in that same way by mental consciousness.
"Of these" refers to the sense-spheres of visible form and so forth being apprehended by mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*).

Why was it said, "Because the statement is untenable"? Is it not the case that the statement, "he experiences their range and domain," is indeed tenable with reference to the element of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) occurring at the five doors? No, because there is no such restriction. For the mind is not necessarily brought [to the object] solely by the five doors.

Here, since there is a restrictive reason for stating "mind" (*mano*), it is precisely with this objection in mind that the inclusion of the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) and so forth was made.
Because of the statement beginning with "of such a color" (*evaṃvaṇṇo*), the knowledges of past lives, the past and future, and others are also possible here.
"Otherwise" means by way of [the categories] such as "form" (*rūpa*) and "sound" (*sadda*).
"By food... by enthusiasm, etc."—this is an indication of the conditions for that wieldiness (*kammaññatā*) by which the material body attains fitness.

For when food is properly digested, when the appropriate climate and food are utilized, and when physical and mental energy—which is termed "right application"—is exerted, the body becomes capable of action and conducive to all activities due to the presence of lightness and the other qualities.
Alternatively, the phrase "by means of food... [and] by means of enthusiasm, etc. is a statement of the causes for the body's affliction, just as it is for its well-being.
For from irregular eating, indigestion, and so forth, the bodily humors such as wind (vāta) arise, which cause affliction to the body.

The word *anuvattantassa* ("of one who conforms") should be understood in the sense of a causal factor (*hetu*), as in the phrases "victory breeds enmity" and so on; for [the following is] the sign of wakefulness.

Here, "conforming" (anuvattana) is intended. Alternatively, the phrase "of one who conforms" is a demonstration of the arising of bodily pleasure and so forth, which are produced by the healthiness and other qualities resulting from the objects coming into the range of the senses through their natural state as visible forms and so on, and through their status as decisive supports (upanissaya).

For one who does not conform to the healthiness of the body and so forth, because of the absence of the aforementioned decisive support and mental application (ābhoga), the aforementioned type [of suffering] occurs.
"May there be no coming into the range [of the object]. Just as adverting (*āvajjana*) is the fixing of the mind upon an experienced object such as a form, and the directing of the mind;

so too, with respect to what is similar, dissimilar, and related to that experienced form and so forth—namely, the seeing and so on of that which is similar, dissimilar, and related—the directing of the mind and the seeing and so on of the similar, dissimilar, and related... [etc.]... [are likewise].

And it should be connected thus: "the mind... [and so on]... seeing and the rest are those conditions. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "disturbance of the elements, etc.," one includes such things as the intervention of deities.
"Similarity to that" means similarity to what has been seen or heard. "Association with that" means being bound up with what has been seen or heard.
By the phrase "spoken by someone," he expresses that faith is produced from what has not been heard from another. "Investigation of the mode" refers to those various...
The investigation of the mode of appearance regarding the possibility [of a state] refers to a certain meaning.

"Of that which is determined" means of that which has been determined thus: "I must produce only what is wholesome. The absence of clarity and affection occurs due to an abundance of hatred; therefore, he said that rough persons abound in hatred. "By way of being a basis" means by way of being a cause.

Regarding the phrase "when the requisite object exists": by this, the over-zealous assertion of some—that "merit consisting in giving is accumulated through the mere arising of the thought alone, even without the relinquishing of the thing to be given"—is refuted.

"Proclamation of the hearing of the Dhamma" means the announcement of the hearing of the Dhamma. "Of that" refers to the act of causing the production of sound from the objects of sound—such as drums and so forth—which serve as the basis for sound, with the intention, "I shall give the gift of sound.
"Reflection" means the generating of the thought in various ways accordingly.

"In another place" means in the Suttas. "In another sense" means in the Abhidhamma passages. The commentary on the word *apariyāpanna*—namely, the commentary beginning with "the flavor of enjoyment" (*paribhogarasa*) and so forth—is written in many manuscripts after the commentary [on the preceding term], but it should rather be brought back and stated in its proper place.

In that context, because they do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), the designations of characteristics (*lakkhaṇapaññatti*) [are included] because they belong to a different sphere (*aññāyatana*).
It should be connected thus: "The six internal bases are not included within the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana).
Why was it said, "Kamma that has one door arises at another door"?

Is it not the case that, just as a consciousness directed toward a single object such as visible form does not have another object because a specific state of consciousness is intended, so too [the same applies] when a specific type of kamma is intended?
Kamma that functions through one door, such as the body-door, does not arise in another door because it reaches its completion right there.
Now, if what is intended is merely the commonality of being "kamma," would this example—"one object among form and so forth"—not be inappropriate?
No, because it was cited for the purpose of illustrating a dissimilar state; otherwise, this consciousness would be nothing other than mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa).
Because it operates upon all objects, it is said to have "unrestricted objects" (*anibaddhārammaṇa*);

by way of providing a similar illustration, one might say that the door is also unrestricted like its object. However, since he will later explain the mutual distinction between doors and kamma based on their predominant operation and frequent occurrence—despite the fact that kamma may occasionally pass through other doors—he [states this].

Therefore, having taken action (kamma) as a single unit by way of the commonality of its existence as killing living beings and so forth, it is said that "action is not restricted" because of its occurrence through the doors of speech and the rest; thus he said:

"An action belonging to one door, such as the body-door, does not arise in another door. However, a consciousness directed toward a single object among visible forms and the rest [arises] with that very object.
"Delimited" (*paricchinna*) means that only a specific [state] is grasped; it is said to be "bound to an object" (*ārammaṇa-nibaddha*).

Thus, a particular state of consciousness (*cittavisesa*) alone is grasped, not consciousness in its general sense (*cittasāmañña*). [Objection: But is it not the case that the object is also stated without restriction, as in:
"Whether having a visible-form object... or a mental-object (*dhamma*) object, or whatever [object] it may be"? [Reply: That is true. However, in that context, regarding visible forms and so forth—

A consciousness has a single object; it does not arise without that object. However, karma—divided into types such as those pertaining to the body-door—does not fail to arise in the door of speech and so forth.
To illuminate this distinction, only the "object" (ārammaṇa) is mentioned in the text and not the "door" (dvāra).
This point is shown by the phrase, "the object alone is fixed," and so on. Even when [karma] arises in the door of speech...
The meaning is "killing living beings and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the door of bodily action regarding wholesome states of the sense-sphere.
By the phrase "the doors of kamma," etc., he shows both the actual nature of that which is to be explained and the method for explaining it.

"By way of determinate materiality" means by way of the determinate materiality specified in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. Otherwise, even the heart-base would have to be included within the body produced by kamma.
Here, the "body acquired by clinging" (upādinnakakāya) comprised within a single continuity is what is taken; thus, [it refers to] the eye-base and so forth.

It cannot be said that among those mentioned, only one entity— the heart-base— is included [in the definition of the sense bases], because the arrangement [of the bases] has been clearly demonstrated by the statement,
"The eye-base and so forth have life as their limit. Furthermore,
since the apprehension of intimation is intended to follow immediately after the apprehension of the appearance of vibration, the air element is indeed characterized by the mode of motion.
One might occasionally suspect that [the mind] is accompanied by a modification of intimation; therefore, to preclude that, he says, "arisen from the first impulsion.

By the phrase "to move by way of being the cause for arising in another location," he shows that movement is the arising in another location, and that the status of being an agent is metaphorically attributed to that which is its cause;
otherwise, the momentariness and the lack of functional activity of phenomena would not be possible.

"Characterized by the modification of being directed toward that": "directed toward that" (*tad-abhimukha*) means facing that; the state of being so is "the state of being directed toward that" (*tad-abhimukha-bhāva*); that itself is the modification.
Or, the air element possessing that [state] is "characterized by the modification of being directed toward that.
Now, showing that this modification of being directed toward that constitutes intimation (*viññatti*), he says: "Co-existent with the intention," and so forth. And having done so, etc.
This shows the quality obtained from this commentary on the meaning. Therein, "of adverting" means of mind-door adverting (*manodvārāvajjana*).
By the passage beginning with "from which thirty-two," he shows that it is impossible to deny its status as the originator of intimation (*viññatti*).
"Capable of being a condition" refers to the ability [of the aforementioned air element] to perform the functions designated as stiffening and moving.
He states that this particular mode of appearance (*ākāravisesa*) functions as a cooperative cause (*sahakārīkāraṇa*).

He says, "it shows its non-existence in the ultimate sense" because, like invisibility and resistance (*anidassana-sappaṭighatā*), this particular mode of appearance is merely a specific state of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and does not exist as anything at all in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
Thus, its status as being originated by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*) is denied in the ultimate sense; however, its status as being originated by kamma (*kammamuṭṭhāna*), and so forth, [is not].

However, since there is no possibility [of such a thing], if the aforementioned modification were to exist in an ultimate sense, it would follow that it is causeless, because it would not have arisen from anything.
For there is no material form (*rūpa*) that is causeless; and if something were causeless, it would follow that it is eternal.
Yet, with the exception of Nibbāna, there is no functional phenomenon (*sabhāva-dhamma*) that is eternal. [Furthermore,] its being originated by mind...
This shows that the status of manifestation (*viññatti*) as derived matter (*upādārūpa*) originating from consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*) is established by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*).
[The phrase] "by means of manifestation" refers to manifestation acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*). "That which is the instrument" refers to that mental activity or mental operation.

"Made known by manifestation" refers to this disclosure of intention, namely, "this person is causing this to be done," [which occurs] in those things devoid of any alteration caused by manifestation.
It is not seen in the case of the movement of a tree and so forth, but it is seen in the case of the movement of the hand and so forth;
therefore, it is understood that there exists some modification distinct from the mere appearance of quivering which indicates the intention (adhippāya) known as a bodily action.
And a cause that indicates makes known the object to be indicated only when it is itself known, not by its mere existence; thus, immediately after the apprehension of the color...
The grasping of a modification is also understood. For it is only sound that has attained the state of being an object (*visaya*) which reveals the meaning, and not any other.
Therefore he said, "For it is not intimation" (*na hi viññatti*), and so forth.

However, if intimation were the mode of movement of mind-born material phenomena (*cittajarūpa*), then since the visual consciousness has as its object a color-form (*vaṇṇa*) that is vibrating, it might be apprehended by that [consciousness] as well; thus, in order to dispel this suspicion:
He said, “Of eye-consciousness,” and so forth.
By the phrase “forms such as palm leaves,” etc., he demonstrates that the intimation (viññatti) is cognizable by [eye-consciousness] and is also cognizable by mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) alone.
It is called *saññāṇa* because one perceives (*sañjānāti*) by means of it; the perception of water and so forth is *taṃ-saññāṇa*. Of that...
"Ākāra" means the mode of that cognition; and it is both the mode associated with water and the like, and that mode of the cognition of them—thus [it is] "udakā...kāro.
Having grasped that, having known it. "Tadākārassa" means of the mode that makes known water and the like.

If the apprehension of the aforementioned modification itself is the cause for the apprehension of the intention (*adhippāya*), then why is there no apprehension of the intention for one who has not grasped the convention (*saṅketa*)?
The apprehension of a modification is not the sole cause for the apprehension of the intention; rather, as he says, "But of this...
and so forth. With the words "Now then," etc., he shows that the intimation (viññatti) is to be apprehended through inference. Regarding the phrase "sādhippāya... anantaraṃ":

it refers to the stream of eye-door consciousness, which is characterized by the apprehension of the visible-object base (vaṇṇāyatana) arising simultaneously with a modification accompanied by intention.
"Immediately after. "Of the grasping of the intention" means of the impulsion (javana) in the third stage, which determines the intention.
"Because of its non-existence in the absence of a modification co-existent with the intention"—by this, one infers the aforementioned modification by means of the grasping of the intention.
"This being so," etc., he shows the matter thus inferred by way of conclusion. In that context, "by the very grasping of water and so forth..."

It occurs precisely through the recognition of the presence of water and so forth there, aided by a previously established relationship following the perception of the color of the palm leaves and the like.
Just as the mode of recognition— the concomitance of the palm leaves with the water and so forth—

is indeed consciousness itself and not due to immediate succession, so too [is it here] following the perception of the color of the quivering [object], aided by a previously established relationship.

The application of the simile is as follows: by the very act of discerning the intention, such as the desire to go, the intimation (*viññatti*) is known; for in the absence of that [intention], it does not exist.
"Consisting of its own nature" means existing in accordance with its meaning. It is twofold: both as the act of intimating and as that which is to be intimated.

When bodily intimation occurs in such a manner, the status of bodily action (*kāyakamma*) is accomplished for the karma consisting of volition (*cetanā*), because it is to be characterized by that [intimation].
However, showing that it is not by way of any one among the twenty-four conditions [that they are included], he said, "established at that door," and so forth.
By this, he shows the inclusion of killing living beings and the rest even when they arise at the door of speech; thus, he demonstrates their state of being included.
Alternatively, it is by way of the volition (cetanā) that constitutes bodily action, which arises at the door of the body, that [the phrase] "because of being cognizable through that door" is stated.
This was stated with reference to that very [consciousness] which has arisen in another door, by way of its "obtaining a name through that door.
Since it is certain that even mind-door adverting consciousness possesses the quality of originating intimation, he said, "of the eleven functional consciousnesses.
"Moving in other doors" means occurring by way of being present in other doors. "Confusion of doors" means due to the mixing up of the doors.
For if one door were to attain the state of being another door, it would follow that the body-door becomes the speech-door and so forth, and the speech-door becomes the body-door and so forth;
thus, there would be a confusion even among the kamma arising from those respective doors. Therefore he said, "there would also be a confusion of kamma.
This being the case, bodily kamma... [and so on] ...there would be no clear distinction. If kamma were to operate within the domain of other types of kamma, [then such a confusion would result].

Because bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and so forth could become verbal action (*vacīkamma*) and so forth, there would be no mutual distinction such as "bodily action is the door of bodily action" on the grounds that "there is a confusion of doors due to the confusion of actions.
To address this point, he said: "The same principle applies when one action enters into another action.
"Entering into another action" means being characterized by another action. For this very reason, he said: "by way of being a door."
"Moving from one door to another" means arising at another door. "Door" refers to one's own door; "another" refers to another door.

"Kamma" refers to kamma pertaining to a specific door; "other" refers to kamma pertaining to a different door. "Doors do not move from door to door" means they do not proceed by way of being another door, nor do they transfer to another door. Even though [there is] intimation (*viññatti*)...
Among the twenty-four conditions, there is no conditionality of volition (cetanā) by means of any one of those conditions;
rather, it is only when manifestation (viññatti) occurs that killing and so forth take place, and not otherwise. Thus, manifestation may be said to have the status of a cause for volition.
Therefore, it is said: "by way of the doors acting as causes. "Bodily action" and "verbal action" refer precisely to the definition of action (kamma).
Or, with reference to their status as causes, it is said: "by means of the doors which have become the causes.
Even though it was stated, "kamma-s by means of the doors," because it was also stated that they are "mutually defined," the point that the doors are also defined by the kamma-s is established;
this is shown by the phrase beginning with "not only," etc. Regarding the term "advāracārīhi" (those who do not move through the doors): [the doors].
He states that [the doors] are themselves determined, and not undetermined; the intention is that they are indeed determined.

He now clarifies that determination with the words "independent of karma," and so forth. Therein, just as time is determined by the mind restricted to time, the doors are determined by the karmas restricted to the doors—this is the summary meaning.
"Because they have such a nature" means because their nature is to be characterized by the body and so forth, which serve as doors. "Command...

[down to] pride" refers to the fact that bodily and verbal actions must be manifested through verbal and bodily intimation (*viññatti*). "By the body and so forth" means by bodily and verbal intimation.
"Therefore" means that even actions proceeding through other doors proceed only as characterized by their own respective door.
Therefore: "Nor does karma belong to the door" means that the door through which karma operates—that door itself—is not-self (anattaniya).
"That very door" means its own respective door. "Of karma" means of each respective karma.
If the doors are determined by karmas, how is the statement "because karma is unattached" to be understood? To this he says: "But previously," and so forth.
“Intimation” (viññatti) refers to that [action]. “Of that” means of the action. “In some way” means in any one of the twenty-four modes of conditions.

By the phrase “co-nascent with it,” he clarifies by way of a formal argument that the existence of bodily action is contingent solely upon the presence of bodily intimation, and not otherwise; for this very reason, he says: “by way of being its source of arising.”
"Thus it was said. By the phrase "according to the rule as stated," etc., he expresses the absence of deviation regarding the state of being the locus of the arising of kamma.
Therein, "according to the rule as stated" means by the rule consisting of the method of determination described in the manner explained in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
"In the case of proceeding through another door" means when proceeding through a door other than [the one intended].
The commentary on the discussion of the door of bodily action is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the door of verbal action:
Regarding the phrase "by four factors," here [it means]: one speaks only what is well-spoken, not what is ill-spoken; one speaks only the Dhamma, and only what is pleasing.
In order to show that those factors mentioned in the Sutta—“He speaks only truth, not falsehood”—have volition as their intrinsic nature, it is said:
“the speaking of well-spoken words,” and so forth. “Proceeding in such a manner” means proceeding by way of speaking well-spoken words and the like.
“Because they arise together” means because they originate simultaneously; for there is no vocal intimation devoid of sound.

For it is said: "That which is the intimation by that speech. Having spoken of vocal sound as something not too subtle—by means of such phrases as "speech, utterance, articulation," and so on—it is stated that "that which is the intimation by that speech" refers to vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti).

Since this is stated in conjunction with that [sound], the sphere of sound (saddāyatana), like the sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana), exists as an object of non-sensory faculties (anindriya-gocara) by way of its being a limited physical basis (vatthu-parittatā) and so forth.
And with this underlying intention, he said: "That which... [etc.

...is cognized by it. Now, since the fact that sound produced by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-sadda*) is an object of ear-consciousness is stated in the Canon without distinction, the following passage—beginning with "produced by mind"—is given to show the contradiction between the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*)’s position (that the sound resulting from the impact of applied thought [*vitakkavipphāra-sadda*] is not cognizable by the ear) and the Canon.

Thus, having demonstrated that the position of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā must be rejected by adhering to the intention of the author of the *Saṅgaha*, he now says, "But in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā... and so forth, in order to resolve that [objection] by adhering to his own intention.
[This is because] sounds produced by the manner of impact of the primary elements (*bhūta*) serve as the support for sound; therefore, together with the impact itself—
Sound arises. "The state of being its condition" means the state of being a condition for the impact of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*).

There exists a specific mode of the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) originated by consciousness that is capable of acting as a condition for the impact of what is clung-to upon the earth element born of consciousness.
For, because they possess that mode, it is said—following the stated meaning—that their earth element impacts what is clung-to.

Because it must be understood, he says, "it should be understood in the same manner as already stated," and then clarifies that very method with the words beginning "of those [factors] which are its modifications.
In this context, the meaning is that the state of being a condition for one another has been stated as "the state of being its condition" (*tappaccayabhāvo*).
Furthermore, regarding all other rules, he explains: "By the phrase 'not mind-originated,' he shows their non-existence in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*)," and so forth.
The procedure stated by oneself [is as follows]. However, regarding the procedure stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it says, "It should be understood in the same manner as stated above";
thus, it is precisely what was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
The production of each respective conditionally arisen phenomenon in another location through a continuous succession is "the continuity of production in another location."
"By means of what has been acquired" (*laddhāsevanena*) means by means of a previously acquired volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
"By the mind alone" (*citteneva*) means by the very first consciousness. Having rejected the claim that "seven impulsion moments produce seven syllables," they say:

"The consciousnesses included within a single impulsion series produce a single syllable. Although the striking together [of the vocal apparatus] is accomplished even by the first consciousness, [the full production occurs through the entire series].
However, since there is indeed a distinction arising from the repeated occurrence of a single [consciousness], it cannot be said that there is no "support" (upatthambhana),
because the impact produced by the seventh javana— which has acquired habituation through the impacts initiated by the preceding javanas— brings about a clearly articulated syllable.
This is so even by the first consciousness when it possesses volitional effort (abhisaṅkhāra).
Since the impact is powerful, it may be said in the Commentary that "there is no function of support";
all of this should be accepted after careful investigation.
The commentary on the discussion of the door of verbal action is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the door of mental action (*manokamma-dvārakathā-vaṇṇanā*) states:

"In order to show that just as all bodily and vocal intimation possesses the nature of the doors of body and speech, so too all consciousness possesses the nature of the mind-door, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: 'This [particular] mind does not fail to be the mind-door.'"
Having said, "It should be stated," he remarked, "It was said, 'This is the volition,' etc.,

for the purpose of showing that very door-bearing dhamma. Just as the doors of bodily action and the doors of verbal action were mentioned because they serve as the doors for the threefold and fourfold actions of body and speech,
so too [is] mental action [mentioned] because of the covetousness and so forth already stated.

It should be understood that the determination is made that the mind itself—associated with mundane wholesome and unwholesome states which serve as the causes for the round of existence—is the "door of mental action" (manokamma-dvāra) by virtue of its being the gateway. When volition has begun its own specific function, the associated states also begin their respective functions;
thus, it is said that volition "sets those [states] in motion in their own functions," and while setting them in motion, it likewise sets the associated states in motion.

It is said that it "makes" and "exerts itself" with respect to a single, undispersed object; likewise, it is the "making undispersed," the "collecting," the "accumulating," the "inducing exertion," the "exerting," and the "volition" of the associated states.
Showing the distinction between accumulating and volition, he says, "by means of the factors such as contact," and so forth.
"Acting in such a way" means acting in the manner that contact and the other factors [perform] their respective functions.

They become intent; such is the manner of acting. By that very mode of non-diffused activity as described, it should be understood that there is the acting and proceeding of the associated mental states.

Regarding the phrase "because it brings about the destruction of karma," the intended meaning is that it is not logical for the mind—which brings about the destruction of karma—to be considered a door of action (*kammadvāra*).
For this reason, they say: "The discussion of the courses of action (*kammapatha*) pertains only to the mundane."
The commentary on the discussion of the door of mental action is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Action:

Even when the cause, the fruit, and the activity are simultaneous, it is indeed appropriate to speak of them as if they were sequential, just as in the case of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
He said “or else,” etc., in order to show that “eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and forms.
He mentioned the two types of intimation (viññatti) as the act of intimating.

For since that [act] must be performed by means of body and speech—either by body and speech originating from mind, or by the preceding instances of bodily and vocal intimation—it is said: “one performs the act of intimating by means of body and speech.”
Because the primary elements (bhūta) undergo transformation accordingly. Alternatively, "by body and speech" means by bodily and vocal intimation (viññatti).
"The action of moving" refers to the action of stiffening and moving the material body, as well as the action of striking the clung-to (upādinnaka) matter.
For this action is capable of being a condition for stiffening and moving the material body, and for the striking of clung-to matter.
Because it is stated that [it] "is a condition," it is produced by bodily and verbal intimation (*kāyavacī-viññatti*). And by establishing it thus, these statements are also validated:

"Body and speech are the supports for the action of moving," and "By means of the body and so forth acting as instruments, they perform actions such as moving, covetousness, and so on, just as axes and other tools perform cutting and so on.
Furthermore, existence is not merely the state of being currently present.
Then, showing that the rapture has not been cut off by the path, he said, "even while unceased.
And it should be understood that this non-interruption occurs precisely through the non-eradication of the defilements that serve as the proximate cause for the body and so forth.

By the phrase, "performing the acts of covetousness and so on through the body and so forth acting as instruments," it is shown that it is indeed volition that is produced by way of the door of producing the acts of covetousness and so on.
With this underlying intention, he said: "And thus... [as follows]... they are appropriate.

By doing so, the statement beginning with "when there is body, when there is speech," and so forth, is brought into conformity. Furthermore, the instrumental designation "by which volition" is stated for the purpose of showing that the body and so forth, as well as the actions such as covetousness and the rest, have volition as their cause.

Because they exist by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), because they are beneficial, and because they exist within the path, the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are included within the path; thus he said, "And it is not impossible," and so forth.

Even those [mental states] that have not reached the level of a course of action (*kamma-patha*) are connected through their respective doors just as those that have reached the level of a course of action are;
likewise, even for those that have not reached the level of a course of action, when they arise in other doors, they receive their names according to their own respective doors.
They say: "If that were so, there would be a contradiction with the *Aṭṭhakathā*, and there would be an absence of a second meaning.

Therefore, they are 'correlated according to their respective doors' (*tantaṃdvāre saṃsandanaṃ*). This means that whichever door unwholesome volition and the like have occurred without yet reaching the state of a full course of action (*kammappatha*), they receive their designation by way of that very door.
Furthermore, this is because it establishes their belonging to the category of those respective doors.

In this context, it is said "enclosure" (*avarodhana*). For just as volition—comprising bodily action and so forth—that has reached the level of a course of action (*kammapatha*) receives the name "bodily action" and so on even when it arises through another door [such as speech], it is not so for that which has not reached the level of a course of action.
However, wherever those [volitions] arise at a door, they receive the names "misconduct of body," "misconduct of speech," and so forth, according to that very door.
They obtain [the result]. Indeed, it is said that for them, the mere taking of the name constitutes the performance of the respective door-adjunct (dvārapakkhika).

For this very reason, it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Although it has reached the path of action (kammappatha) at the door of speech, because it has not reached [the body], it does not constitute bodily action;
it is merely called verbal misconduct."

Furthermore, when consciousness associated with volition such as killing living beings proceeds through the doors of speech and so forth, its classification as bodily action and so on—due to its occurrence in the manner described as "mostly" or "frequently"—and the classification of the body and so on as the respective doors, constitute the distinction between the doors of action (*kammadvāra*).
For that establishes the doors of action in their unmixed state. It is with reference to this that it is said: "In those [cases] originated by command."
The commentary will explain this. However, some say that "the convergence of doors" refers even to the manifestation of many kamma-formations at each individual door.
In order to show how ill-will (vyāpāda) becomes a course of action (kamma-patha) as it actually occurs, the manifestation of ill-will in the form "May these beings be slain" is shown.
This is because [such an intention] serves as a cooperative cause for the volition (cetanā) belonging to the door of the body.

Because they lack the designation of bodily action (*kāyakamma*) due to the absence of the appropriation of another’s property for oneself through covetousness and so forth—such as the thought, "May these beings be killed"—and because they lack the designation of mental action (*manokamma*) since they do not proceed by way of such thoughts; or alternatively, because their nature is non-volitional, they are "not subject to designation" (*abbohārika*) in terms of killing living beings and so on.
The meaning is that they cannot be described as having the status of killing living beings and so forth. "In this regard" means in the state of being not subject to designation.
“The tenfold supernormal power... [it should be] recited in detail”—this is the intended meaning.
By this it is meant: when one says, “unwholesome verbal action originates at the mind-door,” that is what is intended.
Why was it said, “It is not stated in the Uposatha Khandhaka”? Is it not true that by that [statement], the discourse [is shown to be] from the Uposatha Khandhaka?

[The opponent] asks: "Is it brought [from elsewhere]? Even though it is brought, he says "even though not stated there" and so forth, showing that although it was not actually stated in that context, it is understood as having been stated by him. [He further explains:
"Rebirth in happy or miserable destinies does not occur from well-done or ill-done karma alone; rather, it occurs through the 'seam of the aggregates' (khandhasīva) and other such factors."
They say that this is stated because, for one who has grasped [the object] and misapprehends it by thinking "there is no gift" and so forth, [the Buddha] says, "He holds wrong view...

and performs such acts as paribhaṇḍa. By the phrase "because of the predominance of covetousness and so forth," it is meant that even though ill-will and other [unwholesome roots] may be present, when volition (cetanā) is powerful at the doors of body and speech while the others are not, then volition is [the unwholesome root] due to its predominant state.

It receives the conventional designations "bodily action" and "verbal action. Furthermore, its status as the primary factor is understood through the accomplishment of acts such as the taking of life.

However, when covetousness and other such states are predominant at those very doors and volition is not so, then even though volition exists there, it does not receive the designations "bodily action" or "verbal action" because it is not the primary factor.

It is not obtained. However, he shows that covetousness and the rest, because they are the primary factors, are called mental action (*manokamma*) by their own specific definition even when there is movement of the limbs of body or speech.

As for those who say: "Because it does not attain the status of a course of action (*kammappatha*) in all three doors, and because it occurs together with the mental action that has attained the status of a course of action in all three doors, volition (*cetanā*) is what is meant here by 'action' (*kamma*)."
When they say, "It is not so called," they may have spoken with reference only to the primary nature (*padhānasabhāva*) of covetousness and the rest.
Alternatively, because volition (*cetanā*) constitutes action (*kamma*) in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*), it need not be restricted to the secondary sense (*pariyāyakamma*);
thus it is said to be "inclusive" (*abbohārika*). However, by its own intrinsic nature, it is still called "action" even here. As it has been said: "I say, volition is action..."
“Monks, I say it is action (kamma),” and so forth. And in the Commentary, it is stated by emphasizing volition alone, saying, “The volition established at that door,” and so on.
For this very reason, he says, “By its very nature, that is mental action,” and so forth.
Alternatively, the volition co-nascent with covetousness and the rest—which have reached the state of courses of action—at the doors of body and speech, functions as bodily and verbal action.
It is mental action (manokamma) consisting of volition (cetanā) designated as covetousness and so forth.

If covetousness and the rest were predominant and not volition, then in that case covetousness and the rest would be the action here, and not volition; or else that [volition] would belong to the side of covetousness and the rest.
Having considered this objection, he said, "Bhikkhus, it is threefold," and so on. "Volition also... arises only at the mind-door."
