Having considered this as a demonstration of the non-distinctive nature of volition (*cetanā*) in its status as mental action (*manokamma*) within the door of the mind—due to factors such as covetousness—he said:
"Volition... [is] intention. For here, the only distinction is that volition is volitional action, whereas covetousness and the rest are actions associated with volition.
And herein, there might be the suspicion that volition could also take the form of bodily or verbal action; [therefore...]
It should be understood that it is not stated to be "indeterminate" (*abbohārika*) because of its non-existence at the mind-door and because unwholesome bodily and verbal actions do not arise there.

By the phrase "distinguished by abstention," he expresses that volition is predominant over abstention. In this regard, he demonstrates the logical justification through the scripture: "Bhikkhus, there are three kinds of bodily volition," and so forth, showing that [volition] is the opposite of killing living beings and the other [unwholesome deeds]. Because...
And in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is volition alone that is called the "kamma-condition," not the abstentions (*virati*) or covetousness and so forth;
therefore, it should be understood that in the primary sense, kamma is "volition," while non-covetousness and so forth are said to be "on the side of volition.
When defining the doors of action without confusion, [the text] says "it guards" (*rakkhati*), and conversely, "it breaks" (*bhindati*); thus, guarding and breaking are mentioned.
"How are they spoken of as 'without having destroyed' and 'having destroyed'?
The commentary on the Discussion of Kamma is finished.
The third alternative is found only in the first and fourth consciousness-doors, and not elsewhere, [as indicated] by the passage beginning "the ear, the nose," and so forth.
Because it has not been explicitly stated, or else because it is obtainable even from the analysis that omits case endings.
Since it is by way of restraint (*saṃvara*) that the morality of the Pātimokkha proceeds, he said, "Immorality (*dussīlya*) is volition such as killing living beings," referring to that [restraint].
Other unwholesome states—which are dissociated from restraint, associated with covetousness and ill-will, or dominated by them—are the unwholesome states that are the opposites of mindfulness.
Negligence (*pamāda*) is an unwholesome arising of consciousness that occurs by way of the relinquishing of the mind from its object.
Sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*) is called "indolence" (*kosajja*) because it has the nature of counteracting energy, or it is an arising of consciousness dominated by sloth-and-torpor.

"Impurity" means incompleteness, that is, being mixed with something else. For a door, while being the door for an action performed in the space between doors, [is not the door for the action itself].
Thus, it is as if mixed with that. For this very reason, he said: "Because there is also the occurrence of false speech and so forth at the door of the body.
Some, however, say: "It is called 'pure' because, in the intervals between moments that are not to be discerned, there is no occurrence of thoughts belonging to other doors";
but that [explanation] refers to the continuity by way of several sequences of impulsion (javana) having the nature of bodily action and so forth.

It is stated on the grounds that it exists during its occurrence. It is "not contradictory" because, having specified non-restraint by way of its nature as unwholesome bodily action and so forth, there is then the statement regarding its arising in the doors of verbal non-restraint and the rest;
thus, when explained in this way—that non-restraint characterized by the bodily door is indeed "of the bodily door" even when occurring in other doors—there is no contradiction.
This is the meaning. Now, he clarifies that manner of non-contradiction with the passage beginning, "Non-restraint (asaṃvara) is... and so forth. "In one's own door" means in one's own sense-base.
Even though non-restraint arises in another door, it is said to have arisen by way of its own door;
thus, even though bodily non-restraint arises in the door of vocal non-restraint, it is indeed said to have arisen by way of the door of the impulsive-body non-restraint.

It should be understood as "it is said. This same method applies to the other cases as well. The phrase "action by another door" is stated with the intention that the movement of action through another door is evident.

"This being so" refers to when only "non-restraint" is taken, in reference to the door of bodily non-restraint known as "copana. [This applies] only to that which has attained the state of a course of action (kamma-patha).
Since the state of being action (*kammabhāva*) is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he says: “Because it has reached the state of a course of action (*kammapatha*), it is verbal and mental action.
“The rest” means that which is not characterized by another door. “It is not so called” means it is not called bodily action (*kāyakamma*).

“We shall explain right there” means we shall explain it in the section on the convergence of the courses of action (*kammapathasaṃsandana*): “For that [bodily intimation], having reached the door of the body...”

By such statements as "it becomes unwholesome bodily action," and by such statements as "that which arises through the door of non-restraint of the moving body becomes precisely unwholesome bodily action," [the author] addresses the consequence that if speech-action and so forth—
which have reached the status of courses of action (kamma-patha) and consist of non-restraint— were to be reduced to the nature of bodily action and so forth,
then one would have to say: "The fourfold misconduct of speech becomes precisely unwholesome vocal action," and so on.
"It should be seen as included by way of negation"—this was said with reference to what will be stated later.
The intention is that it should be seen as included because the virtue of livelihood-purification dependent on the requisites must be accomplished through knowledge and energy.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Unwholesome Courses of Action.

Sarasena means by its own nature. That volition which, while the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is proceeding, acts as a cause for inflicting injury upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as conditions for it—such that, due to those primary elements being conditioned by that [volition], the primary elements arising from them will not come into being—that kind of volition which originates such an application is called "taking life" (*pāṇātipāta*). For once the primary elements have received the injury, they do not...
Because they are clear, like those that existed previously, they do not serve as causes for material phenomena (*bhūta*) of the same class.
The magnitude of the application (*payoga*) is due to the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) which has gained proficiency through many occurrences of javanas—
arising suddenly to accomplish the task even from a single application— and also because it is sometimes small.
And when a large living being is killed with an equal degree of effort, the volition (*cetanā*) arising for one who kills a large being is more intense;
thus, the "greatness of the object" occurs through the very strength of that volition. Therefore, he said: "by way of the effort... and by way of the state.
"Even in the reversal of the aforementioned conditions" means even when the conditions such as the effort and the object are not great.
"By various conditions" means by conditions such as the victim's possession of virtues and so forth.
In this context, the great culpability of one who kills a virtuous person should be understood as being like the "greatness of the object" (vatthu-mahantatā).

The minor and great culpability of the defilements and the methods [of killing] should be applied according to their mildness and intensity, respectively. The preliminary requisites consist of a living being, the perception of it as a living being, and the murderous intent.

The preparatory effort (*upakkama*) is that which is originated by the volition (*cetanā*) to kill; the volition of taking life possesses five constituent factors (*sambhāra*). That [volition] should be understood as being distinct from those five constituent factors.
This same method applies to taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and the other offenses as well.
Taking what belongs to another through the recitation of mantras is "based on knowledge" (*vijjāmaya*); [taking] what belongs to another without mantras...
The application consisting of psychic power (*iddhimaya-payoga*) is the drawing [of an object] toward oneself through bodily or vocal exertion by means of such a kind of psychic power;

thus, one should understand that there are six modes of application for taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), beginning with "by one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*). Sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*) is a great offense when committed after having overcome [the other person], but not so when both parties share a common desire.

They say: "Because it is stated that there are four constituent factors, even when one overcomes [the restraint] and transgresses while enduring the practice of taking what is not the path as the path, there is no wrong conduct (*micchācāra*) for one who is being overcome, because of the absence of the prior arising of the intention and the application of service.
However, the absence of application is not a valid criterion when the mind of service is present, since the application of service toward a woman occurs in the majority of cases.

Because of its absence. For, since the effort of engaging [in sexual intercourse] generally belongs to the man, it would follow that even if a woman lies down after first arousing the intention to engage, there would be no wrong conduct;

therefore, it should be understood that four factors are stated from the perspective of the man as the maximum. Otherwise, at the time when a woman performs the function of a man, for the man as well—
Because there is an absence of the application of cultivation, there would be no wrong conduct (*micchācāra*). However, some say:
"There are three factors for that which proceeds by one's own preference, and three for that which proceeds by force; thus, by including both what is taken and what is not taken, there are four.
This should be examined and accepted [only after due consideration].
Harsh speech is the volition of harshness arising from a bodily or verbal application that issues from a corrupt mind with no intent to kill.
However, when there is an intent to kill, both killing and ill-will occur, depending on whether the objective is achieved or not.
Harsh speech reaches its head—that is, its full consequence—only in the presence of the person against whom it is directed. Even if [the person] is absent...
"one becomes one of harsh speech," they say.

If it is argued that because volition (cetanā) is not always present as a path of action (kamma-patha), its status as a path of action is indeterminate, and therefore it is not mentioned in the category of paths of action—

then would it not follow that covetousness (abhijjhā) and the others are also indeterminate in their status as paths of action, since they too exist in states where they have not yet reached the level of a path of action?
Does this not result in their being excluded from the collection of courses of action (*kammappatha*)?

It does not result in such exclusion, because they are included therein by virtue of sharing the same nature as the courses of action. If that is so, should volition (*cetanā*) also be mentioned there? This is true;
however, since its status as a course of action is evident from its being [the mental factor] underlying killing and so forth, it was not explicitly stated. For as regards volition—
The state of being karma is illuminated by such statements as: “Bhikkhus, I say that volition is karma,” and “Bhikkhus, the threefold unwholesome bodily volition is unwholesome bodily karma.

Furthermore, since it is precisely karma that proceeds as the path for both happy and miserable destinations, as well as for the pleasure and pain arising therein, its status as a course of action (kamma-patha) is evident. [This applies] to covetousness and the rest...

However, because volition (cetanā) possesses the nature of striving and constitutes good and bad conduct, and because it serves as the path for the arising of happy and miserable rebirths and their corresponding pleasure and pain—by virtue of being produced by volition—it is not as manifest in its status as a "course of action" (kammapatha).

Therefore, only those [factors] are spoken of in the sense of a collection of courses of action. Alternatively, volition is not mentioned along with them because it does not belong to that same class.
It may be so. One should accept it after due consideration.

By stating that "the objects of the five training rules (sikkhāpada) such as abstaining from taking life are themselves the objects of the abstention from those acts, and thus they have limited objects (parittārammaṇa)," one raises an objection regarding the contradiction with the statement that [the objects] of taking what is not given and so forth have sentient beings as their object. For it is thus:
He will say: “For it is precisely because [an action] is to be transgressed that it is called ‘abstinence’ (veramaṇī).
He says this with reference to the commentary on the interrogation section (*pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā*) in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*. For therein it is stated:
“Because it takes as its object only those formations (*saṅkhāra*) that have been reckoned as ‘sentient beings,’ they are therefore said to have limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*).”
Regarding the phrase "misfortune and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (ādi), such states as "not obtaining what has not been obtained,
the loss of what has been obtained, the difficulty of acquiring desired enjoyments, having enjoyments shared with kings and others, dwelling in suffering, and dwelling in fear" are included. However,
some say that "the loss of wealth and so forth in this very life is the outflow-result (nissanda-phala)."
Commentary on the Discussion of the Wholesome Courses of Action (Kusalakammapathakathāvaṇṇanā):

The intention is that because these abstinences are associated with volition (cetanā), it is logical that volition serves as the "path" for happy and miserable destinies, as well as for the happiness and suffering that arise therein.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Concordance of the Courses of Action (Kammapathasaṃsandanakathāvaṇṇanā)
"Thus" refers to those [unwholesome and wholesome states] that have reached the level of courses of action (*kammapatha*). "Some" says this with reference to the Elder Dhammasiri.

For he maintains that the "conjunction of the courses of action" is the demonstration that unwholesome conduct (*dussīlya*) and so forth, as well as virtuous conduct (*susīlya*) and so forth—which have reached the level of courses of action—possess no difference in meaning from the courses of action themselves;
or alternatively, it is the illumination of their non-contradiction with the doors of contact (*phassadvāra*) and so forth. This is their status as courses of action.

By the word "there is not," he shows that the aforementioned non-restraints and restraints are not included in their [the Abhidhamma] system when they are compared with the paths of action (*kamma-patha*).
To show that there is no purpose in including those which do receive such inclusion, it is said: "threefold...
by way of seeing. Having thus briefly stated the fault in the first position, he proceeds to state it in the second position as well.

He says, “And not of misconduct,” and so forth. By this, he shows that those instances of misconduct, good conduct, non-restraint, and restraint which are practiced are established as being bodily action and so on.

For it has been stated [elsewhere] that, “Non-restraint arising by way of the five doors of contact is indeed unwholesome mental action,” and so on. With the words, “If, however,” and so forth, he expresses the absence of a complete exhaustion [of the subject].
"‘It should not be said that it arises’ means that for those who say [the path of action]... [etc. ... ‘mental action arises by way of the six doors of contact,’ it should not be so stated.

Alternatively, if the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā who state in the Aṭṭhakathā that only those instances of immorality and so forth that have reached the level of a path of action are designated by the names ‘bodily action’ and so on, then for them mental action [would likewise arise] by way of the six doors of contact."

The meaning is that its arising cannot be predicated. He says this with reference to such passages as, "The threefold misconduct of body is itself unwholesome bodily action," because it has been stated that each specific state of action [is so].
One might suspect that even a separate action could be an action by way of that door; thus, he suspects that killing and so forth might constitute verbal action and the like.
Therefore, since for some non-restraints and restraints there is no status as courses of action (kamma-patha),
and since there is no purpose in demonstrating the lack of difference between bodily misconduct and so forth from the courses of action,

and since the arising of misconduct and so forth has not been explained by way of the doors of contact, and since this method does not include everything without exception, and because it would result in a confusion of kamma;

And there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows in the commentary; such is the meaning. "Having a common name" means being [classified as] bodily action and so forth. "Not abandoning the general name" means not abandoning the state of being bodily action and so forth.

"Of both" refers to those that are paths of action and those that are not paths of action. By the phrase "due to the absence of a statement regarding the mode of arising," it is shown that although there is no difference in meaning between the doors of contact, the doors of non-restraint, and so forth, on the one hand, and the kamma performed through those doors on the other, it is nevertheless the case that...

This shows that they have been analyzed by way of the teaching as it occurs [in the texts]. The second determination begins with: "Unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five doors of contact," and so forth.

By the phrase "from the establishment of [unwholesomeness] in body and speech...," it is shown that unwholesome mental action which has reached the stage of impulsion (*copanappatta*) is distinguished from that which has not yet reached impulsion (*copana-appatta*).

It is stated as "bodily and verbal action" (*kāyavacīkamma*) in order to show it by way of its specific distinctions; however, this does not mean that it is shown merely by virtue of being bodily and verbal action.

Therefore, it should be understood that the mention of "body and speech" clarifies only that which has reached the state of "instigation" (*copanappatta*) as previously described. For this very reason, he said:
"That unwholesome [state] which has reached the state of instigation becomes mental action (*manokamma*) at the door of the body and at the door of speech. When the word "that" (*taṃ*) is uttered...
Since the word *yaṃ* (which) is used precisely because it denotes an invariable relationship, it is said: "that which arises.

By the phrase "delimited by mere arising," the meaning is "by kamma functioning through the six doors of contact. By the word *matta* (mere), in the sense of excluding other qualifiers, it excludes the specific quality of being mental kamma (*manokamma*).
Because the restrictive particle *eva* has not been employed, [it does not exclude] bodily and verbal kamma.
Because it was not stated [otherwise], namely, "it happens. Now, demonstrating the benefit obtained by not making a restrictive rule (*niyama*), he says, "But not even all...
and so forth. The phrase "because no restriction was made" and so on refers to the previous method.

Since the occurrence of words follows the speaker's intention, even a single part of a compound word may be drawn in by virtue of the governing context; with this intention, [he speaks] by means of the word *kamma* alone...
It is said, “having established the connection. However, by the words “but as for what they say,” etc., he demonstrates the incorrectness of the commentator’s (Padakāra) position here.
In that context, “belonging to the side of volition” (*cetanāpakkhikānaṃ*) means belonging to the side of volition consisting of bodily and verbal action. “Satam” means of those that are similar.
“And of the respective doors and courses of action” (*taṃtaṃdvārakammapathānañca*) refers to that which occurs as the course of action of this consciousness.
This was said with reference to a specific time, not at all times, because [these restraints] proceed only by way of being paths of action (*kamma-patha*).

Alternatively, by the word "and" (*ca*), the inclusion of those that are not paths of action should be understood. Or else, the phrase "respective doors" (*taṃtaṃ-dvārā*)—referring to both the respective doors and the paths of action pertaining to those respective doors—should be understood as including the restraints that are not paths of action. By that nature...
The intention is that [the mind] is not [the agent] by virtue of being the door for mental action (*manokamma*).

"In the same way here too" means that the state of being a door for the action associated with the mind—which is produced by the mind—is metaphorically attributed (*upacāra*) to the mind as well. There is indeed nothing to be said [against this], because there is no such thing as a consciousness devoid of the mind that serves as the immediately preceding condition (*anantarapaccaya*).
The commentary on the "Discourse on the Doors" is finished.

By the word "etc. in the phrase "taking all objects, etc.," when there is an absence of order and an absence of fixed rule, he includes [other factors]. He shows that because it is impossible for [the object] to exist when the primary [factor] is present, the non-primary is what is taken as the subject. This concludes the discussion on the section concerning the Enumeration of Phenomena (Dhammuddesa).
Regarding the commentary on the "five factors beginning with contact" (*phassapañcamaka-rāsivaṇṇanā*):

by the passage beginning with “At that time there is contact,” it is shown that in the demonstration of the status of contact and the other factors as belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth, there is no emphasis on their being the primary factor; rather, the emphasis is only on the demonstration of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). This is shown by the phrase “for [there is no such thing] for contact and the others,” etc.

“By way of mental activity” (*cittakiriyābhāvena*) means by way of the operation of the mind. The accomplishment of contact is simply its arising. Because of its occurrence through a coming together (*sannipatitappavattiya*).

"Is a condition" (paccayo hoti): by this, he shows that contact (phassa) is stated to be the cause for the meeting of the mind and the object, and that it is the meeting of the mind and the object. For contact, proceeding by way of touching the mind's object, is called the condition for its proceeding as a meeting with that object.
And that proceeding of its in the mode of touching is like [the hand] on the tip of a branch.
It becomes clearly manifest in such cases as seeing the movement of the legs of a man standing on the ground who is not a coward;
the production of saliva in the mouth upon seeing someone eating sour mangoes or similar fruits; and the trembling of the body of a compassionate person upon seeing another being slaughtered.
"Material phenomena" (rūpa-dhammā) refers to those specific factors which, by way of resistance, [interact] with one another.
The term "impact" (*saṅghaṭṭana*) is used for specific material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) that arise in close proximity;
likewise, the process by which mental objects become the domain of consciousness and attain the status of being its objective field occurs in the manner of an impact.

And that specific phenomenon dependent on consciousness is spoken of by way of the term "impact," as when it says, "In this way," and so forth. However, some maintain that "contact (*phassa*) has the nature of impact."
Some say, "It belongs only to the five doors, not to the other [the mind-door], because of the absence of the impact between the physical base and the object";
however, that is not tenable, because such an impact is established only figuratively (metaphorically). Otherwise, even for the five doors, that [impact] would not be possible.

When the sense-faculties and attention proceed in their respective ways, consciousness arises with respect to each corresponding object; it is precisely through their proceeding in that manner [that consciousness arises].
It is the making of consciousness an object.

Because of such statements as, “Monks, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence upon these five cords of sensual pleasure, this is called the gratification (assāda) of sensual pleasures,” it is said that pleasant feeling itself is the gratification; hence the phrase “because of its state as gratification.”

The grasping of an object by way of touching and so forth is the experiencing of a portion [of it]; thus, he states that the function of experiencing belongs to contact and the other [mental factors] in a non-figurative sense.

"By means of a sign" refers to a sign such as blue or long and so forth. "By this method" shows that just as perception conforms to knowledge in a mental state where knowledge is predominant, so too does it conform to concentration in a state where concentration is predominant.

It "binds" (paṭṭhapeti) means it establishes; it establishes the associated mental states in their respective functions. For that very reason, explaining its meaning, he said "it sets in motion" (pavatteti).
The word *hoti* expresses existence; and since existence for conditioned phenomena does not occur without arising, it was stated:
"In this sense, consciousness does not not arise. By this, it is shown that because consciousness does not fail to arise, it indeed arises.

Thus, "therefore, consciousness exists" is what was stated; this is the meaning of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) here. Since this is established thus, no purpose is seen for the words *hoti* (exists) and *uppajjati* (arises), as they have the same meaning.
Alternatively, "existence" (*bhavana*) means being (*sattā*), and being consists in being possessed of arising and so forth;
therefore, because contact and the other factors are included within the three moments, in such expressions as "contact exists," the word *hoti* [indicates their presence].

It has been stated. In that regard, whatever state possesses arising does not fail to exist; therefore, it is not impossible for the meaning expressed by the word "arises" (uppajjati) to be expressible by the word "exists" (hoti).

However, in the phrase "that which has arisen exists" (uppannaṃ hoti), although the possession of arising and so forth is expressed by the word "arisen" (uppanna) itself, there is nevertheless no deviation from that very state [of having arisen].
Because the word *uppanna* (arisen) can denote a state even when the three moments have passed— as expressed by the word *hoti* (is)— therefore, here,

just as there is no contradiction in showing the presence of the same meaning as the word *uppajjati* (arises), so too the showing of *uppajjati* is not contradictory, since it serves to make [the state] manifest. Otherwise,
by the very phrase "consciousness has arisen" (*cittam uppannam hoti*), the existence of consciousness would already be established.
It cannot be said that it is not possible to say, "What is the use of showing again what already exists?

For although the mind has already been mentioned with specific distinctions according to its temporal determination, it is mentioned again here to show that, because it arises simultaneously with contact and the other factors, it is even more indistinguishable from them.
Furthermore, in this section on the exposition (niddesa), there is an analysis only of those phenomena already listed, and not as in the Vibhaṅga.

The meaning that "all the words have been ascended by way of the text (pāḷi) for the purpose of summarizing in the section on enumeration (uddesavāra) and for the purpose of analyzing in the section on exposition (niddesavāra)" is also unshakable.
For instance, in such passages as "At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm," the path and so forth are not analyzed there.
Furthermore, [the analysis occurs] through contact, feeling, perception, and volition, just as [they are distinguished] among the faculties by way of their predominance.

Since it must be included within the aggregate common to all mental states (*sabbacittuppādasādhāraṇa*), the consciousness mentioned in the "Analysis of Occasions" (*samayavavatthāna*) should also be understood as being mentioned in the "Fivefold Contact" (*phassapañcama*).
Commentary on the Aggregate of Jhāna Factors.

"Applied thought" (*vitakka*) refers to the act of applying the mind; and since that is merely the occurrence of applied thought by means of its own conditions, this description in the abstract serves to exclude the notion of mastery over it.
When the mind applies itself to an object, applied thought makes that object fit for apprehension, as if striking it or turning it over.

Its characteristic is said to be striking and its function is said to be pounding. This characteristic is stated by way of dependence on its activity (*kicca*), for there is no such thing as an action or a mode of apprehension that is separate from the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.

Nevertheless, although a phenomenon possessing an intrinsic nature is in the ultimate sense of a single nature, it is described by various figurative expressions in accordance with the needs of those people who are to be enlightened.
It is manifested in many ways through various superimposed forms. For in this way, it is well manifested.

"Expansion" (vipphāra) is the opposite of sloth and torpor (thinamiddha); it is the lack of shrinking back or contraction regarding the object. However, because its nature is that of directing [the mind] toward the object, it is like a movement;
with this intention, it is said: "Expansion means connected with movement."

It has been said. By the phrase "occurring through a continuity in access and absorption," he shows that while applied thought (*vitakka*), being the initial impact upon a previously unencountered object, is expansive, it is not so when occurring as an uninterrupted succession upon the very same object;
rather, in that case, it is not overly expansive because of its settled nature. For this very reason, he said:
“Being unshakable,” and so forth.
Because of such statements as “He drenches with rapture and bliss,” the pervasion by rapture has the body as its object; in order to show how that occurs, it is said, “by means of sublime forms.

Non-distraction (*avisāra*) is the essential nature that is the opposite of diffusion (*visāra*), which is the state of being scattered; it is not merely the absence of diffusion. Of non-distraction and non-wavering...

Although there is no difference in meaning because both consist in the state of concentration (*samādhāna*), it is stated that "both [non-distraction and non-agitation] are mentioned" by way of their direct expression and by way of their associated factors, in order to show this.
Alternatively, the word *visesato* should be understood as meaning "by way of excellence.
For pleasure (*sukha*) is a specific cause for concentration, according to the statement: "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated."
The Commentary on the Faculties (*Indriyarāsi*).
"Therein" means in that which has the characteristic of resolve (*adhimokkha*), known as faith (*saddahana*).
By the phrase "the person has faith," this too clarifies that the states associated with it—which have acquired their specific qualities through faith—are indeed the agents of the act of believing.
For the function of the parts is figuratively attributed to the whole. It is not only unwholesome lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) that arises in the form of non-confidence toward an inspiring object;
rather, it is also shown to include that which arises in the form of confidence toward an uninspiring object. To demonstrate this, the term "wrong resolve" (*micchādhimokkha*) is used.
By this, he indicates that the confidence placed in Pūraṇa and others is itself a state of lack of faith. [The phrase] "become confidence" (*pasādabhūta*)...
By this, he excludes lack of faith (*assaddhiya*), which is the opposite of clarity. By the phrase "situated in the object" (*vatthugata*), he excludes wrong resolve (*micchādhimokkha*).
However, by the phrase "clarity that is a settled conviction" (*pasādabhūto nicchayo*), making the already explained meaning manifest, he says:

"it is not a mere incidental resolve" (*na yevāpanakādhimokkho*). Clarity (*pasāda*) is the state of being untroubled; furthermore, because it is a state of being undisturbed, it is described as "the state of being unsullied" (*anāvilabhāvo*). For that...

Among the associated mental states, faith manifests as clarity (*akālussiya*). Furthermore, because it must be grasped in the manner of resolving that "it is so," it manifests as resolution (*adhimutti*).
Regarding the phrase "the bases such as the Buddha," it should be understood that this includes the connection between this world, the next world, and the results of kamma. As it is said:
"The noble disciple, Mahānāma, has faith as his hand," and "In this world, faith is wealth."

Because of such statements as, “Faith is the seed, austerity the rain,” faith should be regarded as being like the hands and other limbs in the undertaking and so forth of wholesome states. [As it is said:
“In this case, a task must be done by a bhikkhu. It occurs to him: ‘A task must indeed be done by me;’”
"Moreover, while I am performing work, it is not easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas;
come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, and for the realization of the unrealized.
This is the appropriate preliminary reflection.

"Rooted in that" means rooted in the path to be traveled and so forth. Here, it should be understood that "the path is to be traveled" and so on are stated according to the method of exposition in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, and not according to the sequence in which they appear in the *Pāḷi*.

Just as at the time of performing an action, mindfulness—which functions by making its object clear even when that object was performed long ago—approaches that object, remains there, and does not let go. That object which has been forgotten is as if it has slipped away.
It is as if it has moved, yet because it is the opposite of that [distraction], it is not confused; showing this meaning, he said, "like a gourd in water," and so forth.
Therein, by the word *sāraṇa* (remembering), he clarifies this very meaning: "they remember by means of it.
For mindfulness (*sati*) is the state of predominance over those mental states that are occurring as the act of remembering.
[It is] a condition. For when it exists as a condition in that way, those phenomena are remembered, not forgotten, and not confused.
[It is so called] from the perspective of "origination," because of the arising of these phenomena through such causes and conditions;
and from the perspective of the "fruit," because by the arising and ripening of phenomena, they are said to be "accomplished" by producing such and such a fruit.
“Becoming the basis” means becoming the object.
Although all dhammas that possess an object take an object, the mind is said to “know by way of delimited apprehension,” because—unlike other [mental factors]—it grasps others as delimited.
For among the mental concomitants (cetasika), some grasp the object after delimiting it...
Some are unable to grasp [the object], while others remain at the mere limit [of perception] and do not grasp the object as consciousness does;
thus, in order to show the absence of that [grasping] in those who might be suspected [of it], he said: "Not perception... by way of piercing.
And regarding the statement "joy (pīti) attains the state of mental happiness (somanassa)": this refers to the compound *pītisomanassa*, meaning joy and mental happiness.

This was said with reference to their equal conjunction. However, just as one says "a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds" (*ājaññaratha*), it is intended that the predominance of joy associated with rapture is expressed as "joy-with-rapture" (*pītisomanassa*);
thus, rapture does not itself become the state of joy. For when the predominant factor is present, the subordinate factor is not [separately] employed.
And here, the mention of "rapture" is for the purpose of specifying that the joy associated with rapture is generally [of that kind].

It is performed by way of its essential nature and its manifest function; yet there is no exclusion of joy that is devoid of rapture (*nippītika-somanassa*), because in conventional terms (*ruḷhīsadda*) the action is not necessarily present.
However, showing that this meaning is well-established when *pīti* (rapture) serves as a defining characteristic (*upalakkhaṇa*), he says: "or characterized by rapture," and so forth.

The occurring [state] is the appropriated aggregates (*upādinnakkhandha*). By the phrase "it endures for a long time," it is shown that life is the cause not only for the momentary persistence (*khaṇaṭṭhiti*) of those phenomena that must be maintained, but also for the non-interruption of the continuity (*pabandhānupaccheda*).

Otherwise, death through the exhaustion of the lifespan would not be tenable. "Without distinction" means by way of the commonality of being the life-faculty (*jīvitindriyatāsāmaññena*), independent of any specific causes.

Even though material and immaterial phenomena do not occur in the formless and non-percipient realms, nevertheless, because the final and initial phenomena in those preceding and succeeding existences are not separated by anything of a different nature, they are indeed called "uninterrupted. Thus it is said:
"It proceeds uninterruptedly until final Nibbāna. Regarding "guarding and so forth," this refers specifically to guarding, proceeding, and establishing.

It says: "Because it is the condition for the specific state of being alive" means because it is the condition for the specific quality of being alive in those factors that arise simultaneously with it.

For the distinction between what is bound to the faculties (i.e., living matter) and dead matter, and between what is born of karma and what is born of the seasons, is produced by the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
*Commentary on the Collection of Path Factors* (*Maggaṅgarāsivaṇṇanā*)

"By way of being non-perverted and leading to liberation": this is stated because the word *sammā* (right) and the words *diṭṭhi* (view), etc., stand in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇatā*), such that the quality of leading to liberation—which is common to view and the others—is qualified by the word *sammā*.

For the word *sammā* has the sense of "non-perversion," not the sense of "leading to liberation. Or rather, the word *sammā* itself possesses the sense of both "non-perversion" and "leading to liberation."
For particles have many meanings. "Just so" means by way of being unerring and leading to liberation. Regarding the commentary on the "mass of power":
with the intention that "assent" (*patissava*) is the reception of speech, [the text says] "with assent," "consisting of assent," and "of the same nature as that."

"Whatever respect there may be," he said. "By way of being manifest in various instances" means by way of the function of making [the qualities] clear—through the reviewing appropriate to shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) regarding internal factors such as birth and so forth, and external factors such as monks and so forth;
the meaning is that it is like the manifestation of the earth element and so forth within the earth and other elements together with their constituent parts.
The Commentary on the Root Simile:

Thus it is said that it corresponds to the simile; for just as a man who has fallen into filth, despite his body being in contact with it, is not attached to it in his being, so too non-greed (alobha), even when an object is grasped by way of making it an objective support, is unattached in its state of non-clinging.
It proceeds with a form that is entirely unattached. For such is the nature of that phenomenon. Any instance of immorality arises from hatred;
all immorality has hatred as its decisive support. Thus it is said: "arising from hatred and having hatred as its decisive support.
By this, he shows that non-hatred is the direct opposite of hatred itself, and by extension, the opposite of immorality.
Therein, "development" (*bhāvanā*) is in the sense of non-transgression of the states arisen therein... [and] in the sense of repetition.

That which is the arising of consciousness in absorption—beginning with the first *jhāna*—which has attained unity, which possesses the specific excellence brought about by the proximate access, which is purified by the cleansing of obstacles such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and which, being free from the objects that veil it, is characterized as the intermediate absorption (*appanā-samādhi*) proceeding in equilibrium.
One who has entered upon the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta), by virtue of having so entered, approaches that state and leaps into it;

and because of the absence of distraction—which must be purified—and of contact with defilements, one looks on with equanimity at the mode of establishing unity through the practice of pure serenity, free from the activity of establishing purification and concentration.
This is done by means of the innate, co-nascent, and perfectly neutral equanimity (tatra-majjhatta-upekkhā) in its most manifest form.
By way of function, it is nourished by equanimity; in that very state, the factors known as concentration and wisdom arise as a yoke-fellow pair.
Their development (*bhāvanā*) is their cultivation (*brūhanā*) in such a way that they proceed without one overstepping the other.

Likewise, those faculties (*indriya*) therein, such as faith and the rest, having become of a single flavor through the taste of liberation because they are freed from various defilements, [proceed in the same manner].

[The factors] have proceeded. And whatever energy is carried forth—that is, set in motion—as appropriate for those [factors] which possess a single flavor in their non-transgression [of their respective functions], and whatever cultivation there is at that moment, consisting in the attainment of a state of proficiency and strength;
the development, production, and increase of all these modes is here [the nutriment] for those [factors] born therein... [and so on].
It is called "development" (bhāvanā) in the sense of repeated practice (āsevana).
Furthermore, since this mode of development has already appeared in the Pāḷi as "the purification of the way for the first jhāna," and so forth,
and because one sees, by means of knowledge, the various dangers and benefits in both defilement and purification, [one develops accordingly].
It must be accomplished; therefore, it is said: "of the development consisting of the fifty means thus described.

Regarding "non-occurrence": the intention is that when a certain state exists, the aforementioned development does not occur, and that state is called "non-development" because it is characterized by a development that is its opposite.
For it is not logical that mere non-existence should be the opposite of non-delusion.

The unwholesome states such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth, which are the opposites of those [wholesome qualities], are to be understood here. Alternatively, non-cultivation (*abhāvanā*) is a specific kind of negligence (*pamāda*).
For it has been defined as: "the non-practicing, non-cultivating, and non-multiplying of wholesome states," and so on.
It is stated as "subject to aging" (*jarādhamma*) in order to show that its sight is absolutely impossible to obtain; for thus it is said in the Pāli: "of those subject to birth... [and so forth].
By the passage beginning, "Monks, such a desire arises in beings," the failure to obtain what is desired has been analyzed.

Since the accomplishment of the contemplation of the body through the power of non-greed, and the accomplishment of the contemplation of the mind and mental objects through the power of non-delusion, are already evident, he spoke the words beginning with "In the change of pleasure" in order to analyze the accomplishment of the contemplation of feelings through the power of non-hatred, which is not yet evident. And this...

This interpretation was made with reference to the specific conditions of non-greed and the other [wholesome roots]; however, in a general sense, all [wholesome roots] are conditions for all [of them].
Hatred arises by way of the very inability to endure suffering that has arisen through its own nature and through volition;
thus, it is the immediate opposite of the vision of that [truth], not a remote opposite like lust.

In the commentary on the section on the heap of courses of kamma (*kammapatharāsa*), it is said: "Because of their being courses of kamma and because of their similarity to them. This is stated because non-covetousness (*anabhijjhā*) and so forth, like covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and so forth, are not exclusively courses of kamma.
For these are included within the heap of courses of kamma by virtue of their being kamma that occurs as mental courses of kamma (*manokammapatha*).

"Not always only the courses of action (kamma-patha)," he says. By this, he shows that there is no contradiction in speaking of "course-of-action-ness" even for other phenomena that are indeterminate as to being courses of action yet are manifest as such.
[The Explanation of the Pairs: Tranquility, etc.]
"Samanti" means "rightly. "For the purpose of worshipping the cetiya, etc. means for the sake of worshipping the cetiya and so forth.

Because it serves as the observation of beneficial and non-beneficial phenomena at all times—by way of the meditation subjects of the four truths of tranquility (*samatha*) and their respective divisions, by way of the application of all meditation subjects, by way of the distinctions such as dull, medium, and sharp faculties among all yogis, and by way of the appropriate time for the mind’s states such as lethargy and agitation—it is [beneficial].
In the state of penetration (*paṭivedha*), mindfulness and clear comprehension should be understood without distinction as the removal of obstacles and the increase of cultivation,

respectively, by way of their realization of things according to their true nature. Just as there is no serenity (*samatha*) without skill in absorption (*appanā-kosalla*), and no awakening to reality as it is (*yathābhūta-avabodha*) without serenity,
so too concentration and wisdom— occurring at different moments— are the specific causes for one another in the context of penetration.
Showing that even [the factors] exist in a single moment, he said: "By way of being mutual signs.
For when the object is being exceptionally illuminated by wisdom, concentration is able to settle through unification;
and when concentration has entered upon the middle sign of serenity, wisdom flows clearly regarding its objects. They proceed evenly because they do not overstep one another.
They proceed equally and without unevenness by way of a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

Having become a pair joined together—like a pair of noble steeds pulling the yoke of a chariot when drawing the burden of a meditator’s aspirations—they are called "yoked in pairs" (*yuganaddha*) because they are bound as if tied together, not overstepping one another.
Thus, for those devoted to higher consciousness (*adhicitta*), energy and concentration must be yoked together evenly.

In order to show that those [factors] previously mentioned are taken up again for the sake of demonstrating this specific distinction, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "for the purpose of joining energy with concentration.

However, since that constitutes an elucidation of the conjunction of concentration and energy, he said: "the meaning is 'for the purpose of expressing the term "conjunction" (*yoga*). [End of] the commentary on the miscellaneous factors (*yevāpanaka*).

"In whatever way" means either rightly or wrongly. "Without resolving" means not desiring a resolution at the time of application, which is caused by a prior resolution such as "I shall do this" or "I shall do that.
For where there is no desire, there is simply no undertaking. "Crawling about" (saṃsappana) is doubt; for it is said, "creeping along, crawling around."

It is said: even when there is no active effort, because of the presence of equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*), the states associated with it proceed neither deficiently nor redundantly, and they become neither sluggish nor agitated.

Thus, being the condition for their proceeding in such a manner, it is said to have the function of preventing deficiency and redundancy, as if warding off an imbalance. Precisely because it is the condition for proceeding in that way—
"Equanimity toward those states" is what is said. "Of the word *jhāna*" means of the term *jhāna*.

"In them" refers to the five [factors]. For it is with reference to this particular arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*) that it is stated, "the meaning of the word *jhāna* consists of five factors," because it is precisely this that is being commented upon. Indeed, this is not the case in every arising of consciousness.
There are exactly five jhāna factors. A "sentence" (*vākya*) is a collection of words, or a portion of words, such as the group of phenomena beginning with contact as the fifth.

It is said to be "fulfilled" (*pūrita*) by way of fulfilling [the requirements] starting from the fifty-sixth [verse]. Contact is the condition for feeling and the other [mental states], because of such statements as:
"One who is touched feels; one who is touched perceives. Even though desire and the rest lack the function of a "ruler" (*rāsi*) as previously stated, [they are included].

Regarding those [categories], it cannot be said that they are not to be mentioned; however, considering the objection that they ought to be mentioned in their own form as distinct groups, he says, "Even though they have been stated," and so forth.
The commentary on the section concerning the Enumeration of Phenomena (Dhammuddesavāra) is concluded.
Explanation of the Exposition of the Section on the Wholesome of the Sense-Sphere (Kāmāvacara-kusala-niddesavāra-kathāvaṇṇanā): 2.

"In what exists" (*sante*) means in that which exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Because contact is to be grasped by way of the manner in which the object and the subject meet, [it is said to exist].

"Contact" is said to be the convergence of the mind upon an object. Since words such as "citta" and "mano" clarify their own meaning by way of functions such as "thinking" and "mentating"—as in the passage, "In the sense of thinking it is *citta*;
in the sense of mentating it is *mano*"—he says, "without regard for specific functions, as in the case of *citta*, *mano*, and so forth.
Just as in the world, what is cut up (*vikatam*) is itself called "cutting" (*vekatam*).
The object itself is called "the objectifier" (*vesayanti*); likewise, the mind itself is the term "*mānasa*," being merely a distinction in sound.
Just as with words such as "blue" and so forth, the application of the word "white" (*paṇḍara*) to minds—such as those directed toward cloth and the like—is based on their state of purity;
thus, its dependence upon a specific quality is stated. As in the expression "bodily pleasure" (*kāyikaṃ sātaṃ*), the meaning here is "dependent upon the sensitivity of the body."
In the phrase "thus the mental [state] is pleasant," the expression "dependent on the mind" (*ceto-nissita*) indicates a dependence upon a specific support.
The term "stability of consciousness" (*cittassa ṭhiti*) refers both to that which is simultaneous with the mind and to that which occurs at different moments;

it is a description of a particular state of the mind, thus indicating a dependence upon a specific state. This applies to the mode of occurrence of either the consciousness or the person that was described as "not being greedy."

"Non-greed" (*alubbhana*) is stated as "non-greed" (*alobha*); this designation "non-greed" is made with reference to a specific distinction regarding the absence of another action. In the same manner as previously stated, the state of one who is non-greedy is "non-greediness" (*alubbhitatta*);
this designation is stated with reference to a specific distinction regarding the state of being another [quality].
The agent, instrument, state, and so forth, are established only by way of superimposition upon intrinsic phenomena (*sabhāvadhamma*); such is the designation of a state (*bhāvaniddesa*).

However, when it is independent of superimposition (*ajjhāropana*), and for that very reason free from and turned away from other specific qualities—specifically because of its state of being devoid of life and substance—it is called a "description of the intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvaniddesa*).
Thus, the term "contact" (*phassa*) is said to be "a term for the intrinsic nature that indicates a mere phenomenon" in the sense of touching.
Since the mode of occurrence of the mind as it touches an object is the functional activity of touching, it is called "the act of touching."
It is said, “the mode of touching. Since the prefix *sam-* in the word *samphusati* indicates the sense of coming together—as in “origination” (*samudaya*) and so forth—it is said, “meeting-touching.
However, since in such passages as “I touch the bliss of renunciation,” obtaining is also called “touching” and “contacting,” he says, “not obtaining-contacting.”
By another synonym: the term "wisdom" (*paññā*) refers to the state of being learned (*bahussuta*), which brings about the perfection of wisdom;
it refers to "skillfulness" (*kosalla*) as proficiency in the various arts and sciences; it refers to "cleverness" (*nepuñña*) as sharp and subtle discernment in any matter whatsoever;
and it refers to "discernment" (*vibhāvanā*) as the correct exposition of the Dhamma. In this way, these terms are applied to those various specific distinctions of wisdom.
Those specific modes of expression proceed with distinction; thus, it is stated that those specific types of wisdom are obtained at different times.
The intention is that the others also follow for the most part. "By way of difference in meaning" means by way of the specific meanings such as wisdom and so forth.

Expressions such as "anger," "being angry," and "the state of being angry" are merely by way of phrasing (*byañjana*), intended to illustrate the existence of their respective intrinsic natures and modes.

The term "analytical statement" (*vibhāgavacana*) refers to the fact that terms such as "cleverness" (*paṇḍicca*) and so forth are analytical statements by way of their meaning, because they are based on specific qualifications of wisdom (*paññā*).

He expresses this point with the words "Alternatively," and so on. Furthermore, the phrase "of such a nature" states the reason for its classification according to meaning, which distinguishes it from the preceding mode.
"Refusal" (*paṭikkhepa*) means rejecting or denying; the variety of that—that is, its distinction—is "the variety of refusal."

Rejection out of reverence for the true Dhamma is *saddhammagarutāpaṭikkhepa*; by means of that rejection out of reverence for the true Dhamma, there is diversity, which is *saddhammagarutāpaṭikkhepanānatta*.
Furthermore, since that diversity of rejection out of reverence for the true Dhamma is divided into categories such as reverence for anger (*kodhagarutā*) and so forth, it is said:
"by way of the distinctions of reverence for anger and so on. It is distinguished by anger and the rest.
The rejection and prohibition [of anger and so forth] is distinguished by its respect for the True Dhamma (*saddhamma-garutā*). It is precisely the respect for anger and so forth;
through their diversity, there is a diversity of opposites to the respect for the True Dhamma. Thus, respect for anger is the opposite of respect for the True Dhamma.
Respect for flattery, gain, and honor is the opposite of respect for the True Dhamma; therefore, [it is abandoned] by means of respect for the True Dhamma.
Through the distinction of being opposed [to virtue], the esteem for what is not the true Dhamma (*asaddhammagarutā*), though unified with that state, has become manifold.
For in its essential meaning, anger (*kodha*) is simply hatred (*dosa*).

Slander (*makkha*) consists of unwholesome aggregates (*akusala-khandhā*) that proceed in the mode of destroying the virtues of others, dominated by hatred. And esteem for that [slander] is simply the occurrence of activity through the process of forming them with reverence. Esteem for gain (*lābhagarutā*)...
There is honor and respect for the four conditions, and a desire to obtain those very same things when they are well-prepared.
Furthermore, the performance of reverence toward both of these is merely a manifestation of craving. Therefore, it is said:
"By way of the diversity that is the opposite of reverence for the True Dhamma, the non-True Dhammas have reached diversity. For thus, the four non-True Dhammas are indeed enumerated.
Regarding the phrase "due to a lack of respect for the true Dhamma" (*asaddhammagarutā*): in the first alternative, the meaning is that there is no respect for the true Dhamma (*na saddhammagarutā*).
In the second, it is the opposite of respect for the true Dhamma; or rather, respect for the true Dhamma itself is the opposite.
Thus, the meaning here is "by way of the diversity of the opposite of respect for the true Dhamma."

It should be understood thus: for those who value anger, slander, and ill-will, loving-kindness—which is distinguished by the True Dhamma—is the antidote because it differs from them in its mode of occurrence.
For those who value gain and honor, fewness of wishes and contentment are the antidotes. Therefore, the meaning stated here is that one who values anger does not value the True Dhamma;
thus, valuing anger is the opposite of a certain kind of valuing the True Dhamma. The same applies to valuing slander and so forth.

And by doing so, the scriptural passage that has come down, “There are four true qualities: reverence for the True Dhamma, not reverence for anger... [and so on] ...reverence for the True Dhamma, not reverence for honor,” is also validated.
“Greed does not exist” means non-greed (*alobha*); “the state of being greedy does not exist” means non-greediness (*alubbhana*).
In this way, the negation of greed and the other [defilements], such as non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth, is distinguished from greed and the rest. Contact (*phassa*)...
Because they differ in nature from [the terms] beginning with "contact" (*phusanā*), it is stated that "there is a distinction by way of contact and so forth.

Here, it should be understood that non-greed (*alubbhana*) and the rest are also included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). The phrase "by way of the opposites of greed and so forth" should be applied as follows:
"non-greed is the opposite of greed," and so on. The remainder is exactly as before. [This is due to] the absence of discordance in non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

And since it is obtained by way of being an opposite, it is understood through its mutual dissimilarity [to greed], through its state of negating greed and so forth, and through its state of being the antidote to greed and so forth;

thus he said, “It should be connected as ‘non-greed’... and so on. The quality of having great meaning consists in the fact that the matter must be illustrated in many ways for the sake of the listeners' respect.
3. Even if there is only a single object at one moment, it is said “or by those [six bases],” etc., because they are capable of arising with respect to all six types of objects.
“Of that”: of the gratification that is pleasure (*sukha*). To show the meaning of the word “born” (*jātā*), it is said:

“functioning for the sake of contact (*phassa*) by way of being its cause. This is what is meant: just as the feeling of mental joy (*somanassavedanā*), which is reckoned as the gratification of mental factors (*cetasika-sāta*), [arises].
It arises together with that; thus, having occurred in association with a contact corresponding to it, it is called "of that kind" (*tajjā*).
It causes to decay (*sādayati*); that is, by the desire for attainment, it makes [the mind] incline toward nothing else. Regarding the phrase "not of that kind" (*na tassā tajjā*):

whether one takes it as "not born from that" (*na tassā jātā*) or as "not of the same nature as that" (*na tassā rūpā*), it refers to the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). In both ways, it is so designated.

“Arising from that” (tajjatā) is not tenable. Even if contact is not a specific condition for consciousness, it nevertheless remains its condition; thus, with reference to the objection that it should be called “arisen from contact with the mind-consciousness element arising from that,” he says, “And not that very [contact],” and so forth.
By the meaning of “arisen from those objects” (*tajjā*), it is also called “arisen from contact with the mind-consciousness element arising from that” (*tajjā manoviññāṇadhātusamphassajā*).
It is not possible to speak [of consciousness itself in that way]. However, the designation of consciousness as "conditioned by such-and-such" (tajjatā) is indeed obtainable.
For it is said, starting with "What is the use of this?", that contact and the other factors should be taught in that same manner.

7. Vitakka (initial application) occurs in the mode of bringing the mind toward its object; in its actual meaning, it is as if it draws the object toward the mind. Therefore, it is stated: "Vitakka is the drawing of the object."

8. Sustained thought (*vicāra*) occurs as a mode of repeatedly rubbing over the object; because it moves all around it, as if wandering about there, it is said that "wandering all around is *vicaraṇa*. 11.

Likewise, "by way of the state of being established" means by way of the state of being established in the performance of killing living beings and so forth; the intention is that it is not by way of its being powerful. 14.

That quality by which the object stands near to and shines forth in the mind is called "standing near" (*upaṭṭhāna*) and "shining forth" (*jotana*). Therefore he says: "Standing near and shining forth are mindfulness itself."
16. "In the sense of being subtle" means in the sense of being refined.
30. "State of being" refers to the act of feeling shame.
33. "One should not harbor ill will" expresses the objective case of the term *abyāpajja*.
42–43. If lightness (*lahutā*) is the capacity for very rapid transformation in those states that are blameless (*anavajja*), then how is it so for states that are blamable (*sāvajja*)?
To this he says, “of those hindered by ignorance,” and so forth.

By the phrase “the state of these is heaviness” (*garutā*), he shows that although all immaterial states (*arūpadhamma*) are equal in their momentary duration, those associated with delusion (*moha*) possess an especially sluggish mode of occurrence.
However, their sluggish state is manifest within the continuum.
44–45. Non-resistance is non-opposition.
46–47. "Moistened" means permeated.

50–51. Retreating is deceit; it is also called "that which exceeds. Anointing a wound is the application of ointment to a sore. A bamboo stalk itself, when taken as something to be given, is called a "gift of bamboo.
The commentary on the section of the Niddesa is finished.
Commentary on the section of the Divisions (Koṭṭhāsavāra).

58–120. "Those beginning with contact as the fifth": "By way of inclusion alone" means by some common characteristic such as shared nature, and not by way of being separate entities like contact and the others;
this is the meaning. Likewise, "because they are not scattered" means because they are not stated individually in their own form, as contact and the others are.
Even though desire and the rest [are mentioned] in their own form in the sections on inclusion and emptiness...

They are not explicitly mentioned [there], but it is said "because, however... and so forth to show that they are indeed included within the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).

In the "Description of That" (taṃniddesa)—that is, in the description of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)—since there is no deviation from the aggregates' being bases and elements, one should understand that by precluding their status as non-aggregates, their status as non-bases and non-elements is also precluded. They are not merely occasional (na yevāpanaka).
"They should be excluded" is said with reference to their being included within the aggregates and so forth. However, regarding the enumerations (uddesa) and so on, the Commentary states:
"It is appropriate that those which are described as 'only-included' (yevāpanaka) should be grouped exactly as such. Thus it says, "having excluded the only-included ones.

Even for those factors not mentioned by name, their status as aggregates and so forth—which are comprised within the arising of consciousness—cannot be denied; therefore, they are not "only-included."
The phrase "it should be set aside" is stated; this is the intended meaning for both [the preceding and following passages].
By the term "nutriment-condition" (āhāra-paccaya) is meant that which is reckoned as a supporting condition (upatthambhaka-paccaya).

This is stated because the status of nutritions as supporting conditions is well-known, not because they lack the quality of being productive (janakatta). For it is through the nourishing of the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence (oja) and of feeling and the other [mental aggregates] that they function as nutritions.

"Their status as producers is obtained. If "condition" here is intended in the sense of a supporting condition (*upatthambhaka-paccaya*), then let that apply to physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) for now;

but how does it apply to the others? To this he says, "Just as... and so forth. By "co-nascent and other conditions," he refers to the co-nascent (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), association (*sampayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*) conditions, or else to the Great Tetrad (*mahācatukka*).
By the phrase "in one way," he expresses the state of being helpful through the manner of supporting both the material and the immaterial.

And such is their function of bringing [the path] about. Because of the statement, "With volitional formations as condition, consciousness," the status of volition as a condition for consciousness is particularly prominent;
thus he said, "consciousness by way of distinction.

It should be understood that the expression "the path as it has come" is used through the metaphorical treatment of cause and fruit as non-different; [it refers to] the eightfold path belonging to different moments.

“Having this as its decisive support” means having the eightfold path as its decisive support (*aṭṭhaṅgikamaggūpanissaya*). When the noble path is spoken of by way of its designation as the “path already traversed,” it clarifies the following point:
that [the path] is not too dissimilar from the state of arrival (*āgamanāvatthā*) which existed previously as its undifferentiated basis and was established through figurative usage (*abhedopacāra*).
Therefore, he said: “The preliminary stage... is illustrated. The variegated nature of consciousness (*viññāṇassa cittavicittatā*) refers to specific distinctions in the mode of cognizing.

Thus he said: “The very act of cognizing is the variety of consciousness. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “the aggregate of feeling, etc.,” he includes the mental base (*manāyatana*) and so forth mentioned in such passages as “there are two bases.
“Its negation” means the negation of that state of being a description by way of genus (*jātiniddesa*).
By the words “is made,” [it is implied] how many causes—namely, nutriment, faculties, jhāna factors, path factors, and fruits—there are in this consciousness.

He shows that all those [nutriments] which can be obtained—even if not explicitly stated in the passage beginning with "There is one nutriment, consciousness"—are nevertheless already stated by implication.
This same method applies elsewhere as well.
The commentary on the section concerning the analysis of components is concluded.
Commentary on the Section on Emptiness (Suññatavāra), §§121–145.
"In the aforementioned occasion" means in the collection of the types of occasions already described.
§146. "Ussāhanaṃ" means instigation, sending forth, or enjoining.

156–159. “Not too concentrated” (*nātisamāhitāya*) is said with reference to the proximity of various acts of adverting (*āvajjana*). It shows that there is no distinction [from other wholesome states] even among the “miscellaneous” (*yevāpanaka*) states, because compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) also arise therein.

“Bodily and verbal action” (*kāyavacīkiriyā*) refers to the occurrence of body and speech, or simply to intimation (*viññatti*). “Incomplete development” (*asamattabhāvanaṃ*) refers to the preliminary stage of development (*pubbabhāgabhāvanā*).
The commentary on the wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) is finished.
The Fourfold Method of the Wholesome States of the Fine-Material Sphere:
An Exposition of the Discussion on the First Jhāna.

160. It should be understood that by eliding the latter member of the compound, "form-existence" (rūpabhava) is spoken of as simply "form" (rūpa), as in such cases as "one possessing form sees forms" (rūpī rūpāni passati) and "lust for form" (rūparāga).
Since the jhāna of form achieved through practice serves as a means even for transcending form-existence, this restriction—that it is a path only for rebirth in the form realm—is not tenable;
likewise [it is not tenable] due to the absence of other requisite conditions and so forth.
Since that which does not produce rebirth in the form realm also exists [as a factor], the restriction that "this alone is the path to rebirth in the form realm" is likewise untenable.

And this being the case, it raises the following objection: "It follows that only that which produces rebirth in the form realm possesses the status of a wholesome state of the form realm associated with it, and not that which does not produce it."
"Not of all wholesome jhāna," and so forth. In that context, even though it is a general term (*sāmañña-sadda*), it is indicated as a specific qualification by virtue of the topical heading;
thus it is said: "the state of being a path for wholesome jhāna.

The nature of producing rebirth in the fine-material realm is the nature of ripening into the fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*); therefore, although that [existence] also possesses the quality of being a result-of-ripening (*vipāka-dhamma*), [it is not the path].

The commonality of being a state subject to result (vipākadhammabhāva-sāmañña), which is shared by all wholesome and unwholesome states, is stated as an illustration in the phrase "just like the state of being subject to result.
For even a commonality is expressed by distinguishing it from its particulars.

"Common to all" refers to everything that has been attained, whether it is productive of rebirth in the form realm due to the presence of other requisite conditions, or non-productive due to the absence of such conditions.
It is common to jhāna. By this, he shows that the restriction of the subsequent term is encompassed.

Through the phrase "there is no other path than this," it should be understood that the state of being the means for rebirth in the form realm (rūpūpapatti) for this jhāna has been stated as being common to its own class, excluded from other classes, and not shared by anything else. The other two are faith and moral shame (hirī).

Now, if the determination of the occasion (*samayavavatthāna*) was made by one who develops [the path] through a teaching preceded by the person (*puggalapubbaṅgamā*), because it is to be accomplished by means of the practice (*paṭipadā*), then how is it [accomplished] for those devoid of such practice?
To this he says, "of some" (*kesañci*), and so forth. Therein, "of some" refers to those who have performed the preliminary work (*katādhikāra*) in the development of serenity (*samatha*).
For prior to their attainment of the Path, while they have not yet attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and so on [arise].
Just as by the attainment of the path, those [qualities] are accomplished;
"other" means other than what is established by the noble path. "Even in those" refers even to those devoid of the practice, because they are established by the noble path.
But is it not the case that even for one established by the noble path, the practice is indeed found by way of its approach? Otherwise, "not..."

Would this not contradict the statements: "It arises without a path of practice, just like that pertaining to the sense-sphere," and "Even most mundane jhāna does not succeed without a path of practice"?

No, because [the former statement] refers to the majority of cases and because it depends on a specific type of person. For jhāna that brings about the Noble Path occurs only for some; therefore, the other, more common mundane jhāna—
It is stated with reference to the worldling and the noble one who has not yet performed the preliminary service that [the attainment] is not accomplished without the practice (*paṭipadā*).

Even for the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) accomplished by the Noble Path, because it lacks similarity to the wholesome Noble Path—just as in the case of its results (*vipāka*)—and because it does not have that as its result, the designation "practice" is not applicable in the sense of proceeding along the path; thus, its lack of practice is established.
And by doing so, even the "pure" teaching for novices is properly brought to its conclusion. Thus he will say in the discussion on the supramundane:
"Even mundane jhāna," and so forth.

By way of attenuating the craving that serves as the specific condition for the inclination toward the round of existence (*vaṭṭāsayo*), there is an increase in the inclination toward the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭāsayo*).

He said: "By the cleansing of the defilement of craving, there is the nourishment of the disposition. And "nourishment of the disposition" refers to the perfection of underlying inclination (ajjhāsaya-sampadā), established through previous application and other means, which serves as a condition for the development of jhāna.
Since that [perfection] occurs through the removal of the torment of craving, he said:
"by the cleansing of the defilement of craving."
“Of sloth and torpor, etc. means of sloth, torpor, restlessness, worry, and doubt. “Abandoning” means that which abandons.
“In those similar to it” means in those similar to the concentration of the first jhāna by way of their sublime state and so forth.
Showing that the jhāna possessing rapture and pleasure is called “rapture and pleasure,” as in the expression “the noble son,” he says: “Rapture and pleasure….”

"The letter 'a' has been spoken," he said. Alternatively, the state of being a contemplation on the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇa) should be applied to the Path as well, because it has Nibbāna as its object.
"Of a nature not subject to confusion" means having a quality of non-destruction.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Second Jhāna.

161–162. The terms "stilling" (*vūpasama*), "fading away" (*virajjana*), and "abandoning" (*pahāna*)—referring to the state of being subject to non-arising at the moment of each respective *jhāna* for those [hindrances] whose dangers have been seen—apply here only to the applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth that constitute the *jhāna*-factors;

they do not apply to the contact (*phassa*) and other factors associated with them. Thus, the statement regarding the stilling and so forth of applied thought and the rest is logically established. For:
However, just like applied thought (*vitakka*) and the others, the mental states associated with them are also seen as coarse because of the disadvantages [of those states] perceived by this [path];
therefore, when the subsiding and so forth of applied thought and the rest, along with their co-nascent factors, should be stated without distinction,

the fact that only the subsiding and so forth of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are mentioned indicates some specific distinction, according to the principle that "the mention of a superior term makes known another meaning."
Showing this, he said, “By those applied thought and sustained thought,” and so forth. He stated, “Of these...

it is called the illuminator,” showing that although the terms “surmounting applied and sustained thought” and so on stand separately, they are taken as a collective whole by means of a common mental factor—namely, the designation of what is to be abandoned—and thus a part is used to characterize the whole. Now, [regarding] the characterization of the whole by a part:

By stating "Alternatively," etc., he shows that the expressions "fading away of rapture" and so forth perform the same function regarding their respective objects even without the explicit mention of the subsiding of initial application and sustained application.
"When that has been shown" refers to when "serenity" has been shown in the *Jhānavibhaṅga* by the passage beginning, "That faith which is believing... and so forth.

"By the very same grammatical coordination (samānādhikaraṇa) exposition" means by the statement of the single common substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatā*) for faith and jhāna as "tranquillity" (*sampasādana*) in the very same Vibhaṅga,
within the extraction of the summary phrases (*uddesapada*) and so forth.

The suppression of the respective attachment to each jhāna— which was described as "mindfulness in accordance with that" (*tadanudhammatā sati*)— is effected by way of the coarse factor (*oḷārika-aṅga*).
