It is said that [the cessation of applied and sustained thought] is revealed by such statements as "the subsiding of applied and sustained thought"; thus he says, "The abandonment of craving is their subsiding.
Since the statement "the subsiding of applied and sustained thought" indicates a state of detachment from applied and sustained thought, the phrase "and those which...
and so forth was spoken to show how it further indicates the absence of both of them.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Third Jhāna (163).
It is said that "equanimity is energy" because it is "regarded with equanimity by not performing any intervention in either stimulation or suppression.

It is "equanimity regarding formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) because it regards formations with a state of neutrality during the act of grasping; it is the wisdom of insight proceeding in such a manner.

Regarding its classification by way of object, he says "the first jhāna," etc., showing the remainder of that scriptural passage in which it was stated as "the eight equanimities toward formations" and so forth.
Therein, "arising" (uppāda) means the occurrence here through the condition of prior karma;
"occurrence" (pavatta) means the continued existence of what has thus arisen; and "sign" (nimitta) refers to the entire range of conditioned phenomena.
Because it appears as a sign (*nimitta*). "Accumulation" (*āyūhana*) refers to karma that serves as the cause for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the future.

"Rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*) refers to arising in the future. "Destiny" (*gati*) refers to the particular realm of existence in which that rebirth-linking occurs. "Generation" (*nibbatti*) refers to the manifestation of the aggregates (*khandha*).

"Arising" (*upapatti*) refers to the occurrence of result (*vipākappavatti*), as expressed in the phrase "of one who has entered [a meditative attainment] or of one who has arisen [in a new existence]."
Birth (*jāti*) is that which serves as the condition for aging and the rest; it is "birth conditioned by becoming" (*bhavapaccayā jāti*). Aging, death, and so forth are indeed well-known.

Here, only the five beginning with arising (*uppāda*) are mentioned by way of being the objects of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*); the remaining terms are synonyms for them.
Indeed, this pair—"origination" (*nibbatti*) and "birth"—are synonyms for both arising and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Destination" (*gati*) and "reappearance" (*upapatti*)...
"And ‘and’" refers to these two [aging and death] which pertain to what is occurring.
"Aging and so forth" pertain to the sign. "Of the become" means of the five aggregates. "By these" means by the material phenomena produced by the jhāna-consciousness.
The commentary on the fourfold method is concluded.
Commentary on the Fivefold Method (Pañcakanayavaṇṇanā) 167.
"Difference in aspect" (ākārabheda) means a distinction in aspect. For phenomena possess manifold aspects, and the Blessed One has fully awakened to them all exactly as they are, without exception.
As it is said: "All phenomena in all their aspects are [known] by the Buddha, the Blessed One..."
"It comes within the range of the door of knowledge. The intention is that it belongs to the category of the second jhāna, not the category of the first jhāna.
For this very reason he said, "Indeed, it is the first jhāna itself," and so forth. In terms of actual meaning, the fourfold and fivefold methods do not enter into one another.
In the fivefold method, is the second jhāna on the side of the first jhāna because of its possession of vicāra, or rather because of its absence of vitakka?
The phrase "belonging to the second jhāna" might give rise to doubt; therefore, this was stated in order to dispel that doubt.
He states the reason for this with the words "Why? and so forth. The connection is: "And in the teachings of the Suttantas, they associate [it] with the second jhāna itself.

By the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that this applies not only here, but also in the teachings of the Suttantas—in other words, that the aforementioned jhāna is treated in the same way in other discourses as well.

This shows the absence of being a factor belonging to the first jhāna. Now, in order to show the classification as well, "with the stilling of applied thought" and so forth is stated. By this, he shows that the fivefold method is also found in the Suttanta.
But is it not the case that only four jhānas are analyzed in the Suttanta, so that the fivefold method does not exist there at all? No; for [it says] "with applied thought and sustained thought..."
Because the fivefold method (pañcakanaya) is obtainable through the designation of the threefold concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth;
however, since the fivefold method is analyzed by way of the fourfold method, the fivefold method must also be extracted from that context.
For it can be said that "the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought" refers to applied thought, sustained thought, and both applied and sustained thoughts.
Likewise, regarding the phrase "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (*avitakka-avicāra*),

it is possible to include all three types— *avitakka*, *avicāra*, and *avitakka-avicāra*— by taking *avitakka* as the abandoning of applied thought either with or without sustained thought, and *avicāra* as the abandoning of sustained thought either with or without applied thought.

"Second" refers to the teaching that has come down by way of the proper method (*ñāya*) for those [meditations] devoid of applied thought (*vitakka*), and for those devoid of both applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicāra*). It is "second" because it is to be attained secondly;
furthermore, even in the case of that which is devoid of sustained thought alone, it is so called because the state of attainment is the same through the abandoning of the pair [of thoughts].

And having established this, in the exposition of the fivefold method (*pañcakanaya-niddesa*), it is said that in the second [jhāna], although applied thought has subsided, it is not "completely subsided" because its companion, sustained thought, has not yet subsided; thus, it is [the stage] devoid of both applied and sustained thought.

By showing that its subsiding occurs through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicāra*) alone, and that it shares the same nature as the remaining factors, the third jhāna— described as "with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,

he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and is born of concentration, consisting of rapture and happiness"— is shown to be indistinguishable from the second [jhāna] in the fourfold system.

It is analyzed. Because both types share the quality of being "without applied thought" (*avitakka*) due to the absence of a companion [thought] and the abandonment of applied thought in another way, and because they share the state of "joy and bliss born of concentration" (*samādhija-pītisukha*), it is designated as "the second" on account of these common characteristics.

For even that which consists of mere sustained thought (*vicāramatta*)—being like that which is devoid of the pair of applied and sustained thought—is described thus: "At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, which is without applied thought and with mere sustained thought... (*yasmiṃ samaye rūpūpapattāya maggaṃ bhāveti avitakkavicāramattaṃ*).

"Having attained and dwelt in the second jhāna, which is born of concentration and possesses rapture and happiness"— thus it is analyzed as "rapture and happiness born of concentration without applied thought.
Or else, having transcended one of the two concomitants, applied thought and sustained thought, in the first jhāna,
and seeing even the second as faulty for being present there, for one who transcends both together, this is the third [jhāna] according to the fivefold method.
The third [set] is so called because it is to be attained. Furthermore, its status as the second arises by virtue of its immediate succession to the first.
But why is the fivefold method not analyzed here according to its own specific form? Because of the inclination of those to be trained; for the teaching of the Suttantas follows a progressive order.
Commentary on the Fourfold Path, etc.
(176–180). "Conformable to that" means having a nature corresponding to that first jhāna and so forth.
Having viewed the jhāna as it was attained as peaceful and sublime, one relishes it; the attachment associated with that [relishing], or the aggregates that serve to protect it, [is what is meant].
Or rather, mindfulness is called "conformity to that" (tadanudhammatā) because it is suitable for that very jhāna.
"Sometimes" means when, having attained the first jhāna, one attains the second and subsequent ones while remaining in the same posture without further effort; this is the meaning in such a case.

It is said they are "trainers" (sekkhā) because they have attained wholesome jhāna. He says this not because they do not actually produce them, but with reference to the fact that fine-material-sphere jhānas do not arise at the moment of the noble path (ariyamagga).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Kasiṇas (Kasiṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 203.

And the fact that they serve as a basis for the formless attainments is shown by their absence [in the higher stages]; for there is no capacity to produce the cessation attainment without the capacity to produce the formless attainments.
"Quickly attending" (khippanisanti) means attending, observing, or perceiving by way of the creation of the object desired to be created.
"Attainment of this" means "quick penetration. Its state is "the state of quick penetration," which is why it is said: "quick vision, quick direct knowledge.
The commentary on the discussion of the kasiṇas is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) follows.
204. It is called a *kasiṇāyatana* because its cause (*āyatana*)—meaning its basis—is the counterpart sign known as the *kasiṇa*-object;

thus it is the jhāna. Alternatively, it is both a *kasiṇa*—in the sense of pervading the object without remainder—and an *āyatana*, because it serves as the foundation for the yogi’s specific types of happiness and because it constitutes the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*), together with its associated states.
Jhāna is the kasiṇa base. For this very reason it was said: "Even though the bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) have the nature of kasiṇa bases.
The sign for development is the "sign of development" (bhāvanānimitta); its diversity consists in the limited or immeasurable extent of the object and its being perfectly pure blue and so forth.
Alternatively, the development itself in its prior stage is the "sign of development," and the diversity of that is the "diversity of the sign of development."
For the preliminary development (pubbabhāgabhāvanā) possesses various intrinsic natures due to the differences in the mode of its occurrence toward the aforementioned specific objects.
The diversity of the signs of the preliminary development that overcomes the kasiṇa-sign should be connected [to the diversity of the kasiṇas]... [and thus] the diversity [of the bases].
And here, the first four bases of mastery have the primary kasiṇas as their objects; and among the primary kasiṇas—

That which cannot be described as either "beautiful" or "ugly"—the first and third bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) that occur therein, occurring everywhere without the application of attention to color—have the color-kasina as their object.
If this is so, what is the distinction between the fifth and subsequent bases compared to the second and fourth?
[The answer is: "The fifth and subsequent ones are more delightful in terms of color."
They say, "The others are not like that. The first four [liberations] also have the eight kasiṇas as their objects;
therefore, that is merely their opinion because they are stated as being "among the eight kasiṇas. Among the liberations, the first and second liberations have the eight kasiṇas as their objects.
The third has a color-kasiṇa as its object. Alternatively, the first and second also have a color-kasiṇa as their object.
This is because it has been stated: "One sees external forms, such as the blue kasiṇa and so forth, with the eye of jhāna.
For in that case, due to the agreeableness of the object, they proceed without having emerged from the attainment. This being so, what is the distinction of the third [jhāna] from the others?
It is the mental application to the aspect of the beautiful (*subhākārābhoga*). For it is only the third that proceeds by way of inclining toward "the beautiful," whereas the others do not.
Knowledge is the wisdom of absorption (*appanā-paññā*). By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even when existing," he shows that it also applies when not existing.
The intention is that limited magnitude is the cause for mastery in these four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

But is it not the case that because the expression "beautiful and ugly" occurs everywhere, they are understood as being accompanied by attention to color (*vaṇṇābhoga*)? Showing that they are not so understood:

He says, “And therein,” and so forth. “Therein” means in the Āgamas. “Likewise immeasurable” means that all immeasurable [forms], being devoid of the apprehension of color, are both beautiful and ugly; this is the meaning.

If this is so, how does one bring to mind together those distinguished forms—both those devoid of the apprehension of color and those possessing it? Not together; rather, the attention toward them is distinct for each.

If they are distinct, how can they be one? Because they share the commonality of being limited (*paritta*). If that is so, [the objection] that "it is redundant to mention both 'beautiful' and 'ugly'" is not redundant; showing this, he says, "For there is this method," and so forth.

In that context, without grasping the specific distinction produced by the mental application to color, but rather leading them to unity through their commonality of being limited, [he says]: "The limited..."
Having said "having overcome," in order to further show the classification of the phenomena included therein according to the persons to be trained, he says:
"If those [objects] are at times attended to by way of color—whether beautiful or ugly—one should say 'having overcome';

thus, having mentally attended to them both together and separately while devoid of attention to color, in both cases there is the overcoming of the limited (paritta) while being devoid of attention to color.

The intention is this: by taking the commonality of "overcoming the limited" (*parittābhibhavana*) with "overcoming the limited together" (*sahitaparittābhibhavana*), the expression "one" (*ekaṃ*) is used;
such a methodological approach (*pariyāya*) exists.

Having thus demonstrated the absence of contradiction with the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) despite the differences in the readings of the Sutta and Abhidhamma, [the author now addresses] the readings of the Sutta and Abhidhamma...

In order to show that there is no contradiction by clarifying the intended meaning, he said, “And therein,” and so forth. Thus, in the Abhidhamma, they are described both separately and together, being devoid of attention to color.
But in the Suttanta, it is said, “both together as one”; how is this to be understood? To this he said, “That which here,” and so forth.
Therein, “of what has come” means of what has come in the Suttanta; for therein [it says]: “Internally...”
The phrase "perceiving forms" has been stated. Regarding the term "because it is not mentioned": this means because it is not mentioned in the Abhidhamma.

Even though the liberations (vimokkha) are taught separately, since the spheres of mastery (abhibhāyatana) possess the function of liberation just as the kasiṇa-bases do, one might object that a confusion between the spheres of mastery and the liberations here is unavoidable.
Bearing this objection in mind, he says: "Because they share the status of being terms common to all the functions of liberation."

This shows that just as the functions of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) were stated in their entirety in the teaching on the bases of mastery, so too are the functions of the liberations (*vimokkha*) stated here in the teaching on the liberations; thus, there is no confusion between them.
Furthermore, for those who do not accept the aforementioned definition [of these functions], there is a distinction in the textual readings of the Suttantas and the Abhidhamma.
Another reason might be stated. What is there to be said?

Has it not been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—after saying, "But why [is it not mentioned] as in the Suttanta," and so forth—that the reason is "because internal material phenomena are not to be overcome"? No;
showing that that was not the statement of the actual reason for this case, he says, "Because internal material phenomena," and so forth. In that context, the word "which" (*yaṃ*) refers here to...
He says this with reference to the statement in the Sutta: "he sees forms externally. For it is only external forms that are to be mastered.
"Having another cause" means that its cause for being mastered is something other [than internal form], owing to the elegance of the teaching.
It is precisely by virtue of the perception of non-materiality internally, and not by virtue of the perception of materiality internally as in the Sutta.

The meaning is as follows. Regarding the phrase "because it is not clearly manifest": this is stated on the grounds that for those whose knowledge is supreme, the production of absorption (appanā) together with the arising of the sign is impossible without the object being in a state of perfect clarity; thus, the "overpowering" of the object occurs. Now, one might ask:

"But was it not stated in the Commentary that the distinction between the two readings is due to the cause of the Teacher’s skill in exposition? To this he replies: "And the skill in exposition is by way of the aforementioned definition."

“It must be understood. For what is called the "elegance of teaching" (desanāvilāsa) is the elucidation of an existing method of exposition in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, and not just any method whatsoever.

And therein, by the phrase “because it is a teaching by way of a method” and so forth, he states the basis for the elegance of the teaching, which is the aforementioned determination of its specific mode.
Indeed, the elegance of the teaching is thus elucidated further on.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Bases of Mastery is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Liberations: 248.

The word "that" refers to the color of the hair and so forth mentioned as "matter included within one's own continuity. Furthermore, because that [color] is like the husks in a threshing floor and so forth...
Because it is, as it were, the cause of jhāna through a continuous succession, he said, "by way of being the cause of jhāna. "By which" means by the specific kind of form already mentioned.

"By the distinguished" refers to the jhāna of form—which is called simply "form" here through the elision of the latter member of the compound, as in the expression "rebirth in the form realm" (*rūpūpapatti*)—which has reached a state of excellence (*atisaya*).
By the word "distinguished," he shows that one who possesses such excellent form is called "possessed of form" (*rūpī*).
“Having attained and dwelling in the first jhāna with the earth-kasiṇa,” and so forth—in these cases, it is the jhānas themselves that occur in the mode of being kasiṇas.
In the Sutta, however, it is the objects that occur in the mode of being kasiṇas, as in: “One perceives the earth-kasiṇa,” and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the liberations is finished.
251. Furthermore, the feeling of equanimity associated with ignorance is "equanimity-ignorance" (*aññāṇupekkhā*). As it will be stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*:
"Equanimity is the feeling of equanimity associated with ignorance; 'equanimity-ignorance' is also a name for these very same [states]."

Even though they have as their object a sign that has no counterpart, how can those [perceptions] that occur with reference to one or a few beings be said to have an immeasurable range (*appamāṇagocara*), given that they occur within the scope of limited form and so forth which serve as their material cause? To this he says: "And not by way of conventional truth," and so on.
Even in this case, just as the wrong view that "there are no spontaneously born beings" has formations as its object even though it occurs in terms of beings, [so too here].
If it is argued that, by way of clinging (*upādāna*), even loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables] occurring by way of a living being (*satta*) might have formations as their object,

[the author] says "without misapprehension" (*aparāmāsa*) and so forth, demonstrating that for loving-kindness and the others which occur without misapprehension, it is impossible for them to be grasped together with clinging.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Abodes is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Foulness:
Regarding the nine charnel grounds described by way of color in the passage beginning, "One dead for one day, or dead for two days," and so forth:

The jhāna occurring in a charnel ground is the jhāna on the appearance of a corpse. Is it not the case that its apprehension by means of the color-kasiṇas would be more appropriate than by means of the foulness [meditations]?
No; for, having taken the appearance of a charnel ground as a simile, it proceeds by way of color without abandoning the repulsiveness in one's own body.
Therefore he said: "by way of the commonality of attention to repulsiveness. This is the meaning of the jhāna on the appearance of a charnel ground.
Explaining that this should also be applied here, he says, "That too," and so forth.
The commentary on the discourse on foulness is finished.
The commentary on the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Wholesome States of the Formless Sphere (Arūpāvacarakusala-kathāvaṇṇanā) 265. "The sign of form" means having form as its cause, having form as its basis.

"In regard to the signs of form and formlessness" means in regard to both material phenomena and the signs such as the earth-kasiṇa, etc. "In the jhānas that have those as their object": here, by the word "those" (taṃ), the sign of form is referred to.
One attends to form (*rūpa*) as well, because fine-material-sphere jhānas can have both forms and mental states associated with forms as their objects. "In regard to forms, etc.
means in regard to the signs of form and the formless, the jhānas having those as objects, and those phenomena connected with form.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes such factors as the lack of desire to attain [the jhāna].
“Cutting off” means transcending those things that are liable to arise by bringing about their state of non-arising...

By this phrase, "because it is to be transcended," he shows that there is no distinction between the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the resultant or functional states of the fine-material sphere, because [the latter] have not yet been attained.

To show those perceptions of form (*rūpasaññā*) and so forth for which the transcending and so on through the development of the immaterial (*arūpa*) is possible, [he says]: "By the development of the immaterial..."

It is said that "in the absence [of form], there is no arising after death for those who are incapable of rebirth. Here, "form" refers to the remaining limited resultant perceptions and so forth, which depend on a specific form.

Since the non-percipient state, the attainment of peace, the experience of bliss, and rebirth in a particular existence are the purposes of the formless attainments, he says: "The perception of form...
there is no purpose. The intention here is that, by way of the "opened kasiṇa," there is a limited infinity, as this is a teaching according to the direct method (nippariyāya).
If this is so, how is it that the term "base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) is used when the limited kasiṇa has been removed?
Because even there, the state of infinite pervasion exists. For this very reason, he said: "Because of the existence of infinite pervasion.

If infinite pervasion exists everywhere, then why was it not stated as "infinite space"? He replied: "Because of the establishment of a specific occasion," and so forth. In that context, "practice" (*paṭipatti*) means...
He states the mode of development for the jhānas. 266.
*Ugghāṭima* is the state of being opened up, just as *pākima* [is the state of being cooked]. 268.
Having extracted the term "third" based on its logical connection and scriptural authority, [it follows] from the transcendence of consciousness that functions in space.
To clarify this meaning, he said, "Because of transcending that," and so forth.

Since the formless attainments (ārūppasamāpatti) are to be reached by transcending their objects, the specific observation of faults in the object is the logical reason why that very object must be transcended.
Furthermore, when the object is transcended, the jhāna which had that as its object is also necessarily transcended. This is the disappearance of the object through meditative development (bhāvanā).

“Removal” means elimination. “In the text” refers to the Vibhaṅga. But has it not been stated in the text without qualification as “that very consciousness,” rather than “not the consciousness of the base of infinite space”?
Showing that this meaning is established by the specific statement “not that very consciousness,” he says: “the base of infinite consciousness,” and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of wholesome states of the formless realm is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the wholesome states of the three planes. 269.
"By means of seven great sections" refers to the sections on the questions concerning dependence, co-nascence, conditionality, support, association, and conjunction.
The methods such as the positive-negative, the negative-positive, and the negative-positive-positive are the "positive and other methods.
Just as there are forty-eight fundamental lineages in the world, such as the Bhāradvāja and Gotama, so too are there forty-eight branches, such as the Kaṭṭhakalāpa;
thus he said, "forty-eight," and so forth. In that context, "of them" refers to those who are capable and incapable. By way of the "gate" (dvāra)...
With the intention that "those which possess doors are to be grasped," he said: "or the various doors, such as the body and so forth. That which is done without careful attention is inferior;
that which is done with equanimity is middling; that which is done with thorough care is sublime. Alternatively, that which is done for the sake of material gain, fame, and the like is inferior;
that which is done out of a desire for the fruit of merit is middling; [that which is done] by one established in the state of a noble one, thinking simply "this must be done," is sublime.
It is "excellent" (paṇīta). That which is set in motion by greed for success in existence is inferior; that set in motion with an intention free from greed is middling;

that set in motion for the welfare of others is excellent. Or, that which is done to a limited extent is inferior; that done to a moderate extent is middling; that done to an excessive extent is excellent.
Furthermore, among the sublime states, that which is merely attained is inferior; that which is not well-cultivated is middling.
It is middling, well-developed, reached its peak, and sublime.
It should be understood that even for each of these [types], a distinction such as "inferior" and so forth is indeed obtainable by way of their different modes of exertion and so on.

Alternatively, the meaning here is this: the state of being dominated by the mind—which belongs to the mental factors associated with the mind and is produced by the power of the mind—is metaphorically attributed (upacāra) to that mind which serves as their basis.
The exposition of the wholesome states of the three planes is finished.
Regarding the exposition of the supramundane wholesome states:
the passage beginning with “In what sense is it ‘supramundane’? is a statement from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* cited in the commentary; therefore...

Therein, since it is summarized by the passage beginning, “The unsurpassed Dhamma, in its threefold way, crosses over the world,” he says, “By this [phrase] ‘crosses over the world,’ etc.,” in order to demonstrate that by connecting it with the three terms.
This should be applied to each [term], because the state of reaching the end of the world and so forth is found even in the paths and other factors.
Or rather, all three meanings should be connected to the path alone; such is the connection. “Not overstepping, etc. means:

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes these three specific kinds of development (*bhāvanāvisesa*): the single-flavor state (*ekarasa*) of the faculties, the driving of the energy that conforms to them, and cultivation (*āsevana*).

And because these specific kinds of development are accomplished through a particular kind of knowledge produced by preliminary wisdom—which consists in seeing the respective dangers and advantages regarding defilement and purification, as well as the rounds of existence and its cessation—therefore it is said: "They mutually... increase."
"It is a support" (*nissaya*) means that it is designated as such by way of being a basis, like a tree for its branches.
The statement regarding the fruit-knowledge and the factors of the fruit as "support" is because they possess the condition of a support (*nissaya-paccaya*).

Precisely because of this state of being a support and a foundation, the Noble Ones—having relied upon the Noble Fruits, having accomplished their task, and being thoroughly disenchanted with all states of existence—remain in the world for a very long time for the benefit of others.

Although the Noble Paths abandon the defilements specifically, they nevertheless function by way of a particular mode of abandoning even those things to be abandoned by other paths, because they are the universal opposites of all unwholesome states and are opposed to all wholesome states.
To show that mode of abandoning, [the author] said: "Of the others, as darkness by the flash of lightning.
This refers to the comparison of the knowledges of the lower paths to lightning found in the Pāli.
[The defilements] have been shown. If that is so, then those defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths are intended here as "the others.
It would not be appropriate to speak of their complete eradication (*samuccheda*), for the path of seeing cannot eradicate what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If that were the case, they would necessarily be [defilements] abandonable by seeing alone. Alternatively, if "abandonment" is intended here in the sense of "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*), then—just as by the flash of lightning...

It is stated, “as if by darkness,” which is established only for preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) and is not appropriate [to say] that the supramundane path abandons defilements by way of their suppression (tadaṅga).
The same principle applies to suppression as well, because that has been accomplished pre-eminently by conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) alone.
However, if it is intended that the other defilements are those to be abandoned specifically by the first path, [then it is acceptable].

This being so, there would be no state of "the others" for them; nor is there any defilement that is not subject to falling away which is to be abandoned by seeing, nor is it reasonable to say that the defilements to be abandoned by the first path should be cut off by that flash of lightning-like [knowledge] as darkness is by light.
Thus this phrase, "the cutting off of the others...," should be examined. This also applies to mundane jhāna.

"It does not succeed without the way" (na vinā paṭipadāya ijjhati) is to be understood according to its underlying intention (*adhippāya*), as it has a meaning that requires further interpretation (*neyyattha*).

To clarify that intention, he says, "for one who has not performed the preliminary service" (*akatādhikārassa*). By this, he shows that the aforementioned statement is qualified by specific conditions (*sappadesa*).

But is it not the case that even for a Noble One (*ariya*) who has performed the preliminary service, the attainment of *jhāna*—though accomplished by means of the Path—is nevertheless [achieved] by way of the Path's method of practice (*maggapaṭipadāvasena*)?
"Only when accompanied by the practice" means that it can be said that [the goal] does not succeed without the practice;
therefore, with reference to the objection that this statement is thus incomplete, he says, "But for one who has performed the preliminary service," and so forth.
Now, showing that the intended meaning of that statement is to be understood even from the Pāḷi itself, he says, "As stated... performed."
“‘Whoever’ is a non-specific term”—showing an exception to this, he said, “once, twice,” and so forth.

“Full understanding” (*parijānana*) is grasping by way of delimitation. “Of the determination of name-and-form, etc. refers to the determination of name-and-form, the discernment of conditions, the penetration of characteristics, and the exhaustion of craving.
“From the accomplishment of the task” means from the accomplishment of the task of some or of all [these factors], such as the determination of name-and-form.
This same method applies to the second section and those that follow, as far as applicable. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of the attainment of ease":

the difficulty in accomplishing tasks such as the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāpana*) and so forth is not an absolute cause for the state of dullness in the manifestation of the path;
rather, it shows that the dullness of the faculties associated with insight (*vipassanā*) is the absolute cause thereof.

"Because this is the end of the way": by this, he shows that the quickness and slowness of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) regarding the Path—according to whether it arises quickly or slowly—is stated by way of the insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) known as purification of knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*), from the standpoint of the definitive meaning (*nippariyāyato*).
"Of the former" means of the previous sections, or specifically of the penetration of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*) and so forth. "Three times at the lower limit."

Because it has been determined that when defilements are suppressed, there is the state of being a "difficult practice" (dukkhāpaṭipadā) and nothing lower than that, he said, "by way of three occasions of suppression.
The intention is that its state as a "pleasant practice" (sukhāpaṭipadā) should be understood by way of its excellence.
In whatever person there occurs deception, breaking [of trust], and the joining with undesirable states, therein [the absence of suffering] is due solely to the lack of affection.

Their occurrence and the fact that such a person is not included [in the wholesome categories] are stated as the harshness and lack of supportiveness of false speech and the rest, due to their functions of deceiving and so forth.
Right speech, being of a nature opposed to and contrary to those, possesses a quality of lubricity and a supportive nature.
Alternatively, its lubricity should be understood as arising from its association with a particular degree of faith (*saddhā*). "It originates" means...
It causes [the mind] to proceed. It is called "cleansing" (*vodāna*) because while living, a being is cleansed by it, or associated states are cleansed by it, or it cleanses itself.
285. It is the establishment through craving and views; the accumulation through the remaining defilements and volitional formations.
It is the establishment through the view of eternalism; the accumulation through the view of annihilationism. It is the establishment through dullness; the accumulation through agitation.
Establishment by way of devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires; accumulation by way of devotion to self-mortification.
Establishment by way of all unwholesome volitional formations; accumulation by way of all mundane wholesome volitional formations.

These modes of establishment and accumulation should also be understood by way of those aspects not mentioned here, among the alternative explanations given in the commentary on the *Oghataraṇa Sutta*.

Alternatively, by the mention of "defilements" (kilesa), craving, eternalism, views, and all unwholesome volitional formations (abhisankhāra) are included, because they share that same nature and are associated with them.
Likewise, by the mention of "volitional formations," the remaining defilements, annihilationism, views, and all mundane wholesome volitional formations are included.

Since the indulgence in sloth and agitation, sensual pleasure, and self-mortification have been stated separately, they should not be combined with those [categories]; thus, it is by way of defilements and volitional formations [that the classification is made].

Having stated [the application] regarding establishment and bringing together, a coordination has also been made by way of both [craving and views] in order to illuminate their specific conditional relationship therein.
Or rather, this should be seen as a demonstration of the underlying method (*naya*) in that context. In the same way, the other modes should also be coordinated.
In such passages as, "Bhikkhus, a person endowed with four factors... the word *aṅga* (factor) should be understood in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*).

299. When speaking such things as false speech, what action is one performing that is yet to be spoken of? And what is that? It is the action of false speech and so forth; this meaning is already understood. Or rather, the construction here should be seen in this way. 301.

"Of the requisites already produced" means of the requisites such as robes and so forth. "Grounds for scheming" refers to the state of being near to noble qualities by representing oneself as such—through the practice of using coarse robes and so on based on evil desires—by saying, "He who dwells in this monastery is an Arahant," and so forth.
Unwholesome states of consciousness that arise through one’s own maintenance— acting as if one has attained distinction by means of speaking after having performed [meritorious deeds]—
are the grounds for hypocrisy (*kuhanavatthu*), which cause wonderment in others.

(343) Although the Path does not, in the ultimate sense, receive the names "signless" and so forth when its objects are virtuous qualities, it is nevertheless not [the case that] insight (*vipassanā*) is not [the signless].
Regarding the phrase "called signless": because the path does not receive the name "signless" from the perspective of its arrival, he says, "But it is not established...

[as] by means of qualities and objects. However, since for the path—which has received the names "emptiness" and "wishless" from the perspective of its arrival—there is never an absence of those names when considered from the perspective of its qualities and its object, therefore, for the sake of fulfilling the triad of names, from the perspective of its arrival...
He says, "Because it is the cause for the perfection of the name," with the intention that [the path] does not obtain a name [prior to this].

"Of all" refers to all paths that have entered the doors of liberation (*vimokkhamukha*). "The conjunction of the three names" is the conjunction of the names emptiness (*suññatā*), the wishless (*appaṇihita*), and the signless (*animitta*).

"Determination" means non-confusion. 350. Conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are the signs (*nimitta*); they appear as if possessing signs and having a graspable form. Therefore, for one who has not cultivated the cultivation of these...
Showing the mode of manifestation for one who has cultivated the meditation, he says, "from the aggregate," and so forth.
By this, it is stated that "through liberation, the faculty of faith becomes predominant," not that [faith is predominant] "in that liberation. Therefore, it is said:
"'Signless liberation' refers to the contemplation of impermanence. The same method applies to the other cases as well. Regarding the signless, there is no absence of its state of being signless.

Why was it said that "it does not exist"? Is it not the case that, while the state of the signless liberation exists figuratively through the contemplation of impermanence, its absence as a non-figurative teaching certainly exists?
And this being so, it cannot be said that "there is no bestowing of the name 'signless' upon the signless," whereby the application of the simile would be even more appropriately fitting.

Likewise, it is indeed not tenable that the signless nature of the path [is established] by means of the signless [object]. Therefore he said: "In the ultimate sense, it is not possible to give it a name.

This is true; however, having taken the signless nature of the contemplation of impermanence as established by way of conventional designation, this investigation was undertaken for the purpose of purifying the path: "The absence of the signless nature in the signless liberation..."
"It seems contradictory [to say] 'it does not exist'. And having done so, he himself will later state: "The signless... is thus illustrated.

By the term *sāmañña* (commonality), he refers to the relationship between the simile and that which is to be compared. "Not having the Path as its dominant factor" (*na maggādhipati*) means that this designation of "Path-dominant" does not apply to desire or consciousness; nor does the Path [have them as its dominant factors].
"Because the path has desire and consciousness as its dominant factors, it is called 'path-dominant' (maggādhipati)"—this designation does not apply to the path itself. Why?
Because those [states of] desire and consciousness are not factors of the path.

By the phrase "the jhāna having names such as 'emptiness' (suññatā) and so forth," it is shown that the faculties, powers, and other factors also receive names such as "emptiness" due to their association with the path.
It should be understood as "shown. Even though there is an opposing factor, that path is not as clearly manifest as its own inherent nature (*sarasatā*);

therefore, he says "predominant in its own nature" (*sarasappadhāna*). "By two" means by the two opposing factors of its own nature. "Independent of anything else" means independent of [any other] arrival.
"Therefore" means because, if the name were obtained solely from its own nature, there would be the consequence of non-determination for everything.

Because the Path attains all names, therefore [the text says]: "Self... and so on, up to "...Path. By this, it shows the state of attaining a name through its opposition to the attainment of a name by way of coming from that [source].

"In another sequence of words" means in such states as signlessness (*animitta*). "By a sequence of words accompanied by its opposite" means by way of emptiness (*suññatā*) and wishlessness (*appaṇihita*), which are the arrivals at those [states].
"Non-prevention of the grasping of signs" refers to the grasping of the sign of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*).

Regarding "by way of non-restraint": since only the paths of emptiness (*suññatā*) and the wishless (*appaṇihita*) have been mentioned, one might suspect that the path for one emerging from [the contemplation] of impermanence (*anicca*) is not included here; anticipating this, he says "contemplation of impermanence" and so forth.

The intention is that there would be no emergence from the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) themselves, but rather emergence only from their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*); thus, there would be no penetration of the characteristics because they would not be the object of that [path].

This is the meaning. For the conventional designations "impermanence" and so forth apply to the modes of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) that consist in their non-existence after having been, their arising, their passing away, and their being oppressed by these [changes].
Since the mode itself is grasped when those possessing the mode are grasped, he said:

"The characteristics are also penetrated through the grasping of the conditioned phenomena that possess those modes. This is according to the aforementioned intention, namely, by way of the terms "impermanent," etc., and "conditioned phenomena," etc.
In the sense already stated. "Thirty" means having excluded the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
[This concludes] the commentary on the miscellaneous discussion regarding supramundane wholesome states (*lokuttara-kusala*).

He points out [the objects] in five ways: having divided and not having divided the five aggregates of clinging by way of the internal dyad and the form dyad, he points them out by means of the term "sign" (*nimitta*) alone.

This is because the process of occurrence (*pavatta*) does not transcend the nature of being a sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*), and because there is a commonality in the fact that both must be emerged from.

For that very reason, even after dividing and demonstrating the process of occurrence into two types—by way of the appropriated (*upādinnā*) and the unappropriated (*anupādinnā*)—[he continues as follows].
“This, first of all, is the analysis by way of the sign” thus he concludes by means of the sign alone. And here, the sign is both internal and external, whereas the occurrence is only internal;

this is the distinction between them. “The distinction of the enlightenment factors, etc. refers to the dissimilarity of the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga), jhāna factors (jhānaṅga), and path factors (maggaṅga).

“Cultivation of dispassion consisting in the lack of desire to attain” is the cultivation of dispassion toward applied thought and so forth, characterized by the lack of desire to enter [the higher stages].
"Of the other" means of the foundational jhāna and so forth. "Due to the absence of that state" means due to the absence of the cultivation of dispassion as previously described.

This is what is meant: just as when insight proximate to the path is accompanied by joy, the path possesses the first jhāna and so on, and when it is accompanied by equanimity, it possesses the fifth jhāna;
and according to those [factors], there is a distinction in the factors of enlightenment and so forth.

For those [arahants], insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*) is the proximate cause and the primary cause for their fixedness; it is not so with the foundational jhānas and the like.

Now, because the paths produced by those who have used the first jhāna without a foundation—as well as those produced after having comprehended the miscellaneous formations and the first jhāna—are invariably characterized by the first jhāna, here it is exclusively the fixedness of insight that is the primary factor.
Explaining this point, he said, "By the very rule of insight (vipassanāniyama)," and so forth. In that context, "the others" refers to the paths consisting of the second jhāna and beyond.

For those who have transcended the factors of the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna), the insight leading to emergence—which consists of the cultivation of dispassion and the desire not to attain further factors—is the determiner of the specific qualities such as the jhāna-factors of the path, because it has been infused with excellence by the foundational jhāna which serves as its basis.
It is said: “By means of the basis-jhāna, insight, and the rules.

And just as by the basis-jhāna which serves as the foundation, so too, when both are present—namely, the jhāna that has been comprehended as the object—the insight, having acquired its specific distinction through the influence of the underlying aspiration (ajjhāsaya), brings about the rule;
thus he says: “In the same way, this should be applied to the remaining doctrines... and so forth.
"In the volitional formations of the foundational jhāna" means in the volitional formations of the first jhāna; for it has been said, "having made the first jhāna the foundation.
"By way of the state of developing fading away from or non-fading away from this or that" means by way of the state of developing the fading away or non-fading away of applied thought and so forth.
By this, he states that the object-jhāna also serves as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the attainment of distinction in insight.

The foundation jhānas and the jhānas attained through reflection are themselves the decisive support (*upanissaya*) and cause for the specific factors such as the enlightenment factors; thus, they are called "the decisive support of the foundation jhānas and the jhānas attained through reflection.

"In its presence" means: because of the presence of that inclination (*ajjhāsaya*). "Because of its absence when that is absent" means: because of the absence [of the enlightenment factors] when that inclination is absent.
Since for a path belonging to the fourth jhāna, only an immaterial jhāna can serve as the foundation in the immaterial realm, he says: "excluding those belonging to the fourth jhāna."

The second jhāna and those following it, which serve as the basis and object for insight (vipassanā) that provides the necessary support for transcending the gross factors of the Noble Path, [are meant]. "By five factors" means by the five jhāna factors.

With the intention that "the foundational jhānas and so forth, when being demonstrated by various doctrines, are called 'doctrines' (vāda) because of their association with those doctrines," he said, "These three doctrines. They speak thus.
Or, "by these" refers to the discourses (*vāda*) consisting of the foundational jhānas and so forth that serve as the instruments for debate.

By the phrase "because of the well-composed nature of the resultant continuity," it is demonstrated that whatever action arises in a particular continuity produces a specific refinement right there at the moment of its arising; therefore, its result occurs in that very same continuity and not elsewhere.

"Just as with the preceding conformity": the continuity is such that, just as the knowledge of preceding conformity (purimānulomañāṇa) arises following the conformity that has arisen at the stage of the lineage (gotrabhu), so too does it follow that very conformity.

"That too" means that even the knowledge of conformity arisen at the stage of the lineage would follow another instance of conformity-knowledge itself; it would arise immediately after that. "That plane" refers to the five aggregates subject to clinging.

It is called "ground" (*bhūmi*) because it is the locus for the arising of defilements. By stating that "one existence" (*eko bhavo*) is taken [as the basis], he shows that even the expression "seven existences" or "two existences" must be understood according to the intended meaning (*adhippāyavasena*), and not according to the literal sense (*yathārutavasena*).
Herein, this is the intended meaning: even by way of mixed rebirths, such as being born once among the gods of the sense-sphere and once among humans.

This limitation applies only to a single rebirth among those [beings]. As for what was said, "They do not take an eighth existence," that too was stated with reference only to existence in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara-bhava*).
They say that there is no such limitation for existences in the sublime realms (*mahaggata-bhava*).
Likewise, regarding the phrase "except for two existences," here too it refers to the mixed nature of existences as gods and humans in the sense-sphere realm.
Therefore, "the two existences in the sense-sphere realm" means the two existences by way of sense-sphere devas and humans.

In the previous alternatives, having distinguished the path according to the difference between individuals—stating that for some it wavers and for others it does not—the meaning was stated without the restrictive term "it certainly wavers.
However, since in the Commentary it says, "Just as... [the meaning is established].
And since it is said, "In this way, even the dominant influence (adhipati) wavers," therefore, when all the modes of practice (paṭipadā) are taken without distinction,
wavering is necessarily possible; thus, the third alternative— "it wavers indeed"— is stated as an emphasis on wavering, meaning "it wavers, not that it does not waver."
The commentary on the miscellaneous discussion of supramundane wholesome states is finished.
357. Commentary on the First Path: The Twenty Great Methods.

“Awakening factors” (bojjhaṅgā) are intended here as those spoken of by way of such designations as jhāna, path, and so forth. Specifically, with the intention that in the prior stage one possesses an inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) such as, “I develop jhāna; I develop the path,” he says, “for whom, in the prior stage,” and so forth.
358. "By way of proximate cause" (*upanissayavasena*) means by way of the prior formative activity (*pubbabhāgābhisaṅkhāra*) known as the occurrence of consciousness in such a manner.

For this very reason, he said, "For one who... and so forth. "By power conforming to that" expresses the possession of a specific capacity through the acquisition of the dominant condition (*adhipatipaccaya*).
If the state of dominance of desire and the rest is due to the influence of prior formative activity, for what purpose are these alone stated in this way?
One might object: "Is it not the case that a prior-formative-activity (pubbabhāga-abhisaṅkhāra) is also found for faith and the other [faculties]? To this he says:

"Of the remaining states," and so forth. "Because they lack that nature" means because they are devoid of the state of being followed in an especially eminent manner by their associated [mental factors].

For although faith and the others also follow their associated factors by virtue of being faculty-conditions, nevertheless, within a single arising of consciousness, they cannot exist without another [factor] of equal strength alongside the associated factors.
Their state of being to be followed is not like that of desire and the other [mental factors]; therefore, they alone are stated as having the status of predominance (*adhipati*).
By doing so, the distinction between the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) and the co-nascent predominance-condition (*sahajātādhipati-paccaya*) becomes clearly evident.
Commentary on the Four Thousandfold Method of the Path.
362. The mode of occurrence of conceit (māna) is similar to that of views (diṭṭhi). For, like a dominant factor, it does not occur together with another dominant factor, namely, with views.
This is an illustration by way of partial similarity (*ekadesa-sāmañña*), not by way of total commonality;

otherwise, just as darkness would envelop the world upon the setting of the sun, there would follow the consequence that the concealment of the truths would persist even when the supreme path has arisen.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Mutually" (*aññamañña*) means one with another. The case ending in the phrase "this sutta has been brought forward" (*ānītaṃ idaṃ suttaṃ*) must be transformed [into the nominative].
"By the method already stated" (*yathāvuttanayena*) means by the method stated in this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

"Because it was not stated as a simile" (*na upamāya vuttattā*) means because the state of being stated as a simile does not exist in this sutta. Alternatively, "by the method already stated" means by the manner stated in this sutta.
This is because, according to the method of this commentary, the simile is not stated here.

It should be understood that they are called "mental factors" (*cetasika*)—as in "they are like limbs," "they are joined to the mind," or "they belong to the mind"—but not as "contactual" (*phassika*), and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the wholesome is finished.
The Section on the Enumeration of Phenomena: The First Explanation of Consciousness in the Unwholesome Category.
365. Because the three moments [of consciousness] cannot exist in unwholesome states, the word *samaya* has the sense of a collection, time, or a combination of causes.

With reference to such points as the fact that a state accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata*) occurs only when one is overcome by greed, through the apprehension of an agreeable aspect in a desirable object or otherwise, it is said “according to what is appropriate.
[It is also said] because of the presence of the blemish of defilement (*kilesavajja*), in the sense of being unwell due to the affliction of defilements.
"It is unwholesome (akusala) in the sense of being blameworthy (sāvajja), in the sense of being produced by ignorance (avijjā), and in the sense of being produced by lack of skill (akosalla)"—and:

"It has the characteristic of being blameworthy and having painful fruition; its function is to produce what is harmful; its manifestation is defilement (saṃkilesa); its proximate cause is improper attention (ayonisomanasikāra).

Alternatively, it has the characteristic of being blameworthy because it is censurable; its function is the state of defilement; its manifestation is undesirable fruition; and its proximate cause is exactly as stated above."
It is said, "having followed the stated method," because it is to be understood according to the method described by such phrases as "and so forth.
It is said, "merely gone, merely going, merely occurring," taking "gone" (gata) to mean "going" (gamana) or "occurrence" (pavatti);

for the occurrence of a view is indeed its very going. It is said, "because it is the proximate cause," meaning because it is the proximate basis (padaṭṭhāna), just like appropriate attention (yonisomanasikāra).
Improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is the proximate cause of the unwholesome (*akusala*).

For even when there are other causes such as listening to what is not in accordance with the Dhamma, if one does not attend improperly and does not determine [the object] improperly, there is no occurrence of the unwholesome. And so it will be said in the Commentary:
"Improper [attention] is unwholesome. By this, its status as the single, absolute cause is stated. Reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhā*) is the endurance of cold and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "dwelling in heedfulness," it is said that "heedfulness is endurance. Therefore, the intention here is that "restraint through mindfulness" refers to restraint through patience (*khantisaṃvara*), since restraint of the sense faculties has already been mentioned. "Restraint through abandonment" is restraint through energy (*vīriyasaṃvara*);
for that is described as "not tolerating, but abandoning, an arisen sensual thought," and so forth.

The mode of being grasped as the opposite of right practice is delusion (*moha*); it is the mode of grasping [the object] as being the opposite of right practice. For by that [delusion], people are shrouded and do not practice rightly. The specific application of covetousness (*abhijjhā*) constitutes the attainment of a course of action (*kamma-patha*).

Lack of investigation is delusion; and here, this should be understood as being devoid of wrong view (*diṭṭhi*). However, when associated with wrong view, because it conforms to that view, it is included by the very mention of the view itself.
"In an improper basis" means in a basis that is not to be believed. It is accompanied by persuasion (*sānunaya*).

“Adhimokkha” (resolute conviction) refers to that which most closely resembles faith among delusion, wrong views, and so forth. It is [so called] because of the state of negligence caused by the factors of shamelessness (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), delusion (*moha*), and the like.
“In a mind devoid of protection” (*ārakkharahitacitte*) shows precisely the absence of mindfulness (*sati*) in the mind; for mindfulness is manifested as protection.
By this, the meaning of the two phrases “in a mind lacking faith” and “in a mind blind and foolish” is explained. “Enmity and so forth” (*upanāhādi*)...

By the word "etc.," lust and the other [defilements] are included. Because lust and the others have the nature of obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) and so forth, it is said "without distinction" (*aviseseṇa*), since no specific [distinction] is possible.
"Here" means in this consciousness. The locative case is used for the purpose of that which is to be accomplished, as in "he kills the leopard on the skin";
or else, the object is [so called] by metaphorical transfer of the fruit, as in "the phlegm is sugar," where the lack of tranquility [is the cause].
The commentary on the section concerning the enumeration of phenomena (*dhammuddesavārakathā*) is finished.
Commentary on the Section of Exposition (*niddesavārakathā*): 390.

Because it is the support and the cause for the apprehension of what is non-existent—such as a "natural self" (*pakati-atta*)—by way of concealing its true nature (*sabhāva*), [ignorance] is "non-existent" (*asanta*).

It is called "delusion" (moha) because it understands incorrectly—due to its being the support for the perversion of perception and so forth, which grasps the impermanent and other things as permanent and so on;
this is said figuratively by treating the sign (nimitta) as the agent. And this meaning should be understood by way of delusion associated with wrong view (diṭṭhi).
Furthermore, in this context, "nature" (pakati) refers to the primary principle (padhāna) of the followers of Kapila.

400. Just as the term *apaṇṇaka* (infallible) might sometimes indicate a state of certainty, the phrase "factors worthy of arising" is used to indicate uncertainty, because conceit (*māna*) is not certain.
For if conceit were certain, [the text would not have used that qualification].
The occurrence of sensual lust (kāmarāga) would not be devoid of conceit (māna), nor would that of existence-lust (bhavarāga).
This being so, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, there would be no fourfold conjunction with sensual lust, but only a threefold one; furthermore, it would not be rooted in existence-lust.

And thus, the conjunction of the fetters (saṃyojana) by way of the eightfold method of the fetters would occur, rather than the tenfold method as it is shown. Therefore, [the text] states... as previously mentioned.
By this construction, the inconstant nature of conceit (*māna*) is made clear. Alternatively, there are five *apaṇṇaka-aṅga*s (infallible factors) including conceit;

and when the question "What are they? arises, it is understood that these are the *yevāpanaka*s (residues). For here, the fact that the *yevāpanaka*s are five is being enjoined, not that the *apaṇṇaka-aṅga*s are five.
Therefore, it should be construed accordingly. [End of] the dyad on defilements (*kilesa*).

In the sections on "Dependent Arising" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and so forth, such as: "Dependent upon a defiled state (*dhamma*), a defiled state arises by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*)," and so on;

[it is said]: "Dependent upon greed (*lobha*), there arise delusion (*moha*), conceit (*māna*), sloth (*thina*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*).
Dependent upon greed, there arise delusion, conceit, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing. Dependent upon greed, there arise delusion, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness..."

“Lack of moral dread (anottappa). In dependence on greed (lobha), there arise delusion (moha), restlessness (uddhacca), shamelessness (ahirika), and lack of moral dread (anottappa)”—because it is analyzed in this way, it is said:

"Likewise in the dyads of defilements. For this variation in the reading occurs according to the types of consciousness dissociated from wrong view that are prompted (sasankhārika) and unprompted (asankhārika).
"Sensual lust (kāmarāga) arises together in four ways; aversion (paṭigha) in three ways; conceit (māna) in one way; likewise doubt (vicikicchā) and lust for existence (bhavarāga)."
"Having enumerated them, lust for sensual pleasures [is associated] with the fetter of conceit and the fetter of ignorance, as well as with the fetter of ignorance alone;

conceit [is associated] with the fetters of existence-lust and ignorance; and existence-lust [is associated] with the fetter of ignorance"—this is because it will be explained in the commentary on the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*.
Therefore, it was said: "And here it will be stated," and so forth. In that very same place...
Having stated: "Greed arises together with six [factors], aversion in two ways, and likewise delusion," it continues:

"Greed is without volitional effort (asaṅkhārika) when dissociated from views, along with delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; it is with volitional effort (sasaṅkhārika) when associated with delusion, lethargy, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing;

it is without volitional effort when associated with delusion, conceit, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; and it is likewise with volitional effort when associated with delusion, conceit, lethargy, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing."
Because it will be explained later, it is said: "Likewise, the eightfold defilements.
Because it is grasped as "I," its grasping is also called "exaltation" (*sampaggaha*).
Commentary on the Fourth Consciousness.

402. "Generating enthusiasm" (*ussāhaṃ janenta*): here, "enthusiasm" (*ussāha*) refers specifically to the mental formation (*saṅkhāra*) consisting of the application of the mind, not to the enthusiasm of energy (*vīriya-ussāha*). 413.
The spreading forth [of anger] arises from an undesirable visible form; by means of this, when one is provoked, the entire body trembles and the appearance of being provoked [manifests].
It is manifested. By this, the "flavour" (rasa) in the sense of excellence is shown; or alternatively, it is the flavour of pervasion by way of its mode of occurrence.
For, generally speaking, the prosperity of one whose [anger] is provoked becomes a cause for the arising of resentment in that enemy.
By this, the "flavour" in the sense of function is stated.
418. It is simply the meaning of the words; it is simply a synonym for the words. 424.
"Due to the absence of certainty" means due to the absence of resolve (*adhimokkha*). "Due to not persisting" means because it does not remain fixed upon a single object by way of continuity.
Commentary on the Twelfth Consciousness (429).
There is no co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*), because there is an absence of such mental occurrences as "If doubt arises in one who possesses desire, it might arise in me.
Since it is not mentioned, its prohibition implies its non-existence; for in the teaching that accords with the Dhamma, even non-mention indicates absence.
By the term *avacana* (“non-statement”), it shows that the letter *a* has the sense of denoting something other than that [which is stated].

And by this demonstration—that the establishment of the fruit follows from the establishment of the cause through the statement of the non-existence of those things to be abandoned—it is first said, “because it does not draw forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-anākaḍḍhana*),” in order to show the very cause for that non-existence therein.
By that, the nature of that arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*) is stated. And from that, [it is shown that] the rebirth-linking is powerful...
“[The kamma] draws [the rebirth-linking], but that which is weak does not draw”—this refers to those things whose intrinsic nature is to give rebirth-linking.
However, for that which lacks the very nature of giving rebirth-linking, its state of strength is not a cause for drawing the rebirth-linking; this is the meaning demonstrated here.
He establishes the non-drawing with the words, “For if it were to draw,” and so forth. And because it has not yet arrived, therefore it does not draw.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Because it was stated, "But since that [kamma] does not give rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), therefore it has not come," it was said, "In order to establish its non-arrival due to not being drawn along.
Regarding the phrase "leading to the states of misery" (*apāyagamanīya*):
it leads to the states of misery, thus it is "leading to the states of misery"; the meaning is that it possesses that nature. In the drawing along of rebirth-linking...
If it were accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*), it would necessarily lead to the states of deprivation (*apāya*). Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

“For the other [type of consciousness] as well, the giving of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) would occur only here [in the sense-sphere realms]. For an unwholesome rebirth-linking is not possible in a happy destination (*sugati*).

And because of the statement, “He is liberated from the four states of deprivation and is no longer subject to falling into ruin,” it is shown that [this consciousness] does not lead to the states of deprivation through vision (*dassana*).
It is to be abandoned. Therefore he said: "Because it is to be abandoned by seeing that leads to the states of deprivation.

And yet, it cannot be said that this is abandoned by seeing, nor that it is comprised within that lust, hatred, delusion, and the defilements associated with them which lead to the states of deprivation;
for it is stated as being necessarily abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā). For this has been said:
“Which phenomena are to be abandoned by cultivation? A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness.

The status of being a kamma-condition as stated in the formula, “Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma,” refers to the status of a asynchronous kamma-condition.
And that [restlessness] would be [a condition] if it were accompanied by restlessness...

It might draw forth rebirth-linking; that too could be so. And if that were the case, [the defilement] accompanied by restlessness would have to be abandoned by seeing, because it has been stated that only those [defilements] abandonable by seeing function as kamma-conditions at different moments.
But this is not abandonable by seeing; thus everything recurs as before.
"Co-nascent only" means that in the *Vibhaṅga* on what is to be abandoned by seeing (*dassanena pahātabba*), after stating both the co-nascent and the asynchronous [conditions]—
namely, "A state to be abandoned by seeing is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for a state not to be abandoned by seeing or by cultivation"— it says:
"Co-nascent volition to be abandoned by seeing [is a condition] for mind-originated [matter]..."

It has been analyzed thus: "Volition to be abandoned by vision, being asynchronous, is a condition for resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of kamma-condition"; yet it has not been analyzed in this way:
"Volition to be abandoned by cultivation is a condition for mind-originated matter by way of kamma-condition."

Only this much was stated; it was not stated that "volition belonging to a different moment is a condition for resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of kamma-condition.
By this, it is understood that there is no state of being a kamma-condition belonging to a different moment for that which is to be abandoned by development (bhāvanā).
This is also the case when, in the negative (paccanīya) [section], the extraction of conditions is performed according to possibility by way of the inclusive conditions.
"And in the other case" refers to the states to be abandoned by vision. For therein it is stated:
"A state to be abandoned by vision is a condition, by way of object-condition, for a state not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation;
it is also a condition by way of co-nascence, decisive-support, post-nascence, and kamma-condition. Thus, the kamma-condition is also mentioned there.

"Because of their absence" means because of the absence of the condition of karma belonging to different moments. Since there is no drawing forth of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) without the condition of karma belonging to different moments, it is said:
"They do not draw forth rebirth-linking there; therefore, they are future in that regard. "In this context" refers to the statement:
"Excluding that which is accompanied by restlessness, the remaining eleven alone draw forth rebirth-linking. "Of the fruition in the course of existence" (pavattivipākassa)...

"Pavattivipākaṃ" means that for this [kamma], there is a result (vipāka) during its occurrence (pavatti), or a result that has come into being during its occurrence because it is a part of that occurrence;
thus it is "pavattivipāka," referring to the kamma. Alternatively, "pavattivipāko" means a result during occurrence.

However, in this sense, the word-division (*padaccheda*) should be understood as follows: "nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayo etassāti nānā... and so on, up to "...yo, tabbhāvo... and so on, up to "...tāti. It cannot be denied.
Because a resultant state does not arise without the condition of asynchronous kamma.
Now, in order to show that the occurrence of resultants is explicitly stated as being due to their acquisition of the condition of asynchronous kamma, he said, "And it is said," and so forth.
Thinking that the giving of a resultant consists in the nature of rebirth-resultant states, he said, "If [it were] cultivation," and so forth.

He says, "of the super-knowledge consciousnesses, etc.," because the state of being subject to ripening (vipākadhamma) is established even in the absence of giving a result for others, as it is found in other such [states] as well.

By the word "etc.," he includes that which is to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) and that which is to be experienced upon rebirth (upapajjavedanīya), both of which have transcended their own time.
This might be said because of the acquisition of an auxiliary condition (sahāyapaccaya) for those existing in the continuum of an ordinary person (puthujjana).

It is stated that it is logical for a state accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*) to produce its result, and because of the absence of that [restlessness], for its result not to arise in the continuum of a trainee (*sekkha*).
For this very reason, he said: "But this point must be thoroughly investigated," and so forth. And likewise he will say:
"Of the desire, lust, and so on toward one's own belongings that arise in worldlings (*puthujjana*), [there is] the arising of a thought accompanied by restlessness..."
Furthermore, since it is impossible to deny that the three fetters and the defilements associated with them produce a result when their companions have not been severed and are not yet exhausted,
the production of a result for states accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*) is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*. Thus,
while such a statement regarding the production of a result holds true when such companions exist, it contradicts the statement that no result is produced when they do not exist.

Or, having taken into account that [volition] which gives rise to the result during the course of existence (*pavatti*) for one accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*), it is said, "it might be stated. Some explain:
"For it was stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-vibhaṅga* with reference to the result during the course of existence: 'Knowledge regarding their result'.
Thus, even the volition of restlessness does not exist [in this context], and it too must be excluded from being a condition for consciousness.
This too was said with reference specifically to rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*).
The commentary on the section on unwholesome states is concluded. [Now begins] the section on indeterminate states (*abyākata-pada*).
Commentary on the Rootless Wholesome Resultant (Ahetuka-kusala-vipāka) 431.
Regarding the phrase "The sense-sphere... etc., has been stated," the word "etc.

(*ādi*) here includes the term "because of being accumulated" (*upacittattā*), since it was stated [in the preceding section] as "by way of the condition of uncommon kamma" (*asādhāraṇa-kamma-paccaya-vasena*). Some explain: "Because of being accumulated means because of having been repeatedly practiced (*laddhāsevanattā*)."

They say that this [simultaneous arising] is not tenable for the first impulsion (*paṭhamajavana*) because it lacks repetition (*anāsevanattā*). And if that were the case, it would not even be capable of yielding its result (*vipākadāna*).

Therefore, showing the meaning in another way, he said "Just as" and so forth. In that context, "facing toward the result" (*vipākābhimukha*) means facing toward the giving of the result, having been granted an opportunity.
And the state of having been granted an opportunity [occurs] because many karmas have been performed throughout beginningless *saṃsāra*.
"By way of obstructing another's existence" means "having obstructed the result for another," and so forth.
And "augmentation" is the state of being conditioned by its own causes through the capacity to bestow strength upon its own karma.
The name is mentioned by way of its specific characteristic, as in "the sound of a drum" or "a barley sprout. "Of consciousnesses" refers to eye-consciousness and the rest.
"By way of being a specific condition" means by way of being an additional condition.
By the phrase "that which is dependent on the eye and is the cognition of form," he demonstrates the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) of the compound;

furthermore, therein, regarding the two terms "dependent on the eye" and so forth, he states their relationship as qualifier and qualified, just as in the case of words such as *nīluppala* ("blue lotus").

"Another consciousness" refers to mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) having visible form as its object. However, when it says "having visible form alone as its object," one should understand this as referring to divine-eye consciousness (dibbacakkhuviññāṇa), applying that designation to things similar to it, just as one might say, "That is the very same partridge;
those are the very same medicinal herbs. Since the condition of jhāna is absent, there is no status as a jhāna factor;
thus, in the fivefold sense-consciousnesses, equanimity and the other factors are considered jhāna factors only by way of metaphorical application (upacāra).
