He establishes this. For it is not the case that, having stated that the factors of jhāna possess the conditionality of jhāna, their status as jhāna-conditions is thereby denied.

If this were so, then equanimity and the other factors would not be mentionable in the context of the fivefold group of consciousness (pañcaviññāṇa) under the heading of "jhāna"; thus he says, "In the absence of the status of being a jhāna-condition," and so forth.

"Because of the presence of equanimity and the rest" means because of the presence of equanimity, pleasure, pain, and one-pointedness. "Because of the absence of another place" refers to the stability of consciousness (*cittatthiti*).
It was said with this very intention.

436. Unwholesome [kamma] is called "white" by way of its outflow from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), for if the life-continuum itself were not white, how could there be whiteness in the unwholesome rooted in it?
Thus it is said, "And of the unwholesome. The reason for its whiteness must be stated.
If it is "white" for other reasons, it is said to be the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of consciousness because its intrinsic nature is free from defilement (*akilesa*);

however, this does not imply that contact (*phassa*) and the other factors are also white. For the Blessed One, who knows the specific distinctions between the intrinsic natures and functions of phenomena, designated consciousness alone in that way.

439. By way of development through non-transgression. "Having struck the sensitivity and come into the range" means that the striking of the sensitivity is its establishment in a suitable location for the object.

Regarding the phrase "it strikes against the great elements," here it does not itself strike anything, nor is it struck by anything, because its intrinsic nature is not tangible. It has become both object and subject.

However, because it serves as the cause for the arising of consciousness through the attainment of a state of confrontation, it is designated by the term "possessing resistance" (*sappaṭigha*) due to its specific nature of being struck and striking back;

therefore, the designation "possessing resistance" applies to them. Furthermore, expressions such as "it strikes the derived matter" (*upādārūpa*) should be understood merely in a figurative sense (*upacāra*).
But when the great elements that serve as the support for the body-sensitivity are struck by an object consisting of the great elements, [the sensitivity is said to be struck].
Having stated that "confidence too is indeed called 'struck' (ghaṭṭita)," they say it "should be investigated.

By means of a simile expressed through a partial commonality as intended, he says, "for the purpose of showing the striking of both," demonstrating that even though there is a temporal sequence between the striker and the struck, they are to be understood as a simile because of their similitude.

455. “Because of the state of having vision and so forth” means that, since the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) lack vision and so forth, this [latter] is their specific distinction.
“Because of not having another support and having the mind as the forerunner” means due to the absence of having another support or of the mind being the forerunner.

By the phrase “due to the absence of being a condition of contiguity (*anantarapaccaya*) for consciousness supported by another,” the distinction from the functional mind-element (*kriyā-manodhātu*) is also indicated.
Because it has been stated [thus], it is said: “because of the absence of the state of being the exit-gate for the mind-door,” but it is not said:

“because of the absence of the state of being the exit-gate and entrance-gate. For in all three ways, the distinction of the mind-element and the consciousness-element from the mind-consciousness-element is shown.

Precisely for that reason, because of the lack of a specific mode of cognizing. If the mind-element is not called “mind-consciousness,” then [the question arises regarding] the groups of sensory consciousnesses...
How is there an inclusion of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) therein? It is indeed an inclusion because it is a teaching given by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya-desanā*).
For there is this figurative expression: "mere thinking consciousness is mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*), just as "the element that is mere thinking is the mind-element.
Furthermore, it is because of its similarity to mind-consciousness in terms of its basis and function, because of its state of ceasing and arising, and because of its being the end and so forth.

And the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is comprised within the body of mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇakāya*), but it is not comprised within the other bodies of consciousness because it does not share their nature;
however, here, in the non-figurative sense, "mental consciousness" refers to that which has arisen from the mind and is associated with the specific function of the mind.
Since that [function] is absent [in this case], it is said: "It is not called 'mental consciousness' either. To establish this very point, it is stated: "For that is not consciousness..."

The passage beginning with “from the mind” (*manato*) and so forth was stated; by this, it shows that the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is, in the primary sense, devoid of the function of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*).
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with “but as for seeing and so forth,” it shows the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the mind-element as being distinct from other types of consciousness.

If, among the great resultant states (*mahāvipāka*), the state of right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) and so on in volition (*vitakka*) and the rest consists in their similarity to the producer, then [this applies] from the three-rooted [state].
"Let it be that those born from a three-rooted [state] possess right intention and so forth, as do those born from a two-rooted state who possess two roots;
but how is it for those possessing two roots who are born from a three-rooted state? To this he says, "In that regard... and so on.

It cannot be included in that stream because it does not follow immediately after it. For that very reason, by the subsequent statement, only that which is said to be included in the stream by the phrase beginning with "for that very reason" [is meant].

It is capable. If it is the case that even when they are present, mental factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so on are not counted among the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the rest—just as they are not counted among the fivefold sense-consciousnesses (*pañcaviññāṇa*)—then how is it that their status as a condition for *jhāna* is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*:
“An indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of the *jhāna*-condition”? [As in: “Resultant-indeterminate or functional-indeterminate states...”
For it is said: "The factors of jhāna are a condition, by way of jhāna-condition, for the associated aggregates and for the mind-produced matter.
In the negative formulation as well, [it is stated]: "In dependence on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises not by way of jhāna-condition;
for example, in dependence on one aggregate accompanied by the fivefold sense-consciousness, three aggregates [arise]," and so forth—thus [the fivefold] sense-consciousnesses [are excluded].
Thus, it is these [factors] that are elevated, not the mind-element and so forth; therefore, he says, "merely by way of the function of being a condition for jhāna," and so on.
For here, the relative strength or weakness of the jhāna factors is not emphasized; rather, the intention is merely their status as conditions for jhāna.
469. Having obtained the proximity condition with a common basis, [the mind-element] is strong in its function of seeing and so forth.
This is a statement of the reason. "According to the object" means in conformity with the object.

If it is argued that because the resultant mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy is stronger than the mind-element due to having the same basis (*nissaya*), how then can the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) have a neutral feeling (*majjhatta-vedanā*)?
Having considered this inquiry and accepted its forceful nature, [the answer is given] through a specific function of transforming the continuity (*santati-pariṇāmana*).
Stating the resolution that it is not a feeling of mental joy (*somanassavedanā*), he says, "the determining consciousness" (*voṭṭhabbana*) and so forth.

It is stated [thus] because, unlike a result (*vipāka*), there is no mere experiencing; for while results invariably experience the flavor of the object due to their functional capacity, this is not the case here.
The commentary on the rootless wholesome resultants is concluded.
Commentary on the Eight Great Resultant Consciousnesses: 498.

Regarding the doors for resultant states, it was stated in the *Dvārakathā* (Discourse on the Doors): "The mind of the three planes, consisting of the wholesome and unwholesome, is of twenty-nine kinds.
By "effort" (*payoga*) is meant the exertion of effort performed by oneself or by others. Just as with the wholesome and unwholesome [states],...

For those [consciousnesses], that [resultant consciousness] is their object and follows as a consequence. Since the second, sixth, and other [moments of consciousness] are also investigated by examining the mutual strength and weakness of the first and fifth moments of consciousness, it is said:
"In order to investigate which among these is strong and which is weak.

Just as, depending on whether the soil for rice and other crops is hard or soft, there is the non-extraction or extraction of weeds and the like, so too regarding the remaining conditions such as temperature and so forth...

And there is the connection with specific results by way of misfortune and success; thus, the transformation of karma into a distinguished result—by way of rebirth in happy or miserable destinies, by way of impure or pure application, and by way of misfortune or success—is like the connection of seeds with specific results during the summer, rainy season, and so forth.
Therefore, he said that there is a connection of karma with specific results according to the distinction of those respective times.

“It transforms by way of time. Regarding the phrase “of the semen and blood as conditions,” he states that the semen and blood are the cause for the specific lifespan because they arise within a continuum permeated by a particular type of karma;

for it is on account of the semen and blood that differences in complexion and other qualities are observed, whereby it is said, “the son conforms to the appearance of his parents. The phrase “rooted in that” means rooted in the karma conducive to a short lifespan.
"In nutriment, etc."—by the word "etc.," poison, assault, and so forth are included.
Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the extraction of kamma-result (*vipāka*):

"From which [kamma] consisting of three roots, etc."; and "in which place" refers to the place of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth, or to a happy or miserable destination (*sugatiduggati*).

The intention is that one does not accept a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) from a three-rooted state to a two-rooted state. However, one certainly accepts resultant [consciousness] in the course of existence (*pavatti*) even when it proceeds from a three-rooted state to a two-rooted state.
For thus it will be said in the Commentary: "That which is not compatible with the attainment of the previous exposition of roots.
As for those who say, "By the remainder of the result of that very same kamma," and "Having offered a single flower, for eighty koṭis of eons..."

Not understanding the intended meaning of such statements as, “I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth,” they fall into doubt, wondering, “Could it be that even by a single kamma there are multiple rebirths?

And failing to discern the meaning of such statements as, “Having seen the prince endowed with a hundred marks of merit,” they wonder, “Could it be that by various karmas there is only a single rebirth? Thus they are beset by uncertainty.

Because it has been determined through the simile of the seed and the sprout that "rebirth-linking occurs from one [cause] as one, and from many [causes] as many," he states the connection for the mention of the prominence of the discussion on the extraction of the result in the Sāketa Question—following the establishment of kamma as the rebirth-linking factor—by saying: "By way of kamma...
to show. By way of the kamma that generates rebirth-linking, there is the resultant rebirth-linking.
The meaning should be understood as follows: these are the causes for the excessive presence of qualities such as non-greed and greed, and so forth.
For it has been said: "Having been reborn through that karma by way of a bestowed rebirth-linking, he is greedy," and so on.

And herein, there are three single factors—greed, hatred, and delusion—and three pairs: greed-and-hatred, greed-and-delusion, and hatred-and-delusion; [thus,] by way of greed, hatred, delusion, greed-and-hatred, greed-and-delusion, hatred-and-delusion, and greed-and-hatred-and-delusion.
There are seven instances on the unwholesome side alone by way of viewing greed and so forth as "one triad" (eko tiko).
Likewise, there are fourteen instances obtainable on the wholesome side by way of viewing non-greed and so forth.
Among these, regarding those that appear on the wholesome side as "non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion; non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion; powerful non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion":
By the third, second, and first sections, the sections on the predominance of hatred, the predominance of delusion, and the predominance of both hatred and delusion are included.

Likewise, on the unwholesome side, by the third, second, and first sections where it is stated that "greed, hatred, and delusion; greed, hatred, and delusion; greed, hatred, and delusion are powerful," the sections on the predominance of non-hatred, the predominance of non-delusion, and the predominance of both non-hatred and non-delusion are likewise included.
Thus, there are three [sections] each for the unwholesome and wholesome sides.

Having included the "both" category within the [previous] categories, only eight categories were shown. However, there are another forty-nine categories—such as those where greed or non-greed predominates—that ought to be shown by way of mixing both types;
these were not shown precisely because they are impossible.
For it is not possible within a single continuum, without a change of state, for greed to be strong while non-greed is also present, because they are direct opposites.

For this is the state of being strong or weak among these [mental factors], whether by way of their co-nascent states or otherwise. Among them, greed (*lobha*) is strong because it is not overcome by its opposite, non-greed (*alobha*);

likewise, hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*) are strong because they are not overcome by non-hatred (*adosa*) and non-delusion (*amoha*). However, non-greed and the others are strong because they overcome greed and the rest;
and all [wholesome factors] are strong simply by virtue of arising while equally overcoming those of their own kind through their co-nascent states.
This refers to the state of being strong or weak. Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Lobha is strong; alobha is weak. Adosa and amoha are strong; dosa and moha are weak.

And that state of being weak or strong in them should be understood from the influence of previous supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) and the extent to which the underlying disposition (*āsaya*) has been cultivated.

Furthermore, in this context, by means of the first and second sections, or the seventh and first sections, [it is shown] how rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*) arise from kamma possessing three roots (*tihetuka*).

The result of a three-rooted [kamma] is distinct; furthermore, this distinction should be understood as follows: from among other three-rooted and two-rooted kamma, the results of two-rooted and rootless [kamma] are shown according to possibility by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
"Here" refers to the matrix of the exposition of results. By this, he specifies the enumeration of roots. It is the sign of misfortune such as being born blind and so forth.
Delusion, or all unwholesome states. The connection is with the phrase "but what has been said.

By that statement from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, when there is attainment of a [favorable] rebirth-state (*gatisampatti*) and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) associated with knowledge is to be produced, "elsewhere" refers to the moments of attachment and rebirth-linking.
"Similarity to the kamma" should be understood here as intending a preeminent state of similarity; otherwise, even those [rebirths] with three roots or two roots would [not be included].

This is shown by the phrase "mutually similar. Regarding the term "eye-consciousness, etc.," here the fivefold consciousnesses, as well as the mind-element—which lacks the specific mode of cognizing and which proceeds based on a support not previously occupied—are not capable of grasping the desirable and other such portions [of objects];

thus they are not described as "manifest" (*pākaṭā*), or they are included by the word "etc. The phrase "all impulsion moments with that as their object-condition" refers to all impulsions having those [preceding moments] as their objective condition.
[This is] together with the entire occurrence of the impulsion (javana) which serves as the condition for that object.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "Here, because of the ripening of the sense-bases. "At another time" means at a time when consciousness is occurring without directed thought (abuddhi).
"In conformity" means in conformity with the Dhamma. "By way of repetition-condition" means by way of conditions that constitute repetition. [This applies] to the path, not to non-path conditions.
"He too might obtain the 'futile' category" means: if even determining (voṭṭhabbana) were a condition by way of repetition (āsevanapaccaya), as in the positive-negative formula:
"Dependent on a state associated with pleasant feeling, a state associated with pleasant feeling arises by way of repetition-condition, not by way of path-condition";
and in the negative-positive formula: "Pleasant... [etc. [and so forth].
And when it is said, "not by way of path-condition, but by way of repetition-condition," this is stated with reference to the consciousness that arouses laughter.

Likewise, by way of determining (voṭṭhabbana), there may be a reading according to the method previously explained, beginning with: "dependent on a state associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
And that being so, in the enumeration according to the two occasions, it says: "By way of repetition-condition, but not by way of path-condition, there are two."
"One might have said, 'By way of path-condition and by way of repetition, there are two,' but it was not so stated;
therefore, this section on the futile (mogha-vāra) would not be applicable"—this is the intended meaning.
If even the "determining" (voṭṭhabbana) were a repetition-condition, then as in the second section on the futile, it would likewise [occur] in the third and fourth sections.

If that were so, then there would also be [a condition] for oneself between the wholesome and unwholesome states. For it is not... [omitted] ...because it has been stated without exception in such passages as, "Preceding wholesome states... and so forth. As for the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), it is not stated...

[omitted] ...because there is no statement saying, "An indeterminate state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of the repetition-condition (*āsevana-paccaya*); [it is] a condition for an unwholesome state... and so forth.

It is not only when unspoken; rather, it is wholesome... [and so on] ... even when rejected. Furthermore, the phrase "if there should be" and so forth is stated solely for the purpose of purifying the path.
Because it demonstrates that the status of being a condition through repetition applies only to those with identical feeling, it is said:
"by way of those with non-identical feeling. Thus, it could also be stated: "it is a condition by way of the condition of repetition," specifically by way of identical feeling.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). In the phrase "and of one whose birth is undifferentiated" (*abhinnajātikassa ca*), the word *ca* has the sense of a conjunction (*sampiṇḍana*) meaning "and of one whose feeling is undifferentiated" (*abhinnavedanassa ca*).

In the triad of feelings (*vedanāttika*) as well, the construction is: "because of the absence of the status of being a condition by repetition (*āsevanapaccayatā*) for the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*). In the phrases from the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*) onwards, as shown in the cited portions of the scripture, the word *pi* has the sense of a conjunction (*sampiṇḍana*).
When there is counting—that is, when counting is being performed as the cause of the enumeration—[the following applies].
Or [it is] within. The second section on "futility" (moghavāra) should be investigated:

because it lacks the status of being a condition through repetition (āsevanapaccaya), it is not logical for it to remain in the position of impulsion (javana). For there is no occurrence of impulsion without repetition;
this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, in this context, it will be stated later: "That which has reached the state of impulsion is like a flower from a tree whose roots have been cut."
If the roots of existence were not severed, the functional nature of the apprehending consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) as it occurs would not be possible; yet it is stated:
"At whatever time the mind-consciousness element has arisen, which is functional, neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and is neither the result of kamma, but is accompanied by equanimity.
Therefore, "standing in the place of impulsion" means standing in the place where impulsion arises.
"Having occurred twice, but not by way of impulsion"—and regarding the phrase "having obtained repetition," if it is said that "repetition is like repetition," there is no contradiction;
for here, the similarity to repetition consists precisely in its occurring twice while being expansive.
Indeed, because of this expansiveness, its capacity to originate intimation (*viññatti*) is also stated. Even though it is expansive...
Because it is weak due to not occurring many times—just like the javana—it would not function as a condition by way of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*) in the primary sense;
therefore, the meaning of "repetition" is not stated for this [consciousness] in the text. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated figuratively (*pariyāyato*), just as it is said:
"In the case of fruition-consciousnesses, the path-factor is included within the path. This is my own opinion on this point. This too...
It should be carefully examined because it was not commented upon by the ancient masters.
And as for the phrase "having done so": since there is no difference in meaning between determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) and adverting (*āvajjana*), it is stated simply as "adverting";
the intention is that this refers even to the stage of determining. Therefore: because determining is, in actual fact, nothing other than adverting.
Because it is a state of rootless functional mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, therefore— intending that mindfulness, like advertence,
would function as an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) exclusively for sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and functional impulsion-moments at the moment of their arising,
and not otherwise— he said, "from determining" (*voṭṭhabbanato*), and so forth. "Of the four" refers to [the moments of consciousness] at times such as fainting, near-death, or the limit of sleep.
It is stated with the intention that four impulsion moments (*javana*) might arise for one whose momentum has become weak.

By saying "this is its intrinsic nature," he demonstrates the fixed order of consciousness (*cittaniyāma*) even by way of the object. Although it was said, "due to the non-completion of the impulsion...

[etc.]... it is not fit," because it was further stated that "it is unable to serve as a condition for the adverting consciousness and so forth," this is shown by way of the occurrence of consciousness.
There is no distinction between this [consciousness] and the first "Infallible" (Amogha) category. For that very reason it was said: "This too... must be understood.
Since the term "bhavaṅga" is used for the rebirth-linking consciousness itself during its course of existence, there is no differentiation of it by way of its cause;
thus, one cannot say, "A bhavaṅga with root-cause is a condition for a bhavaṅga without root-cause by way of proximity-condition. And so it has been said. Therefore—
It is understood that the "bhavaṅga with cause" is said to have that [object] as its object (*tadārammaṇa*).

The state of being a condition for one's own fruit by means of its own intrinsic function, or the state of being a condition for those things which are its fruits by means of their own intrinsic functions, is "the state of being a condition through its own intrinsic function" (*sabhāvakiccapaccayabhāva*).
This should be seen as not prohibited [in the following case]: "at the conclusion of a double-rooted, joy-accompanied, unprompted impulsion..."

This is because that specific meaning is not intended here. And just as it is not prohibited for those with rootless or two-rooted rebirth-linking to have a rootless or two-rooted registration (tadārammaṇa) following a three-rooted javana,
so too it is not prohibited for one with a three-rooted rebirth-linking to have a two-rooted registration immediately after a three-rooted javana,
nor for one with a two-rooted rebirth-linking to have a rootless registration immediately after a two-rooted javana.
It should be understood that this is not prohibited. For it has been stated: "Three-rooted kamma gives its result whether it is three-rooted, two-rooted, or rootless.
By the phrase "of the full result," he establishes by this very means that the aforementioned object-representation (*tadārammaṇa*) following a three-rooted impulsion is indeed not prohibited;
for in the absence of the completeness of other conditions, the object-representation does not occur at all.

"Kamma that has not yet ripened becomes one whose result is fulfilled"—this is merely a way of indicating the mouth [of the process], because the occurrence of the aforementioned object-conditions has not been fully analyzed.
For in the case of superior three-rooted (tihetuka) kamma, there are sixteen [resultant moments];
for the other [two-rooted], twelve; for superior two-rooted kamma, twelve; and for the other [one-rooted], eight. Thus, there are sixteen resultant consciousnesses and so forth.

They should be applied. "Therefore" means because this is merely an illustration of the opening for the exposition of result by way of kamma that produces rebirth-linking when its result is complete; therefore.
And "having done so" means that the arising of the object-representation (tadārammaṇa) from various types of kamma can also occur in other ways than this.

Regarding the statement, “Equanimity... arises,” by what function does it arise? First of all, it does not have the function of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), because the object of the impulsion (*javana*) is no longer present as an object.
Nor does it have the function of investigation (*santīraṇa*), because it does not proceed in that manner.

It cannot be said to have the functions of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) or death (*cuti*). By process of elimination, it is logical that it has the function of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). Not...
For it is precisely the consciousness that has become the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) which is called the "life-continuum" (bhavaṅga).

The connection is: "inclined toward that" means the advertence (āvajjana) is inclined toward the object that has entered the range of the senses. "As for another," such as the first jhāna and so forth;
the intention is that this [advertence] must also possess the quality of being accompanied by advertence (sāvajjanatā). Regarding the phrase "not for that purpose": here, by the word "that" (taṃ),...

One recollects its cessation. "By way of arising" means from the perspective of arising. "That" refers to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "Of that cessation" refers to the cessation of that [base].
And the phrase "it arises in such a way" explains the meaning of the expression "it is the proximity condition.

"As stated" means of the kind already described. "Purification" is the knowledge that precedes the second path and so forth. "Of these" refers to the noble path-consciousness, the consciousness immediately following the path, and the resultant consciousness.
"Of this" refers to the aforementioned resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*).

"By way of decisive support" (*upanissaya*) means, for the purpose of showing that very resultant [consciousness] such as eye-consciousness, etc., the sense bases such as the eye, etc., are so called by virtue of their function of seeing, etc., their fruit of seeing, etc., or their purpose of seeing, etc.
"The preceding minds" refers to adverting (*āvajjana*), etc. "In the state of being devoid of another physical basis" (*vatthantararahatta*)...

Because it does not apply even to another object in the same way it applies to another base—as if it were being shown in a different instance—it is said to be "devoid of another base and another object.

If it must necessarily be similar to the kamma by way of its result, then in this case there would be no possibility at all for rootless results, since they are not similar to kamma; bearing this point in mind, he said: "Of the rootless..."

"Panā" means "mere impact. This refers to the function of the five types of consciousness (*pañcaviññāṇa*), for they operate merely by way of impinging upon visible forms and other objects that have come into range.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the functions of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*) and so forth are included.

Furthermore, the state of being "prompted" (*sasankhārika*) or "unprompted" (*asankhārika*) existing within wholesome states—or indeed within both wholesome and unwholesome activities—is not similar to one another.
Because it stands in opposition [to the state of abandonment], it might seem as if it were contrary to the results;

however, since that [opposition] does not exist for those [states] which, due to the absence of a root, lack such functions as the mere falling upon their own objects without being well-established, it is said: "it is not opposed to the prompted" and so forth.
By both [of these terms], he allows for their arising, with the intention that they are like "matter produced by past action" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*). [The term] *vipākadhammadhamma*...
"A resultant state is a condition for [another] state by way of object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya).

One contemplates the aggregates that are subject to result (vipākadhammadhamma) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; one relishes them and delights in them; taking them as an object, lust arises, and grief arises.

Since it is stated, "When wholesome or unwholesome [states] have ceased," and so forth—as in the triad on results (vipākattika)—there may well be a corresponding text in the triad on the wholesome (kusalattika) as well.

Having stated this, it was said: “And in the *Kusalattika*,” and so forth. For there, after indicating that “a wholesome state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*),” it is explained:

“Whether trainees (*sekkha*) or worldlings (*puthujjana*), they practice insight (*vipassanā*) into the wholesome as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; when the wholesome has ceased, its result arises with that as its object; the wholesome...”
It is said: "One relishes it and delights in it; with that as its object, lust arises, views, doubt, restlessness, and grief arise;
when the unwholesome has ceased, the resultant [consciousness] arises with that as its object.

By the phrase "for it is expansive," etc., he demonstrates the logical justification for that statement, intending to show that it is not mentioned precisely because it does not exist [in that specific state].

Here, some say: "Even though it possesses the sixfold equanimity, because it is a functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*), the expansive functional nature of the functional impulsion (*kiriyajavana*) cannot be denied; thus, the example of the leaf-bundle brought forward is inappropriate.

Furthermore, the fact that the absence of a registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) immediately following a functional impulsion is not mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*) is no reason [to deny its occurrence], since it is found in some places by some intention."
"Because it is not mentioned. For instance, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, although the predominance (*adhipati*) is found in the description of the unwholesome, it is not stated;
therefore, one must investigate whether there is an absence of registration (*tadārammaṇa*) immediately after functional impulsion (*kiriyajavana*)," they say.

Even though it consists of function, for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) who have attained equanimity (*tādibhāva*) in all circumstances, the impulsion consciousness is not expansive as it is for others.
However, because it has the nature of being peaceful (*santa*), it may have the function of settling; thus, its leaf-cup was shown.

In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, in the exposition of the unwholesome, there is no apparent reason for not mentioning the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*)—which is obtainable immediately after functional impulsion (*kiriyajavana*)—just as [the registration] following the predominance (*adhipati*) is mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
For it is stated in the commentary on that passage: "Because the method has been shown below."

Nor can it be said that the method has not been shown here, because it would be inappropriate to demonstrate a method for those states—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that possess the nature of producing results (vipākadhammadhamma), since they do not share the same intrinsic nature [as the factors being discussed].

Furthermore, in that context, it could be said that [the method] was "extracted" in order to show a teaching of a single flavor, owing to the absence of any dominant influence (adhipati) in some cases or in all cases; but here, such is not the case.
It was stated that "there is no reason for not speaking" because a reason for not speaking could have been found.
By the phrase "by way of intention," he shows that this is merely the opinion of that elder, based on the statement:
"When the wholesome or unwholesome has ceased, a resultant consciousness accompanied by roots arises as its object-condition (*tadārammaṇatā*)."

However, since even a "caused" (*sahetuka*) object-recognition (*tadārammaṇa*) exists immediately after an unwholesome state, the intention [of the author] in saying "by way of grasping what is appropriate" when explaining its arising is as follows.
By the statement "no reason is seen here," he shows that all three types of object-recognition are appropriate immediately after a three-rooted (*tihetuka*) impulsion.
Regarding the phrase "by which intention": first, according to the Elder, a single kamma produces many object-recognitions.
Because there is no distinction in the kamma itself, it becomes distinguished by the specific condition known as the respective impulsion (*javana*);

with this intention, the classification of the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) as "with effort" and so forth was stated by way of the impulsion. For a resultant state must correspond to its kamma, not possess a nature contrary to that kamma;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the result] being disagreeable. It is with this intention [that this was said].

The second elder spoke of a specific difference in the object [of rebirth] by way of karma alone. Thinking that just as knowledge is the opposite of the signs of misfortune such as birth-blindness and the like in the miserable destinies,
it might also be the opposite of the signs of misfortune in the happy destinies, the third elder—

following this method— [stated] that "one does not admit a two-rooted rebirth-linking from a three-rooted karma," thus [explaining] those doctrines in a way that does not contradict their underlying intention.

What is appropriate should be taken. Regarding the passage from the *Mahāpakaraṇa*: “A conditioned phenomenon (*sahetuka-dhamma*) is a condition for an unconditioned phenomenon (*ahetuka-dhamma*) by way of the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*).
In the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of this [statement], it says: “A conditioned life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is a condition for an unconditioned life-continuum by way of the proximity-condition;
conditioned aggregates (*khandhā*) are a condition for emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) by way of the proximity-condition.”
The meaning is: "by such passages as these found in the *Paṭṭhāna* under the 'Duo on Wholesome States with Roots' (*sahetuka-duka*) and so forth.
The commentary on the wholesome and resultant [consciousness] of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) is concluded.
Now follows the commentary on the discussion of the resultant [consciousness] of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).
499. "Of the desire and so forth existing at that moment": by this, he shows the non-existence of the state of being a "difficult progress" (dukkhāpaṭipadā) and so on in the resultant jhāna.
For the resultant jhāna is not produced by means of preliminary work (parikamma) in the same way as the wholesome jhāna.
Nor, in this case, is there an ultimate distinction of object for the result corresponding to the distinction of the wholesome progress.

"It may be" means it can be so stated because immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) invariably possess an object, and because the resultant consciousness (*vipāka*) exists even with reference to objects other than the sign of the action (*kamma-nimitta*).

"At different moments, with different predominants" is said considering that "in whatever moment a particular jhāna has a certain predominance, at another moment that same jhāna does not invariably have that same predominance. "Only of the fourth jhāna" means...
And it shows this very point: that the predominances (*adhipati*) are not as one-sided as the path (*paṭipadā*).
The commentary on the discussion of the resultant states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the supramundane resultant states.
505. Worldly kamma, when it has acquired a specific distinction through craving, ignorance, and so forth, becomes capable of producing a result, but not otherwise;

thus it is said, "conditioned by craving and so forth. "Of the other" means of that which is devoid of the designations of emptiness and the wishless—that which is manifested by the pure path and which is called "signless" (animitta) according to the method of the Suttas. For this very reason he said:

“Even for the path immediately following the contemplation of impermanence,” and so forth. The intention is that there is an opening... [and so on] ...up to “there is a breaking [of the continuity] by way of the proceeding of the path.

Having regard for the statement, “Only in the fruit-consciousness immediately following the path,” he spoke with hesitation, saying, “when there is the acquisition of names such as ‘emptiness’ (suññatā).
And it acquires the name ‘signless’ because there is no distinction in the acquisition of the fruit’s name once the path has proceeded.
The intention [is as follows]. "Of such a kind alone" means: of precisely the same kind as the faith in the path, so too is the faith in the fruit.

(555) Because of the statement, "Which phenomena are leading out? The four paths," and because it is said in the description of the non-leading-out state that "it is the result in the four planes," the fruit does not, in the ultimate sense, possess the nature of leading out; rather, it is the nature of leading out... [of the path].
However, because the fruition (vipāka) occurs by way of the subsiding and abandoning of the defilements (kilesa), it is called "such" in a figurative sense;

thus he said, "of that which has the nature of leading out," and so forth. By the phrase "and five-factored," he shows that in all sections of the *Maggavibhaṅga*, the designation of the fruit as the "path" is employed.

For therein, even though [the factors] exist at the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga)— [The rest of the sentence continues: ...it is shown that the designation of the fruit as the path is used in all instances. Therein, although [the factors] are present at the moment of the Noble Path—

In the case of the abstinences, the five factors of the path are also mentioned in the Pāḷi for the purpose of showing that the remaining five factors—the factors of causing others to act—have additional functions.

Thus, regarding the "enlightenment factors as well": the meaning is that just as with the path, the enlightenment factors are also mentioned in the *Maggabojjhaṅgavibhaṅga* and in the [discussions on] the fruits.
The commentary on the discussion of supramundane resultant [consciousness] is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of functional indeterminate [consciousness]: 568.
"The prior occurrence" refers to the occurrence of the great functional consciousness; for it is by means of that that one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) reflects in this way.
For this very reason he said: "But this consciousness is devoid of investigative wisdom.

The word "thus" (evaṃ) indicates that just as it occurs at the ear-door, so too at the nose-door and the others, this consciousness functions by means of the "this-is-the-purpose" (idamatthika) determination regarding each respective object through the great functional consciousnesses (mahākiriyacitta).
"Obtained while being associated with the five doors" refers to the great functional consciousnesses that arise in the five doors.

This was said with reference to the occurrence of this consciousness by way of its "rounding of the back" (piṭṭhivaṭṭaka-bhāva), or else the connection is that it occurs only in the five sense-doors. Because it is stated [in the text] as "greed... [etc.]...
arisen," one first becomes joyful through this consciousness in the five sense-doors, and subsequently investigates each respective object with the great functional (mahākiriyacitta) consciousnesses.

This meaning appears as if it were already stated. However, they say that even before this, for one who has delimited the suitability for exertion and so forth by means of mind-door consciousness, such a consciousness proceeds toward such objects as visible forms and so on at the five doors.
This meaning also [arises] precisely at the five doors, as the cause for the reflection upon the abandoning of craving for what is alluring and so forth.
It can be stated by connecting it thus: "That which has arisen is the cause as previously described.
And this being so, the statement, "The preceding occurrence is the condition for this consciousness," is also established.
Furthermore, in this context, at the five sense doors, one should understand that this consciousness merely produces mental joy (*somanassa*), not physical happiness (*sukha*).
Because the five-door consciousnesses do not produce intimation (*aviññatti*), the arising of joy occurs at the mind-door (*manodvāra*).

For this very reason, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), regarding the five doors it is stated merely that "he is gladdened" (*somanassito hoti*), whereas regarding the mind-door it says "causing laughter" (*hāsayamānaṃ*).
By means of this consciousness that arouses laughter (*hasituppāda-citta*), even though the Blessed One’s smiling was occurring, [the smile was produced].
Because it conforms to the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of future existences, and the knowledge of omniscience, it is indeed a "concomitant of knowledge" (*ñāṇānuparivatti*).

When there is thus the state of being a concomitant of knowledge, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the scriptures or the commentaries; and having established this, it is stated in the commentary:
"At the conclusion of the practice of those knowledges, this consciousness arises. And this must necessarily be so.
It must be so intended; otherwise, even the occurrence of the Buddha’s advertence-consciousness (*āvajjana-citta*) would not be logical.

For its status as an originator of intimation (*viññatti-samuṭṭhāpaka-bhāva*) is certain, and when it functions as an originator of intimation, its nature as advertence does not obstruct the bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and so forth produced by that intimation.
“Tato eva” means precisely because they are not well-established due to the absence of roots.
In the phrase “jhānaṅgāni balāni ca,” the word “ca” has the sense of a conjunction, meaning “and jhāna factors.
If, because their status as powers is incomplete, the powers are neither mentioned nor included in this pair of rootless consciousnesses, then why are they pointed out? To this he says: “Because...”

“...panā” and so forth. Since even the resultant [consciousness], which is a counterpart of the wholesome states that possess the nature of leading to liberation, might have that same nature like a fruit, [the author] has stated “in the great functional consciousnesses” (*mahākiriyacittesu*) by excluding the resultant consciousnesses with roots (*sahetuka-vipākacitta*), because they are merely functional (*kiriya*).
Alternatively, it should be understood that by the word “and” (*ca*) in the phrase “and in the great functional consciousnesses,” the resultant consciousnesses with roots are also included.

574. “The faculties... [etc. ...arise immediately after this”—this is stated because those knowledges belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Because the others belong to the sublime sphere (mahaggata), it is stated that they arise “immediately after the preliminary work” (parikamma).

577. That wherein the conceit “I am” (ahaṃ māno) is established is the self (attā). That very thing comes to be, arises; it is not permanent as imagined by others—thus it is the individuality (attabhāva). Or, it is called individuality because it comes to be, proceeds, in the manner grasped by those held to views (diṭṭhigatika).
The commentary on the discussion of the indeterminate (abyākata) as action is concluded.
The commentary on the Section on the Arising of Consciousness is finished.
2. The Section on Material Phenomena (Rūpakaṇḍa): Commentary on the Summary (Uddesa).

"By what? means by either form (*rūpa*) or non-form (*arūpa*). First, regarding the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), it is impossible to establish a temporal determination for matter (*rūpa*), because [consciousness] is not all-pervasive and is not invariable.
Showing this point, he said: "Because of the existence of matter not originated by consciousness," and so forth.

In that context, according to the first position—that matter not originated by consciousness arises during the three moments of consciousness— ... [the text continues] ...in this view, [matter] arises at the three moments of consciousness.
Let there be no defining of the moment of material rebirth by the moment of the arising of consciousness;
however, in this alternative view—that all material form arises at the very moment of the arising of consciousness—how is it so?
Even here, non-mentally-produced matter, despite arising simultaneously with the mind, does not arise as bound to the mind, just like matter that is not bound to the faculties.
It is said that "the time [of arising] must be determined by the mind" because of the presence of non-mental-originated [matter].
By this, he shows that the determination of matter's time by that particular mental state is not universal. The connection is:
"because there is no determination due to being originated by multiple minds. For if the originating mind were fixed, there might be a determination of the matter originated by the mind.

“Of some” means of the wholesome [kamma] of the sense-sphere and so forth. “In some places” means in the formless realm (ārūpa). Alternatively, “of some” refers to the resultant [consciousness] of the five-aggregate plane;

“in some places” refers to the moment of rebirth-linking and the final moment. By the statement “at that time there is contact,” etc., the determination of the occasion is made for those factors coexistent with consciousness by means of consciousness itself;
thus it is said, “because of their non-coexistence with consciousness. “Of these” refers to the derived material phenomena (upādārūpa).
That which is beneficial to something by way of coexistence is itself described as that which establishes its temporal determination; thus he says, "co-nascent... because of its own nature.
Furthermore, by the phrase "nor from the great elements," etc., he demonstrates the very absence of such a determination. "Of some" refers to those things such as the non-kamma-born.
"By some" refers to those such as the kamma-born. "From their occurrence" means from their arising. "Together" means at one and the same time.
"Non-existence" means non-existence by necessity.
"Intimation" ... [etc. ... "cannot be said" because, when the time is determined by the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is not manifested by them;
this is the intended meaning. By the phrase "at one time," etc., he further clarifies the very absence of determination when the time is restricted by the great primary elements.
Regarding the phrases “for the purpose of analyzing thus” and “to show that there exists what is unanalyzed and undeclared,” their connection is with the statement:
“He spoke thus, encompassing both the analyzed and the unanalyzed in their entirety.

Since it is impossible for that which is being demonstrated after establishing a temporal distinction to be demonstrated without limitation [if taken literally], he provides a general conclusion after demonstrating only a portion.

However, without establishing a formal definition of the occasion (*samaya*), he stated this meaning—namely, that it is "thus"—by way of a direct description through the phrase beginning with "by the establishment of the occasion" (*samayavavatthānena*).
"Unanalyzed" (*avibhatte*) means not previously analyzed like the indeterminate states of fruition (*vipāka*) or functional (*kiriya*).
"To be analyzed" (*vibhajitabbe*) means worthy of analysis because of its possessive nature. "Shown" (*dassite*) means shown by way of enumeration. This very same meaning has already been stated.
In order to show this in detail, he said, “But here...,” and so forth.

The leading (*nayana*) of phenomena such as results (*vipāka*) is the method (*naya*); that very thing is the "exposition of the method" (*nayadassana*). What was previously called "the teaching" (*desanā*) is precisely what is meant here by "exposition of the method.
In the second alternative interpretation, however, it is called "method" (*naya*) because it is led (*nīyati*) by way of being sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so on.
It is functionally indeterminate (*kiriyābyākata*). Its "seeing" should be construed as "seeing by way of method" (*nayadassana*).

In the sections of the exposition concerning the dyads and so forth, because the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*) has not yet been introduced, it is not included and thus the first alternative is stated; however, in the section on the single factors (*ekaka*), the basis is also included, and therefore it is stated in the second alternative as "and the heart-basis.
But what is the reason for this in the sections of the exposition concerning the dyads and so forth?
And why is the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) not included? Because it does not belong to the same category as the other bases and because there is a difference in the teaching.
For while visual consciousness and the others have the eye and so forth as their supports exclusively, mental consciousness does not have the heart-base as its support exclusively;
furthermore, the teaching regarding the number of bases and so forth proceeds by way of what [consciousness] is supported. Even that which has the heart-base as its support exclusively—

By virtue of that [distinction], even when the pairs and so forth are stated as "there is matter that is the basis (*vatthu*) for mind-consciousness" and so on, the corresponding pairs of objects (*ārammaṇa*) and so forth are not possible.
For it would not be possible to say, "There is matter that is the object of mind-consciousness; there is matter that is not the object of mind-consciousness," and so forth;
thus, the teaching of the pairs of bases and objects would be of different categories rather than of the same category.
And it is the Blessed One’s intention to teach this; for this is the natural mode of the Blessed One’s teaching.

Precisely because it is not stated in the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* by way of the classification of the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), one cannot say "sustained thought" (*vicāra*) in response to the category of "without applied thought and without sustained thought.

Therefore, although applied thought (*vitakka*) is applicable in the response to the category of "without applied thought and with sustained thought only," it was not mentioned; otherwise, [the teaching would have been inconsistent].

"It should be stated as 'and applied thought' (vitakko ca). Thus, because it does not belong to the same category as the other bases and because of the difference in the teaching, it is not included in the enumeration (uddesa) within the dyads and so forth.
Since one explains only that which has already been enumerated, they say it is also not included in the exposition (niddesa) as "the heart-base" (hadayavatthu).
"Seven decads of the eye, etc. means the seven decads consisting of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, and masculinity;
or, in terms of a single continuum, the seven decads consisting of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, sex, and base.

Although there is no ultimate division in Nibbāna, it is stated that it has divisions such as "with remainder" and so forth, because even a conceptual division is indeed a division when considered within the sphere of conventional discourse.

584. Although the term *parimaṇḍala* is seen elsewhere in the sense of being shaped like a hen’s egg, here, since it refers to the Cakkavāḷa which is wheel-shaped (*cakka-saṇṭhāna*), the word *parimaṇḍala* may be used as a synonym for "round" (*vaṭṭa*).
With the intention that words have multiple meanings, he said: "Round and circular. And herein, [the height] of Sineru, Yugandhara, and so forth...
Its height is stated in terms of its upper and lower portions relative to the ocean; it is also eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, Sineru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in length and eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in breadth.
It stands surrounding Sineru by way of a wall-like enclosure.
There are the Yugandhara mountains and so forth; between Sineru, Yugandhara, and the others, there are also what are called the Cold Seas.
They say that "in terms of their breadth, they are respectively equal in measure to the height of Sineru and the other mountains.
A single world-system of one hundred thousand million is the field of authority (*āṇākhetta*), while a world-system of ten thousand is the field of origin (*jātikhetta*).
It should be understood as being by way of the very nature of things (*dhammatā*).

Since the particle *vā* functions in the senses of restriction, non-restriction, alternative, and conjunction—as in the cases of *vikappa*, *samāna*, *samuccaya*, and *vibhāvana*—the construction has been made accordingly. For particles (*nipāta*) have many meanings; therein, the sense of "non-exclusive" (*anekantikatta*) is the sense of non-restriction (*aniyamattha*).
By means of accomplishing the purification of virtue and so forth, or by means of the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*), it is [described] as "great" due to its great function.

By way of effort (*vāyāmena*). Although there is a distinction based on characteristics and so forth, because they exist as many hundreds of thousands of groups (*kalāpa*) at one time within a single continuum, these great elements (*mahābhūtāni*) exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) as vast and numerous, just as one speaks of "the great multitude" (*mahājana*).
Thus, when the meaning is "occurring by depending," dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppannatā*) is stated, because it indicates arising from conditions.
The intention is that "upādāyati" means "it depends upon" (upādāyati). For this very reason, he says, "of that which is absolutely dependent.

[The phrase] "for there exists a state of ownership among things that have the nature of being supported" means that even though a thing is the support (ādhāra), it is spoken of as having a state of ownership (sāmibhāva) due to a desire for a relationship of mutual sharing (saṃsāmisambandha), in the absence of a desire for a relationship of container and contained (ādhārādheyyasambandha);
the intention is, for example, as in the expression "the branch of the tree."

Commentary on the Compendium of the Threefold Matter (Tividharūpasaṅgaha) 585. Regarding the phrase "and the dyad of intimation," it should be understood that by the word "and" (*ca*), the dyads of [matter] coexistent with consciousness and following consciousness are also included.
For by this same method... [omission] ...it can be known. Herein, first, among the twenty-five dyads of bases:
The first dyads, pentads, and so forth, together with the fourteen remaining miscellaneous dyads,
the twenty-five remaining object dyads, the five external base dyads, the five beginning with the visible-form element dyad,
the three final faculty dyads, the twelve subtle-materiality dyads, and the remaining dyads of bases, elements, and faculties— excluding those beginning with the first.

And they proceed by way of combination (*yojana*). Furthermore, among the twenty-five dyads of objects (*ārammaṇa*), the first group of five dyads proceeds by way of all the miscellaneous dyads—with the exception of the dyads of "clung-to," "not clung-to," "subject to clinging," "with visible form," "consciousness-originated," and "coexistent with consciousness"—by way of all the dyads of bases (*vatthu*), by way of the dyads of bases and elements excluding the dyads of the visible-object base and the visible-object element, by way of all the dyads of faculties (*indriya*), and by way of all the dyads of subtle matter (*sukhumarūpa*).
In the case of the second group of five dyads and so forth, it proceeds according to their respective order.
The sound-base, the sound-element, and the dyads beginning with "sound" do not travel a league (*yojana*);
the form-base, the form-element, and the dyads beginning with "form" do travel it. Among the miscellaneous dyads, the only distinction is the dyad of "with visibility.

And just as it is with the dyads of the physical bases (*vatthu*), so it is with the pentads of dyads beginning with the eye-base, the eye-element, and the eye-faculty. And just as it is with the dyads of the objects (*ārammaṇa*), so it is...
The application of the triads (*tika-yojanā*) occurs within the five dyads such as the dyad of the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) and the dyad of the visible-form element (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, the dyads of the female faculty (*itthindriya*), male faculty (*purisindriya*), and life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), as well as the dyad of subtle matter (*sukhumarūpa*), enter into combination with all the dyads. Thus, first of all, the application of the triads is to be understood in this way.
[Objection: But surely this application was not taught by the Blessed One; therefore, it should not be done. [Response: This is not an absolute rule. Why?
The application according to the method given by the Blessed One is indeed the teaching of the Blessed One himself. For it is said in the commentary on the matrix (mātikā):
"It is also possible that 'states which are both causes and causeless' [be included]," and so forth. Furthermore, "possibility" (sambhava) is the basis for inclusion.
The commentary on the threefold classification of matter is concluded.
586. Regarding the commentary on the fourfold inclusion of matter and so forth:

taking the meaning of "cittasamuṭṭhāna" to be "that which originates from consciousness alone," it is stated that "the dyad of consciousness-originated matter follows the same course as the dyads of intimation and so forth.
For when the commonality [of the term] has been set aside, whatever matter [is produced] among the productive conditions...
"It originates from consciousness; it originates from consciousness alone.

By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "from the dyads of intimation, etc.," the dyads of co-existent with consciousness and following after consciousness are included. Regarding "that which is obtainable":
of that derived matter, some is mind-originated and some is not mind-originated. Of that non-derived matter, some is...
"Originated by mind" (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*) and "not originated by mind" (*na cittasamuṭṭhāna*): it is thus that [the pair] is obtained. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*) in the phrase "the dyads beginning with 'with visibility'" (*sanidassanadukādi*), dyads such as "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*) and "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) are included. "By that" refers to the dyad of "originated by mind.

"Of that" refers to the very same dyad of "originated by mind. "But others," however, [are included] by means of the dyads of "intimation" (*viññatti*), "originated by mind," "co-existent with mind" (*cittasahabhū*), and "concomitant with mind" (*cittānuparivatti*).
There are other miscellaneous dyads as well.
Because the sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*) is exclusively not-clung-to (*anupādinnatta*), it is stated:
"excluding the dyads beginning with those having ear-contact as their object. Regarding the tetrads that are obtainable: that form which is clung-to (*upādinna*) exists as the object of eye-contact.
There is that which is not the object of eye-contact. That form which is non-clung-to (anupādinna) is the object of eye-contact;

there is that which is not the object of eye-contact—and so forth. The connection is that fourfold sets (catukka) are obtained by applying this method to all the dyads (duka) such as "object" and "external base. "By the remaining" refers to the dyads beginning with "object," "external base," and "form-element."

"By the remaining dyads among those mentioned as 'attainable dyads'" means by those dyads other than the ones already stated. "Of these" refers to the dyads consisting of what is clung-to (upādinna), what is not clung-to (anupādinna), what is subject to clinging (upādāniya), and what is mind-originated (cittasamuṭṭhāna).

"Of others" refers to dyads such as what is subject to clinging (upādāduka) that are other than the dyad of what is clung-to (upādinnaduka) and so forth. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "by the dyads of bases etcetera," the dyads of the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so on are included.
Here too, the connection is that "quaternaries are not found" when one applies the remaining [dyads] to both "these" and "others."
The commentary on the fourfold classification of matter, etc., is finished.
The commentary on the enumeration is finished.
The Exposition of Matter.
594. Just as the nature of being subject to change (*ruppana-sabhāva*) is common to earth and the other phenomena, the state of being a cause (*hetu-bhāva*) and so forth is not common;
therefore, it is not to be analyzed among the causes. Thus it is said, "of that which has no division. This, however, is merely a demonstration of the very nature of its lack of division.
This is the exposition. And having done so, because even Nibbāna is devoid of differentiation, it is stated in the exposition merely as "the unconditioned element" (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).

Although the factors such as non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth are exclusively expressible by the term "cause" (in the sense that "by means of this, wholesome states and the like proceed and are established"), [they are nevertheless included].

Furthermore, since even the great elements (mahābhūta) and so forth are denotable by the word "cause" (hetu) due to their commonality as causal factors, [the author] specifies them by means of the second word "cause," which expresses the sense of being a root (mūla), saying: "causes that are causes" (hetuhetu).

Because they establish a state of firm foundation for wholesome and other phenomena in the sense of being roots, these very factors that assist are called "the three wholesome causes" and so forth in the *Paṭṭhāna*, and they alone are termed "the cause-condition" (hetupaccaya).

He said, "The meaning is either 'root-cause' (mūlahetu) or 'condition-cause' (paccayahetu). He stated that the word *paccaya* is used as a synonym for the word *hetu*, intending to show that these two terms—*hetu* and *paccaya*—do not have different meanings, based on the following etymologies:

it is called *hetu* because by means of it (*etena*) or from it (*etasmā*) the fruit proceeds (*hinoti*); it is called *paccaya* because depending upon it (*paṭicca*) the fruit comes into being or proceeds (*eti*). Thus he said: "Of the words *hetu* and *paccaya*..."

"Because they have the same meaning. Since the primary elements (mahābhūta) are dependent upon the three elements of existence, and derived matter (upādārūpa) is dependent upon the four great elements, all matter at all times, in all places, and in all modes has the four great elements as its cause.
Furthermore, since the primary elements are taken in their general sense without specifying their particular divisions, it is said: "The causes of the aggregate of matter."

“Of undertakings of action” (*kammasamādānānaṃ*) means of actions that have been undertaken, or of actions performed after having undertaken them. “In other conditions” refers to craving, ignorance, and so forth, which are the conditions for the ripening [of kamma].
“Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a desirable, pleasing, or agreeable ripening should arise from bodily misconduct;
such a case does not exist. But, bhikkhus, it is possible that from bodily misconduct...”
“An undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable result might arise. This is possible. [The same applies to] speech...
mind... this is possible... It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen that an undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable result should arise from bodily good conduct.”

“Kamma divides beings, that is to say, by way of inferiority and superiority”—from such statements as these, it is said that kamma determines the desirability or undesirability of the result (vipāka), hence the phrase:

“because of its determining the desirable and undesirable result. The states of success and failure regarding destiny (gati), physical basis (upadhi), time (kāla), and effort (payoga) constitute the “occasion” (ṭhāna), because they provide the opportunity for the result; for no result whatsoever arises without them. In the aforementioned occasion...
When it exists, the desirable or undesirable object to be attained is said to be "the destination... [and so on]... accomplished.

Since a result (vipāka) cannot exist without an object, the object is also its primary cause. Regarding the phrase "because of having no other intrinsic nature," this means because it lacks the intrinsic nature of a cause (hetu) and so forth.

Matter (rūpa) is that which is subject to transformation (ruppana). In the statement "it has this [transformation]," the referent "its" (assa) refers to the very thing—earth and so forth—that undergoes transformation.
He says, "It is called so because only that which possesses the characteristic of being affected (ruppana-lakkhaṇa) has the state of being material form (rūpī-rūpa-bhāva).

"This is its intrinsic nature" (etaṃ sabhāvaṃ) restricts this to material form alone, meaning that when it exists in an arisen state, it has the intrinsic nature of being cognizable by the six consciousnesses, since that is the specific nature of material form.

"Material form is not in this" (na rūpaṃ etasmin) [is said] because material form that does not possess that nature also exists due to the difference in time; therefore, material form is not present there.
This shows that [the object] must be determined. With the words "For there is," etc., he clarifies precisely the absence of the necessity for determination in the case of form alone.
With the words "This very same," etc., he correlates the summary (uddesa) with the exposition (niddesa).

Here, the meaning is that by the word "only" (eva) in the exposition, he determines—that is, he restricts—this very same nature of form as previously stated, making it the thing to be determined. The "determination" mentioned is as follows:
When there is the state of having arisen, the state of being cognizable by the six consciousnesses is called "determination" (*niyama*) because it is fixed;
this exists in form (*rūpa*) alone, since that is the very nature of form. Alternatively, determination is simply the aforementioned restriction of specific time;
this determination exists only in form, it is possible only in form, and unlike in the case of the formless (*arūpa*), it does not fail to occur.
The meaning should be understood as follows. "Difference in time" (*kālabheda*) means a specific distinction of time. "Without taking into account" (*anāmasitvā*) means not grasping it.

"All that" refers to all material form (*rūpa*), including that for which the difference in time has not been taken into account, and which, for that very reason, possesses a nature cognizable in the same way as immaterial phenomena (*arūpa*). By the word "arisen" (*uppanna*), he distinguishes [material form] from this non-grasping of the difference in time, saying: "That which is arisen... and so forth."
All material form existing in the present time possesses the nature of being seen, heard, sensed, and cognized;
it has precisely the nature of being cognizable by the six consciousnesses according to each respective sense, and is not uncognizable by them.

Nor does it have the nature of being cognizable by the six consciousnesses only when it has already arisen, as that would entail the fallacy of there being no fixed rule regarding its characteristics. Thus, although the meaning has been explained without error in this way...
The challenger, not understanding the intended meaning, challenges by saying "Is it not so? and so forth, implying that everything would then become an object for every consciousness.
The other clarifies his own intention with the words "Having grouped together all material form" and so forth.
Here, "having taken [them] as a unity" is a synonym for "having grouped together. The single-characteristic [of materiality] is [perceived] by the six consciousnesses.
It has precisely the nature of being cognizable. This is what is meant:

although it is not the case that everything is an object for all [six] consciousnesses because the five consciousnesses do not operate upon other objects, nevertheless, since every form serves as an object for eye-consciousness, there exists for each its own state of being cognizable by the six consciousnesses according to their respective capacities; that [state] taken collectively—
Having taken them by way of inclusion, it is said: "All matter that has arisen is cognizable by the six consciousnesses," just as it is said:

"The fifth jhāna attained through direct knowledge (abhiññā) has six objects. For just as in the case of the fifth jhāna attained through such direct knowledges as the divine eye or divine ear—although it does not individually have all things as its object—it is nevertheless grasped as a unity by way of its single, uniform characteristic.
In order to show the distinction of the fifth jhāna from the first jhāna and so on by way of its object, it is said: "The fifth jhāna, when attained through direct knowledge, has six objects.
Likewise, in order to show the distinction of form from the formless by way of its objective domain, it is said:
"arisen... cognizable. The state of being cognizable by the six consciousnesses must be restricted to form.
However, material form (*rūpa*) need not be restricted to that [present time], for the particle *eva* has an indefinite scope; thus it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*):
"Only present material form is to be experienced by the six, beginning with eye-consciousness. By the phrase "only present material form" and so forth, he points out the fault in that [Commentary].
Therefore, because the particle *eva* is used in the Canon as "only that which is cognizable," and not through an application [of the meaning] to its [the particle's] absence.
There is no attainment of a desired goal here; rather, there is only the attainment of what is undesired, because one does not see any absolute uniformity of characteristics in all forms.

Therefore, if a fixed rule were accepted merely according to the literal expression, there would be no arising... [text missing] ...and consequently, there would be no purpose even in its inclusion within the scope of the hearing (sotapatita).
"By the method stated" means by the method stated in the passage beginning with "incompatible with the formless" (*arūpato vidhura*).
The preceding knowledge is the basis and cause for the subsequent knowledge; thus it is the "basis of knowledge" (*ñāṇavatthu*).

Regarding the term “sajātī,” the letter *sa-* is shown to have the meaning of the word *samāna* (similar/equal); hence it is said “of those of similar kind” (*samānajātikānaṃ*). And the state of being of similar kind for right speech and so forth is precisely the sense of “virtue” (*sīla*).
By this, it should be understood that inclusion within a similar class means having a common nature. [Regarding] the mind’s [engagement] with an object...
Just as encouragement and mindfulness are particularly helpful for the occurrence of non-distraction, so too is non-distraction itself;

thus it is said, "by way of mutual assistance. For this very reason, even though other co-nascent states exist, only these [three] are shown to be included within the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*).
As for that which was stated in the *Visuddhimagga* and elsewhere in the commentary on the *Saccavibhaṅga*:

And as for the statement, "The applications of energy are included under the heading of activity," that was said with reference to their lack of the nature of concentration and their being conducive to concentration.
For this very reason, it was stated there: "In this context, only concentration itself is included under the aggregate of concentration by way of its own genus.
However, here, inclusion by way of genus refers to the place of arising of both concentration and those factors conducive to it.

"Comprehension (saṅgaha) has been stated": penetration (*paṭivedha*) is the grasping of the intrinsic nature of the object without violating it, and absorption (*appanā*) is the firm settling upon the object, which is indeed its plunging into it; thus it is said that "the function is similar to penetration.

Alternatively, because they are alike in being conducive to the striking and hammering of that [object] for the sake of penetrating the object, the similarity of function between wisdom and applied thought (*vitakka*) has been stated.
The commentary on the Singlefold Exposition is finished.
The Doublefold Exposition:
Commentary on the "To Be Analyzed by Way of Clinging."
596. To show the meaning of "the universal eye" (*samantacakkhu*) as the eye in the sense of seeing in every way and entirely, it is said: "seeing all the conditioned and the unconditioned.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) should be applied individually to each of the three sections: "Suffering is to be fully understood; it has been fully understood. [As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye... [and so on].
For the Pāḷi proceeds with such words as, "knowledge arose, vision arose," and so forth. "By way" means by way of the twelvefold aspect.
That [knowledge] also belongs to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) because it is the knowledge of reviewing through insight (vipassanā).

They say: "The 'eye of knowledge' is appropriately called both the noble path together with its factors and the knowledge of insight. However, together with the supreme path, it is the knowledge of reviewing through insight.
It appears as if it were a single entity.

Regarding the aforementioned lump of flesh together with its constituent parts (*sasambhāra*), the conventional designation "eye" occurs by depending upon the material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) arising from four sources (*catusamuṭṭhānika*) that proceed as a continuum;
thus it is said: "the four... constituent parts. As for "shape," it is simply the sense-sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*); therefore—
It is said because the sense-sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*) is cognized by way of this or that shape when the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are situated in that manner;
it is not because the sense-sphere of visible form itself is the material cause (*upādāna*) for the designation of shape.
For in this way, even in the dark, a shape is cognized by touching it. And so he will say: "Even by touching, it is possible to know [the shape] as long and so forth."
And [it is said]: “Depending on a collection of primary elements (bhūta-samudāya) arranged in long and other shapes.

Although those [qualities of] arising and shape are not distinct from the water element and the sphere of color (vaṇṇāyatana), they are mentioned separately as the arising and the shape of those very elements that have become such.
By this it is shown that, by way of the water element and the sphere of color, there is a specific state occurring which constitutes both arising and shape.
This meaning has been shown. Therein, "origination" (sambhava) is of fourfold origin and arises at the age of sixteen;
they say that for him, there is speech from a position by way of lust. "Of those who are not such" means of those who have become otherwise than that.
"In what was stated," namely, in what is reckoned as the basis of requisites (sambhāra-vatthu). "Because of its existing" is said in the sense of being more frequently occurring. Likewise...
