For indeed, there is no arising for those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) nor for Brahmās. Because of the distinction of the water element (āpodhātu), "arising" refers to that which is connected to the water element;
it also pertains to what is dependent upon that [water element] as its support. Thus, its dependence upon the four elements is stated without contradiction.
Regarding the phrase "being sustained by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment," here it is intended that "temperature and nutriment included within the [material] group (kalāpa) are meant."
They say this to show that the eye exists even when its film is impaired, because it has existed throughout many kalpas.
"Impact" (*paṭigha*) is the state of being directed toward an object, due to its condition of striking (*nighaṃsa*). "Striking" (*nighaṃsa*) is the attainment of a state of dependence.
Therefore, perception based on the eye and so forth is called "perception by impact" (*paṭighasaññā*).
"Multiplicity" (anekatta) is the reason for the non-statement [of a cause], not because the state of being understood as a causal activity is absent.
That, however, should be understood precisely through its establishment by way of dependence. For the activity of the fruit is dependent upon the activity of the cause.
Thus, even though the eye does not actually become the support for visual consciousness, it is designated by that conventional term because it does not deviate from its own nature.
In this context, he demonstrates the conventional usage [of the term].

Since the function of guiding vision is indeed the sovereign function (*indattha*) of the eye, the simile of a lord is stated by the passage beginning, "Just as a lord," and so forth. Eye-consciousness guides the function of seeing;
thus, the eye—and its co-nascent factors such as eye-contact—is said to guide them there. Therefore, it is said: "He guides those states... and so on.
This was stated, but not because visual contact and the others possess the function of seeing. Alternatively, showing that this is a figurative expression (pariyāya) for the following purpose:
the eye-consciousness, which assists visual contact and the others by acting as their faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya), directs them toward the function of seeing;
and the eye, in directing [consciousness] there, also directs the visual contact and the others that follow it. Thus, he demonstrates this figurative usage.

It says: "He sees those phenomena... [and so on]. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the words *cakkhati* (he sees) are explained as having the senses of "leading across" (*pariṇāyati*) and "manifesting" (*pakāseti*).
Furthermore, since shape is indeed a form-object (*rūpāyatana*), it is said: "The eye is that which sees forms, whether even or uneven.
Its function of "wandering" (*vaḷañjana*) consists precisely in its being the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for contact and the other mental factors associated with that door.

599. “The door leading to that... [etc. ...arising is stated” means that when eye-consciousness has arisen, since the javana necessarily arises with respect to a powerful object—taking into account the functions of receiving and so forth—it is so stated.
For it is certain that there is no possibility of turning back after having stood in the interval between the eye-consciousness, the receiving, or the investigating.

"By that condition" means by a condition of that specific kind. "Of those similar to it" refers to the mind-element, investigation, and determining consciousnesses, which are similar to seeing because they lack the specific mode of activity consisting in esteem and relishing.

Since five-door javanas do not function by esteeming in a manner other than relishing and so forth—because their object is material phenomena—they are said to be "of the nature of relishing and delighting."

Only this much has been stated. For it cannot be said that even the post-impulsions of mind-door javanas proceed by treating visible form as a weighty object (*garuka*) through the state of relishing and delighting, in the same way as the five-door javanas do. Thus, visible form is an object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*) only for unwholesome consciousness.
Accordingly, in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "An indeterminate state is a condition for an unwholesome state by way of the predominance condition."

By the passage beginning, "Taking the eye as an object and making it an object-condition (ārammaṇādhipati), one esteems it, relishes it, and delights in it," material phenomena (rūpadhamma) are also analyzed as object-conditions.
However, in the statement, "An indeterminate (abyākata) phenomenon is [a condition] for an indeterminate phenomenon;

an indeterminate phenomenon is [a condition] for a wholesome (kusala) phenomenon," only the fruit (phala) and Nibbāna are analyzed specifically by way of being object-conditions. And according to the enumeration: "Object, object-condition, decisive support (upanissaya), prenascence (purejāta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata)."
It is said, "one. If it were also [possible] for the wholesome, it would have to be said, "two. "Those" refers back to the aforementioned impulsions (javana).
"And those associated with them" means associated with the impulsion. "Others" refers to eye-contact and so forth.
If what is intended is merely the state of being an object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) for form, this would be established by the phrase "having that form as its object" alone.

One might say only this much. However, since matter (*rūpa*) is also a specific condition for the impulsion consciousnesses (*javana*) associated with that door, the word "taking as an object" (*ārabbha*) was stated in order to illustrate that specific quality. Therefore, he said:
"It indicates the state of being another condition, even apart from the condition of the object (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)."
600. In the occurrence of ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*), there is the conventional expression "the act of hearing.
Thus it is said that the ear’s status as the agent of the act of hearing is by way of being a condition for ear-consciousness: “It hears by way of being the support (*nissaya*) for ear-consciousness.

Because it inclines toward life (*jīvita*)—wherein the nutritive essence (*āhārarasa*) is the sign of life—it calls out to that [life]; thus, by this derivation, it is established as the tongue (*jivhā*).
It is said, "the act of tasting, known as the invitation to flavors, is obtained by means of the word 'tongue' (jivhā-saddena)," because it is manifested through the word "tongue.
And so he will say later: "it is called the tongue (jivhā) because it invites (avhāyati) life.
The term *āya* refers to the place of origin. This is because the sensitive body (pasādakāya) serves as the basis for bodily pain and pleasure.
Because they serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the others, it is said that they are "the source of the suffering of suffering and the suffering of change.
"Pervasive" (*byāpitāya*) means in the state of being pervasive, or by way of pervasiveness. "The state of the bodily sensitivity" (*kāyappasādabhāvo*) means the presence of the bodily sensitivity.

"Pierced through" (*anuviddhattā*) means because of being permeated, which is to say, because of being conjoined. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because, to whatever extent there is the occurrence of the appropriated (*upādinnaka*) in this body...
It is said that the body-base exists everywhere, like oil in a cotton pad; therefore [this is so].

Because the translucent sensitivities (pasāda) manifest—as it were—by acting as the cause for the arising of consciousness toward an object that has come into the range of perception due to their white nature, their function of illuminating the object is stated. "Of those with a common basis" means having a single basis. For, among things that are inseparable...

Whatever material form is the support for visible form, taste, and so forth, that very same support is [the support] for taste and the rest. By the phrase "not assuming each other's intrinsic nature," he states the absence of confusion regarding their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).

This is because the sensitivity of the eye (*cakkhuppasāda*) functions only when accompanied by other conditions through the process of impinging upon visible forms, and not when devoid of other conditions.

Therefore, whether or not there is an impact upon the form, it is stated as "capable of being impacted by form" (*rūpābhighātāraho*) in order to show that such is the inherent nature of that material phenomenon (*rūpadhamma*), just as [it is said] "wholesome and unwholesome [states] have the nature of being capable of producing result" (*vipākārahasabhāvā*).
Impact (*abhighāta*) is so called because the mutual facing of object and subject is like an impact;
that occurs either of the form in the eye, or of the eye in the form. Thus it is stated.
“Regarding form, or the striking against form. For this very reason he said:

“In that eye which is non-manifesting and impinging, visible and impinging form has struck,” and “The eye, which is non-manifesting and impinging, has struck against visible and impinging form,” and so forth.
And here, by way of the aspiration for various respective states of existence...

Regarding the eye and the other [senses], the first characteristic of the eye was stated by way of the common karma that produces the personal existence (*attabhāva*) for one who has not yet abandoned lust for them;
the second was stated by way of the specific (*āveṇika*) karma produced with the thought, "May the eye be capable of grasping even visible forms that are extremely distant, subtle, and so forth.

This same method applies to the remaining [senses] as well. Alternatively, although there is a commonality among the five in their nature as sensitive matter (*pasāda*), [the distinction lies] in what is termed the illumination of their respective objects...

The first [statement] was spoken by way of showing the function of confidence (*pasāda*); the second was spoken by way of showing the distinction between the causes of confidence, despite their commonality in being kamma, through the specific difference of their own respective causes.

"Craving for sense-pleasures" (*kāmataṇhā*) means craving for the realm of sense-pleasures (*kāmabhava*). Likewise, "craving for form" (*rūpataṇhā*) should be understood. These are the root causes of their respective realms of existence.

Since craving has as its object the sense bases that are capable of arising in this or that particular existence, it is said that craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*) and the others are fit to be designated by such terms as "desire to see" and so forth.
For "desire to see" means a wish to see, which is to say, craving for forms (*rūpataṇhā*). The same applies to the remaining types of craving as well.
And herein, "desire to see" and the rest refer to the moment of accumulating (*āyūhana*) the karma that produces those respective individual existences (*attabhāva*).

If there were a prior production, there would be nothing further to be said. Even if such production does not exist, it should be understood that the reason [for its designation] is precisely its state of not having been eradicated by the Path.
Since it has not been cut off by the Path, when it encounters its causes, it arises and enters into the state of being a cause for its own fruit;
thus, while existing, it is spoken of by way of the synonyms "arisen" and "existent": "the Noble..."

In such passages as: "One who develops the Noble Eightfold Path, making much of the Noble Eightfold Path, causes arisen evil unwholesome states to vanish even on the spot," and "When sensual desire is present within him, he understands:
'Sensual desire is present within me,'" and so forth.
Here it is asked: Do the sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, arise from a single karma, or rather from various karmas?
The ancients say: "In both ways. In that regard, first, if they arise from various karmas, there is no need to state a distinction among the eye and the others, because their causes are distinct.
But if they arise from a single karma, how is there a distinction between them? Precisely because their causes are distinct.
For craving, which consists in the aspiration for this or that state of existence, by virtue of its longing for the bases included within such states of existence, is itself manifold in form;
through its status as a decisive support (*upanissaya*), it establishes the manifold variety of the kamma that produces those respective states of existence.

Consequently, that kamma—having acquired specific qualities through that [craving] and being endowed with such capacity—produces a fruit that, as it were, assumes many forms and possesses a manifold, distinguished nature.
It produces [the result]. And thus he will say: "Kamma alone is the specific cause for these.

Nor should anything other than the capacity [of the kamma] be understood here as the specific cause, because there is no capacity to produce a distinguished fruit for that which has received a distinction through a specific cause.

For if that were the case, even a single kamma would possess the connection with the distinction of being the cause of multiple faculties, as stated in the passage beginning with "even a single kamma... and so forth.

He himself will later explain this both through reasoning (*yutti*) and through scripture (*āgama*). Likewise, it is stated that a single wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*) is the cause for the production of sixteen or more resultant consciousnesses (*vipākacitta*).
In the world as well, it is observed that a single grain of rice (*sālibīja*) is the cause for producing a fruit consisting of either full or incomplete grains.
What is the use of such deliberation on reasoning? This indeed need not be deliberated upon; for the ripening of karma (*kammavipāka*) [produces] the eyes and so forth.
The ripening of kamma (*kammavipāka*) in all its aspects is the domain only of the Buddhas, who are endowed with the fruit of the knowledge of the ripening of kamma;

it is not the domain of others because it lies beyond the reach of mere reasoning. For this very reason, the Blessed One rejected it after demonstrating the danger, saying: "The ripening of kamma is inconceivable and should not be speculated upon;
whoever should speculate upon it would partake of madness and distress. [Next is] drawing forth (*āviñchana*).
It is the state of being a cause for a person or for consciousness to reach a state of being inclined toward that [object].

Not understanding the specific meaning obtained from the word "all" either through the context (*pakaraṇa*) or by way of elimination (*pārisesa*), one who takes the meaning according to the literal expression alone objects, saying, "What is the distinction here?
and so forth. The other [responds] regarding the individual predominance of fire and the other elements.
Since it is understood that even when there is an excess of two or three [elements], the clarity of the body does not arise due to the deficiency resulting from that aforementioned excess—
even though it is obtained by way of being "one" and so forth— then, either by way of context (*pakaraṇa*) or by way of elimination (*pārisesa*),
the meaning is established that the body exists through the equal proportion of all four primary elements (*bhūta*); thus, the word "all" (*sabba*) here indicates equal proportion.

He said "But this... and so forth in order to show this. And by saying "it illuminates this meaning," he shows that this meaning is obtained from the word "of all" according to the method already stated, and not because that [word] is its direct synonym.

For that very reason he said, "because it is stated by way of... following after... and so forth. For by the very exclusion of the state of being more than a single part, the exclusion of being merely a single part is also understood.

A "part" (*ekadesa*) is a component (*avayava*). For the sensitive matter (*pasāda*) which is the basis for the aggregate of the four elements, there is an "excess of a part" when one of those elements is predominant.
Regarding this, they say: "Both of the first two theorists here belong to other schools.

It is a "quality" (*guṇa*) that the eye and so forth possess the capacity to manifest visible forms and so on only when accompanied by cooperative causes such as light, and that the aperture serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for ear-consciousness.

With the intention of presenting their respective doctrines, it was said: “by the qualities of this or that primary element,” and so forth. Because an opening lacks the nature of a primary element—unlike fire and the others—it was said: “according as applicable.
Alternatively, showing the opponent’s intention—that even an opening, like visible form and the rest, is a quality of a primary element—he said:
“by the qualities of this or that primary element. However, for fire, by means of its visible form of light, and for that which is reckoned as space...

With reference to this meaning—that [the ear] is [conditioned] by the sound of space, [the nose] by the odor of air, [the tongue] by the taste of water, and [the body] by the tangible of earth—it may be said:

"by the respective qualities of those elements as appropriate. Regarding the phrase "in the apprehension of visible form and so forth," the meaning is that eye-consciousness and the rest are to be produced with respect to the objects such as visible form.
Regarding the phrase "by way of being beneficial," it means by the aforementioned qualities of the elements acting as cooperative causes.
Because it is helpful for the eye and other faculties in performing their respective functions. "Being heard by its own nature" is said because it is perceived even when not being uttered by anyone.
Furthermore, there is no sound of wind without impact;

or rather, it should be understood that the opponent's own tenet is that "sound is heard by its own nature in the wind," just as they hold that "the taste of water is sweet. This applies to the second proponent as well.
Because he holds such a view, [the opponent] maintains that there is a restraint [of the elements], and that for them too, qualities such as heat (tejo) consist of visible form (rūpa) and so forth.
"By means of specific qualities such as visible form" means by those endowed with specific qualities such as visible form. "Fire... wind" refers to the atoms of fire and so forth together with space.
"Dissimilar to cotton" means possessing a distinction from cotton-wool earth, and thus possessing a greater capacity than it.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāyo*). "Of that very [earth]" means of the cotton-wool earth itself.

Because it stands having overwhelmed even those existing elements that are indistinguishable from it by virtue of being impossible to perceive, therefore its fragrance alone would be more predominant;

this is the sense. And all of this subsequent explanation is found in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) in the passage beginning with, "Due to the predominance of this or that primary element" (*tassa tassa bhūtassa adhikatāyā*).
This was stated by way of Kaṇāda, who spoke while accepting the doctrine of the Tathāgatas because it had been so taught.
However, according to his own view, Kaṇāda, Kapila, and others hold the tenet that there are only substances such as earth and so forth;
and some say, "This doctrine belongs to certain individuals who are devoted to the teaching of Kaṇāda but have not yet fully penetrated its system. Regarding both of these [positions]:

Because the scent of cotton is superior to the scent of fermented liquor, and the color of hot water is superior to the color of cold water—since both of these [superiorities] are observed—and because no specific distinction of visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth is seen when the constituent elements such as fire (*tejo*) are predominant, it is established that visible form and the rest are not the specific qualities (*visesa-guṇa*) of fire and the others.
Thus he said: “In the absence of that... [up to] ...heat. Therefore, visible form does not belong to fire.
A specific quality (*visesaguṇa*) is not invariably and specifically perceived in a constituent (*sambhāra*) such as fire and so forth;

this shows that whatever is a specific quality of something is not invariably and specifically perceived in a constituent that exceeds it, just as the water element is not [specifically perceived] in a constituent where earth is predominant.
In the same way, this should be applied accordingly to the remaining elements as well. What need is there to mention different groups (*nānākalāpa*), given their distinct intrinsic natures?

He shows that even in the absence of diversity [of parts], there is some distinction due to the diversity of the root cause—that is, because the capacity for such actions as death and so forth is observed only in certain [beings] and not in others.

By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "not even one," he shows that there is nothing at all to be said regarding multiple [such beings]. Regarding the state of existence consisting of the five sense-bases (*pañcāyatanika-khandha*):

That which is produced by the aspiration described as the state of desiring to see and so forth—by this specific cause, he states the specific result. With the words "For it is not," etc., he supports the very point already stated.
"That" refers to the kamma. "By way of distinction" means by its own cause, through the excellence (atisaya) it has brought about.
The intention is that for that very reason it is not a condition for the ear, but rather it becomes one by means of something other than that.

By this reason—that it possesses manifold characteristics—it is shown that even a single kamma, when imbued with specific qualities, is capable of producing a result characterized by manifold characteristics.
Now, he states the fault that would arise if the kamma lacked the aforementioned specific qualities: "Because of the resulting absence of other faculties.
The meaning of this is: since a specific result is impossible in the absence of a specific cause, [if] that kamma which is endowed with such specificity...

The eye is the cause; if there were no specific distinction in it other than that [general cause], it could not produce other faculties either, and thus the ear-faculty and the rest would simply not arise from it. The same applies to the other cases as well.
And here, by "distinction" (visesa) is meant the capacity of karma to produce this or that particular faculty, and that is precisely the nature already demonstrated previously.

It cannot be understood that the production of the kamma-produced material phenomena (*kaṭattārūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking occurs through many sublime volitions (*mahaggata-cetanā*) or through a single limited volition (*paritta-cetanā*);
therefore, it is said: “For all... [it] is understood. Now, in order to demonstrate in detail that very impossibility, it is said:
“By various volitions,” and so forth. This is its summary meaning: “At the moment of rebirth-linking... [etc.]

Regarding the phrase "condition": if the arising of the faculties here were intended by way of various kamma, then at the moment of respective rebirth-linking, both sublime kamma and sense-sphere kamma would have produced the kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*).
But this is not logical, because it has been stated that "sublime volition is a kamma-condition. Nor [is it logical] by way of the material faculties fixed to their respective realms of existence...
The state of having deficient faculties is appropriate at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) within the womb of spontaneous birth (*opapātika-yoni*) when there is perfection of destiny.
Now, if it is produced by various sublime volitions (*mahaggata-cetanā*), then a single rebirth-linking is not produced by multiple kamma-formations.
For this has been determined in the Sāketapañha. Thus, by means of a single sublime kamma, [there is the production] of the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, and the heart-base.

By this statement, which indicates the arising [of faculties], it is shown that even by a single limited kamma, the arising of multiple faculties occurs accordingly; thus it is said: "The arising of multiple faculties is established by a single kamma.
In order to show the meaning that "only when attained" means "performing the function of having been attained," it says: "From the moment... [etc. ...is produced."

It has been stated. Because it is of an extremely subtle nature and thus not within the range of the fleshly eye, and because it exists as a composite of form-objects (*rūpāyatana*), it is said to be "like the wind.

A sound-object (*saddāyatana*) originating from mind could never be an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for ear-consciousness, because [sound] that strikes through a succession of elements is temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*). Therefore he said: "For... [it] does not reach [the ear]."

And in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated without qualification: "The sound-base is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*). The intention [of the objection] is:
"Is it not the case that there is no quick hearing for those standing at a distance because sounds are heard only after a long time?

Or, if there were quick hearing even for them, would there not be no distinction between being far and near? [Response: No. ... [The text continues: "...because of the distance... It is not the case that the sounds of washermen and others are not heard by those standing at a distance.

They are heard by ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*) only after a delay. If that sound is within the range of hearing, for those standing far away and those standing nearby, when the sound has duly entered the field of perception, there arises the conceit that it was "heard slowly" or "heard quickly," due to a specific mode of grasping [the object] by means of what is termed mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*).
Showing this very meaning in detail, he said: "Just as... and so forth. *Nicchaya*... etc.
There is conceit; however, the occurrence of ear-consciousness is the same in both cases, because that sound...
[as before] ...comes. If sound does not proceed by way of a succession of elements (*dhātuparamparā*), how is it that echoes and the like arise?
To this he says: "In the distance... [as before] ...it is the condition. By the phrase "arrived by way of arising," it is shown that even material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*) are present wherever—
It shows that [sounds] arise right there and break up right there, and do not migrate to another place.

"Having the nature of striking" refers to those primary elements (bhūta) being the cause for the production of sound. "Of the location of the ear" means of the region of the ear; the meaning is "situated in the region of the ear.
"By way of the inclination of a person with vision" refers to the fact that, for the most part, sentient beings [are inclined] toward the variegated and diverse sense-sphere of visible forms.
This was stated with reference to the occurrence [of consciousness] by way of drawing after the javana that functions through the eye-door.
By the phrase "because it occurs only in the aperture of the ear-hole," he refutes the claim that the sense-faculty (indriya) operates outside its physical basis (adhiṭṭhāna).

For the sense-faculty functions only in the location of its basis, since its application of function and so forth is seen there. Nevertheless, even though it has an outward operation, [it does not depart from its basis].
It does not possess the capacity to grasp an object; otherwise, there would be grasping of an object even when [the mind] is fixed on or burned by something else.
"And because it is the cause for grasping an object" means that it serves as the cause for consciousness—which makes an object—by remaining right at the opening of the ear-canal.
"By way of that designation" intends that even the odor is spoken of in that way because it is associated with the grasping of the odor.
"Gandho paccayo" means that odor is a concomitant condition (*sahakārīpaccaya*). It should be construed as "saliva and so forth are conditions.
Likewise, "earth" refers to internal and external earth that has become another concomitant condition;

the meaning is that it is a condition for the apprehension of the object. "Serving as a support" means serving as the support for the fire and air elements. "Of those that have become the basis" means of the great primary elements that serve as the basis (*nissaya*).
Of the elements of water, fire, and air. "At all times" means both at the time of compression and at the time of non-compression.
"Therein" refers to the aggregate of material form known as the upper body, which is divided into eighty-four types.
"Impossible to separate" means impossible to separate even by way of groups (kalāpa), such that one could say, "this is the eye-decad," "this is the body-decad," or "this is the sex-decad."
616. “By touching [the object] of long and so forth, it is to be known”: this is not said because long and so forth are the domain of body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*);

rather, it is said because they are to be known even by the mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) that occurs subsequent to the course of body-consciousness after having touched the tangible object consisting of the forms designated as "long" and so forth.
"The configuration of long and so forth" means possessing the configuration of long and so forth.
By stating that one exists in the absence of the other, he expresses the non-coexistence of shadow and sunlight, as well as light and darkness.
But how does light dispel darkness? At the very moment light arises, the sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*) that was occurring by way of the intrinsic nature of darkness is destroyed.
The primary elements (*bhūtāni*) that were occurring as the support for darkness gradually [transform], and in such a manner...
Some say that [the visual consciousness] goes toward the state of being supported by the sphere of visible forms (*vaṇṇāyatana*).

It should be understood that together with darkness, immediately after the cessation of those [visible forms] which constitute its support, there arises within that same continuum—given the convergence of such conditions—those [visible forms] which constitute the support for light.
For there is no occurrence of light without the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as its support, nor is there [light] apart from what is reckoned as darkness.
Only the sense-sphere of visible form ceases, because it ceases together with the primary material phenomena (upādārūpa) that constitute the single group functioning in dependence upon it.
They say that darkness proceeds even after leaving behind the earth, walls, trees, and so forth, like the flame of a lamp or the rays of a jewel.
However, when faint, it is not clearly perceived if it lacks a support such as a wall; when thick, [it is clearly perceived].
They also say that it is logical [to define it] as "that which proceeds depending on a basis.

Regarding the phrase "the sound of non-humans" (*amanussasaddo*): here, the letter *a-* does not have the purpose of excluding the mere state of being human, because its function as indicating similarity is not intended;
rather, it is shown that its purpose is to exclude [the sound] from being anything other than human, by stating: "non-humans... such as spirits and so forth."
He said: "It should be praised in such a way" means it should be praised by way of its basis (*vatthu*), starting with the phrase "the sound of splitting bamboo," and so forth.

632. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "kamma, consciousness, and so forth," temperature (*utu*) and nutriment (*āhāra*) are included. "Those respective forms" refers to the forms of the female gender and so on.
"Arising in dependence upon the female faculty" means that the female gender and so forth, which are generally mutual conditions (*aññamañña-paccaya*), arise [in dependence upon it].
Because they exist only in a continuum accompanied by the femininity faculty (*itthindriya*) and are absent elsewhere, they are said to have the faculty as their cause.
"In another way" means in a manner other than the appearance of feminine gender (*liṅga*) and so forth, or in the absence of the femininity faculty.

"And of the apprehension of 'woman'" refers to the mental activity [arising] from the thought "she is a woman. "Of those forms" refers to the forms that constitute the appearance of feminine gender and so forth. If the femininity faculty...

[The opponent asks: "Since the female organ and so forth are the cooperative causes (sahakārīkāraṇa) for the forms that have the appearance of the female gender and so on, why then is their status as a condition such as a faculty (indriya-paccaya) not mentioned for those [forms]?

[The author replies: To show that they are not indeed a cooperative cause, but rather are called a "cause" merely because the existence of those [forms] arises when they exist, he says: "But because... and so forth.
633. Because a changing sex organ changes only in accordance with the species that was the basis for its previous sex organ, it is said:
“As in the case of rebirth-linking, so too in the course of existence. By the word “etcetera” in the phrase “For whom... not?
and so forth, the statement “Or, for whom the male faculty arises, does the female faculty arise for him? No” is included.

635. Because they are the locus for the occurrence of the base, corrupting *āsava*-states, the application of the designation "body" (*kāya*) should be understood to apply to the specific intimation as well, just as it does to the specific clarity [of the physical body].
Alternatively, because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is distension, the stiffening of the air element is called the "function of the air element" (*vāyodhātukicca*).
For even the function of phenomena is nothing other than their intrinsic nature. [The same applies to] the earth element.
The construction is: "It is appropriate to say that the mode [of expression] is vocal intimation.
(636) Regarding the phrase "thoughts... are grasped," this is stated with reference to the occurrence of the intention to produce speech that manifests the intended meaning;
for at that time, it is said to be "grasped" by them. Even a single syllable, by many...

Because they must be produced by the impulsion-moments (*javana*), and because their nature is incapable of being produced otherwise, they do not possess a discernible distinction nor are they different;
thus it is said: "All... are not different. Regarding the term *abbokiṇṇe* (uninterrupted), it means unmixed with those arising at intervals.
With the intention that the phrase "the final consciousness" refers to the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) without qualification, it is said: "The death-consciousness of others also... is known."

Alternatively, by the statement: “In the case of those who, having been reborn in the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere, will attain final nibbāna, at the time of their death, their verbal formation will cease, but their bodily formation will not cease,” this implies that even for those being reborn in the fine-material or immaterial spheres, the bodily formations are not produced by the death-consciousness of the sense-sphere;
thus, [the same applies] to others besides those whose taints are exhausted...pe...
It is said: "It is known. And because it has been stated:
"Is it the case that for whom bodily formation ceases, for him verbal formation will cease? Yes. And:
"Is it the case that for whom bodily formation ceases, for him mental formation will cease? Yes."

Because of the initial statement: “At the moment of the dissolution of the final consciousness, neither the bodily formation nor the mental formation ceases,” it is established that the in-breaths and out-breaths do not arise together with the sixteenth consciousness preceding the final consciousness, or with any consciousness prior to that.
If they were to arise, [then at the moment of the dissolution of the final consciousness...]
One should not say, "Their bodily formation does not cease," for this has been stated.
Therefore, the inhalations and exhalations that arose seventeen moments prior to death at the very lowest limit cease together with the second consciousness immediately preceding death.
By this, it is meant: "That consciousness after which the final consciousness of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) will arise."
It has been stated that even for a consciousness that serves as an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for the final consciousness, there is no production of bodily formations (*kāya-saṅkhāra*).
Alternatively, the phrase "of whichever consciousness" should be understood as referring to that consciousness by which the very last bodily formation arises;
it does not refer to [the final consciousness] being the immediate condition for the subsequent consciousness. For "immediately" refers to the production of the bodily formation.
“Without an interval,” meaning that the final consciousness will arise immediately after, without being separated by the production of bodily formations.
Why? Because it is stated: “In others, both vocal formation will cease and bodily formation will cease.
Otherwise, [the cessation would apply] to those possessing the third consciousness prior to the final consciousness.

"One falls into the position that the bodily formation arises. Thus, having shown the scriptural authority (*āgama*) for the fact that the death-consciousness of all beings does not produce matter, he now states "For it is not," etc., to show the logical reasoning (*yutti*).

Therein, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "entering the womb, etc.," he includes those submerged in water, those who have lost consciousness, those who have passed away, those who have attained the fourth jhāna, those possessing the form and formless realms, and those who have attained cessation.
637. Because many groups (kalāpa) arise together as a single, solid mass, it is said that those groups belonging to one aggregate are in contact with those belonging to other aggregates.
This is because their distinctness is difficult to discern, not because they are inseparable.
"The separation from their respective elements" means the distinct state of each of those elements from the elements belonging to other groups.

The meaning of *vibhattasabhāvatā* (distinct nature) is non-confusion (*asaṅkīrṇatā*). Since, however, the aforementioned seclusion (*vivittatā*) constitutes the limit of material forms (*rūpa*), it is therefore called "the limit of form" (*rūpapariyanta*).
Alternatively, it is the emptiness (*suññatā*) of each respective primary element (*bhūta*).

For that which has space as its delimitation, its state of being empty should be characterized by its limitation through those [elements]. And for that very reason, it [is distinguished] from the other elements...
"It is said that it is not touched by them as if they were [separate]. "In another way" means in the absence of the state of being untouched by those things which are to be delimited.
638. Regarding the phrase "by means of the various specific qualities of transformation": how is it that softness and wieldiness are found in leather and gold?

Is it not the case that transformations such as lightness occur only in matter bound to the sense faculties (*indriyabaddha-rūpa*), and not in matter not bound to the sense faculties (*anindriyabaddha*)?
"Are they obtained? Yes, this is true; however, it is stated here by way of applying that designation to things similar to them.

For instance, the designations "light" and so forth are applied to cotton wool and the like because of the presence or absence of an excess of the primary elements (bhūtas) that serve as the causes for heaviness and so on.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the phrase "by means of forms exceeding those respective modifications" was said with reference specifically to the nature of the support (nissaya) of the dhamma to be demonstrated. All [dhammas] are conditions for all.
The intention is that lightness (*lahutā*) and the other [characteristics] do not abandon one another.

641. "By the word 'accumulation' (*ācaya*) alone" means by the very word *ācaya* as stated in the *Niddesa*. That which is the accumulation (*ācaya*) of the sense bases (*āyatana*) because they are being accumulated from the beginning—that same thing is intended as "growth" (*upacaya*) because of the subsequent building up (*upari-caya*) of matter as it is being produced again and again. This is the meaning.
The phrase beginning with “In the Pāḷi, however,” is stated in order to show [the meaning] by applying it to the canonical text.
The prefix *upa-* has the sense of “first,” as in such passages as “Bhikkhus, giving is ordained by the wise”;

and it has the sense of “above,” as in such passages as “When the canopy was spread and the parasol set up, they sat down in the pavilion. “Otherwise” means when one takes the prefix *upa-* only in the sense of “above.”

643. *Phalavipaccanapakatiyā* means by way of the nature of the ripening of the fruit. Alternatively, the meaning is that "aging" (*jarā*) is a designation for the nature of the fruit itself—such as the withdrawal of life-span and so forth—by way of its being the fruit-nature.

For it is said: "They are spoken of by way of a metaphorical application to the fruit. This refers to the time when well-transformed matter reaches maturity, such as during the decad of decline (*hānidasaka*) and so on.

645. *Kattabbasabhāvato* means by way of the nature of what is to be done; that is, because the food-bases intended here, such as roots and fruits, have the nature of performing actions like eating and so forth.
"In a state of imbalance or compression, the nutritive essence (*ojā*) becomes dull" means that its subtlety is described due to the absence of its own specific quality.

"The pith of the sap that follows limb by limb" refers to the moisture that serves as the internal nutriment-condition for the bodily parts, having entered them via the network of nutrient-carrying vessels (*rasaharaṇī-dhamani-jālā*);
this is what is called the "sap-element" (*rasa-dhātu*) in the world.

The commentary on the discourse concerning what is derived from clinging (*upādābhājanīyakathā*) is finished. The commentary on the discourse concerning what is not derived from clinging (*noupādābhājanīyakathā*):

From such statements as, "Dependent upon one great primary element (*mahābhūta*), there are three great primary elements; dependent upon three great primary elements, there is one great primary element," and so forth...
One great primary element depends upon the remaining great primary elements, and it is also depended upon by them and by derived matter; thus it is said, "it depends and it is depended upon.
(647) Because the great primary elements do not abandon one another, there is more than one tangible object even within a single group (kalāpa).

Therefore, even when several objects possessing the nature of tangibles have come into the range of the senses, [the mind] attends to only one through the process of mental application (ābhoga) and so forth.
This analysis has been shown [regarding how] it becomes the cause for the arising of consciousness. However, this should also be demonstrated, as appropriate, for the others as well.
In that regard, first, by adhering to the sense-faculty which is its support, the object of taste becomes the cause for the arising of consciousness;
thus, even when many tastes come into the range of perception, at one moment it becomes the cause for the arising of a single type of tongue-consciousness according to the method already stated.

The same applies to the object of smell. As for the objects of visible form and sound, however, because they become causes for the arising of consciousness even without reaching the physical basis of the sense faculty, it cannot be said that as many of them as are situated in a suitable location and receive assistance from other concomitant conditions do not become a single combined object at one moment. For instance, in the case of sound, such as shouting and so forth...
In the same way, even though color consists of many groups [of atoms], it becomes a single object of consciousness by means of its being carried in a palanquin.
Here too, due to the predominance of the object through its being brought together, consciousness certainly arises in some instances despite the gathering of many groups.
The predominance of the sensitivity (pasāda) is the sharpness of the sensitivity due to the absence of obstructions such as bile (pitta). But how?
"Of the mind": he asks this by way of the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*) based on the commonality of "mind.
"Such as that": it refers to that which is not even grasped by ordinary people as "existing"; it is simply "present. "In this way":
he shows that just as water together with its constituent parts binds the earth together with its constituent parts, so too does ultimate water bind ultimate earth.

“By means of conditions corresponding to it” refers to the preceding elements such as earth, which are being bound by conditions suitable for their own binding and which possess functions such as supporting.
By the phrases “it becomes a support without touching” and “it binds without touching,” he states that the state of being touched and the act of touching do not exist in the water element;
thus, he expresses its dual nature by way of the tangible. Mutual dependence is *aññamañña-nissayatā*.

Alternatively, mutualness and dependence constitute "mutual-dependence. If there were mutual-dependence between the tangible and intangible elements without their being tangibles by way of the state of tangibility, then since the intrinsic nature of earth and so forth—such as hardness—is itself the state of tangibility, how could they possess the state of being a support for the water element in its absence?
Therefore, he says: "In those that exist inseparably," and so forth.
By the phrase "in those that have become mutual conditions," he excludes derived matter (*upādārūpa*).

Alternatively, having previously stated—standing on the intention of the *Aṭṭhakathā*—the distinct mutual dependence of the tangible and intangible elements, he now says "existing inseparably" (*avinibbhogavuttīsu*) and so forth, stating it without distinction while standing on his own intention. That very [dependence] is undifferentiated.
Demonstrating the firmness of their mutual dependence, he said, "Nor among those that are co-nascent," and so forth.
In this regard, non-contact need not be examined, as it follows from the fact that they belong to a single aggregate (kalāpa). But how is contact [to be understood]?

Precisely because they belong to a single aggregate. For contact is observed only in the case of objective great elements (mahābhūta) that are established separately, when they serve as the support for the bodily sensitivity (kāyappasāda).
"It heats up" means it ripens. Regarding the phrase "not having become hot," this is stated as meaning "having become of a hot nature";
thus, it is said that "it rejects the very state of being of the nature of heat. Since cold is the opposite of heat, there might be a suspicion that it allows for coldness when rejecting hotness;
therefore, he says, "it does not admit coldness. Or rather, [the text implies] even by coldness, it is only the state of being of the same nature as heat.
To demonstrate this, it is said: "It does not allow for coldness. For that very reason, he says: "For heat itself is cold.
For when the state of being hot is dull, there arises the perception of cold; thus, heat itself is cold. But how is this to be understood?

Because the perception of cold is not fixed, like [the shifting] between the near shore and the far shore. For instance, the perception of cold arises in those who have entered the shade after standing in the sun.

There is a perception of heat precisely where things have emerged from the womb of the earth. If fire itself were cold, then the state of coldness would also be perceived within the same aggregate (kalāpa) as the state of heat;
therefore, he said, "And of cold and heat," and so forth. There is no occurrence of both cold and heat within the aggregates of heat and cold respectively.
The intention is that while the coexistence of two [elements] such as earth and fire is logical, it is not logical for the water element and the air element to possess the state of coldness.
For if the water element and the air element were to exist together in a single group (kalāpa), the state of coldness might be found alongside the state of heat;

however, it is not so found. Nor can it be understood here that the state of coldness exists in a group where the water element predominates or where the air element predominates, because such a state of coldness is not found in any such groups whatsoever.
[This applies] to that which possesses a predominance of intrinsic natures such as hardness and so forth.
The attainment of a state characterized by an excess of the nature of devas and so forth within the aggregate of the primary elements (bhūtasaṅghāta) is "change of state" (bhāvaññathatta).
To show how that occurs, he said: "Dependent... [etc. ...attainment. 652.
By the word "etc. in the phrase "exclusively mind-originated, etc.," he includes such categories as exclusively non-clung-to and subject-to-clinging, and so on.

Regarding "of the former" as well: from the statement "or whatever else," this refers to the former non-clung-to (anupādinnā) sound-base, bodily intimation, and so forth, as well as the eye-base, ear-base, and so forth, which are not mind-originated (nacittasamuṭṭhāna).

"The absence of the state of being non-kamma-born, etc. means the absence of the state of being non-kamma-born (nakammassakatattābhāva) and the absence of the state of being non-mind-originated (nacittasamuṭṭhānabhāva), and so on. "In the case of those that are exclusively kamma-born, etc. means...
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), that which is exclusively non-mentally-born (*acittaja*) is included. Those [qualities] are decay (*jaratā*) and impermanence (*aniccatā*).

The meaning is: since they are taken among those things that are exclusively not born of kamma—namely, the sound-base (*saddāyatana*) and so forth, and the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth, which are not mentally born—they are not included among the "non-exclusive" (*anekanta*) bases such as the visible-form-base (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth, because those arise from four origins (*catusamuṭṭhānika*).
666. "Unproduced" (*anipphanna*) means not being established by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) independently of anything else. "Of that" refers to the two types of intimation (*viññatti*).
The commentary on the discussion of what is not derived from clinging (*noupādābhājanīya*) is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of Pairs (*Dukaniddesa*) is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads (Catukkaniddesa-vaṇṇanā) 966.
Since it is stated that "all form is cognized by the mind," if there were no seeing and so forth other than what is cognized, then the questions beginning with "Which is that form seen?
would not have been asked; such being the case, how can there be the state of being a tetrad?
Having kept *anuyoga* (the inquiry) in mind, he said: "By way of the distinction in the apprehension of seeing, etc. This means:

by way of the distinction in the apprehension of seeing, hearing, measuring, knowing, and fully cognizing. By this, he shows that through the difference in the apprehender, there is a difference in the object to be apprehended.
Now, in order to show that the difference in the object to be apprehended is also obtained directly, he said: "Seen... [etc. ...by way of existence."
969. This method of exposition has been applied to the three compendia beginning with the "Sixfold" [Compendium].
Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussion (*Pakiṇṇakakathā*).

975. Because torpor (*middha*) is exclusively an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), it is included by the statement "there are no hindrances" [in the case of the first jhāna]; this is shown by the phrase "of torpor, which is also an hindrance.
And yet, material form (*rūpa*) is not to be abandoned here, because what is intended here is abandonment in the absolute sense (*nippariyāya*). On this point, some say:
"Torpor is twofold, being of the nature of sickness for both the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the physical body (*rūpakāya*)."
Regarding this, they say that the former is described by the term "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*), while the latter is of the nature of form (*rūpa-sabhāva*).

In that case, even if one were to imagine a *middha* (torpor) distinct from the immaterial, since that too is a hindrance by virtue of having the nature of *middha*—just like the other *middha*—it is impossible to deny the status of being a hindrance even for that imagined *middha*. Thus they [argue].
Showing the contradiction with the statement regarding the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇappahāna*), he says, "And not the material body," and so forth.

Alternatively, because those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) have the nature of sleeping, and since sleep has torpor (*middha*) as its cause, he offers the reply, "And not the physical ailment of the material body," and so forth, with reference to the claim that there exists the form of torpor. In this context, it is torpor alone that is the cause of sleep.
This restrictive definition is not intended; rather, it is intended that *middha* (torpor) is the cause of sleep alone. Thus, there is another cause of sleep besides *middha*. What is it?
It is the physical debility of the material body (*rūpakāyagelañña*). And the construction should be understood as: "and not from the sound of speech... and so forth. By the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in the phrase "the sound of speech, etc.," sounds such as the utterance "huṃ" are included. The sound of snapping fingers and the like is produced solely by temperature (*utusamuṭṭhāna*).
The mind-condition, however, does exist. "Merely the state of matter" means that for material phenomena whose intrinsic nature is aging and death, there are merely those properties;

for that very reason, they do not possess properties such as birth, which is why it is said, "they do not themselves possess an intrinsic nature. Just as aging and impermanence are merely the state of matter, so too is birth;
thus, the word "likewise" (tathā) serves to apply this same principle of being "merely the state of matter" to birth.
Of those material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*). Just as the word *saṅkhāta* and others, the word *abhinibbattita* can also refer to the present time;
thus it is said: "at the moment of the phenomenon being produced" (*abhinibbattiyamānadhammakkhaṇasmiṃ*).

Even so, although aging and dissolution are the inherent natures of phenomena that possess the states of aging and dissolution, because they do not exist at the moment of the efficacy of the producing conditions, the conventional designation of their causal status [is applied]...
The connection is that even though they do not receive the designation of "rebirth," their state of being "clung-to" (upādinnatā) must still be affirmed.

By the statement, "Old age and death are dependently arisen," he clarifies its figurative nature through the passage beginning with "when there is the arising of those [aggregates]. "If it were so" means:
if birth and the rest have an existence dependent upon a support, then, in that case, [the question arises regarding] "derived matter of the great elements."

Since, among things dependent on primary elements (*bhūta*), there is only conventional expression based on derived matter (*upādāya-vohāra*), the intention is that even those things dependent [on the primary elements] must be stated by distinguishing them with another word "derived" (*upādāya*);
thus he said, "it would result in a state of being derived from what is derived.

Showing that a conventional expression occurs even for the cause of a cause, just as it does for the cause itself—as in the case of "the village was burned by thieves"—he says: "from the primary elements...".

He said: Now, in order to show—without resorting to a succession of stages and directly—that the states of arising and so forth are bound to the primary elements (bhūta), together with an illustration, he spoke the words beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Even though the specific qualities (*vikāra*) and delimitations (*pariccheda*) exist as modifications of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), they do not cease to be bound to the primary elements;

thus, within a single group (*kalāpa*), each of these qualities, such as modification, exists as one [unit]. Therefore, like the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), it is that which sustains the group by virtue of being the state of the group's modification and so forth.
And because they are indeed called "derived forms" (*upādāyarūpa*), he says: "In this way, the modifications... [etc.]...
should be applied. The state of being fully accomplished (*parinipphannatā*) was stated for the purpose of excluding the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).

This is because that which possesses an unaccomplished nature is not perceived, and thus, like a rabbit's horn, it might be considered "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) since it is not conditioned by anything.

This is stated by way of turning back this suspicion. Alternatively, just as the state of being "form" (rūpa-bhāva) arises from the existence of form and its modifications, so too, since their status as dependently arisen is established—such that they exist when form exists and do not exist when it does not—their "perfectedness" (pariniṣpannatā), which has been proven, establishes their conditioned nature (saṅkhata-bhāva).
Thus, it is said: "for the purpose of precluding their unconditioned nature (asaṅkhata-bhāva)," because that perfectedness serves to exclude the possibility of them being unconditioned.
"...the state of being fully accomplished has been stated.
The commentary on the miscellaneous discussion is finished.
The commentary on the Section on Form is finished.
3. Nikkhepakaṇḍa: Commentary on the Exposition of the Triplets (Tikanikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā) 985.

Having set aside certain phenomena because they lack the function of being grouped as pentads with contact as the fifth, as previously stated, [the author] does so for the purpose of including specific qualities not yet mentioned, such as being easy to admonish (*sovacassatā*), and so forth.

Alternatively, because desire and the rest are mentioned according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*), the reason why they do not deserve to be explained by extracting their individual terms as "included" (*yevāpanaka*) has been stated.
When explaining the reason why the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*) likewise does not deserve to be explained in that manner, he says:
"Because of its subtle nature... for one who is benefited. Even though it is subtle, the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) possesses the specific characteristics of the faculties and so forth.
They are manifest by way of predominance and so forth, but the subtle derived matter (upādāyarūpa) does not possess that same nature;
therefore, it is stated that it is unworthy of being explained in the word-commentary on the triad of wholesome states through the extraction of the heart-basis (hadayavatthu).

Precisely because of its subtlety, it is [not mentioned] even in the Great Treatise (Mahāpakaraṇa), where it says: "That matter depending upon which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element proceed."

It should be understood that it was not shown by way of the heart-base through the extraction of the heart-base [in this context] because it was already shown by way of the "dependent phenomena" (*nissitadhamma*).

However, the intention for which the heart-base was not mentioned under the two-fold inclusion of matter and so forth in the *Rūpakaṇḍa* has already been clarified in the commentary on the *Rūpakaṇḍa*. Regarding the word "having set aside" (*nikkhipitvā*):
"Having included" means that, according to the intended sense, it is said "having made the detailed exposition included within.

For wholesome and other states taught by way of roots and so forth are indeed also taught by way of their respective arising of consciousness and so on, because they do not deviate from their own intrinsic nature.
"By way of roots" means by way of establishing the state of being well-established. These terms beginning with "cause" (hetu) [are so called] because the fruit proceeds (*hinoti*) from them.
It causes to proceed, thus it is a cause (*hetu*); it goes by depending on this, thus it is a condition (*paccaya*); it generates, thus it is a generator (*janaka*);
it brings about, thus it is a producer (*nibbattaka*)—this is the meaning of the remaining terms. Why was it said, "The meaning of 'root'... has been stated"?

Is it not the case that the state of being a root is the meaning of 'root'—just as in the expressions "the meaning of oppression" and so forth—and that "the three wholesome roots" is an extraction from the word "root"? No; [it is not so] because of the root... [text continues].

“Meaning” (*attha*) is the sense of being a root (*mūlaṭṭha*); it is precisely that sense of being a root because, in the sense of establishing firm footing, it intends the specific function of the wholesome factors—such as non-greed and the rest—which possess the nature of roots among the wholesome states. For this very reason, he said: “‘Meaning’ is the function of the dhamma.
Alternatively, “by way of meaning” means by way of the meaning reckoned as the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of those roots mentioned as “the three wholesome roots.”
This is not by way of the meaning expressed in the verse. However, because that [meaning] is indeed the sense of "root" (mūla), it was said: "of non-greed and so forth.
Just as non-greed and the others [are roots], the aggregates of feeling and so forth are also to be indicated by the word "that" (taṃ) because they are included;
thus it was said: "those wholesome roots associated with that. In the phrase "by those non-greeds and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) also includes the aggregates of feeling and the rest.
In order to show that they are included, it is said: "those roots of skillfulness are associated with them.
Having asked, "Which phenomena are skillful? and having shown the four aggregates by way of their divisions such as contact and so forth, it is stated, "these phenomena are skillful";
thus, it is said that the aggregates are skillful "in terms of their intrinsic nature (sabhāvato) through the aggregates."
"...it fulfills. [This refers to] the aggregate of feeling, or... up to ...the aggregate of consciousness. "Of another fruit of its own":
this is stated because the roots show the cause for the faultlessness of the wholesome states;
it is not said because the roots establish the faultlessness of the wholesome state itself, but rather because they establish the state of being well-established for that faultlessness.

For if the faultless nature of wholesome states were produced by the roots, then the material form originated by them would also possess that nature, or else those roots would not function as its conditions;
yet it does so function. For this has been said: "Roots are roots... [and so on] ...a condition.
Furthermore, like the wholesome states, the unwholesome and indeterminate states would also have their respective natures dependent upon roots.
If that were so, then unwholesome and indeterminate states, being causeless, would lack that status [of being well-established].

Therefore, it should be understood that the wholesome and other qualities of wholesome and other states are dependent upon appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and so forth, rather than being dependent upon roots;

the roots, however, are the means for accomplishing the state of being well-established for the wholesome and other states. For phenomena accompanied by causes, like trees with well-developed roots, are well-established and firm.

"It is not thus without cause. As for the statement, "The nature of blamelessness is produced by association with that," this too is not said because the nature of blamelessness is actually produced by association with that;
rather, it is said in order to show the nature of blamelessness by way of its specific distinction.
For it is through association with non-greed and so forth that the state of blamelessness of the wholesome aggregates and so on becomes well-established and arises.
It is not well-established, unlike [the roots] that are rootless and indeterminate. If this were so, would the wholesome nature of those aggregates not be shown?

No; for their wholesomeness is understood by virtue of the context (*adhikāra*). Unlike the word "root" (*mūla*), the terms "aggregate" (*khandha*) and "root" do not denote the state of being subject to ripening (*vipākadhammatā*), as is the case with the word "kamma.
And since that [word "kamma"] is used here without distinction, he says: "He shows the state of having a pleasant ripening through kamma."
The construction is: "It shows the goodness at the beginning of wholesome states. One should see the excellence of the cause, nature, result, ripening, cultivation, source, and so forth;
furthermore, the excellence of the source and so forth should be applied by way of appropriate attention being the opposite of what is blameworthy and by way of having a pleasant ripening as desired.

For from appropriate attention, wholesome states are rooted in non-greed and the rest, and through association with non-greed and the rest, they arise precisely as having a pleasant ripening that is the opposite of greed and the rest.
986. Having been questioned with “Why was this said?”, the objector reveals his own intention with the words beginning “Is it not so...”.
The other, accepting the statement that the aforementioned delusion (*moha*) is not expressed here by the term “associated” (*sampayutta*), replies with the refutation beginning “By that...”.
Its meaning is as follows: although the aforementioned delusion [is indeed] included by the phrase “associated with that,”...
It is not included by way of being the primary factor (*padhāna*), but rather it is included as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) because it is an immediate consequence (*ānantariyaka*).

"In the absence elsewhere" means in the absence elsewhere than in the aforementioned associated states; for delusion accompanied by doubt or restlessness does not exist apart from the states of doubt, restlessness, and so forth.

(987) The terms "impermanence, suffering, and non-self" are stated for the purpose of excluding the conditioned characteristics (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*) such as arising (*uppāda*) and the rest. Arising and the rest...
However, because they are modifications of the states existing in those particular conditions, they are indeed included by the apprehension of those respective states. For it has been said:
"Old age and death are comprised within two aggregates," and "the accumulation of form," and so forth.

All names such as "hair," "skull," and so on, are *nāmapaññatti* (conceptual designations of names); whereas those based on the appropriation of form, feeling, and so forth, which have the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and the like as their objective domain, are *upādāpaññatti* (conceptual designations of derived matter).

The "concept of a being" (*sattapaññatti*) is that which is to be grasped by taking as its basis the respective primary elements, their signs, and specific modes of development; the "concept of a kasiṇa" (*kasiṇapaññatti*) is a specific range of meditative objects to be grasped by taking those same bases.

By the phrase "expressed without abandoning the ultimate sense," he shows that concepts such as "monastery" or "bed" are similar to the concept of a being, since they are included under the grasp of the concept of a being.
This is because [these things] possess the nature of being subject to the oppression of non-existence after having existed, and the lack of mastery over their own mode of being.

Because they are the modes of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*)—which are specific modes of conditioned phenomena—should be spoken of as being like intimation (*viññatti*) and so forth;

however, since those [characteristics] cannot be found independently of their support (*nissaya*), they are not mentioned here because they are merely conceptual entities (*paññatti-sabhāva*) consisting of the corresponding conceptualization (*tajjā-paññatti-bhāva*).
Nevertheless, they are mentioned in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) for the purpose of showing the distinction from "being" (*satta*), "pot," and so on.
"Stated separately": for it is not appropriate to say... [omitted] ...because the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*) is without exception. 988.

That wherein something exists is a "plane" (*bhūmi*). Because it serves as a supporting condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), it is the "plane of pleasure" (*sukhabhūmi*), meaning a state of consciousness accompanied by pleasant feeling.

For the purpose of determining that [consciousness] according to its classification of planes, the associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) which constitute its support are termed "belonging to the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).

It has been stated. Or, because that which constitutes a part of it is considered as a support (*ādhāraṇa*) by virtue of being the whole (*samudāya*), it is described as "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) by way of sharing the same plane with it.

In this context, both locative expressions—"on the plane of pleasure" (*sukhabhūmiyaṃ*) and "in the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacare*)—are stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as having different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, in order to show the application of the meaning through their state of having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*), [the text says]: "The plane of pleasure..."
It is said that "the sense-sphere [consciousness] and so forth are also applicable.

For just as with consciousness, so too all phenomena associated with limited pleasure are called the "sense-sphere plane" because they serve as its support. It should be understood that this very meaning is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For "consciousness" (*citta*) refers to a "mental state" (*cittuppāda*) as well. Therefore it was said: "consciousness has arisen."
"In this context, it is not the mind alone that is taken up, but the mind together with more than fifty wholesome states.
And "having done so" means because the arising of consciousness is understood as being on a plane of happiness. "Showing the division" means showing the distinction.
"That which is to be spoken has been spoken"; that itself is the meaning, hence "the spoken meaning," i.e., the expressed meaning. "By making that meaning known."
By means of [the term] *tikadukānaṃ*, which illuminates the meanings of "wicked" (*kucchita*) and "flowing" (*salana*), etc.
994. What need is there to mention the case of the aggregates as objects?

For when the aggregates of an Arahant exist in a temporal sequence of prior and subsequent moments, clinging (*upādāna*) arises by taking them as its object through the mode of identity (*ekattanaya*) within that continuum, thinking, for example, "This is our uncle, the Elder."

He grasps only the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). Even though supramundane aggregates (*lokuttarakkhandha*) are included within that same continuum, they are incapable of occurring therein;
what then need be said regarding [the mind] occurring with reference to the [mundane] aggregates?
By this, it is shown that wrong view and so forth—which occur by way of such thoughts as "there is no path to purification" and "there is no Nibbāna"—[are likewise excluded].

It is thus demonstrated that [the objects] such as the path are not the objects of the respective designations [of the aggregates], but rather the objects of those specific designations. 998. By the phrase “thus... up to ...lesika,” he states that there is no difference between the non-clinging factors (*anupādāniya*) and the non-defilement factors (*asaṃkilesika*).
1006. The word-division for *avi...pe...sākāro* is: “that [object] does not exist, and it has the aspect of the inversion [of perception] such as permanence, etc. Regarding the view (*diṭṭhi*):
Even though it is apprehended in the form of permanence and so forth—which do not exist—it is not non-existent in the ultimate sense like those forms;
rather, the existing body is "personality" (*sakkāya*). Thus, by means of the qualifying term "personality," it is distinguished from the non-existent distorted modes such as permanence.

Therefore, those beyond the world (*lokuttara*) do not require this qualification, for [to them] "personality" is simply the existing, peaceful body. In this way, the underlying entity remains undifferentiated.

This statement, "when there is the body" (*satī kāye*), is said with the intention that here the word "body" (*kāya*) refers to the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) without specifying any particularity,
because it signifies a collection (*samūha*). However, if the meaning were taken as "body" in the sense of being a locus for the arising of base things such as lust and so forth—
just like the "body of sensitivity" (*pasādakāya*)— then the basis for the view would indeed be specified, and thus [the view] would also be supramundane (*lokuttara*).
[They] have been removed. For the supramundane aggregates are not called "body" (*kāya*) by virtue of being a place of arising.

"By that which is not a cause for purity" means by cow-vows (*gosīla*) and so forth, or by mundane morality (*lokīyasīla*), which is not the proximate cause (*apadaṭṭhāna*) for supramundane morality. Alternatively, "morality" (*sīla*) is so called because it is not to be transgressed and must be constantly practiced;
"vow" (*vata*) is so called because it is undertaken through the state of practicing asceticism (*tapas*). Morality is the undertaking of one's own state as a cow and so forth.
They state the distinction between virtue (*sīla*) and ascetic practice (*vata*) as follows: "Virtue is the performance of actions such as eating, tending cattle, and so forth;

or rather, virtue is the turning away from what is considered improper to do. Ascetic practice, for one who has undertaken that [virtue], is the specific mode of conduct such as eating at a fixed time, wandering about, and so on.
Regarding the statement "with the arising of this, this arises," the term "arising" does not intend the mere act of being born; rather, it refers to... [the causal relationship].
"Even non-ceasing," he says, "is called 'the sound of people' (janasadda) because it is not afflicted. Herein, this is the method regarding the word *jana*:

they are "people" (*jana*) because they have been born (*janita*); the meaning is "unafflicted" (*avihata*). Those who possess many people are "worldlings" (*puthujjana*), referring to beings who pride themselves on being ordinary teachers.

Alternatively, the word *jana* has the sense of "volitional formation" (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*) and so forth, due to the multivalence of verbal roots (*dhātu*). This is because the aggregates, bases, and so forth, are dependent upon hearing (*savana*).
The term "unlearned" (*assutavā*), which indicates their lack of hearing [the Dhamma], expresses their blindness regarding the acquisition of the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*).
"Knowing what is done" means they know, as it truly is, the wholesome and unwholesome actions performed by themselves and others, as well as the pleasure and pain produced by them;
likewise, they know the assistance rendered to others by themselves and to themselves by others, in the manner already described.

They make it manifest. They perform what ought to be done—such as nursing—for one afflicted by disease and so forth, or they perform such acts for one afflicted by the suffering of *saṃsāra* in the manner previously described.
Regarding the statement, "The noble-making states are the Noble Truths," it was said that "impermanence and so forth are to be seen" by way of the first two truths.
Alternatively, when the meaning is "being seen through the distinctions of full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth," [it refers to the remaining two truths].
By the word "etc. in the phrase "impermanence, etc.," even Nibbāna—which is permanent—is included; thus it should be applied according to the Four Noble Truths.
Alternatively, it should be understood that "impermanence, etc. refers to the states such as impermanence itself.

The remaining defilements constitute the stream of defilements. "Knowledge" (ñāṇa) means knowing things as they truly are (yāthāvato), for by means of awakening to reality as it is (yathābhūtāvabodha), that [stream]...
Because they have been brought to a state where they no longer arise, they are incapable of entering the mental continuum;
thus they are called "restrained" (*saṃvuta*) and "shut off" (*pihita*). "In that way" (*tathā*) means by way of enduring the disintegration of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).

Wisdom is called "patience" (*khanti*) because through it one endures the investigation of things according to their non-perverted nature. It proceeds in such a manner because it possesses the quality of forbearance (*titikkhā*) only when one is free from hatred.
Regarding the term "aggregates" (*khandhā*): since the aggregates dominated by non-hatred (*adosa*) have been mentioned, the third alternative was stated as "or non-hatred itself.
Because covetousness and dejection are the opposites of mindfulness, they are described as "muddle-mindedness" (*muṭṭhassacca*). Impatience is hatred (*dosa*).

Since the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhiti*) is free from extremes such as eternalism and so forth, the grasping at eternalism, annihilationism, and the like is stated to be their opposite. [The view of] Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*)...
It is the state of being contrary to Nibbāna. It is said that the defilements, such as craving, are to be abandoned by the final knowledge of conformity (*carimānuloma-ñāṇa*).

However, the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) functions by way of preventing the occurrence of defilements—just like the knowledges of the path and the knowledge of insight—and it is stated, "the abandoning of formations...," because it functions by way of transcending the domain of the defilements.
The commonality of origin for views and so forth consists in their being cooperative causes for the production of the fluctuation of kamma;
