or else, it is the function of seeing and so on belonging to the eye and other [faculties], while the self possesses the task of seeing and so on. For in this way, one grasps the self as form according to one's own conjecture.
"According to what is seen" means, by implication, "according to what is apprehended through speculative vision. For the holder of wrong views does not [grasp] the sense-sphere of form alone.
"Grasps as 'self'" means: in this process, by way of the general tendency toward grasping form as self—which constitutes a pervasive mode of occurrence.
"Conceit regarding form," etc., refers to the grasping at a self that occurs by taking the nature of the eye and so forth to be the self. "Grasping at non-otherness, etc.
refers to the grasping at non-otherness, at what belongs to the self, at dependence on a self, and at being supported by a self. "Of color, etc."... [text continues].

[The examples given are] "of color, trees, flowers, and gems. But do not trees, flowers, and gems fail to exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*)? It is true that they do not exist;

however, their material basis (*upādāna*) does exist. Therefore, this [basis], which possesses such modes as being "aggregated" and so forth, is here expressed by way of the conventional designations "tree" and so on.

Thus, there is no fault even in using the illustrations of trees and the like, because what is intended is merely the state of being a possessor (*saṃsāmibhāva*) and so forth, just as in the case of a "shadow-tree" and the like, in relation to matter (*rūpa*).

1008. "The intrinsic nature of birth and so forth" means the intrinsic nature of the production and non-production of birth, existence, and the rest; it refers to the capacity for arising and the state of being a condition.

1009. Regarding the term "defilements associated with that" used in a general sense: although views and the others are included because they are obtained either through the method of elimination (*pārisesa*) or by implication (*sāmatthiya*) from the subsequent statements such as "the remaining greed," they are not mentioned here by their specific names or individual distinctions.
Because they have not yet arisen, greed and the rest are called "future"; thus he says, "Here... [and so on]... a bridge.
This meaning is understood from the fact that, having arisen simultaneously with greed and the rest, it is view alone that possesses the status of a defilement as stated in the text.

This interpretation is also appropriate because it serves as a specific designation for the fetters and defilements, and because of their state of being associated and originating together. "By those free from the fetters" means—

By those [factors] devoid of the state of being fetters (*saṃyojana*), namely dullness (*thina*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*), or by dullness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing. 1013. Regarding "a part... and so forth:
he says this because a whole may also be designated by means of its parts. Or, they are "caused" (*hetuka*) because they possess a cause (*hetu*).
"Indeterminate" (*aniyata*) means not determined. Because its meaning is to be grasped by way of the determination of the preceding term, it expresses a meaning that requires further exposition.

"Set forth according to meaning" means that, as in the case of "the three wholesome roots: non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion," these very same states shown by the preceding method are demonstrated here by way of showing their meaning through the classification of those to be abandoned by the cause and those having a cause.

(1029) Because sublime states—excluding those associated with direct knowledge—lack the quality of having limited objects, it is said: "or the types of supernormal power and so forth, which are sublime. Because knowledge of past lives belongs to the sense-sphere, he says: "associated with the knowledge of... the mind... and so on.
1035. "Those connected with the immediate" (*ānantariya*): the fruit that occurs immediately after death is the "immediate" (*anantara*);

those connected to that are so called because they bring it about exclusively and cannot be bypassed—this is the meaning. Alternatively, the performance of the aforementioned immediate [deeds] is the "immediate" (*anantara*);

this should be construed as "those [sīlas] which are the immediate. Even when many immediate deeds have been committed, although the giving of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) occurs only through the most powerful one, [the others still contribute].

It is not so for the others; however, because the task that ought to be performed by oneself has been accomplished by that [volition] itself, and because it proceeds by way of supporting its own result (*vipāka*), the other [wholesome factors] do not have their fruits obstructed by it—how much less so in the case of wholesome states that are its opposites?
Thus it is said: "Because its fruit cannot be obstructed by a contrary factor. "Even in the case of many... there is none."

Why was it said: "Is it not the case that when several *ānantariya* (immediate) karmas have been committed, only the most powerful one grants rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), thereby obstructing the fruition of the others? To this he replied with the words "And not of those," and so forth.
Furthermore, that mutual non-obstruction among them has already been investigated in detail in the commentary on the *Mātikā*.
Without grasping the meaning as it follows from the context, but rather taking the meaning of the text according to the literal expression alone,

the passage beginning with “the former view” was stated in order to show the distinction between the theories of no-cause (ahetukavāda) and so forth, with reference to their occurrence as the primary proponents of those views. Furthermore,

even one who negates the cause of bondage and liberation also negates karma, since the causal process consisting of the accumulations of merit and demerit— which is divided into that which leads to non-emancipation and that which leads to emancipation— is itself the cause of bondage and liberation.

In the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, however, it is stated: "Because it is the cause for resultant [kamma], and for kamma, defilements, concentration, and wisdom, the resultant itself is also a cause for bondage and liberation; thus, one who says 'there are no causes' rejects both.
In that context, by one who denies kamma, the resultant is also denied, and by one who denies the resultant, kamma is also denied; therefore, all three are [rejected].
These doctrines should be understood as negating both [the existence of cause and effect] in meaning. Regarding "fixed wrong view":

when one is intent on the study, inquiry, and determination of false doctrines associated with the doctrine of no-cause and so forth, and while sitting in private reflecting that "there are no causes" and so on, wrong mindfulness becomes established upon that object, the mind becomes one-pointed, and impulsive thoughts (javana) arise.
They continue. In the first momentary consciousness (javana), it is curable; likewise in the second and subsequent moments.
By the seventh moment, it is said to have reached the state of being incurable. It is with reference to such a view as this that it is called "fixed wrong view" (niyatamicchādiṭṭhi).
Prior to that, it is indeterminate (aniyata).

1039. Although [the relationship] is distinguished by such factors as co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata), the fact that it is distinguished by co-nascence and so forth is understood simply by indicating that the path-condition (maggapaccaya) is distinguished by association (sampayoga).
Therefore, it is stated in the Pāḷi as "associated" (sampayutto); thus it is said, "by way of being distinguished by association.
This is for the purpose of showing the path [condition], and not because there is an absence of mutual path-conditionality among the path-factors themselves.

This is the intention. "If this is so" means: if the first method is intended to demonstrate that the path-factors obtain the condition of being a path, then, such being the case, since the path-factors—like feeling and the rest—must also be described as having the path as their cause, they would lack the intrinsic nature of a path.

Therefore, in the third method, there is the illumination of the fact that non-greed and the other [wholesome roots], which do not have the intrinsic nature of a path, as well as other phenomena which possess the intrinsic nature of both, serve as conditions for them.
He said, "They should not be excluded," meaning that one should not say "excluding. "In the first method" means in the first system.
By the word "also" in the phrase "in the second method also," he includes the first method.

This shows that the third method is undertaken to demonstrate the state of being with roots (sahetuka) for right view, since it was already established in the two preceding methods. In the third method...
Not accepting the demonstration of the state of being "with cause" (sahetuka) regarding right view (sammādiṭṭhi), the challenger asks, "How is it demonstrated?
and then reveals his own intention with the words "Is it not," etc.

The other [respondent] explains with the words "For just as," etc., that even though greed and so forth are stated to have causes that are to be abandoned, they are nevertheless mutually co-existent, simultaneous, and associated, and are included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

He shows that just as in the "Inclusion of Roots to be Abandoned by Seeing," even though right view is stated to be a root of the path, its status as a root of the path is also logical because it is included within the aggregate of formations associated with the roots of the path.
"Of something other than that" means of something other than that root consisting of right view—namely, of non-greed and non-hatred alone. "By another" [means...]

“‘The path is the cause’ [is said] by way of something other than this”: because only non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adosa*) are intended, they alone are referred to by the specific method as “the path-cause.

By the common method: because all three causes are intended, those which possess the nature of both path and non-path are referred to by the common method as “path-cause and non-path-cause. “Of these” refers to the causes. “Of others” refers to those associated with the causes.

“By way of a specific meaning” means by way of the specific meaning of the textual passage (pāḷi): “having the Path as their cause. The second and third methods, which proceed by way of showing that the remaining factors possess causes through non-delusion (amoha) and through non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion (alobha-adosa-amoha), are stated as “the demonstration of the cause and the possessor of the cause according to their own form.
“Because it is not seen in its own form” means because it is not seen by way of its own form. “…by way of the meaning… by way of going” refers to the “Path-factors” (maggaṅgāni).

By the statement, “excluding that which is associated with it,” the causal state of associated factors— designated as the path-condition (magga-paccaya) for those phenomena whose intrinsic nature is the Path—
is shown according to its specific form. The meaning is that, by implication, the status of being a cause-of-cause (hetu-hetu) for those factors associated with right view,
which itself is the cause of the Path, is made known.
1040. Because a phenomenon that lacks intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is not to be respected, it is said to be a "phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvadhamma*).
For this very reason, it will be stated in the *Paṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā*: "Predominance by object (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is sixfold according to the division of its classes:

wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, material, and Nibbāna. "Setting aside the Path and so forth" means excluding the Path and the rest. "Of others" means of those other than the Path and so forth. Adhi...pe... [end of fragment]

"Vassati" refers to the state of being the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipatipaccaya*). Because wisdom is supreme among wholesome states and because wisdom is the primary burden in the discourse on the supramundane (*lokuttara*), it should be understood that among the remaining predominances, the predominance of investigation (*vīmaṃsādhipati*) is the most prominent.
(1041) Since the first alternative pertains to a limited scope of beings, in order to show it by way of all beings, [it says]: "Even after the passing of a thousand eons..."
The passage beginning with “or” was stated thus: “that which will have found its opportunity” means that whatever karma reaches its opportunity [for fruition].
Because its result is certain to arise after the passing of a thousand eons, that too... [is] so called.

The non-arisen state of a result that has not attained the moments of arising and so forth—due to not having obtained what was to be obtained—is its state of non-existence, which is the absence of manifest existence.
It is said: “That which is called ‘non-existent’ does not mean it is unarisen.

Therein, in the case of the immaterial life-continuum (*arūpabhavaṅga*), karma whose result has not yet matured—due to the lack of an assembly of auxiliary causes—is said to be “without opportunity,” because it lacks the state of being oriented toward fruition; thus it is described as “similar to karma whose result has matured”:
“not having obtained... [and so forth]... to be given. This is because its functional accomplishment is absent.

The phrase "even arisen karma is as if unarisen" means that it lacks the capacity for [the thought], "there would be no opportunity," which expresses the sense that there would be no possibility [for such a thought].
By this, the absence of opportunity for the function of karma leading to diminution (*apacayagāmika-kamma*) is shown.

Because it was previously useless, the absence of opportunity for the arising of karma is stated due to the lack of purpose (*payojana*), meaning there would be no opportunity for the arising of karma. "From the result..."
The distinction between these [two] is this: by the phrase "there would be no occasion for the occurrence of another," it means [the former] is impossible.
The intention is that this is by way of an illustration through the result of a karma with certain fruition (*dhuvavipāka*).

Because sublime karmas lack the fixed nature (*niyatasabhāvatā*) found in the Noble Path and in deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariyakamma*), the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) are treated under the heading "in the absence of strength" and so forth.
The state of having specific characteristics, being constant, and having fixed maturation has been stated.
And here, the phrase "the five deeds of immediate retribution" (ānantariya-kamma) should be regarded as a mere illustration, since even fixed wrong view possesses the quality of fixed maturation.
Whatever result will necessarily arise from the performance of a particular action receives the designation of "arising" even during its future time. And that designation of "arising"—

In order to show that the path is said to be "unarisen" here by virtue of its future state of being accumulated (*āyūhitabhāva*), even though it is spoken of as being accumulated through kamma, the words "that which will be accumulated" and so forth were stated.

(1050) The connection is with the phrase "taken up by means of clinging" (*upādānehi ādinnā*). "Other" means other than those things which have clinging as their object; that is to say, they are not subject to clinging (*anupādāniya*).
“By the first mention” means by the mention consisting of the reviewing knowledge [expressed as] “I have realized the fruit.
Now, in order to explain the meaning of the word *upādinna* by way of the prefix *upa*, which indicates the sense of “approaching,” it is said: “or by the word *upādinna*,” and so forth.
Therein, because Nibbāna is not internal (*anajjhatta*), it is said: “only those states that are neither the Path nor the Fruit are mentioned.”
He said: "By the others" means by the internal terms and so forth.
The commentary on the exposition of the triads is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the dyads.

1062. *Mettāyana* is the going toward or approaching through loving-kindness (*mettā*). This consists of the attainment and production of loving-kindness within one’s own continuum and the non-approaching of sentient beings; in its actual sense, it is simply "moistening. Thus, having stated "loving-kindness" and "softening," he said "affection" (*sinehana*). 1065.
That by which the mind becomes delighted in various objects is the "delighting of the mind" (*cittassa saṃrañjana*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "craving-investigation, etc.," searching (*esanā*) and so forth are included. The vastness of craving is to be understood either by way of its objects or by way of its mode of occurrence.
The apprehension of form and so forth—which have the intrinsic nature of impermanence and so on—as permanent and so on is "adherence" (*abhinivesa*);

this occurs specifically through the influence of craving (*taṇhā*), since a view devoid of craving does not exist. Thus, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), he describes the sign (*nimitta*) as the agent, saying:
"Apprehending [it] as permanent and so on, it becomes deceptive. Because it is obtained through a manifest sound and because it is understood according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*).
And the intrinsic nature (*visata-sabhāva*) of the word *visattikā* is stated to be its "primary meaning.
This is because it is grasped by Māra through such passages as: "The snare that moves in the sky, which wanders in the mind—with that I shall afflict you.

Furthermore, [it refers to] the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) such as rain and wind, which are not the proper occasions [for harm], because they are not intended for the practice of harmful deeds and so forth.
Just as anger that has arisen toward beings, through the act of attributing [faults] such as doing what is improper (*aṭṭhācaraṇa*) by way of the intention to impute them,

proceeds by means of that very attribution— even if it is not actually an ill-will (*aghāta*) because it does not arise toward an improper object— it can nevertheless be understood that, since its object is a sentient being,
there is indeed a breach of the path of action (*kammappatha*) when the mind is exclusively defiled; this is so even in the case where the arising is toward an improper object.
Thinking that there might otherwise be no breach of the courses of kamma, he said: "One who has given rise to misplaced anger toward beings does so.

Since the terms *paṭigha* (aversion) and so forth are seen to apply to striking, the manifestation of bodily changes during the first watch of the night, conventional designations, and other such instances, it was stated that "the terms *paṭivirodha* (hostility) and so forth serve as qualifiers for those [terms]."
1091. Regarding the statement "two things, three things," because we observe plural forms that possess delimitation through the proximity of other words, it is said [here] "by an undelimited plural.
The word *iti* in the phrase "the enumeration is made" (*uddeso kato*) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
By means of that, it indicates that the making of the enumeration by the plural form is the cause for the question posed by the plural. It follows the enumeration.
"For indeed he asks. For instance, in a summary (uddesa) delimited by a number, such as "Which three?", the question itself is made delimited by that very number.

With the intention that—just as there is no need to delimit the intrinsic nature, plane, cause, fruit, and so forth when one merely wishes to state the mere existence of phenomena through a summary—there is likewise no need to delimit them by number, it was said:
"in a case where the delimitation is not determined," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "states that are not conditions" (*apaccayā dhammā*): although the various classes of states (*dhammā*) distinguished by many divisions were previously mentioned without specific limitation using the plural number,
and are likewise mentioned above, nevertheless— due to their inclusion within that [category] and despite the absence of further subdivisions—

the state that is not a condition (*appaccaya-dhamma*), which is the unconditioned state (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*), is expressed by such terms as "the destruction of lust with remainder," "without remainder," and so forth, as the objects of those designations.

It would be appropriate [to say] that the enumeration was made by means of two words denoting a metaphorical distinction, using the plural number to indicate an indefiniteness such as "there is some mere distinction.
Since the questions and the conclusion follow the enumeration, they too proceed in that same manner.
However, the exposition (niddesa) must be made by way of clarifying the delimitation of the intended intrinsic nature and so forth; thus, [the unconditioned is] unconditioned.
It should be understood that the term *dhātu* is used here for the purpose of illustrating the absence of differentiation from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).
When one asks out of a desire to explain, one does so by formulating a question according to the requirements of the person to whom one speaks;

thus, one asks only by following one's own lack of knowledge or doubt regarding that subject. Therefore it is said: "The question is made from the standpoint of one who does not know the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), etc."
By the passage beginning with "From the exposition" (*niddesato pubbe*), etc., it clarifies precisely the sequence of questions as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

1101. "Having broken down" (*bhinditvā*) means having analyzed. "Visible forms... [etc. ...are cognizable" refers, respectively, to the reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*) of sublime states by means of sense-sphere wholesome or great functional consciousness through the mode of comprehension (*sammasana*), and the reviewing of sublime and measureless states by means of [the same consciousness].

Sensuous-sphere phenomena (kāmāvacara-dhammā) are not cognizable by the aforementioned consciousnesses through the adverting [consciousness] that precedes them—which occurs by way of misapprehension and relishing sublime states (mahaggata-dhammā) associated with lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, and by way of various designations and conventional expressions;
nor are they cognizable by the other [type of consciousness], namely, that which has a limited object (paritta-ārammaṇa). This refers only to those [consciousnesses] belonging to the sensuous sphere.
"Of objects" (*ārammaṇānaṃ*) is the genitive case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*).

By means of consciousnesses having visible form as their object and so forth, it should be understood that among them, by means of the consciousness having visible form as its object, sounds and so forth are not cognizable, whereas visible form is cognizable. The same application should be seen for the remaining [senses] as well, according to the distinction of the doors, such as:
"by means of that which belongs to the eye-door, sounds and so forth are not cognizable, whereas visible form is cognizable," and so on.
It should be applied as follows: "the other" refers to the desirable-neutral, the undesirable, and the undesirable-neutral.
Regarding the designations of the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the supramundane as being [incomprehensible] by way of the sense-sphere resultant and so forth:

it should be applied that the supramundane is incomprehensible by way of sense-sphere resultants; and the fine-material and immaterial spheres are incomprehensible by way of sense-sphere wholesome and functional states dissociated from knowledge, as well as by way of unwholesome states.
The very nature of not knowing *nibbāna* is itself the arising of a self.
(1102) It has been stated that in the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms, greed devoid of wrong view is the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*);

and it is appropriate that greed accompanied by wrong view, as well as greed whose object is all phenomena of the sense sphere as previously described, constitutes the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).

“...the taint of existence (bhavāsava)... may be. For he himself will later state the absence of greed (lobha) apart from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the taint of existence. “In the text” means in the text of the Commentary section (Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa).

Therein, just as it is said, “The taint of sensual desire arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed,” so too it is said, “The taint of existence arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed.”
Because it was stated [elsewhere] that "it arises in the arising of consciousness associated with greed and dissociated from the four types of views," the text says "the taint of existence...
arises only in those associated [with views]," using a restrictive formulation. And so he will say:
"The taint of existence, together with the taint of ignorance, occurs in one way only among the four types of consciousness dissociated from views."
"...arises on one side. That too is lust (*rāga*); it is lust accompanied by the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).
It is appropriate to say that the "taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*) is like the longing for sense-pleasures and existence (*kāmabhava*).

For there is also a way of speaking in which the longing accompanied by the eternalist view and the lust accompanied by the eternalist view may be called the "taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*). Thus: "Lust accompanied by the eternalist view is the taint of existence by way of the longing for existence."

The intention of the Aṭṭhakathā should be understood as follows: it was not stated [in the Sutta] for the purpose of showing that those [other defilements] possess the nature of the *bhavāsava* intended here. For it is said:
"The *āsava* in both kinds of existence—existence consisting of the form and formless realms, which are twofold by way of karma and by way of rebirth—is *bhavāsava*.
In that context, first, the state of being *kāmāsava* belongs to the craving for sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*).

Let it be so; but how can there be a "taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*) regarding attachment accompanied by the adherence to eternalism (*sassatābhinivesa*) within the realms of form and the formless?

That too is indeed called a "taint of sensual desire" because it proceeds by way of longing for the aforementioned objects. For all phenomena belonging to the three planes are "sensual desires" (*kāma*) in the sense of being desirable.
Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence that greed dissociated from views would not be a "taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*), since it exists as such separately.

Because it has been extracted. This must certainly be understood in this way; otherwise, greed (lobha) accompanied by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) in the realms of form and formlessness would also incur the status of being a taint of existence (*bhavāsava*).
The taints of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and so forth are stated as twofold by way of their being taints pertaining to the present life and the future life. 1103.

Here, even according to the text, it is shown that it is not impossible to apply the status of the taint of sensual desire to greed that is distinct from the taint of existence; thus, the passage beginning with "And in the exposition of the taint of sensual desire" was stated. Some say: "The desire for the Dhamma is faith."

1105. It occurs only in relation to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), because in ultimate reality (*paramattha*) there exists no phenomenon apart from them that could be the object of the grasping after a "living soul" (*jīva*).
Furthermore, it does not settle down in form (*rūpa*)... [and so on] ...or in consciousness (*viññāṇa*);

for instead of remaining within the mere unerring intrinsic nature of form and the rest, it adheres to some fabricated mode superimposed upon them, which is established merely through conceptual construction.

For this very reason it says, “having made it other than that. That is, other than those aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). For some proponents of views (*diṭṭhigatika*) even perceive feeling and the rest as impermanent.
Alternatively, “than that” means other than the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), which is reckoned as the body. For it is said: “The soul (*jīva*) is one thing, the body is another.
“It exists” means it comes to be; the sense is that the self (*attā*) is eternal. “Other” means other than Brahmā, Īśvara, and so forth.

Just as the formless existence (arūpabhava) is to be attained by abandoning lust for the fine-material realm, so too the fine-material existence (rūpabhava) is to be attained by abandoning lust for the sense-sphere (kāmarāga).

Regarding the deities of the fine-material Brahma-worlds, it is stated in the Commentary that since their lust pertains to the five strands of sensual pleasure and not to their celestial palaces (vimāna) and so forth, such lust is considered "not lust for sense-pleasures" (akāmarāga) and therefore does not constitute the taint of sense-desire (kāmāsava);
this position was rejected by the commentators (ṭīkākāra), who demonstrated the absence of any greed (lobha) distinct from the taints of sense-desire and becoming (bhavāsava).
Even attachment to the celestial palaces and so forth of the *rūpī* Brahmās is shown to be the "outflow of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*) because it exists as a state of sensual desire and the like;

thus, all greed that is dissociated from views and free from attachment to existence in the form and formless realms is indicated as such. In this regard, one should grasp what is appropriate after investigating it:

it may be associated with an outflow when arising together with sensual attachment or attachment to existence, and it may be dissociated from an outflow when arising together with a different kind of attachment.

By showing the absence [of such a thing] through the passage beginning with “the four types of views,” he demonstrates the absence of greed that is distinct from the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*).

Then, by presenting the passage beginning with “the taint of sensual desire,” he establishes that the lust for views (*diṭṭhirāga*) constitutes the taint of sensual desire. “For the purpose of showing what is to be abandoned” means for the purpose of demonstrating the state of being abandonable.
“In order to abandon” means for the sake of the cause of abandonment.
1121. By "birth" (*jāti*) is meant the excellence of birth such as the nature of a *khattiya*. By "clan" (*gotta*) is meant a noble clan such as the Gotama clan.
By "son of a great family" (*kolaputtiya*) is meant the state of belonging to a prominent lineage. By "beauty of complexion" (*vaṇṇapokkharatā*) is meant the possession of a body endowed with beauty;

for "lotus" (*pokkhara*) is said to refer to the body. "He arouses conceit" (*mānaṃ jappeti*) means he brings about or produces conceit. Conceit that has been produced is "occurring conceit" (*pavatta-māna*).

“Distinction of persons” (*puggalavisesa*) refers to the specific distinctions among individuals, such as “superior to superior,” and so forth. “Conceit of superiority” (*seyyamāna*) is that which proceeds by breaking down [the sense of] superiority.
“Of three” (*tiṇṇaṃ*) means of the three—superiority, etc.—which are stated without depending on another person, beginning with “I am superior.
“Conceit” (*māna*) is the exertion of self-conceit by way of superiority and so forth; its “performance” (*karaṇa*) is simply the occurrence of [thoughts] such as “I am superior.”
It is said: "‘Good’ refers to the performance of primary duties.

(1140) Since all greed has the nature of covetousness (*abhijjhā*), and covetousness has the nature of two taints (*āsava*), while sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) has the nature of the taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*), the distinction between covetousness and sensual lust is stated as being the nature of two taints versus the nature of one taint. Covetousness is not [merely] a mental state (*dhamma*).
Excluding wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) and ignorance (*avijjā*), [the remaining factors] do not have the nature of outflows (*āsava*).

Since covetousness (*abhijjhā*) has the very nature of two outflows, and there is no greed (*lobha*) that does not have the nature of covetousness, it was said with this intention: "The existence of greed that is not an outflow must be investigated.
It was stated that "there are seven by way of enumeration and cause" with reference to the reading of the *Pañhāvāra* (Chapter on Questions); for therein it says: "An outflow-dharma..."

A state that is an *āsava* is a condition for a state that is not an *āsava* by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*). A state that is an *āsava* is [a condition] for a state that is not an *āsava*. A state that is an *āsava* is [a condition] for both a state that is an *āsava* and a state that is not an *āsava*. A state that is not an *āsava* is [a condition] for a state that is not an *āsava*. A state that is not an *āsava* is [a condition] for a state that is an *āsava*.

A state that is not an *āsava* is [a condition] for both a state that is an *āsava* and a state that is not an *āsava*. States that are both *āsava* and not an *āsava* are [conditions] for a state that is not an *āsava* by way of the root-condition.

By way of these sections, it is stated that "there are seven by way of enumeration. Having treated this as the eighth [question], the ninth question— "States that are both taints and non-taints are a condition, by way of the root-condition, for states that are both taints and non-taints"—
should have been stated, but it was not. Thus, having shown the absence of the status of being a non-taint in greed associated with views,
the passage beginning with "and in the case of those dissociated from views" was stated in order to show that same [absence] for the other [type of greed] as well.

1162. Just as when a continuous stream of material form (rūpa) occurs, one says that "a person" goes, stands, or sits, so too the consciousness that produces clear form is what sustains the postures (iriyāpatha).

That [consciousness], however, is divided into fifty-seven types of impulsion (javana), including both wholesome and functional states, comprising the fifth jhāna consciousness—both that which has attained direct knowledge (abhiññā) and that which has not.

"And *voṭṭhabbanan*": thus it is of forty-eight kinds. Because it causes the co-nascent states to become unwieldy, the consciousness accompanied by sloth and torpor does not produce or support clear material phenomena; hence it is said, "unable to maintain the postures.

Even in the case of the opposite [of lightness], because its presence is non-conclusive, it cannot prove the nature of matter (*rūpatā*). The attainment of a state of heaviness is the absence of lightness (*lahutā*).

It should be understood. Although other unwholesome states (*akusala*) and so forth also lack lightness (*lahutā*), it is stated that "matter originated by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha-samuṭṭhita-rūpa*)" because sloth and torpor are exclusively the opposites of lightness and because the effect corresponds to its cause.
By the phrase "not sleep... continuity," he shows that sleeping is not established within the mental body (*nāmakāya*). Regarding the phrase "because it is the fruit of torpor": here...
It should be understood that this is not intended as a fixed rule stating that "drowsiness alone is the cause of sleep"; rather, the intended rule is that "sleep is the cause of drowsiness.

For indeed, in the Aṭṭhakathā, it is shown that for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), the cause of sleep is something other than drowsiness—namely, the weakness of the physical body composed of the four great elements (karajakāya).
“Covering” (*chādana*) or “concealing” (*avattharaṇa*) is “enveloping” (*onāha*); considering that this might be suspected by others to be the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of form itself, he said:
“And ‘enveloping’ and ‘complete enveloping’ are mentioned together with that [sleep]. The state of being expansive is a clear manifestation by way of non-contraction.
By the phrase “as if it were the state of an obstruction,” although sleep has the nature of an obstruction, its opposite [clarity] is shown because of its unique, non-commonality with anything else.

It shows that it has the nature of "crushing" (*onahanādi*) and so forth. For the common characteristic (*sāmañña*) of all five—sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the rest—is their intrinsic nature as an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*);
thus, the intended meaning here is that the state of crushing and so forth, which is similar to the state of being an obstruction and is found in the mental body (*nāmakāya*), is what is grasped.

By the terms "drinking" (*pāna*) and "application" (*anuyoga*), the volition (*cetanā*) that accomplishes those actions is intended; therefore, [the offenses] of drinking liquor... [and] of application... [are established].
And it is said that the state of being weakened by defilements through its unwholesome nature is appropriate.
"The swallowing of fermented liquor and spirits, drinking, and the pursuit of occasions for negligence"—this is the intention of another.

By the words "being an obstacle" (*nīvaraṇaṃ hutvā*) and so forth, this shows that [the term *nīvaraṇa*] refers to an objection directed at demonstrating the state of association with obstacles for those things whose intrinsic nature is that of an obstacle. Thus, it is called an "obstacle."

"In some instances, it is not even logical to include matter that has not been observed in operation and is dissociated [from consciousness], but rather only to include those whose intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is established as being associated with the state of being an hindrance (nīvaraṇa). Thus, only non-material phenomena (arūpadhamma) possessing that nature are shown, not matter.
Therefore, it should be understood that just as stiffness (thina), so too torpor (middha) is purely non-material. Here, "yaṃ" refers to the statement by which [this is known].
"Because of the statement of impossibility" means because of the state of being a statement that [such a thing] is impossible.
"By that" refers to that statement regarding the abandoning of desire and lust for the object of form (*rūpārammaṇa*).

Considering the abandoning of form to be something other [than the abandoning of desire and lust], the abandoning of desire and lust for form is called "another way of acting. This is what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as "in another way."
By the words beginning with "This," he shows that by the passage "Abandon it," the non-figurative (nippariyāya) abandonment is not intended.

"Only the formless is appropriate" means he shows that the mind—which is difficult to see and functions as far-reaching, etc.—is only the formless (arūpa) dhamma associated with it that is capable of obstructing it.
"Obsession of the mind" (cetaso pariyuṭṭhānaṃ) refers to the grasping of wholesome consciousness. The hindrances (nīvaraṇāni).
For it is said that they "seize" the wholesome side by not allowing those states that are arising to arise;
and here, "seizing" means obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), as in such expressions as "thieves have beset the road.
The statement that restlessness and worry are mentioned together refers to the summary, the inquiry, and the conclusion. As for what... [is stated].
However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), after stating the reason why restlessness (uddhacca) is inseparable from worry (kukkucca), it says, "It was stated by breaking [the compound].
This was said with reference to the fact that restlessness and worry are explained separately in the exposition of the phrase "both hindrances and associated with hindrances.
The state of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) being a coarse hindrance refers to its status as belonging to the lower realm (orambhāgiya).

For indeed, because it is more intense than the types of sensual desire consisting of lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, it is called the "exalted hindrance" (*ukkaṭṭhanīvaraṇa*) by way of its superior function.
However, greed is spoken of as the "hindrance of sensual desire" without being distinguished [from other forms].

And when the abandonment of the hindrance of sensual desire is stated to be complete through the path of non-returning, the greed that is to be abandoned by the fourth path is of a nature that is not a hindrance.

He says, "If... it may be," meaning that it occurs. A state of greed (*lobhadhamma*) consisting of attachment to the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*) and attachment to the immaterial realm (*arūparāga*), which is not itself an hindrance (*nonīvaraṇa*), [is related] to an hindrance such as ignorance (*avijjā*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [it is implied]:

"A state that is not an hindrance is related to a state that is an hindrance and to a state that is not an hindrance. States that are both hindrances and not hindrances are related to a state that is an hindrance. And... [the same applies to] a state that is an hindrance... [and so forth].
“Non-obscuring states are related to a non-obscuring state; obscuring and non-obscuring states are related to both obscuring and non-obscuring states by way of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya).

This includes these questions. The statement “four” is made by way of three [questions] rooted in the term *nīvaraṇa* (obscuration) and one rooted in *non-nīvaraṇa* (non-obscuration), as well as those rooted in *nīvaraṇa*, *non-nīvaraṇa*, and both of them.

But it is said that there are nine by way of three sets of three. "Therefore" means because of the absence of a scriptural passage (pāḷi) shown according to the method [previously] demonstrated, and because of the absence of greed that is not an hindrance (nīvaraṇa).
"By that very same" means by the very mode of the prior view as it arises. Regarding those things being spoken of by the holders of views (diṭṭhigatika): "permanent..."

Regarding the words "beautiful" and so forth, as well as worldly conventional expressions such as "sky-flowers," when spoken by those free from [wrong] views, their objects are merely the basis for speech; thus he said, "speech... or. 1221.

"Standing in the other world with the mind": having grasped with the mind that world other than the one in which one is oneself established by way of rebirth, one stands [therein] as the "other world."

1236. By the passage beginning with "Na hi purimehi," he shows that it is precisely those same lusts and other defilements—whose capacity to lead to rebirth in the states of misery has already been eradicated by the first path and so forth—that are abandoned by the second path and the subsequent paths. 1287.

Even when signs of an unhappy destination (duggati) and the like appear, such intense greed does not arise as it would toward signs of a happy destination; therefore, he says, "by the absence of powerful craving. 1301.

The expression "arising together" (sahappavatti) applies not only to things arising within a single moment of consciousness (cittuppāda), but also to things arising within a single continuum (santāna).

"It exists" (atthi) refers to the state of being a refuge for delusion (*moha*) accompanied by lust (*rāga*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*), in the sense of being associated with what is to be abandoned.
Any delusion that is co-nascent with restlessness and doubt is also said to have lust as its refuge, because it shares the same status of being associated with what is to be abandoned.

All [defilements], moreover, are distinguished by way of greed, hatred, and delusion; by way of the defilements associated with them; by way of the aggregates associated with them; and by way of the kamma originated by them.

In order to show that the exposition of the state of being with-conflict (*saraṇa*), which proceeds by way of including the unwholesome, is entirely consistent with the *Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta*, he said, "In the *Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta*," and so forth.
As for the demonstration in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*)— by way of showing their state of being associated, their state of being abandoned together, and their state of being conflict—
that all unwholesome states such as lust and the rest constitute "conflict" (*saraṇa*), that refers to the phenomena as they were shown in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).

It should be understood that there is no contradiction with the *Araṇavibhaṅga-sutta*, which is intent on showing that [the three aggregates] are a refuge for one another and intent on negating the status of being a refuge for other phenomena.

Alternatively, because the teaching in the sutta is a discourse by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya-kathā*), it should be seen that—just as the status of being a refuge is not ultimate—the status of being "without conflict" (*araṇa*) also belongs only to unwholesome states when considered from a non-figurative standpoint (*nippariyāya*). Thus, for one who proceeds accordingly...
It should be understood that there is no contradiction with the Sutta in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Regarding the explanation of the exposition of the pairs (*dukanikkhepa*) in the Suttanta:
"The meaning which [is conveyed] by the word 'I' acting as a cause"—here, the word "meaning" (*attha*) is intended [to mean] the word "I. Its purpose is the comprehension of the meaning.
For [the word] *iti* is the application of sound (*saddappayoga*). Being dependent solely on meaning, it is a signifier of meaning (*atthapadatthaka*);
however, when joined with the word *iti* applied subsequently—which effects a reversal of the meaning—it becomes a signifier of sound (*saddapadatthaka*), as in:

"He says 'gāvī'," which is understood to mean "He says the word *go*. By this, he shows that sound accompanied by a modification of intonation (*viññatti*) is a designation (*paññatti*). For instance, in the case of "Buddhassa... [it is shown].
By the passage beginning, “The Blessed One’s mode of expression would be obstructed by the worldly stream,” he establishes that *paññatti* (conceptual designation) is a verbal entity.
By the passage beginning, “Otherwise,” he states the fault [that would arise] if *paññatti* were not of the nature of a word (*saddasabhāva*).

The intention is: [if it were not a word], it might be a mere synonym (*adhivacana*) and so forth; and if that were the case, there would be no distinction between synonyms and the like from the path of synonyms (*adhivacanapatha*) and so forth, and thus the very category of "fault" (*duka*) could not even arise.

In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is intended that "designation" (*saṅkhā*) refers to a "concept based on clinging" (*upādāpaññatti*)—so called because it is designated as "I" by taking, through a collective and a continuity perspective, the phenomena such as form included within one's own personal continuum; it is reckoned and thus designated.

The same should be understood for the remaining [terms] as far as applicable. For this very reason, he said: "By the mere expression 'given,' [one employs] the designation of a being (*sattapaññatti*)."
"Having shown this, [the author] says 'in order to show another designation based on clinging' (*upādāpaññatti*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the word-meaning" (*padatthassa*):

it refers either to that which is denoted by words such as the term *ahaṃ* (I), or to the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*). With the intention that "sound is a designation" (*adhivacana*), he says "by one who speaks," and so forth.

For sound makes known the meaning that is to be made known by itself only when it has already been known by itself; therefore, for one who has not grasped the relationship [between word and meaning], sound is not capable of illuminating the meaning.
It is said, "by one who has previously grasped the designation. He states that the prefix *sam-* has the sense of distinction (*visesa*) because it is known through distinction (*vi-√jñā*);
thus he says, "it is called *samaññā*. Regarding the word "is made" (*karīyati*), this is a synonym for this meaning;
thus it is set down. He says, "it is called a *nāma*" because, having become a name, that very expression determines each respective object, speaks of it with a reason, and manifests it.
Thus it is said. For that very reason, he says, "For the earth," and so forth. "Designated as 'earth'" means that which is denoted by the word "earth.

"The teachers" refers to the teachers who composed the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), not the teachers of the commentary itself; this is what he intends to say. "In the *mātikā*" means in the commentary on the *mātikā*.
"By that" refers to the words of the commentary on the *mātikā*. [This refers to] the commentary on this canonical text (*pāḷi*).
And there might be a contradiction with this aforementioned teaching of the Master which demonstrates the meaning; he clarifies that very contradiction with the words beginning "For it is not...

(*na hi*). In that context, having made the mere utterance of the word itself—endowed with the modification of intonation (*viññatti*)—the subject matter, [he explains] the occurrence and so forth of the phenomena described as being the domain of designation (*adhivacanapatha*) and so on, by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
It is logical, not illogical; with this intention, it was said: "devoid of the functions of arising and passing away," and so forth.
Therein, "of undetermined intrinsic nature" means of an intrinsic nature not apprehended in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).

"Two-fold" means two-fold by way of the distinction between the designator and the designated. "Of the aforementioned type" means of the type devoid of the functions of arising and passing away, and so forth.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, in the commentary on the *Puggalapaññatti*. But surely other designations (*paññatti*) such as "designation by comparison" (*upanidhāpaññatti*) and so forth are also mentioned there;

why then is it said that "only six designations are mentioned"? It is true they are mentioned, but since those are included within the six beginning with "designation of what exists" (*vijjamānapaññatti*), [the text says]: "In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the designation of what exists... and so forth.
It is said: “Six are indeed designations.
In that context, because they do not exist in the same way as form and so forth, yet are nevertheless to be designated, they are called “designations of the non-existent” (*avijjamāna-paññatti*);

and because they designate objects such as a “being” or a “chariot” which do not [ultimately] exist, they are called “designations of the non-existent. Thus, by the term “designation of the non-existent,”...
Since both kinds of designation mentioned above are included [in this category], he says: “Non-existent... is said.
By the others means by the remaining five, beginning with existent designation (vijjamānapaññatti) and so forth;

because they make known objects such as matter (rūpa), feeling (vedanā), etc., and chariots, etc., in their various modes, the very words that denote them are themselves distinguished as existent designation and so on according to the difference in their objects.
The first meaning is that "conceptualization" (*paññatti*) is expressed by ten terms beginning with "calculation" (*saṅkhā*);
and because it is understood from the text through the literal sense alone, it is described as "conforming to the text" and "straight.

As for the passage beginning with "If," if the aforementioned kind of derivative conceptualization (*upādāpaññatti*), such as "a being" (*satta*), were a non-existent conceptualization, it could not be said to "exist. And since it is a non-existent thing, yet it is nevertheless to be conceptualized...

"And ‘concept’ (paññatti)”: this is the intended meaning, that it is the doctrine of those teachers. Now, by means of that doctrine, he points out the fault in that [position] through the challenge that even those phenomena described as "modes of description" (paññattipatha) would fall into the state of being non-existent concepts, starting with the words "And just as...
Since chariots and so forth do not exist and cannot be made known [as such], they are non-existent concepts.

Because all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) exist and are capable of being designated, they necessarily possess the state of being a "designation of what exists" (*vijjamānapaññatti*);
such is the meaning of the word "therefore.

By the phrase beginning with "Then," [the author] himself [proceeds] from the description of the path of designation (*paññattipathāniddesa*) to the description of the phenomena that are designations (*paññattidhammaniddesa*), which is distinct from the former.
He suspects a reason [for this]. With the words beginning “Nor even,” he shows that the reason for that is unestablished.

Since in such passages as “‘A person’ is a designation,” even designations (*saṅkhā*) and so forth are stated as being non-different in meaning from names (*nāma*) and so forth, he says: “Because words such as ‘designation’ have the same meaning. “Utterance” (*vacana*) means the vocalization of speech.
“Of another” refers to the conceptual designation (*paññatti*) of a name. “Of those” refers to the grasping of conventions (*saṅketa*) and the grasping of utterances.
The construction is: "Incapacity is not possible. He explains that very impossibility with the words beginning "If indeed...
"By designation" means by name-designation (*nāma-paññatti*). Regarding "the designation and the designating":

it is that name-designation by which dependent designations such as form and so forth are designated, and [it is] that [name-designation] which, by means of the previously grasped convention produced immediately after the stream of ear-door consciousness...
It is grasped by the mental-door consciousness-continuum; this is "name" (*nāma*) in the sense of its being made known and established without confusion.
Alternatively, it refers to the causing of the designation to be grasped and delimited by the mental-door consciousness-continuum that arises immediately after the ear-door consciousness-continuum.
Regarding that [designation], another designation might be stated; thus, regarding that designation as name (*nāmapaññatti*):

It should be stated—and indeed it must be admitted—that there exists another designation (nāmapaññatti) which serves as a cooperative cause for the grasping of conventions and the grasping of words during the process of making known. Otherwise, the mere understanding of the meaning would not occur;

for the isolated grasping of conventions and the grasping of words are incapable of making known a designation, just as they are incapable of making known a meaning. Furthermore, it is only when the designation itself is known that it can serve as their cooperative cause.

If one were to postulate a succession of designations for the sake of knowing that [object], there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavatthāna*), and thus the very possibility of attaining the meaning would not exist.

A conventional designation (*saṅketa*) regarding form and so forth is nothing in itself; rather, it is a verbal expression employed by depending upon specific signs such as the primary elements (*bhūta*) and particular modes of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā-viśeṣa*).
Like the designation of the *kasiṇas* and so forth, it is a mere conventional expression based on the act of making a convention and that which is to be designated by that convention;
and since the designation of names (*nāma-paññatti*) is what makes that [object] known, he said, "Nor is there the grasping of a convention," pointing out the occurrence of the aforementioned fault.
But is it not the case that the absence of the grasping of a convention is already shown by the objection regarding the impossibility of cognizing the meaning? True, this is so.

However, regarding conventional designation (*saṅketa*), there exists a difference of opinion among teachers. In this regard, in order to show that this [opinion] belongs to one particular side—that is, to demonstrate the fault in it—it is stated separately:
"The phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are the referents of words, must be designated;
the sound that expresses them is the designation (*paññatti*). With the intention that by this much all linguistic usage is accomplished, he says: "There is no word... nor person."
He said: The status of being speech for a designation (*paññatti*) is established because those readings indicate the state of being struck back and the state of being heard;
this is the intended meaning. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), he includes such passages as: "There are some who hear the terminology (*vohāra*) of the Buddha, the Blessed One;
the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) has the present as its object. Therefore, because of the phrase "designated phenomena" (*paññattidhammā*).
Regarding the position that "meaning" (*attha*) consists of the aforementioned designations (*paññatti*), there are numerous faults:

contradiction with the commentary on the *Mātikā*; the fact that it is not stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*; lack of conformity with this *Pāḷi* text; the necessity of demonstrating that all phenomena (*dhammā*) are designations;

the impossibility of defining the term "path of designation" (*paññattipatha*); and the impossibility of discerning meaning due to the consequence of infinite regress. [This applies] to that which is accompanied by the modification of intimation (*viññatti-vikāra*).
However, if the word *pana* signifies a designation (*paññatti*), there is an absence of the aforementioned faults and a conformity with many scriptural passages;
therefore, with the intention that "what is appropriate therein should be accepted," he says: "The text... [etc. ...should be understood.
By the words "If [it were] beings," etc., he points out the contradiction with the Commentary regarding the word's status as a designation. Thus, regarding its status as a designation:

If sound were a concept (*paññatti*), then because it exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) and because it makes manifest an object such as form, it would necessarily be a concept of something existing, not a concept of something non-existent. For those [terms] such as "being" (*satta*) are not concepts.
And in this way, there would be an absolute absence of the concept of something non-existent. Yet, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated: "the concept of something non-existent."

Because the other [category] lacks an object, it is a "designation of the non-existent" (*avijjamānapaññatti*); thus, showing the absence of the aforementioned contradiction, he says, "of non-existent things," and so forth.

Now, by demonstrating the absence of existence for objects such as "beings" (*satta*) through any method whatsoever, he establishes that the designation referring to them is indeed a "designation of the non-existent."

“And this statement”: beings and so forth, which do indeed exist, are called “non-existent” by way of the absence of their own-nature as form and so on, not because of a total non-existence. For they are cognized as having an existence that is being manifested in such and such a way;
thus, the aforementioned statement is: “Does form exist? Yes, it exists; yes, it does not exist. It both exists and does not exist.”

"It should not be said thus: 'It exists, it does not exist. Yes, [it should not]. 'The meaning of existence is the meaning of non-existence'—this is how the discussion on 'existence and non-existence' (hevatthikathā) proceeds.
For therein, phenomena such as form exist by way of their own nature as form, etc., but do not exist by way of the nature of feeling, etc.;
therefore, with reference to those who hold the view that 'all this exists in this way and does not exist in this way,' [the Buddha said]: 'Form..."
The question, "Does it exist? belongs to the proponent of the first position (sakavādī). The response, "It both exists and does not exist," belongs to the opponent (paravādī).

Then, the proponent, asking him, "If such is your tenet that form itself exists in this way and does not exist in this way, then in that case, is it the very same thing that exists and the very same thing that does not exist?
said, "Does it exist? The other [responded] regarding its existence by way of that very same intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

It is with reference to non-existence that he rejects [the first question]. When asked the second, he admits it with reference to existence by way of its own nature (*sakabhāva*) and non-existence by way of another nature (*parabhāva*). Thereupon, the proponent [of the opposing view] asks:
"Since 'existence' and 'non-existence' are mutually contradictory, how can either existence or non-existence possibly occur in a single phenomenon without a distinction of time?"
He refutes the opponent's argument by demonstrating that [the mind] attains unity.

As for the term "negated" (*paṭisiddha*), it refers to the negation of the existence of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by way of their own-nature (*sakabhāva*) and their non-existence by way of other-nature (*parabhāva), as stated in such passages as: "Form indeed exists as 'form,' but form does not exist as 'feeling,'" and so forth.
By this negation, the same status applies to [the concepts of] a "being" (*satta*) and the rest.
It is stated thus because it has been refuted.

"The visible forms and so forth do not exist" means that they do not possess the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of visible forms and so forth. "In such and such a way" refers to by way of a collection, a continuum, and so on.
A variegated perception arises through the power of conceptual construction (parikappa). If the meaning of the word is dependent upon perceptions such as "a being," "a chariot," and so forth...
Since it does not exist [as a real entity], do not the expressions "seven chariots" and so forth arise as non-noble conventions? To this he says, "And those expressions," and so on.
Because something that exists in its own right is made known only by virtue of the statement that makes it known, it receives the designation of a "conventional expression" (*paññattivohāra*).
It is with this very intention, etc., that the meaning stated in the passage beginning with "not existing in itself" is expressed.
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "That" refers to the inclusion of "beings" (*satta*) and so forth.

In various places in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that [the four divine abidings] are "not to be spoken of" (*na vattabba*) in such passages as: "Because the fourfold set of divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) proceeds by taking the designation of beings (*sattapaññatti*) as its object, it is said to have an 'inexpressible object' (*navattabbārammaṇa*).
If they cannot be spoken of in terms of being limited (*paritta*) and so forth, how can there be a state of being a condition for non-existent things such as "beings"?
He said: “The continuum of the aggregate-mass,” and so forth. “That” refers to the continuum of the aggregate-mass.
“Serving as its basis” means being the cause for the designations of grasping [it] as a person.
If wholesome states and so forth arise for one who cultivates the perception of a person, how is it that seeing a person is prohibited as a wrong view? To this he said: “But because,” and so forth.
The statement "the earth element is apprehended" is an illustration by way of its opposite regarding the non-existence of a person (*puggala*).

This is the inference here: "A person is not apprehended as distinct from form and the rest, because in the absence of their apprehension, there is no such cognition [of a person], just as in the case of rubbing and so forth. [Objection:
"A person is apprehended in the sense of the actual fact and the ultimate truth (*sacchikaṭṭhaparamatthena*), he who is cognizable by tactile consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*)."
He says, "It is the person imagined through such views that transmigrates and is liberated, not the person as a conventional designation," showing this by stating, "The refutation... [of] views.
In the verse, among these five aggregates—form, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness—which phenomenon indeed [is it]?
"Do you perceive a 'being'?"—this shows that not even one among these [aggregates] deserves to be grasped as a "being.

"Or do you think there is some other being apart from these?"—even so, Māra, is this merely a resort to views (*diṭṭhigata*)? The word *nu* has the sense of emphasis, meaning "it is surely nothing but a resort to views.
Why? Because this is merely a heap of pure formations (*saṅkhārapuñja*). He clarifies this very point: "Not here..."
“Because no being is apprehended. The intention is that, whether through direct perception or through inference, because nothing is apprehended, there is here no such thing as a “being. [Objection:
If there is no being, how is it understood that “a being undergoes saṃsāra,” and so forth? [Reply: What is to be understood here?
It is the conventional being (*vohārasatto*) that is intended, because the word “being” (*satta*) functions in the context of conventional usage.

Showing the connection with the second verse, he said, “But the being...,” and so forth. “A collection of parts” means by way of a collection of parts; the meaning is: having taken up the collection of parts such as the axle, wheels, and pole. “Being” is a conventional designation.
“Of that which does not exist” means of that which is absolutely non-existent, such as a hare’s horn. If it is absolutely non-existent—
To the question "How is it grasped?", he says: "It is conceptualized" (*parikappita*). This refers to things such as pots known through worldly convention.

Here, however, just as Nibbāna—though devoid of arising and so forth—is called "the essence of consolation" because it serves as a condition for the state of being comforted by the absence of the torment of defilements in those phenomena that arise with reference to a self and those included within that continuity; [so too is this case].
Thus, it is said that a designation (paññatti), although devoid of arising and so forth, occurs by way of the phenomena that occur with reference to a self.
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as follows: because the sense of "cause" is internalized, it is designated—that is, it is conventionally expressed—as "occurring.

Likewise, a name-designation (nāma-paññatti) makes known the object to be designated only when that object has been apprehended; it makes known [the object] just as a communication (viññatti) makes known the intention. Thus, it [is called a designation].

It is called "being spoken" by way of the meaning being expressed, because there is nothing [else] to be grasped. However, regarding the state of being spoken in relation to the designation that is to be established, there is simply nothing further to be said.

Likewise, by considering it as "making known" through the act of making known in its various modes, and because it is precisely what is to be grasped, the fact that its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is undetermined must be seen as rejected. For indeed...
The hardness, touch, and so forth of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) are expressible by sound through their own specific forms;

however, what is to be expressed is rather the commonality (sāmaññākāra)—which excludes other classes and is shared by those [phenomena] differentiated by time, place, and so on—established through superimposition (ajjhāropa) in accordance with prior convention.
Even in that case, sound does not function without some basis for its occurrence (pavattinimitta).

The ancient teachers maintain that "concept" (*paññatti*) is the specific common characteristic established by worldly convention, determined by the meaning of various words, which serves as the cause for the occurrence [of verbal expression].
For it is called "name" (*nāma*) because it bends the sound toward this or that meaning, or because it gives the designation of a name to each respective meaning;
and it is called "concept" (*paññatti*) because it makes things known through its various modes.

But for whom is that specific mode [of description]? It should be understood as being for the sake of the object to be made known. For objects indeed possess manifold aspects. And by doing so, the statement regarding the necessity of grasping that designation is justified;
moreover, this must necessarily be accepted in this way. Otherwise, there would be a confusion between the expression and the expressed, and everything...
Every word has a meaning to be expressed, and every word is expressive of every meaning;

yet it cannot be said here that their operation occurs through the mere grasping of a convention (*saṅketa*), because the grasping of a convention operates only with respect to those [word and meaning] that have already been established.
Others, however, [argue]: "Just as in the inference of fire from smoke, fire is not cognized by smoke alone; rather, [it is cognized] by the smoke..."
However, just as fire is known through smoke when the relationship characterized by invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with fire is understood,

so too, in the cognition of a meaning from a word, that meaning is not known by the word alone. Rather, when the relationship characterized by invariable concomitance between each specific word and its respective meaning is understood, the meaning is known through that specific word.
It should be understood that [the word] "makes known" (ñāpeti) is used. Otherwise, even without grasping the connection, the meaning might be understood merely by hearing the sound.
Whatever connection exists here in the manner previously described, because it serves as the means of making that respective meaning known, it is called a "name" (nāma).

Since it does not exist in an ultimate sense (paramatthato), but is established or known by way of worldly convention (lokasaṅketa), it is termed "established by worldly convention" (lokasaṅketasiddha).

They explain that it is called "paññatti" (conceptualization) because it makes known (*pakārato ñāpanato*) the various aspects of meaning being manifested by means of sound, owing to its being the cause for the realization of those aspects of meaning. Furthermore,

even if there were no specific object of knowledge distinct from both the conditioned and the unconditioned, then just like the referents of words such as "pot," the referents of words such as "earth" or "tangible" would also [be non-existent].

"Nothing at all is obtained" would mean the abolition of all conventional usage (*vohāra*). And because material and immaterial phenomena proceed only by way of various specific modes (*ākāra*) comprised within a continuity,
and not as mere isolates, therefore— even if those specific modes of configuration, collection, state, and aspect do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*)—
their existence nevertheless exists by virtue of the materiality and other factors that do exist ultimately as their substrata (*upādāna*).
Having obtained each respective basis for apprehension, it becomes the ground for each respective verbal expression.

For a designation based on a substrate (*upādāyapaññatti*), just as it cannot be said to be either "other" or "not other" than its substrate, so too it cannot be said to be "existent" or "non-existent" in every respect.
For all three of these are indeed existent. Thus, first of all, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the commentary on the matrix (*mātikā*). It is reckoned (*saṅkhāyati*).
"It is called *saṅkhā* because it is spoken of (*saṃkathīyati*). This meaning is established only in the sense of that which is to be expressed, not in the sense of the expression itself;

thus, the rectitude of the side of the expression is possible. Since the side of the expression alone follows the Pāḷi, and not the aforementioned meaning which has come down through tradition, how can this be obtained?
For a meaning that is not brought forward does not follow the Pāḷi, nor do all...
It is established that the two kinds of designations mentioned above are indeed stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* according to their occurrence among the six types of designation;
therefore, it cannot be said that they do not exist. If this is a negation of existence in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), then this is acceptable.
But if it is a negation in the conventional sense (*vohāra*), [then it is not acceptable] because of [the existence of things such as] beings, chariots, pots, and so forth.
The employment of expressions such as "seven chariots" would not even be possible; for there is no employment of speech that is devoid of something to be expressed.

The teaching of the triad of duads beginning with "designation" (adhivacana) is for the purpose of showing the distinction between ultimate phenomena (paramattha-dhamma) and designations (paññatti), which are phenomena lacking intrinsic nature (asabhāva-dhamma).
Thus, it does not follow that ultimate phenomena such as form (rūpa) and so forth actually become designations.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to speak of no distinction between the path of designation (*paññattipatha*), the act of designating (*paññatti*), and the description of the dhamma (*dhammaniddesa*);
rather, there may be some slight distinction among them insofar as the word itself constitutes the state of being designated (*paññattibhāva*).

Since what is intended by the state of being designated is precisely the non-ultimate nature (*aparamatthasabhāva*) of that which is to be designated, not every path of designation is expressed by the term "designation" (*paññatti*). Designation...
And since it is stated as being by way of that which is to be made known, it must indeed be called a "term for the path of description" (*paññatti-patha-pada*).

This is how it should be accepted. Otherwise, one could argue that because the word itself is that which is to be made known, it would not be appropriate to call it a "term for description" (*paññatti-pada*), since its status as a path of description would consist merely in its being something to be described—as in the case of the "description" analyzed in the *Nikkhepa-kanda*: "The man Māgaṇḍiya."
It cannot be said that this [distinction] has not been shown here as well.

For even so, because the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of the aforementioned "derived designation" (upādāyapaññatti) and "name-designation" (nāmapaññatti) is possible, the synonymy of terms such as *saṅkhā* and so forth is merely a matter of opinion.
Just like a communication (*viññatti*), the name-designation—making known the intended meaning—designates the object to be designated while being itself already known.

Because it possesses its own intrinsic form, like a lamp that destroys various forms, there is no need for the postulation of another designation (paññatti) in order to designate the object to be designated;
however, in the case of designating by means of a name-designation (nāma-paññatti), there is a separate designation,

just as a dependent designation (upādāya-paññatti) is distinguished by the difference in its material bases, so too a name-designation is distinguished by the difference between the respective words and their referents.

They are indeed intended [to be expressed]. Nor is there the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthāna*), because each respective statement has a fixed nature (*paṭiniyatasarūpatā*) by virtue of being a cooperative cause (*sahakārīkāraṇabhāva*) in the manifestation of that specific meaning.
By this, the absence of the apprehension of a convention (*saṅketaggahaṇābhāva*) should also be understood as refuted; likewise, the absence of purpose for the designation of names (*nāmapaññatti*).
For its purpose was already shown previously.

In such passages as “Conventional usage is struck back by the worldly stream,” it should be understood that conventional usage and the rest—which are the objects of the sound that is to be heard—are spoken of by way of the figurative expression of being "struck back" and "to be heard. Alternatively, it is the sound itself that is so described there because of its association with conventional usage and the rest.
For it cannot be said that the teaching proceeds with a single uniform flavor everywhere; for indeed, in some instances...
"Pleasant is painful" means that even pleasant feelings are called "painful"; "painful is pleasant" means that even painful [feelings] are called "pleasant.
Thus, both these aforementioned two-fold designations are stated in the Commentary as the meaning of the textual passage beginning with "designation" (*adhivacana*).
This is the analysis according to those who maintain that there is a specific object of knowledge distinct from both the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).

1316. Although others possess the state of performing name-giving through such acts as conferring the name "Sāmañña" and so forth, because [the Buddha] is independent of others, the nature of name-giving is here even more appropriately intended in its highest sense as the purpose of name-giving.
To show this, he said, "without depending on anything else," and so forth. The state of having the nature of name-giving does not exist where there is a lack of intrinsic nature (*asabhāvikatā*).

The intended meaning is that it occurs only at certain times. "Because it is established by its own nature" refers to the fact that feeling and the other aggregates possess the property of being designated by the names "feeling," etc.

If the status of being a "name" (nāma) for feeling and the rest is due to their arising while already bearing their own names—being spontaneously named (opapātika) in the sense of having names assigned to them—then it would follow that earth and the other elements also possess the status of being "names"; otherwise, [the definition would not apply].
Reflecting on the objection that "there would be no indication of earth and so forth," he said, "by way of the indication of earth and so forth," and so on.
For a simile exists by virtue of a partial commonality as intended, not by virtue of a complete commonality.

Even so, if feeling and the rest are called "name" because their name is established by their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), then the status of being "name" for earth and the rest would likewise be unavoidable; thus he said:

“Because it is established,” and so forth.
