By this, he shows that although the application of the term *nāma* to feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest occurs by way of a specific cause, nevertheless—just as the word "cow" applies to a collection of beings such as chickens despite their possessing other [grounds for being called cows]—the term *nāma* is applied to feeling and the rest because it is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) therein.
For indeed, in numerous passages of the Suttas, the designation *nāma* is seen to refer to those [aggregates] alone. This is the non-occurrence of the state of being a name (*nāmatā*).

This is stated because [the term] occurs between "hair" (*kesa*), "skull" (*kumbha*), and so forth. He elucidates this very meaning by way of illustration with the words "for indeed" (*na hi*) and so on.

Although the apprehension of non-material phenomena such as feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest also occurs in the form of a lump (*piṇḍākāra*)—due to the absence of a clear analytical distinction (*vinibbhoga*) of the mass and so forth—that nevertheless occurs for the most part by way of a single phenomenon through the medium of a conceptualization of the object’s meaning (*atthātiparikappa*).
"It is not by way of a collection," it is said: "There is nothing... [etc. ...other than this.
The state of being the illuminator and the illuminated is precisely the state of being the subject and the object. Verbal contact (*adhivacana-samphassa*) is mental contact (*mano-samphassa*).
It is stated as an illustration because it is manifest due to its inability to be grasped apart from the name. "Verbal contact..."

By the statement "contact," there might be the apprehension that only those types of contact consisting of mental contact (manosamphassa) possess the nature of "name" (nāma), and not those consisting of impact-contact (paṭighasamphassa).

To dispel this doubt, he says: "There is also impact-contact," and so forth. In this context, contact accompanied by the fivefold sensory consciousness is impact-contact. The word "also" (pi) is used in the sense of inclusion. This is what is meant: [it arises] from the occurrence of the collision between the subject and the object.

Even though contact involving resistance (*paṭigha-samphassa*) is grosser than other types of contact, its mode of appearance is not as distinct as that of material phenomena; therefore, the state of being grasped as dependent upon the mental is a property of the mental alone.

By the phrase "by way of formlessness," etc., he states that contact involving resistance possesses the nature of the mental both generally and specifically by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
The expression "of the latter and the former" is said with reference to this sequence: "mental and material."
By the passage beginning "Mindfulness of form," etc., it clarifies precisely the unique dominant condition (adhipatipaccaya) of Nibbāna as the cause for its designation by the term "name" (nāma);

for this reason, the minds of the Noble Ones (ariya), having escaped from other objects, proceed toward the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) alone through their inclination, tendency, and bias.

1318. Because it conceals the danger (*ādīnava*) in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and because of the delighting in its gratification (*assāda*), it is the root of the round—the primary cause—therefore it is called the "root of the round" (*vaṭṭamūla*).

1320. It is a specific mode of grasping that occurs by superimposing the status of being the basis for the conceit "I am" (*ahaṃmāna*) and the status of being the support for wholesome and unwholesome states and their respective results upon each individual object such as form (*rūpa*), etc., as it has been adhered to.
Any view whatsoever that settles down does so only by way of an extreme misapprehension (*aticcaparāmāsa*) of the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
"It settles" means "it clings," as it has been stated.
Since the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is dominated by volition (cetanā), the phrase "by which volition" and so forth was said.
"Dunnāma" is a name of reproach. By the words "not approaching" and so forth, he explains the distinction between serving and associating.

1336. To demonstrate this point—that there is a method for knowing the delimitation of offenses and their emergence, along with the presentation of the basis and the formal act (kammavācā) and so forth—he said, “From the transgression of the basis,” and so on.

For it has been stated: “Skillfulness regarding offenses and skillfulness regarding the emergence from offenses. Since the fruit is well understood through the knowledge of the cause, he said, “Or of an offense,” and so on, in order to show that.
1342. "Of that" means: due to skillfulness in attention (*manasikāra*).
1344. "Not even arising" means: not even appearing. 1348.
"By way of non-performance" means: by way of disregard; this is the intended meaning.
1350. Of a tree with soft wood, such as the *siggu* and so forth.

1352. "Non-restraint of the eye-faculty" means the non-restraining of the eye-faculty. It is for the very same reason that one whose eye-faculty is unrestrained [is so]; for just as the consciousness belonging to that door [arises], the eye-faculty is the cause for the occurrence of covetousness and other defilements through the eye-door.

This is the primary reason. For it shows the intention of the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that "if the eye-faculty is unrestrained, various [unwholesome states] flow in"; thus, that lack of restraint is said to have the unrestrained eye-faculty as its cause.

Now, standing upon the aforementioned intention, he demonstrates the application of the Pāḷi text beginning with "yatvādhikaraṇan" and so forth. With the words "kassa ca," he asks for the specific manner [of occurrence].
The meaning is: “of what kind” and “how situated. For when the nature [of the object] has already been stated, there is no purpose in asking again about its nature.
“They flow along” refers to covetousness and the rest. The construction is: “the eye-faculty, characterized by those [defilements], is unrestrained, being marked by that which flows along.”
Regarding how they occur: immorality (*dussīlya*) as non-restraint occurs by way of the mind-door; the remaining types of non-restraint should be applied by way of the six doors.
Because forgetfulness (*muṭṭhassacca*) and so forth are unwholesome states that are the opposites of mindfulness, their arising may occur in the five doors;
however, the arising of immorality—which consists of bodily and verbal transgressions—does not occur there, because the javanas of the five doors are incapable of such transgression.
"Because it does not produce intimation" (*aviññattijanakattā*)—this very point is explained according to its possibility by the passage beginning, "For in the five doors...

(*na hi pañcadvāre*). "In what way? (*yathā kiṃ*): the meaning is, "by what manner does the non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) arising in the impulsion (*javana*) come to be called 'non-restraint of the eye-faculty' (*cakkhundriye asaṃvaro*)?
What is that illustration? The sequence of occurrence therein is as follows: when a visible object or other sense-object has entered the range of the five doors...

Having arisen as wholesome or unwholesome impulsion (javana) by way of the restricted [sense-doors] and so forth, once the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has descended, the mind-door impulsion takes that same object and descends into the life-continuum.
Again, at that very same door, having determined [the object] as "woman" or "man" and so forth, the impulsion descends into the life-continuum.
On the subsequent occasion, the impulsion arises by way of the relishing of the sense-faculties and so forth.
It occurs. Furthermore, if that object comes into the range of perception, the impulsion (javana) arising in the five doors and so forth at that time is similar to it;

with reference to such an occurrence, it was said: "In the same way, when unwholesome states such as misconduct arise during the impulsion, if there is non-restraint, the door is also unguarded," and so on.
This, however, is the superior method (ukkaṭṭhanaya), referring to a familiarized object.
It has been said that, having arisen intermittently at the five doors in what is unfamiliar, it likewise arises in the mind door accordingly.
The connection between the door-moments, the bhavaṅga, and so forth, with the impulsion (javana) should be understood as being comprised within a single continuum.
When there is the presence of the door, the bhavaṅga, and so on—even though they do not exist at the time of the impulsion—they serve as conditions by virtue of having been previously produced.
It is said that they are called "existent" only in the sense of being present for the production of their fruit, like the eye and so forth;

for it is not the case that only what is currently enduring is called "existent. The phrase "as if making it external" refers to the fact that, although in the ultimate sense there is no externality to the impulsion (*javana*) nor internality to the other [consciousness], there are such statements as:
"Bhikkhus, this mind is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements."

He shows that the "external" nature of the impulsion (*javana*), which arises only occasionally as something adventitious, and the "internal" nature of the other [mental states], which possess a character contrary to it, are stated by way of figurative expression (*pariyāyato*).

He says "because they become causes for non-restraint" with reference to the evident fact that the doors and so forth become causes for non-restraint; for when non-restraint has arisen, the doors and so forth [become such causes].
Its nature as a cause is thus made known. "Corruption of the doors, the bhavaṅga, and so forth" means corruption within the doors, the bhavaṅga, and so on.
For, in whichever door non-restraint arises, it proceeds precisely by severing the state of those doors and so forth as supports for restraint.
It is for this reason that he said: "the destruction of the commodity of the wholesome."

And here, in the passage beginning with “Having seen a form with the eye,” one should apply the analysis by showing the restraint, that which is to be restrained, the means of restraint, that from which the restraint arises, and that wherein the restraint resides. How so?
By the words “He guards... he enters upon restraint,” restraint is stated. “He establishes mindfulness” is what is meant here.
"Meaning": The eye and so forth are what must be restrained. "He does not grasp at signs nor grasp at secondary characteristics" refers to the means of restraint.

"In whatever way" and so forth indicate the limit of restraint. Visible forms and so forth are the objects of restraint. Furthermore, how is the twofold restraint of the sense faculties comprised within the power of reflection and the power of cultivation?
In that regard, by the former there is the seeing of danger in the objects, and by the latter there is the abandoning of that danger.
Likewise, by the former [type of abandonment], there is the abandoning of the active outbursts (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), and by the latter, the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
Similarly, this distinction should also be understood: the former is included within the mundane path (*lokiyamagga*), while the second is included within the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*).

1353. Regarding "desire for games and so forth": a game itself is the object or purpose, thus it is "for the sake of games" (*davattha*); those things of which that is the first are "games and so forth" (*davatthādayo*).
Among these, "one whose purpose is sport" (*davattho*) means one for whom sport (*dava*)—that is, desire or an object—is the purpose. That which begins with that is "one whose purpose is sport, etc.
(*davatthādi*). To the question "What, then, is that? he says: "desire" (*abhilāso*). "Non-contentment in the enjoyment of food" means lack of satisfaction in the consumption of food.
Non-contentment is the state of desiring more, occurring by way of longing for much and for what is excellent; thus the meaning is appropriate here.
1355. Because it functions in the manner of immersing itself, it is said that "pride itself is the intoxication of pride" (*māna-mada*).

For likewise, the intoxications of birth and so forth are analyzed as being of the nature of pride (*māna*) in such passages as "pride is conceiving" (*māno maññanā*). Hunger (*khudā*) is the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*).
That, moreover, arises both when one has not eaten and when one has eaten; thus, regarding that portion of the body designated as the stomach (*āmāsaya*)—
Because it is oppressive, it is to be designated by the term "affliction" (vihiṃsā); that very point must be demonstrated, and the other [meaning] must be excluded.
Therefore, he said, "the qualification by hunger," because hunger is distinguished by its arising due to the condition of not having eaten.

However, for those who say, "Hunger is painful feeling conditioned by the bodily heat born of kamma," for them, the qualification "arising due to the condition of not having eaten" would be redundant.

It is logical. Even though that explanation refers to the actual state of things, it follows that there would be no distinction between the cessation of violence and the warding off of past sensations;
therefore, the former meaning alone is intended here.

As for the question "What is the difference between these?", the intention is that both types of sensation—those arising from the condition of not having eaten and those not arising from the condition of having eaten—are yet to come.
Mindfulness, although not yet arisen, is similar to that which has previously arisen; the other, however, is dissimilar to that, being absolutely unarisen—this is the distinction here.
For this very reason, it was said of the former, "as it occurred," and of the latter, "not occurring.
Alternatively, the feeling that arises due to the condition of not having eaten is an "old feeling" because it is the result (vipāka) of karma performed in the past.
The term *nāma* [is used here]. Because of improper use—such as lack of reflection and so forth—compared to use accompanied by reflection and so forth, there will be no arising in the future;
thus, the feeling that does not arise due to the condition of what has been consumed is called "new feeling" (*navavedanā*). "Being the cause of violence" means being produced by violence.

Regarding the phrase "the cause of maintaining," since it was stated that "maintenance" (*yāpanā*) refers to the cause for the maintenance of the body, it is also the cause for the maintenance of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
In order to demonstrate this distinction, it is said: "for the sake of maintaining the life-faculty" (*jīvitindriya-yāpanatthāya*).

This indicates that nutriment is not merely the cause for maintaining the life-faculty alone, but rather the cause for maintaining the entire body, which possesses specific modes of activity such as standing and so forth;
thus, the term "subsistence" (*yātrā*) is used. [This is expressed by the thought: "There will be my subsistence," stated without qualification.
Showing what is meant by "stated," he said: "Sustenance (yātrā) is the maintenance characterized by the non-interruption of the four postures.
"The ruin of gifts of faith" (saddhādeyyavinipātana) refers to the destruction of what has been given in faith through such means as using it for improper purposes or failing to utilize it at all.

"By which" refers to the acceptance of food intended for a group (gaṇabhojana), or of food that has been heaped up like a stupa (thūpīkatādi), which constitutes an offense. It is blameworthy and accompanied by censure.
Or the meaning is "he makes use of.

Regarding "conduct" (*iriya*)... it is said [to be] because those [four] modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*), while proceeding comfortably, are grasped and known as the cause for their proceeding in such a manner;
thus, the aforementioned acts of eating and drinking are spoken of as being prior actions in time.

The meaning is that they are described as being like the factors for performing the postures (*iriyāpatha*). For just as it is said, "Having seen with wisdom, his taints (*āsava*) are utterly destroyed," thus describing seeing as the cause for the destruction [of taints];

and just as it is said, "Having drunk ghee, strength arises; having seen a lion, fear arises," thus describing drinking and seeing as the causes for strength and fear respectively—so too, eating and drinking are the causes for the occurrence of comfort in the postures.
"Is said"— thus the meaning should be understood here. Just as the state of being easily obtained and blameless is sufficient for the pleasant dwelling of those living in supreme effacement,
so too, by means of the subsequent verses which proceed by way of permitting the excellence of scarcity regarding robes and lodgings,
the Dhamma-Senāpati here also [teaches] that the excellence of scarcity is sufficient for pleasant dwelling.
"It is understood that it is permitted" means that by the words "again," and so forth, he supports the reading "having eaten.
(1368) "Dhammas such as mindfulness" refers to the dhammas of mindfulness, wisdom, concentration, energy, right speech, and so on, which are comprised within the six dyads.
(1373) "Penetration" is stated with reference to those things to be penetrated. For the object is also spoken of by the name of the subject due to their state of association, just as—
“Having aroused a sense of spiritual urgency through suffering and its cause,
having increased it and reflected upon it, he spoke of the path to liberation”—
and [the phrase] “at the conclusion of the Truths.”

Just as the knowledge of penetration, which proceeds by way of full understanding and so forth regarding suffering and the other truths, is said to proceed without confusion, without distorting, and without contradicting them, so too does insight-knowledge—which serves as its proximate cause—proceed according to its strength without distorting them;
thus it is called "conformable to the four truths. This is the second alternative meaning.

It has been stated. And here, it should be understood that the phrase "of the four truths" is stated without metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), whereas in the preceding case it was stated with metaphorical designation.

Alternatively, because the remaining factors of the path have right view as their predominance, what is stated is the conformity to the penetration of one part of the truth of the path, namely conformity to the whole;
or it is the conformity to the path which is one part of the four truths.
1380. *Khayasamaye* means in the collection of destructions. They also say it refers to "the mass of phenomena occurring by way of the destruction of the defilements (*kilesa*).

1381. Because it is free from obstruction, it is without apprehension; and because its occurrence consists in delighting in the object, it has the sense of "resolving" (*adhimuccana*). Thus he says: "in the sense of being un... [etc. ... resolving. 1382.

The knowledge of fruition (*phala-ñāṇa*) that occurs subsequent to the arising of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) [is so called] because of the various defilements to be abandoned by each respective path.
Because it occurs at the conclusion of exhaustion, it is called "knowledge at the end of exhaustion" (*khīṇante ñāṇa*).

However, since it arises immediately after the path, the second alternative is stated: it is also said to occur at the very first moment of the state of exhaustion, as it proceeds immediately after the defilements have been exhausted by the path and while that state of exhaustion is still present.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Twofold Arrangement is finished.
The commentary on the Section on the Arrangement is finished.
4. The Section on the Commentaries.
Commentary on the Extraction of the Meaning of the Triplets (Tika-atthuddhāravaṇṇanā) 1384.
Regarding "the method of progression" (*nayagamana*): it is called a *naya* because one is led (*nīyati*) by it, or it leads (*neti*), or things are led by it;

it is a *gamana* because one goes (*gammate*) by means of it. Thus, it is either the method itself, or the progression of the method—hence "method of progression. Alternatively, "progression" (*gamana*) simply means going (*gati*). By the first word "beginning" (*ādi*),...

The fivefold method of the *Pañcappakaraṇa*—consisting of the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya* and so forth, the inclusion and non-inclusion, the single [factors] and so forth, the pure [factors], the "with-truth" (*sacchikaṭṭha*), and the roots and sub-roots—is here summarized.
Furthermore, the "conformity" (*anuloma*) and so forth refers to the modes of negative-conformity, positive-negative, negative-positive, and the various types beginning with the single root.
Regarding the phrase "when the meanings have been determined," this refers to the section on the commentary (*aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*) by way of the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*).
When the meanings of all the matrix-terms (*mātikāpada*) have been briefly determined according to their association with specific planes, [the following occurs]:

regarding the "extraction of questions" (*pañhuddhāra*) and so forth, starting from the term "wholesome" (*kusala*)—as in the passage, "Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state may arise by way of the root-condition" (*hetupaccaya*)—there are three groups beginning with the wholesome: those ending in wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; and those beginning with the wholesome, indeterminate, and unwholesome, and ending in wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

There are seven questions beginning with the wholesome, namely: "Three [factors]—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—are one"; likewise, there are seven beginning with the unwholesome, seven beginning with the indeterminate, seven beginning with the wholesome and indeterminate, seven beginning with the unwholesome and indeterminate, seven beginning with the wholesome and unwholesome, and seven beginning with the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Thus, by way of these seven sets of seven, there are forty-nine [answers] for the wholesome triad within the positive order of phenomena (dhammānuloma) under the condition of root (hetu-paccaya).

The same applies to the remaining conditions, the remaining dyads, and the "counter-factual" (paccanīya) dhammas, etc. With reference to this, it is said: "For each of the forty-nine [conditions], for each of the forty-nine [dyads].
By means of such formulations as, "Could a causal state arise conditioned by a causal state through the condition of causality (hetupaccaya)?
and so forth, one should consider: "Conditioned by a cause, a cause; conditioned by a cause, a non-cause; conditioned by a cause, both a cause and a non-cause. Conditioned by a non-cause..."

“Dependent on a non-root [condition], there is a root; dependent on a root, there is a non-root; dependent on a non-root, there is both a root and a non-root. Dependent on both a root and a non-root, there is a root;
dependent on both a root and a non-root, there is a non-root; dependent on both a root and a non-root, there is both a root and a non-root.
Thus, for each pair among the root-condition and the others, there are nine [combinations] for each individual condition.
There are questions. With reference to these, it is said: "In each of the nine [sets of] questions. Regarding that which is obtainable:
first, in the section on dependence within the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*), under the root condition (*hetupaccaya*), it is stated:
"Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of the root condition; dependent on one wholesome aggregate (*khandha*), three aggregates [arise]," and so forth.

By means of the wholesome, the wholesome; by means of the wholesome, the indeterminate; by means of the wholesome, both the wholesome and the indeterminate; by means of the unwholesome, the unwholesome; by means of the unwholesome, the indeterminate;
by means of the unwholesome, both the unwholesome and the indeterminate; by means of the indeterminate, the indeterminate; by means of the wholesome and the indeterminate, the indeterminate;
and by means of the unwholesome and the indeterminate, the indeterminate—this is the occurrence in meaning of nine sets of nine questions.
Extraction (*uddharaṇa*) occurs by way of answering questions; likewise in the remaining sections on conditions (*paccaya-vāra*), the triplets (*tika*), and so forth.

"In those very [questions]" means that because the meaning is possible within the aforementioned questions, the numerical arrangement of the analyzed answers to the questions—beginning with "nine in the case of the root-cause" (*hetuyā nava*) and so on—is established.
"In the phenomena already set forth" refers to how, in the two preceding chapters, it was stated: "At whatever time... and so on.
In such passages as “the wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere,” the phenomena beginning with contact are scattered like loose flowers.
A non-specific description is a general description; the intended meaning is "of a person who has understood the Dhamma.

If, in the sections on the arising of consciousness and matter, there were an exposition of the meaning by way of the arising of consciousness in the four planes and so forth for one who has understood the Dhamma...

[Objection: "This being so, why has the exposition of the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*) been stated here? [In response] he says: "Even though there is an expansion of the triad of the wholesome," and so forth.

By the phrase "because of its status as a qualifier of the phenomena" (*dhammavisesanabhāvato*), he shows that the word "phenomena" (*dhammā*) is the primary term (*padhāna*). For it is because of this that those things denoted by it become subject to inquiry.
By the phrase "for they are understood," he states the connection with the specific characteristics that qualify the planes (*bhūmi*). Herein, "the primary" refers to...

Although in the summary (uddesa) the states (dhammas) are to be qualified by the term "wholesome" (kusala), in this exposition (niddesa)— because they are to be qualified by the planes (bhūmis) as in the phrase "the wholesome in the four planes"—
the word "wholesome" is primary. Since there is no desire for verbal expression in terms of its function as a qualifier,

it disregards the diversity of the states to be qualified— such as those belonging to the sense-sphere or contact and so forth— and refers instead to that which is characterized by blamelessness and pleasant fruition.
Because it proceeds by taking only its own wholesome mode as its basis, it is said that "it proceeds by depending on unity alone.
For all wholesome phenomena (*kusaladhammā*) are indeed of a single nature (*ekasabhāvā*) due to their having blameless and pleasant results (*anavajjasukhavipāka*).

1385. "It should be applied according to what is appropriate" means that, having distinguished them by way of the four planes which serve as their support, they are classified according to their divisions such as occasion (*samaya*), contact (*phassa*), and so forth.
Without treating them as having the nature of fruition (vipāka), one should connect [the text] by bringing them to a single unity and stating: "Fruition exists in four planes.
This same method applies to such passages as "functional-indeterminate (kiriyā-byākata) exists in three planes," and so forth.

It arises in this, thus it is "arising" (uppāda); these are the mental concomitants (cetasika). For they serve as the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) and other conditions for the mind in every respect.

And here, it is expected as the basis for arising. Just as mental factors are [the basis] for consciousness, so too consciousness deserves to be described as the basis for mental factors by virtue of its being a condition such as a support;
thus, its status as denoted by the term "arising" (uppāda), as previously stated, is not negated.
This is what is meant: in the expression "an arising of consciousness" (cittuppāda), [consciousness is the basis] of the arising.

Even though consciousness occurs as a qualifier (*visesanabhāvena*), it functions as that qualifier only while remaining inseparable from the state of being qualified (*visesitabbabhāva*), because of the occurrence of the aforementioned arising and purpose within itself.
As it has been said: "The meaning occurs by way of characterizing the whole through its part.
Since those [mental factors] share the same destiny as consciousness, they are included here by the mention of "consciousness" alone; hence the phrase "the two sets of fivefold consciousness."
Because it will be explained by way of illustration, it is said: "The apprehension of the mind... [etc. ...is made. In that context, "of another" refers to matter (*rūpa*).
(1420) There is nothing at all to be said regarding the five doors, because the consciousnesses belonging to the five doors have exclusively limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*).

By the phrase "the experiencing of desirable and undesirable objects," he states the absence of intentional grasping of the object prior to the arising of the resultant consciousness (*vipāka*). From that...

The intention is this: since fruition (vipāka) occurs in accordance with the kamma, it is fit to occur only with a limited object (parittārammaṇa) because it is the fruition of a limited kamma, and not with a sublime (mahaggata) or measureless (appamāṇa) object.

Furthermore, because even some kamma dominated by concentration that has not reached absorption (appanā) lacks the quality of producing an exclusively similar fruition, the kamma is specified as "having reached absorption. [This applies to] the characteristic of beauty (vaṇṇalakkhaṇa), etc.

"Having taken up" means that because earth and so forth—which have been apprehended solely in accordance with worldly perception—have been produced by means of the preliminary-work perception (*parikamma-saññā*), the object is one under the influence of perception, being what is termed the "counterpart sign" (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*); thus it is "an object under the influence of perception.

"In exactly such a way" means without distinction, just as [the object] is through the attainment of absorption due to the predominance of concentration, so too it is through the object being under the influence of perception. "He too" refers to...

The word *pi* has the sense of inclusion. By this, it is shown: "Just as [the result] conforms to its own action because it takes phenomena belonging to the same plane as its object, so too does the result conform to the action even when taking that [action] as its object-of-objects.

If this is so, why is the result of a limited (paritta) action that has a sublime (mahaggata) or measureless (appamāṇa) object not [itself] a result that takes that [sublime or measureless state] as its object-of-objects?

Is it not the case that [it does] not exist? Because, unlike the ripening of karma that has reached absorption (*appanā*), there is no fixed rule for its having that same object as its cognitive object (*ārammaṇa*), and because it takes various forms according to the nature of the karma;

just as the registration (*tadārammaṇa*) following a sublime impulsion (*mahaggata-javana*)—even when it has a limited object—is not a necessary consequence due to a lack of habituation, so too is it with respect to that [object] which serves as the sign (*nimitta*) for one's own karma.
When the sublime (mahaggata) object is not exhausted by its co-nascent causes and there is an absence of familiarity with it, a limited (paritta) result does not arise;

however, when a rebirth-linking consciousness arises having a kamma-sign as its object, it occurs through that very limited [kamma]. Thus he said, "becoming the rebirth-linking [consciousness] and so forth.

With the words "But because... and so on, he determines the aforementioned meaning by means of the Pāḷi itself. [This concludes the section on] asynchronous kamma-condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya).
For it is this that is intended here, because it has been stated that the condition and the conditioned have different objects. By the words "And not...

and so forth, he shows that only limited (paritta) resultants are mentioned here as being of the nature of the conditioned. "Here" means in this Section on the Extraction of Meaning (Atthuddhāraka-kaṇḍa).

He says "by way of residual impression" (vāsanāvasena) in order to show the possibility of bodily action occurring even for one devoid of mindfulness, in those who have attained fullness of mindfulness.

It has been said. Since there might be mental agitation (*uppilāvitatta*) even toward some limited object for those who are not free from lust, it was stated with the qualification "in the absence of defilements" (*kilesavirahe*).
Regarding the phrase "merely by way of showing respect," the word *eva* (merely) serves to exclude other qualifications;
it indicates that very specific thing to be excluded, and not otherwise. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the term "laziness and so forth" (*kosajjādi*),...

It includes factors such as hatred (*dosa*) and so forth. Regarding the statement "lack of respect is simply a state of indifference," it should be understood that those who show respect do not do so out of a state of indifference;
it does not mean that they fail to show respect at all. However, some say:

"The performance of giving and other acts by those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), though lacking in zeal due to their bodies being unfit for work and their minds being preoccupied with other matters, does not arise from a lack of respect."
1421. "Of those that are very proficient" means of those well-cultivated and having attained mastery to a superior degree.
The intention is that such an occurrence also takes place in the case of proficient jhānas because of the diminished intensity of the investigation and effort therein.
"Shown previously" refers to what was shown previously by the passage beginning, "The three characteristics: 'I am,' etc. "Non-existent, because it lacks ultimate reality; existent..."

The teachers say: "And because it is established by worldly convention and exists as a conventional truth (sammutisacca), its meaning is 'arrived at' (arīyati)—that is, it is reached by the mind and known.

Therefore, since the arising of consciousnesses have that as their object, they are called "having an indeterminable object" (*navattabbārammaṇa*) by way of a *aññapadattha* compound, meaning "those whose objects are not to be stated.
However, this position is like the doctrine of the Hetuvādins. Thus, of that...

Thinking that [the conventional] is absolutely non-existent, and in order to show another way in which there is a designation for what does not exist, he said, "But as for conventional truth," and so forth.
To the question, "How is it that while it is absolutely non-existent, the occurrence of the phenomena within its domain is an inexpressible object?
he said, "Even though it is non-existent," and so forth. Thus, they are not to be called "having limited objects" and so on.
The term "stated" (vuttā) negates its status as something separately established, as in the case of the *paritta* recitations and so forth.
Distraction (*vikkhipana*) is the occurrence of the mind upon various objects. Non-stability (*anavaṭṭhāna*) is the failure to allow it to proceed upon only a single object.

The sense-sphere knowledge that precedes the second and subsequent paths, as well as that which precedes the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), [is excluded] because it has Nibbāna as its object.

And because it is fixed in its function as the adverting consciousness for supramundane consciousness, and because it is considered identical with the knowledge that precedes the first path, it is said:
“Having taken ‘change-of-lineage’ (gotrabhū) by way of the ‘explanation of change-of-lineage’ (gotrabhuvodāna).
The term *sabbatthapādaka* uses the locative case in the sense of what is to be accomplished or for the sake of a purpose, as in the expression “for the non-peace of the mind,” and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is "in all [the qualities] to be accomplished, such as insight (vipassanā) and so forth. For this very reason, he said "in all," and so on.
Because knowledge of the past lives (atītaṃsañāṇa) belongs to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), it should be understood that it is not included among the supernormal powers (iddhividha) and the rest.

However, they say that its range extends from seven days in the past down to the present rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Even regarding those seven days in the past, [it refers to] those things connected with the aggregates (khandha).
Its state of being an object appears as if it were appropriate.
"Having grasped the foundational jhāna consciousness by means of the preliminary exercises" means that, having entered and emerged from the foundational jhāna,
one performs the preliminary exercises of the prior stage with the thought, "May this body move as swiftly as this consciousness," [directing them] toward the material body.

This was said with reference to the fact that even the mind of the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna) must be grasped. However, it should be understood that this resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) proceeds as follows:

having placed the desire to go before him for the purpose of reaching the intended destination, and having entered and emerged from the foundational jhāna, he performs the preliminary work (parikamma) directed toward the physical body as its object, thinking: "May this body move swiftly, just like this mind."
Having performed the preliminary tasks, one descends into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), emerges from it, and enters the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).
When one has again descended into the life-continuum, mind-door adverting consciousness arises taking the physical body as its object, as do the conformity consciousnesses (*anuloma*).
Following that, the resolution-consciousness (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*) also arises taking that very same object. By its power, one becomes as if already gone to the intended destination.

But as he goes with this invisible body, does he go at the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) of that resolve-consciousness (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*), or rather at its moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) or moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*)? They maintain that he goes during all three moments.
"In consciousness" means in the foundational jhāna-consciousness. "He unifies" means he makes it move swiftly, like consciousness that follows the mind.

The meaning is as follows: Just as the mind functions by taking an object even when it is extremely distant at the very moment it so desires, so too, the transformation of the body (kāyapariṇāmanā) consists in bringing about a state of rapid movement in the material body through the power of the mind.

And here, one should not say that the arising of the material body in another location within a single moment of consciousness is untenable because material phenomena are slow-moving; for [this occurs] by means of the resolving consciousness (adhiṭṭhānacitta).
Because a state of light transformation has been induced. For this very reason it was said:
"Having resolved upon the body by means of the mind, and having entered into the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness, he goes to the Brahma-world with an invisible body.
For the domain of psychic power (iddhi) of those possessing psychic power is indeed inconceivable.

"Having merged the mental continuum into the material body" means that because it causes the continuity of those moments of consciousness— by which number the body is seen to reach the intended location—
to proceed slowly, this resolution is applied to the kamma-born body in a manner consistent with that [intention].
Having entered this jhāna which serves as the basis for the resolution and having emerged from it...

Thinking, "May this mind proceed slowly, just like this body," one enters [the attainment], performs the preliminary work (parikamma) having the consciousness that emerged from the jhāna as its object, descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and emerges from the life-continuum.

Having entered the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna) again, when the life-continuum has once more descended, mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) arises taking the foundational jhāna as its object; then the conformities (anuloma) arise.
Then, the resolving consciousness (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*) also arises taking that very same object as its support.
By its power, even when the fivefold sense-consciousnesses and so forth arise in the interval, one does not fall but goes to the desired place.
And while going thus, if one wishes, one creates a path in the sky by means of the earth-kasiṇa and travels on foot. If one wishes—
By means of the air-kasiṇa, having resolved upon the air, one travels by means of the air like a tuft of cotton.

Moreover, the mere desire to go is the measure here; for when there is the desire to go, one who has thus performed the resolution travels while being visible, impelled by the force of that resolution, like an arrow shot from a bow. In that regard, traveling while creating a path in the sky—
Even without the knowledge of supernormal power (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*), he travels as if on ordinary ground; for that very reason it is said, "he goes on foot.
When traveling by resolving upon the air, he proceeds by means of a succession of air elements (*vāyodhātu*) produced by the knowledge of supernormal power.
In both cases, he travels while observing the beauty of groves and such in the interval, and hearing sounds that come within his range of perception.

They say this. However, some say: "When traveling to a desired place by means of an invisible body in a single moment of consciousness, or when traveling on foot or by means of wind with a visible body, it is movement through the projection of bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) arisen from superknowledge-consciousness (abhiññā-citta).
Others say: "The superknowledge-consciousness has no function of producing intimation."

"The two foundations" (adhiṭṭhānadvayaṃ) refers to both foundations: that which consists in the transformation of body and mind by means of mind and body, and that which has the material body and the jhāna-consciousness as its basis and object.

"Associated with those" means associated with the aforementioned two foundations. "Because of the presence of the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness" means because of the existence of the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness; the sense is: because of attaining their state. And here, "perception of pleasure" refers to...
Perception associated with equanimity: for equanimity is called "peaceful happiness.
And that very perception should also be understood as "light perception" because it is liberated from the hindrances as well as from opposing factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*).
When one has entered into those [perceptions], even the physical body becomes as light as a tuft of cotton. Thus, like a tuft of cotton tossed by the wind, being light...
“He travels according to his wish with a single moment of consciousness and an invisible body.

Perceiving the Blessed One’s mental reflection as he thought, “I am indeed freed from that useless and painful practice; it would be well if I were to awaken to perfect enlightenment,” Māra resolved, “I shall prevent his liberation,” and said:
“O youth, those who have departed from the practice of austerity do not attain purity;”
“‘You think you are pure when you are impure;
you have strayed from the path to purity’—it was with reference to such [passages] that it was said: ‘The Blessed One’s knowledge of the minds of Māra and others is also mentioned.

And the connection is as follows: ‘The reviewing of Nibbāna... occurs among those things known by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). ‘Among those things known by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives... [Nibbāna... ñātesu].

This is stated on the grounds that this reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), which occurs subsequent to direct knowledge (*abhiññāñāṇa*), may sometimes occur even with respect to the object of the object of direct knowledge, just as it does with respect to the object of direct knowledge itself. "Having an immeasurable object" (*appamāṇārammaṇata*) means having the immeasurable aggregates as its object.
"Therefore" (*tasmā*) refers to the fact that [the previous passage] demonstrates that the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*) does not have Nibbāna as its object.
There is no such reading; therefore, when it is said "when the function of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇakicca) is being discussed," this does not refer to conventional usage. Rather, the meaning is:

"reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇa) refers to the very function of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa), which is the individual, repeated looking back upon—that is, the recollecting—of the past paths and so forth.
It is seen as "authorized" (anujñātā) in the passage: "from the reviewing of the path, fruit, and Nibbāna."
It was with reference to this very point that it was said. This is the meaning here:
having seen the aggregates with Nibbāna as their object by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, one reflects, "Upon what, indeed, are these phenomena based?
For one who thus reflects, the knowledge of recollecting past lives proceeds with Nibbāna as its object. The same method applies to the knowledge of the future.

If this is so, why is it that in the *Paritta-ttika* (the Triplet of the Limited), it is stated: "An immeasurable state (*appamāṇo dhammo*) is a condition for a sublime state (*mahaggato dhammo*) by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)," and here [it says]:

"Immeasurable aggregates (*appamāṇā khandhā*) are a condition for knowledge of the minds of others (*cetopariyañāṇa*), for knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), and for knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) by way of object-condition";
and likewise in the *Ajjhatta-ttika* (the Triplet of the Internal), "An external state (*bahiddhādhammo*) is a condition for an external state (*bahiddhādhammassa*)..."?
In the analyses (*vibhaṅga*) for the statements “an external phenomenon is a condition for an internal phenomenon by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)”, it is stated only this much:

“external aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of supernormal powers (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of others’ minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of the destiny of deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*), and advertence (*āvajjanā*) by way of object-condition”; it does not state “Nibbāna. [This is because] Nibbāna is not an object for the knowledges of others’ minds, supernormal powers, and so forth.

If it is argued that because they are mentioned together [they must be the same], then even so, they ought to be distinguished separately. For one does not distinguish together what is worthy of being distinguished separately?
No; because there is another reason for not stating it. For Nibbāna is simply outside the range of those knowledge-visions of past and future lives belonging to worldlings (*puthujjana*).
However, for the Noble Ones (*ariya*), who have realized Nibbāna through the reviewing of the Path and the Fruit (*maggaphala-paccavekkhaṇa*)...

It should be understood that *nibbāna* was not mentioned because there is no purpose in making it an object of direct perception through these knowledges; since the knowledges of the supernormal powers (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) and so forth were included in a general sense, it was not stated. It speaks of knowing the aggregates produced [in the future], not knowing the aggregates that have already been produced.

For the function of the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*) is precisely that. The statement "the meaning is possible" was said with reference to the fact that even the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*) does not have *nibbāna* as its object.

1429. Regarding the triad of states having the Path as their object: since among the types of consciousness explained in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*, there are none that have the Path as their object exclusively, yet those that have the Path as their object sometimes have the Path as their dominant influence (*adhipati*), therefore—having posed only the single question, "Which states have the Path as their object?"—the three sections are analyzed according to how they are found to exist.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood from other sources as well in similar contexts.

Regarding the statement, “Because they are not co-nascent (asahajātattā),” which is intended to establish the absence of the state of having the Path as its cause for those very phenomena mentioned as “arising of consciousness” and “having the Path as their object,” it is said that “the meaning is ‘because they are not associated (asampayuttattā).
For this very reason, he says, “For there is no [causality] among immaterial phenomena,” and so forth. “At the time when they have other phenomena as their object...”

Since the restrictive particle "eva" has not been included [in the definition], it should be understood that this point—that [the path] cannot be said to have the path as its dominant factor even at the time when the path is the object because it is not treated as venerable—is indeed accepted in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
For, because it is stated, "at the time of reviewing after having treated it as venerable," it certainly exists also at the time of reviewing without having treated it as venerable. At that time...
Furthermore, the point that those states cannot be said to have the Path as their dominant influence is even more established.
Regarding the phrase "having past objects," although it was extracted [from the text], the reading "having past objects" (*atītārammaṇā*) is seen in many manuscripts as the reading of the Aṭṭhakathā.
Therefore, because in the commentary on the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga* it says: "At the time of death, relatives [say]: 'This one...'"

Having said, "Father, a Buddha-pūjā is being performed for your sake; let your mind be serene," and so forth, [the text] describes the presentation of objects such as visible forms at the five sense-doors and the occurrence of the fourteen moments of consciousness ending with the registration-mind (tadārammaṇa) therein;

it then states that rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) arises upon that very same object—which lasts for only a single moment of consciousness—thereby establishing its status as having a present object.

He will speak of rebirth-linking; therefore, this is the meaning. There are two life-continuum moments, one adverting moment, five impulsion moments—because their momentum has been weakened by proximity to death—and two registration moments, and the death-consciousness:

thus, eleven consciousness-moments have passed. Therefore he says, "with a life-span remaining for five consciousness-moments. "In the other case" refers to a death with a different kind of registration.
Now, in order to show in detail that very point which was stated briefly as "in other cases," he says, "When indeed... and so forth.
Because death lacks an object of consciousness (*ārammaṇa*), and because rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) has a present object, it is stated: "for one passing away from the form realm... etc.
The six life-continuum moments (*bhavaṅga*) have present objects, while nine mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*) are past; thus, when seven mind-moments remain of the lifespan—
It should be understood that rebirth-linking occurs with respect to the sign of the destiny.

By the phrase "it takes as its object only the body that actually exists," he shows that through the emergence of the perception of pleasure and lightness, there is the production of a state of rapid transformation in the aggregate of primary and derived matter belonging to the present alone, and not in that which is yet to come.
"In this interval" means from the time it is unmanifest until the time it becomes manifest; within this interval. However, because for some...
For some things become manifest quickly, while for others it is slow; therefore, it was stated without specifying "one or two moments of the continuity" (*santativāra*).

Some say, "It was stated for the sake of the elegance of expression," while others say, "When the material and immaterial phenomena occurring within this interval are taken as 'present,' that constitutes one moment of the continuity; however, by dividing that into two parts..."
Taking as its beginning the time when it is mostly unmanifest, the period until it becomes manifest is one portion;
taking as its beginning the time when it is mostly manifest, the period up to the time when it is very clearly manifest is another—one such pair of series.

By this method, the distinctions among the remaining series should also be understood. In that context, rather than grasping the commonality of all [moments] by way of time, [the distinction is made].
They say that the delimitation of continuity (*santati-pariccheda*) should be explained by way of the similar occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*).
For even though material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) originated by temperature, consciousness, and so forth, may occur similarly for some time, they are called "units of continuity" (*santati-vāra*).
When [the author] says "extremely brief," etc., the immaterial continuity (*arūpa-santati*) here is also delimited by the aforementioned material continuity.
"It should be understood as 'indeed included'. It is said that "it is drawn together among present phenomena" because it serves as a point of attraction by means of craving and views.

When the mind and mental objects—referring to those phenomena existing within a single existence and included in a single continuum—are taken without making a distinction between subject and object, they constitute the "temporal present. However, when a distinction is made:
He said, "Both of these are present in the sense of a continuity of moments," because the state of being present as a continuum of moments is obtained.

"Of that" refers to the great multitude of people. By saying "without making a distinction between past and so forth," he shows the means by which advertence and the other mental states occur in an identical mode.
"It is established" means that even when the object is present in a single moment, [the knowledge] of the preliminary stage and the knowledge of others' minds [are established].
The meaning is that this Pāli has been well-guided. And thus the "Past Triplet" remains unbroken:

when "present" here is understood as referring exclusively to phenomena present at the very moment (khaṇapaccuppanna), the "Past Triplet" in the *Paṭṭhāna* remains undistorted because it correctly extracts the meaning without division, demonstrating that even that which is included in a different category [of time] can serve as a proximity condition (*anantarapaccaya*).
Alternatively, "the past triad" refers to the textual passage on the past triad in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
By means of this passage on the past triad, for the very reasons already stated, it is non-different and undistinguished; the meaning is that it simply converges and accords [with the present].
Regarding "as far as possible": advertence has the future as its object, while impulsion has the present and the past as its objects.

It should be construed as "having future, present, and past objects. The intention is that there would be no diversity of objects [in the case of direct knowledge] by way of time, because its object is present.

And this meaning is stated by way of demonstrating the possibility that, within the occurrence of a single consciousness in a single impulsion-process (javana-vīthi), the functions such as adverting (āvajjana) can have future and other objects; thus it refers to the intended direct-knowledge consciousness (abhiññā-citta).
In order to show the application of the process within the present moment, he said, "By that," and so forth. "Three" refers to:
"A state with a past object is a condition, by way of repetition-condition, for a state with a past object;
a state with a future object is [a condition] for a state with a future object; a state with a present object is a condition for a state with a present object."
The meaning of “a condition by way of repetition-condition” is that there are three answers to the questions concerning those phenomena included within other categories.
Regarding “there is no non-repetition”: the intention is that when repetition is obtained, there is no reason for its non-mention in the teaching according to the nature of the phenomena;
thus, by this non-mention, the exclusion of the other questions therein is understood.
“Of this doctrine”: of the doctrine that “mind-reading knowledge (cetopariyañāṇa) is established even though advertence (āvajjana) and impulsion (javana) have future and present objects.
“The state of being a support”: the state of indicating the aforementioned method because of the possibility of its meaning.
“That”: the consciousness. “Of that”: of the statement that advertence and impulsion have objects that are present by moment (khaṇapaccuppanna) and ceased.
And in this case, it is not tenable that [the mind] touches upon a specific time while the adverting consciousness (āvajjanā) occurs only with respect to the future.

If, on the other hand, one exercises attention (ābhoga) thinking, "I shall know whatever this person's consciousness will be," then even the preliminary (parikamma) and direct-knowledge (abhiññā) consciousnesses would likewise have only the future as their object;
thus, the state of having both the future and the present as objects for all adverting and impulsion (javana) consciousnesses is not established.
"It succeeds," he says, "because it is stated that... [etc. ... pavatti... It means by way of falling into fault (*dosāpatti*), or from the occurrence of fault (*dosāpajjana*).

Regarding "the penetration of the attention to a portion of the aggregate" (*rāsiekadesāvajjanapaṭivedha*), he states the position of the former teachers according to the literal sense; regarding "the knowing of the attention to each instance as it occurs" (*sampattasampattāvajjanajānana*), he states his own determined position.
"The former teachers would not grant assent" is because [their view] has the continuity of time (*addhāsantati*) as its present objective referent (*paccuppannapadattha*).
They would not grant [this], standing on the intention that the term "present" as it appears in the Abhidhamma Mātikā does not exist.

And here, even though there is a difference in intrinsic nature (sabhāva), because there is no difference in aspect (ākāra), there is no fault of having diverse objects for the minds of adverting, preliminary work, and direct knowledge, according to the method of unity;
thus, for the proponents of the former view, the knowledge of others' minds has a momentary present object.
This has been shown by way of elucidating the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:

"Since there is no absence of the fault of having diverse objects (*nānārammaṇatā*) when there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the state of having a present object is elucidated in relation to a single consciousness itself by way of its temporal continuity (*addhāsantati*).
Therefore, one should examine which of these two positions is logical and accept that.

"By that very reason" means: because in the triad of the past and the triad of the arisen, no reading is found that indicates the state of having present phenomena as an object for the knowledge of penetration of others' minds;
it is for that reason. "In two knowledges" refers to the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of penetration of others' minds.
"Are grasped by way of karma" means that although all four aggregates possess the status of being objects, they are grasped by the knowledge of rebirth according to karma through the door of karma.
This shows that only the wholesome and unwholesome are grasped here, and not their specific classifications.

Since the state of misconduct is characterized by its association with greed and so forth, while the state of good conduct is characterized by its association with non-greed and so forth, it follows that when one distinguishes between misconduct and good conduct, one is indeed distinguishing greed and the other factors as well;
thus he says: "There is the cultivation... [of the distinction] between misconduct... and so on.

1435. Since a phenomenon that lacks intrinsic nature (*asabhāvadhamma*) may be designated as "I" and so forth by way of its being a basis for internal phenomena, it might be considered an "internal" category;
however, this is not the case for a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), because such a thing does not exist within the continuum of a non-existent being.

Thus it is said: "The intrinsic nature... would not exist. For instance, in the passage, "of one who reviews his own aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth," [the term] "having an internal object" (*ajjhattārammaṇā*) is used.
By way of explaining the meaning of the word, he will say: "The word 'beginning' (ādi) includes the designation ‘I’ when it is apprehended internally.
If this is so, should its state of being internal also be mentioned in the triad of the internal? No;
for just as the state of being external, the state of being internal is intended in the triad of the internal in an absolute sense. As he said: "That which is not of the same nature... etc.

"It was not said" [refers to this]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "the base of nothingness, etc.," there are included the faulty preparatory and access-consciousnesses preceding it, as well as the consciousnesses of reviewing, relishing, and so forth that occur with its object.
He speaks of the base of nothingness by drawing it in with the word "that" (*taṃ*), but he does not say "all that"; and as for what...

The meaning is "preceding that. "A statement by way of a part" (lesavacana) means a statement concerning only one part [of a whole] due to its similarity in one respect, namely, the state of having a common object (samānārammaṇabhāva).

For "leso" means it is smeared (lissati), adhered to (silissati), or clung to (allīyati) by way of one part. "Of which" refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, great functional, and advertence consciousnesses of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), as well as the fourth fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) consciousness which is distinguished by its wholesome and functional nature.
Thus [it is said] in the exposition of the [consciousness] accompanied by equanimity (upekkhāsahagata), and so forth.

The meaning is this: among those [states] for which association with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has been stated, having mentioned only one description as "accompanied by equanimity" (*upekkhāsahagata*), the other should not be mentioned.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the descriptions of the sense-sphere states associated with roots (*hetusampayutta-kāmāvacara*) and so forth are included.
For even there, among the phenomena described by way of being limited (*paritta*), having roots, and so on, having mentioned only one, the other...

"It should not be said" means: "by way of the occurrence of the non-existence of the desired state" (*abhāvanāniṭṭhappavattiya*)—the meaning is "by way of the occurrence of the excellence of the mode of non-existence," or "by way of the occurrence of the excellence of non-existence. The intention is that it should not be said that [the consciousness] has arisen as having an internal object, etc.

"Those" refers to the adverting and other [mental states] that share the same object as the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). If this is so, [then regarding] "in the commonality of non-existence" (*abhāvanāsāmaññe*)...

Why was it said [that there is no development]? Is it not because there is no occurrence of states of consciousness—such as those occurring through reviewing or relishing—that which has the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) as its object, in the manner of non-development?

No; for what is intended is the state of being "not to be developed. For "non-development" (*abhāvana*) means that which is not developed (*na bhāvīyati*), not that one does not develop (*na bhāveti*).
Regarding the phrase "produced by a particular mode of grasping" and so forth, this is the intended meaning:

although for the most part sublime states (mahaggata-dhammā) proceed with respect to objects that are merely forms produced by the knowledge of meditation (bhāvanāñāṇa) and which do not exist by way of intrinsic nature (sabhāva), nevertheless, because they grasp external forms, the kasiṇas, etc., are considered external; thus, the states having those as their object are called "external-object" (bahiddhārammaṇa). For, of the kasiṇas...
Setting aside the continuity [of the mind], the establishment [of the object] is understood specifically by way of the developed kasiṇa;
however, the absence of consciousness in the first immaterial attainment possesses neither an external mode nor an internal mode.

Therefore, in that state which is devoid of both modes and proceeds by a mode of occurrence unique to itself, only the base of nothingness is said to have an "inexpressible object," and not the others.
"Arising in another mode. This should be understood as a mere illustration regarding "wholesome states of the sense-sphere.
The grammatical case should be shifted according to the sense: "the fruition of the base of nothingness" [is the cause] for the fruition, etc., of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"Because of the impossibility of directing" means because of the impossibility of directing the attainment-consciousness. It is wholesome only.
Having established that it is the object of fruition (*vipāka*), the passage beginning with "of fruition" was stated.
Although they lack intrinsic nature (*asabhāva-dhammatte*), because they are to be grasped as external forms, the kasiṇas possess an external character;

yet, because they are here exclusively derived from internal phenomena (*ajjhattadhammupādānatāya*), there may be the designation "I," and thus an internal character can exist—hence the statement beginning with "internal."
They say that by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "the aggregates, etc.," the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth are included.
"This method" refers to the principle of exposition beginning with, "having taken the formless aggregates as 'aggregates,'" and so on.

"In the mention of the aggregates, etc., of others" means in the speaking or utterance of this phrase, "the aggregates, etc., of others. The connection is: "by the word 'etc. he has stated every derivative designation (*upādāpaññatti*)."
The commentary on the extraction of the meaning of the *tikas* is finished.
Commentary on the extraction of the meaning of the *dukas* 1473.
“In another way” means in the demonstration of the manner already stated; for it is precisely because of the demonstration of the manner already stated that [this is said] in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

For the impulsions accompanied by volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārika*), when free from sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), a formulation similar to that for the effortless (*asaṅkhārika*) ones has not been shown. "In the case of craving for existence, etc.
refers to the formulations concerning those rooted in craving for existence and so forth.
"Two" refers to the hindrances of restlessness and ignorance. "Three" refers to [the application] with each one of sensual desire, ill will, and doubt.
"The hindrances of restlessness and ignorance. He states that "two or three" is shown by the elision of the word *vā* (or) in the Pāḷi.

Alternatively, even in the presence of particles (*nipāta*), the sense of conjunction and so forth is expressed by nouns and other words alone, not by the particle-words themselves, because those [particles] are non-denotative;
thus, this meaning is obtained even without a particle-word. Such is the case according to the speaker's intention.
In this context, "possibility alone is the authority," which is why it is stated in the Pāḷi as "two or three.
By the passage beginning with "where there is simultaneous arising," etc., the phrase "two or three" expresses a definition that applies universally to all cases.

For it has been said: "And having done so, [this applies] also to the group of defilements (kilesagocchaka). This is the intended meaning: even in the absence of a mental state accompanied by only two defilements, [the number is determined] according to the Pāḷi.
Since two [instances] have been mentioned, yet no mention has been made of all the defilements (*kilesa*) as they arise in their own specific forms,
it is understood that "two" and "three" are used as defining characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
If even for restlessness (*uddhacca*), which arises in all unwholesome states, only a single arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*) is said to be its objective field (*visaya*), [then...]
With the intention that the same should be said for the hindrance of ignorance (*avijjā-nīvaraṇa*), he raises an objection with the words "Why was it said? and so forth.

The other [the respondent] says "In the Sutta" and so forth, in order to show that while the same should be said for the hindrance of restlessness (*uddhacca-nīvaraṇa*), it is not the case that the same should be said for the hindrance of ignorance.
In that context, "among the five hindrances mentioned in the Sutta" refers to those accompanied by restlessness.
This was stated because of the suspicion that restlessness might be accompanied by the hindrance of ignorance (*avijjā-nīvaraṇa*).
But is it not the case that even in the Suttas, in such passages as “of beings hindered by ignorance” (*avijjā-nīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ*), ignorance is called a “hindrance”? True, this is so;
however, in the Suttas, the five [factors] beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) are frequently stated to be the hindrances by virtue of being the opposites of the jhāna factors.
It should be understood that this was stated according to the most common usage.
However, some maintain: "Just as in the *Nikkhepakanda*, the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), though weak, are shown to be the opposites of the wholesome—just as they are presented in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
For instance, in the *Paṭṭhāna* it is said: 'Dependent on a state that is a hindrance, a state that is a hindrance arises.'"

There is no pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*). In the section on the formless realm (*arūpa*), it is stated: "Dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), there arise the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha-nīvaraṇa*) and restlessness (*uddhacca-nīvaraṇa*)," and so forth; however, this is not the case in the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*.

For in the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa*, only those hindrances that are direct opposites of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) are specified, such as: "The hindrance of restlessness arises in a mental state associated with restlessness."

It has been stated [thus]. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the demonstration that the hindrance of restlessness arises together with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the others is done in accordance with the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* for the purpose of showing the classification of their simultaneous arising. For it is said therein:
"In that context, those [factors] are explained in detail right in the *Pāḷi*. And this position [is held] because the hindrance of restlessness is associated with restlessness.

This was stated by taking this very statement—"it arises with the arising of the mind"—as the indicator (*ñāpaka*). Otherwise, it would have had to be stated as "the hindrance of ignorance" (*avijjānīvaraṇa*).

There is no other statement that establishes this meaning—that in the *Atthuddhārakaṇḍa*, only those underlying tendencies (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) that act as foundations for the hindrances are intended—other than this statement regarding the pair [of hindrances].

Because the aforementioned statement encompasses all hindrances in a general sense, and because its status as having been spoken is shown by another purpose—namely, the elucidation of specific objects—it appears not to be indicative [of a definitive rule]. Therefore, it must be understood after careful investigation.

"Without taking [it literally]" means that one should seek the intended meaning in such a way that there is no contradiction with this scripture, according to the *Nikkhepakanda*, the *Paṭṭhāna*, and so forth, rather than taking the meaning solely according to the literal expression; thus he concludes the aforementioned point.

1577. "Of these" refers to others [of the defilements] beginning with greed (*lobha*). How are they shown? First, conceit (*māna*) is associated with greed, delusion (*moha*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), shamelessness (*ahirika*), and fearlessness of wrongdoing (*anottappa*);

likewise, it is associated with greed, delusion, sloth (*thina*), restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing. Similarly, wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) is associated with delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; doubt (*vicikicchā*) is associated with delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; sloth is associated with greed, delusion, wrong view, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing; and greed, delusion, conceit, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing [are mutually associated].
With greed, delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread; with hatred, delusion, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread;

restlessness with greed, delusion, views, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread; with greed, delusion, views, lethargy, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread; with greed, delusion, conceit, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread;

with greed, delusion, conceit, lethargy, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread; with greed, delusion, lethargy, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread; with greed, delusion, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread.

[Conceit] arises together with hatred, delusion, lack of shame, and lack of fear of wrongdoing; with hatred, delusion, sloth, lack of shame, and lack of fear of wrongdoing; with delusion, doubt, lack of shame, and lack of fear of wrongdoing;
and with delusion, lack of shame, and lack of fear of wrongdoing.
Just as with restlessness, so too should lack of shame and lack of fear of wrongdoing be understood by applying them in the same way. How? [First,] lack of shame...

With greed, delusion, views, restlessness, and lack of moral dread; with greed, delusion, views, sloth, restlessness, and lack of moral dread; with greed, delusion, conceit, restlessness, and lack of moral dread;
with greed, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, and lack of moral dread; with greed, delusion, sloth, restlessness, and lack of moral dread;

with greed, delusion, restlessness, and lack of moral dread; with hatred, delusion, restlessness, and lack of moral dread; with hatred, delusion, sloth, restlessness, and lack of moral dread; with delusion, doubt, restlessness, and lack of moral dread.
And it arises together with delusion, restlessness, and lack of moral dread (*anottappa*). Lack of moral dread arises together with greed, delusion, wrong view, restlessness, and shamelessness;

or with greed, delusion, wrong view, lethargy, restlessness, and shamelessness; or with greed, delusion, conceit, restlessness, and shamelessness; or with greed, delusion, conceit, lethargy, restlessness, and shamelessness;
or with greed, delusion, lethargy, restlessness, and shamelessness; or with greed, delusion, restlessness, and shamelessness; or with hatred, delusion, restlessness, and shamelessness.
It should be understood that here, just as greed arises together with hatred, delusion, sloth, restlessness, and shamelessness; or with delusion, doubt, restlessness, and shamelessness;
or with delusion, restlessness, and shamelessness—so too should the simultaneous arising of conceit and the other [defilements] be understood. The remainder is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the Section on the Eightfold Exposition is finished.
Thus ends the sub-commentary (*anuṭīkā*) on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*,
which is the explanation of the meaning of the words in the root commentary (*mūlaṭīkā*) on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
